## Statement refuted

For every nontrivial companion knot and every pattern in its solid torus, the companion torus in the satellite exterior is essential.

## Statement references

[[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]]

## Construction

Let $K$ be any nontrivial knot. Take the core pattern $P=S^1\times\{0\}\subset V=S^1\times D^2$, choose its tubular neighbourhood to be a smaller concentric solid torus inside a companion neighbourhood $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$ of $K$, and use the induced companion embedding. Then $P(K)=K$. The companion torus is the boundary of the larger chosen neighbourhood, while the satellite exterior has boundary the boundary of the smaller tube around $K$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The pattern, the companion embedding, and the two nested tubular neighbourhoods specified in the Counterexample.

[F1] [[def-satellite-pattern-companion-and-winding-number]] defines the core pattern, satellite knot, pattern exterior, and companion torus.

[F2] [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]] defines boundary-parallel torus and essential torus.

## Proof

1.1 The companion embedding sends the core $S^1\times\{0\}$ to $K$, so the satellite knot $P(K)$ is exactly $K$ with the specified smaller tubular neighbourhood. The companion torus is the boundary of the larger neighbourhood. [F1, given]

2.1 The shell between the two concentric tubular neighbourhoods is explicitly $T^2\times[0,1]$, by radial interpolation in the $D^2$ coordinate. It lies in the satellite exterior and has the companion torus and the satellite exterior boundary as its end tori. Thus the companion torus is boundary-parallel and, by [F2], is not essential. This refutes the unrestricted statement. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Remarks

This example shows why a nonproduct condition on the pattern exterior is needed in the essential-companion-torus lemma.

## Remarks references

[[lem-satellite-torus-is-essential]]

kind: counterexample
title: The eigenvalue equation does not imply the matrix relation
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 6
deps:
  - def-sl-two-character-variety-and-peripheral-eigenvalues
  - def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling
justified_by: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: The matrix calculation is choice-free. It refutes only the general
  matrix implication and does not assert that this pair extends to a
  representation of a knot group.
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-generated
sources:
  references:
    - title: John A. Baldwin and Steven Sivek, Torus knots, the A-polynomial, and
        SL(2,C), §2.3
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2
    - title: Léo Bénard, François Florens, and Adrien Rodau, A slope invariant and the
        A-polynomial of knots, §2.2
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151
---

## Statement refuted

Let $U,V\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ commute and have a common invariant line on which their eigenvalues are $M,L$, respectively. For every primitive pair $(p,q)\in\mathbb Z^2$, if $M^pL^q=1$, then $U^pV^q=I_2$.

## Statement references

[[thm-a-polynomial-boundary-restriction-and-surgery-detector|Exact matrix relation for a filling representation]]

[[def-sl-two-character-variety-and-peripheral-eigenvalues|Common peripheral eigenline and eigenvalue convention]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Primitive filling-pair convention]]

[Baldwin and Sivek, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.19197v2)

[Bénard, Florens, and Rodau, §2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.14151)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $U=I_2+N$, $V=I_2$, and the primitive pair $(p,q)=(1,0)$.

[F1] $N^2=0$, so $U$ is upper-triangular unipotent with determinant one and is not the identity.

[F2] The identity matrix commutes with every matrix, and the eigenvalues of an upper-triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.

## Counterexample

1.1 Since $N^2=0$, $U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $U\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$, has only eigenvalue $1$, and is not $I_2$. Also $V=I_2\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$. By [F2], the pair commutes and has common eigenline $\mathbb C(1,0)$ with eigenvalues $M=L=1$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For $(p,q)=(1,0)$, the eigenvalue equation gives $M^pL^q=1^1 1^0=1$, while $U^pV^q=U\ne I_2$. This refutes the statement. The example is only a matrix pair and does not claim to extend to any knot-group representation. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every abstract oriented cobordism between two oriented knot circles in the standard three-sphere can be realized by a smoothly embedded concordance annulus in $S^3\times[0,1]$.

## Statement references

[[def-abstract-oriented-knot-cobordism|Abstract oriented cobordisms of knot circles]]

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth embedded annulus concordance]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The standard unknot $U$, the standard right-handed trefoil $T$, and the claim in the Statement refuted.

[F1] An abstract oriented cobordism is a compact oriented surface with boundary $-C_0\sqcup C_1$ and contains no ambient embedding data. ([[def-abstract-oriented-knot-cobordism]])

[F2] The Seifert matrix convention in the library is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ for a chosen oriented surface and basis; the surface and basis are part of the data until invariance is proved. ([[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]])

[F3] A trefoil Seifert surface admits a rank-two Seifert matrix whose symmetric sum is $\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$; if the cited convention uses the transpose matrix, the symmetric sum is unchanged. For a real symmetric matrix, its signature is the number of positive eigenvalues minus the number of negative eigenvalues. (Collins, Theorem 2.2.9 and Example 2.2.13, https://era.ed.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/1842/5034/Collins2011.pdf?sequence=4)

[F4] The standard unknot bounds a disk in $S^3$; the disk is contractible, so its first homology is zero and its symmetrized Seifert form has signature $0$. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F5] A metabolizer for a rank-two integral Seifert form is a rank-one direct summand $L$ with $V(x,y)=0$ for $x,y\in L$. Thus every nonzero $x\in L$ satisfies $x^T(V+V^T)x=2V(x,x)=0$. This is immediate from the defining bilinear relation, with no signature-invariance or general signature-vanishing theorem. ([[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]])

[F6] Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, a knot is smoothly slice if and only if it is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot. ([[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]])

[A1] Full Axiom of Choice is assumed by the supplied Seifert-pairing definition. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[A2] Full Axiom of Choice implies the countable-choice hypothesis used by [F6]. ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

[F7] For a smooth slice disk, the actual smooth branch of [[lem-slice-disk-induces-seifert-metabolizer]] constructs a metabolizer for every specified smooth Seifert surface: its Proof1.1–2.2 uses the actual smooth hypersurface and positive product constructed in Proof1.1–7.1 of [[lem-locally-flat-slice-surface-bounds-seifert-hypersurface]]. The separate unresolved TOP branches are not used here. This direct finite-form obstruction needs neither surface-choice invariance nor a general signature-vanishing theorem.

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct finite-form obstruction using the proved smooth slice-to-metabolizer branch.

1.1 Let $C_0$ be the oriented circle underlying $U$ and $C_1$ the oriented circle underlying $T$. Take the abstract annulus $S^1\times[0,1]$ and identify its lower and upper boundary circles orientation-preservingly with $C_0$ and $C_1$, orienting the annulus so its boundary is $-C_0\sqcup C_1$. By [F1] this is an abstract oriented cobordism from $U$ to $T$. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 For the fixed trefoil matrix in [F3], $$V+V^T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.$$ Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+4\lambda+3=(\lambda+1)(\lambda+3)$, so its eigenvalues are $-1,-3$ and its signature is $-2$. More directly, for $x=(a,b)\ne0$ over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, $$x^T(V+V^T)x=-2(a^2-ab+b^2)=-(a-b)^2-a^2-b^2<0.$$ Consequently $V$ cannot have a rank-one metabolizer: a nonzero vector in one would have zero value by [F5]. This is a calculation for the displayed Seifert surface and basis; no knot-level signature invariance is being inferred. The unknot's rank-zero form in [F4] still has signature zero. [F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, algebra]

2.1 If $U$ were smoothly concordant to $T$, reverse the interval coordinate to obtain smooth concordance of $T$ to the unknot. By [F6] and [A2], $T$ would bound a smooth proper disk. Apply the proved smooth branch [F7] to the particular trefoil Seifert surface in [F3]. It gives a rank-one metabolizer for $V$, contradicting the strict negative-definiteness calculation and [F5] in step 1.2. Thus the displayed abstract oriented annulus has no realization as a smooth concordance between its specified endpoint knots, refuting the claimed universal realization. No locally flat TOP slice-to-metabolizer assertion is used. [A2, F3, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Sources

[[def-abstract-oriented-knot-cobordism]]

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance]]

[[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]]

## Statement refuted

Assume the Axiom of Choice. An integral homology $3$-sphere is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$ with $H_*(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Z)$; a knot $K\subset Y$ is null-homologous when $[K]=0$ in $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. The assertion that every smooth null-homologous knot in an integral homology $3$-sphere has irreducible complement is false, where irreducible means that every embedded $2$-sphere in the complement bounds a $3$-ball there.

## Statement references

[[thm-rank-one-top-knot-floer-detects-fiberedness|Ni's irreducible-complement hypothesis]]

[Ni, *Knot Floer homology detects fibred knots*, Theorem 1.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0607156v4)

[[lem-poincare-homology-sphere-is-nontrivial-integral-homology-sphere|The Poincaré sphere homology and fundamental group]]

[[thm-rank-one-top-knot-floer-detects-fiberedness|Ni's exact irreducibility hypothesis]]

[Algebraic Topology, Winter Semester 2021/22, §4.5.12](https://loeh.app.ur.de/teaching/topologie1_ws2122/lecture_notes.pdf)

[Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, §2.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf)

## Diagram

The connected-sum sphere separates the two punctured Poincaré summands; the unknot lies in a smaller ball in the left summand.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.95]
  \draw[rounded corners,thick] (-2,-1.15) rectangle (1.45,1.15);
  \draw[rounded corners,thick] (2.55,-1.15) rectangle (6,1.15);
  \node at (-0.25,0.55) {$P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$};
  \node at (4.25,0.55) {$P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$};
  \draw[dashed,thick] (2,-1.15)--(2,1.15);
  \node[above] at (2,1.15) {$S^2$};
  \draw[thick] (-1.2,-0.1) circle (0.55);
  \node at (-1.2,0.15) {$B_0$};
  \draw[thick] (-1.2,-0.1) circle (0.2);
  \node at (-1.2,-0.1) {$U$};
  \node at (-1.2,-0.82) {$N(U)\subset B_0$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the Poincaré sphere $P$, the connected sum $Y=P\#P$, a connected-sum sphere $S$, a standard round unknot $U$ in a $3$-ball $B_0$ contained in the first summand and disjoint from $S$, and a tubular neighborhood $N(U)\subset B_0$.

[F1] [[lem-poincare-homology-sphere-is-nontrivial-integral-homology-sphere]]: $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)=H_2(P;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $\pi_1(P)\ne1$.

[F2] [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]: for an open cover, the sequence $H_1(U\cap V)\to H_1(U)\oplus H_1(V)\to H_1(X)\to H_0(U\cap V)\to H_0(U)\oplus H_0(V)$ is exact.

[F3] [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]], [[cor-homology-of-spheres]], and [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]: $H_1(S^2;\mathbb Z)=0$; for an unknot $U\cong S^1$ in $S^3$, $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus U;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $\widetilde H_1(S^3\setminus U;\mathbb Z)\cong\widetilde H^1(U;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$.

[F4] [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]] and [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]: under AC, a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with $H_1=0$ has $H_0=H_3=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2\cong H^1=0$.

[F5] Every spherical gluing below is made with a retained product collar $S^2\times(-2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon)$, chosen disjoint from $U$. For closed pieces $A_-$ and $A_+$ on the negative and positive sides, replace them by the relative-open sets $O_-=A_-\cup(S^2\times(-2\varepsilon,\varepsilon))$ and $O_+=A_+\cup(S^2\times(-\varepsilon,2\varepsilon))$ in their union. On the added collar of $O_-$, send its parameter $t\ge0$ to $(1-s)t$; fix $A_-$. The analogous formula on the negative added collar retracts $O_+$ to $A_+$. Their intersection is $S^2\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ and retracts to $S^2$ by $t\mapsto(1-s)t$. These homotopies match the identity on the joining sphere and remain valid after deleting $U$, since the collars miss it. Thus [F2] is applied only to these actual open covers, with the same homology groups as the named closed pieces. The collars are the product collars retained in the chosen smooth ball and connected-sum constructions; no collar for an arbitrary wild sphere is asserted.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is the assumption of the local Poincaré-duality suppliers.

## Counterexample


1.1 The unknot $U$ bounds its spanning disk inside $B_0$, so $[U]=0$ in $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$. For $X=P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$, use the collar enlargements [F5] of $X$ and $B^3$ in $P$. They form an open cover, retract to those pieces, and have intersection retracting to $S^2$; apply [F2] to this open cover. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ by [F3], exactness injects $H_1(X)$ into $H_1(P)=0$, so $H_1(X)=0$. The same exact sequence in degree zero, using $H_1(P)=0$ and $H_0(P)=H_0(S^2)=H_0(B^3)=\mathbb Z$, gives $0\to\mathbb Z\to H_0(X)\oplus\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z\to0$. Rank comparison yields $H_0(X)\cong\mathbb Z$, so each punctured summand is connected with $H_1=0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 Put $A=B_0\setminus U$ and let $C$ be the closed ball on the other side of $\partial B_0$ in $S^3$. Identify $B_0$ with the unit ball and $U$ with a round circle in the plane $z=0$. From every point of $A$, the vertical segment in the direction of the sign of its $z$-coordinate reaches $\partial B_0$ without meeting $U$; when $z=0$, the starting point is not on $U$ and the upward segment meets the plane only there. Since $\partial B_0$ is path-connected, $A$ is path-connected. Thicken $A$ and $C$ by collars to obtain an open cover of $S^3\setminus U$ whose overlap retracts to $S^2$. The map on $H_0(S^2)$ is the injection $1\mapsto(1,-1)$. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ and $C$ is contractible, [F2] identifies $H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(S^3\setminus U;\mathbb Z)$; [F3] identifies the latter with $\mathbb Z$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the open collar enlargements [F5] of the two punctured summands in $Y$; the pieces and intersection retract to the punctured summands and $S^2$, respectively. By step 1.1 both summands are connected and have zero $H_1$, and the map $H_0(S^2;\mathbb Z)\to H_0(P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_0(P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3;\mathbb Z)$ sends $1$ to $(1,-1)$ and is injective. Exactness gives $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$. Since $Y$ is closed, connected, and oriented, [F4] gives $H_2(Y;\mathbb Z)=0$ and $H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)=H_3(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. Hence $Y$ is an integral homology sphere. The duality and UCT uses are under [A1]. [A1, F2, F4, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The side of $S$ in the second summand is $P\setminus\operatorname{int}B^3$, which is not a $3$-ball: capping it with a ball would identify $P$ with $S^3$, contrary to [F1]. The other side is the union of $P\setminus\operatorname{int}(B^3\cup B_0)$ and $A$, glued along $\partial B_0$. Apply [F5] to obtain an open cover of this side, relative to its remaining boundary, with intersection retracting to that sphere and pieces retracting to the two named sets. Since $H_1(S^2)=0$ by [F3], exactness in [F2] makes the map from the direct sum of the two pieces' $H_1$ groups into the union's $H_1$ injective. Step 1.2 therefore makes this side's $H_1$ nonzero. Neither side is a $3$-ball, so $S$ cannot bound a $3$-ball in $Y\setminus U$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Therefore $Y\setminus U$ is reducible and the displayed universal assertion is false. The diagram records the separation and location of $U$; the proof uses the homology and homotopy arguments above, not the diagram. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement refuted

The false assertion is that a finite bigraded cochain complex over $\mathbb Q$ is determined in total dimension by its graded Euler characteristic $\sum_{i,j}(-1)^i\dim_{\mathbb Q}H^{i,j}q^j$.

## Source notes

No external statement is cited; the counterexample is finite-dimensional linear algebra.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite bigraded cochain complex over $\mathbb Q$ with zero differential. Its total rank is the sum of the dimensions of all bigraded groups, and its graded Euler characteristic weights degree $(i,j)$ by $(-1)^i q^j$.

[F1] With zero differential, every cohomology group equals its corresponding cochain group by the definition of cohomology.

## Counterexample

1.1 Define $V$ by $V^{0,0}=\mathbb Q$ and all other groups zero. Define $W$ by $W^{0,0}=W^{0,1}=W^{1,1}=\mathbb Q$ and all other groups zero; give both complexes zero differentials. [given, construct]

2.1 By [F1], the graded Euler characteristics are $\chi_q(V)=1$ and $\chi_q(W)=1+q-q=1$, but their total dimensions are $1$ and $3$. Therefore equal graded Euler characteristics do not determine total rank. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This vector-space example does not assert that a nontrivial knot has the unknot's Jones polynomial. Jones-polynomial unknot detection is a separate knot-theoretic problem; a 2026 survey still describes it as open.

## Remarks references

[Manolescu, *From Knots to Four-Manifolds* (2026), §2, p. 5](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/knots4m.pdf)

    - title: "Mikko Salo, Applications of microlocal analysis to inverse problems (2019)"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.03041"
      locator: "§5, Theorem 5.1, boundary determination of all scalar conductivity jets."

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain whose Euclidean metric is isometric to the product metric $dx_1^2\oplus g_0$ on a compact subdomain of $\mathbb R\times D^\circ$, where $(D,g_0)$ is a compact connected simple Riemannian surface with smooth boundary. Let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical scalar conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on every boundary datum, then $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ in $\overline\Omega$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full physical scalar conductivity DN map]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-liouville-transform-and-dn-conjugacy|Liouville potential and boundary conjugacy]]

[[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity|Equality of all boundary conductivity jets]]

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Simple transversal surface convention]]

[[thm-ip-euclidean-schrodinger-calderon-uniqueness|Euclidean Schrödinger full-data uniqueness]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the boundary determination and Euclidean potential uniqueness suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the boundary determination and Euclidean potential uniqueness suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the Euclidean CTA product domain, a compact simple transversal surface, two positive smooth conductivities, and equality of their full physical DN maps.

[F1] [[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity]]: equal full conductivity DN maps imply equality of every inward boundary-normal derivative of the two conductivities.

[F2] [[lem-ip-conductivity-liouville-transform-and-dn-conjugacy]]: for $\rho_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$, $q_j=\Delta_g\rho_j/\rho_j$, the conductivity equation is conjugated by $u=\rho_jv$ to $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u=0$, and $\Lambda_{\gamma_j}f=\rho_{j,b}\Lambda_{q_j}(\rho_{j,b}f)-\rho_{j,b}(\partial_\nu\rho_j)f$.

[F3] [[thm-ip-euclidean-schrodinger-calderon-uniqueness]]: on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain in dimension at least three, equality of the full Schrödinger DN maps for real smooth nonresonant potentials implies equality of the potentials.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 By [F1], all boundary-normal jets of $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ agree, so the boundary values and first normal derivatives of $\rho_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ agree. Put $q_j=\Delta_g\rho_j/\rho_j$. Their Liouville boundary relations in [F2], together with $\Lambda_{\gamma_1}=\Lambda_{\gamma_2}$, now give $\Lambda_{q_1}g=\Lambda_{q_2}g$ for every $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$: substitute $f=g/\rho_b$ into the physical-flux relation, using the common positive boundary value $\rho_b$ and common $\partial_\nu\rho_j$. Multiplication and division by smooth positive $\rho_b$ preserve $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Each $q_j$ is nonresonant. If $w\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)w=0$, then $v=w/\rho_j\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solves $-\operatorname{div}(\gamma_j\nabla v)=0$ by [F2]. Testing weakly with $\overline v$ gives $\int_\Omega\gamma_j|\nabla v|^2dx=0$. Positivity of $\gamma_j$ implies $v=0$, hence $w=0$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The domain is bounded and smooth in $\mathbb R^3$, the potentials are real and smooth, both operators are nonresonant by step 1.2, and their full Schrödinger DN maps agree by step 1.1. Thus [F3] applies and yields $q_1=q_2=:q$ in $\Omega$. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 Each $\rho_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q)\rho_j=0$ and the two functions have the same boundary value by step 1.1. Their difference is a zero-trace solution of the nonresonant operator from step 1.2, hence vanishes. Therefore $\rho_1=\rho_2$ and $\gamma_1=\rho_1^2=\rho_2^2=\gamma_2$ in $\Omega$; continuity extends this equality to $\overline\Omega$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, and let $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$, with $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $[0]=\varnothing$. Write $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{k<d}u_kv_k$. If $m\le2d-2$, then there are $x,z\in\mathbb R^d$ with $z\ne x$ and $z\ne-x$ but $\langle a_i,x\rangle^2=\langle a_i,z\rangle^2$ for every $i\in[m]$. If $m\ge2d-1$ and every list of $d$ distinct measurement labels indexes linearly independent vectors, then equality of all these squared measurements implies $z=x$ or $z=-x$. For every $d\ge1$, this count is attained at $m=2d-1$: for any distinct real numbers $t_1,\ldots,t_m$, the vectors $a_i=(1,t_i,t_i^2,\ldots,t_i^{d-1})^{\mathsf T}$ satisfy the stated independence condition and hence the squared measurements determine the signal up to global sign.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval|Real global-sign phase retrieval]]

[[def-ip-frame-complement-property|Complement property]]

[[def-ip-real-full-spark-measurement-family|Full-spark condition]]

[[thm-ip-real-phase-retrieval-complement-property|Complement-property characterization]]

[[lem-ip-vandermonde-determinant|Vandermonde determinant and moment-curve independence]]

[Radu Balan, Pete Casazza, and Dan Edidin, Corollaries 2.6–2.7](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412411)

[Radu Balan, Corollary 3.3](https://www.norbertwiener.umd.edu/Education/IMA2015/t4/lecture.pdf)

[MIT OpenCourseWare 18.013A, Chapter B §1](https://ocw.mit.edu/ans7870/18/18.013a/textbook/HTML/chapter_b/contents.html)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite labeled family $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ in $\mathbb R^d$, with $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$.

[F1] [[thm-ip-real-phase-retrieval-complement-property]]: real intensity measurements are injective modulo global sign exactly when every partition has one side spanning $\mathbb R^d$.

[F2] [[def-ip-frame-complement-property]]: the complement property is the stated condition over every subset of labels and its labeled complement.

[F3] [[def-ip-real-full-spark-measurement-family]]: full spark means every list of $d$ distinct measurement labels gives a linearly independent list of vectors.

[F4] [[def-linear-map]], [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]], [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], [[def-linear-subspace]], [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]], [[thm-rank-nullity]]: the coefficient map and its image are defined, subspaces are closed under linear combinations, the span is the smallest subspace containing the columns and equals their finite linear combinations, and rank-nullity computes image dimension from a finite-dimensional domain.

[F5] [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-dimension]]: $\mathbb R^k$ has dimension $k$, including $k=0$, and $\mathbb R^d$ has dimension $d$.

[F6] [[def-linear-independence]]: an independent list of columns has no nonzero coefficient vector in the kernel of its coefficient-to-column map.

[F7] [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]]: a linear subspace of $\mathbb R^d$ has dimension at most $d$ and equals $\mathbb R^d$ exactly when its dimension is $d$.

[F8] [[lem-ip-vandermonde-determinant]]: for distinct real nodes $t_1,\ldots,t_d$, the $d$ moment-curve columns $(1,t_j,\ldots,t_j^{d-1})^{\mathsf T}$ are linearly independent.

[F9] [[thm-reals-field]]: the real coordinate and coefficient operations satisfy the field axioms used in the finite linear maps and the Vandermonde construction.

## Proof


1.1 Let $I\subseteq[m]$ have $q$ labels and enumerate them in increasing order as $i_0,\ldots,i_{q-1}$. Define $T_I:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^d$ by $T_I(c)=\sum_{j<q}c_j a_{i_j}$. This map is linear by distributivity of finite sums. Its image is a subspace: it contains zero, and if $u=T_I(c)$ and $v=T_I(c')$, then $\alpha u+\beta v=T_I(\alpha c+\beta c')$. For each $j<q$, the $j$th standard unit vector $e_j$ satisfies $T_I(e_j)=a_{i_j}$, so the smallest-subspace property gives $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)\subseteq\operatorname{im}T_I$. Conversely every $T_I(c)$ is a finite linear combination of the listed measurement vectors, so [F4] gives $\operatorname{im}T_I\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)$. Thus the image equals the span, also when $q=0$ because both are $\{0\}$. [given, F4, F5, F9, algebra]

2.1 If $q<d$, rank-nullity and [F5] give $\dim(\operatorname{im}T_I)\le q<d$, so by step 1.1 this span cannot equal $\mathbb R^d$. [step 1.1, F4, F5]

3.1 Suppose $m\le2d-2$. Choose $S\subseteq[m]$ with $|S|=\min(m,d-1)$. Then $|S|\le d-1$; if $m>d-1$, the bound on $m$ gives $|[m]\setminus S|=m-d+1\le d-1$, and if $m\le d-1$ the complement is empty. Applying step 2.1 to both sides shows that neither side spans, so the complement property fails by [F2]. Hence phase retrieval fails by [F1]. [step 2.1, F1, F2, construct, algebra]

4.1 The lower count is established in step 3.1. For the sufficient count, suppose $m\ge2d-1$ and $\Phi$ is full spark. For any $S\subseteq[m]$, the two sides cannot both have fewer than $d$ labels, since that would imply $m\le2d-2$. Thus one side contains $d$ distinct labels. By [F3], their vectors are independent. The coefficient map $T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ for these $d$ columns has trivial kernel by [F6]; by step 1.1 its image is their span, and rank-nullity [F4] and [F5] give that image dimension $d$. Hence the image, and therefore the span of the chosen vectors, is $\mathbb R^d$ by [F7]. The containing side also spans $\mathbb R^d$. Since $S$ was arbitrary, the complement property holds, and [F1] gives phase retrieval. [step 1.1, step 3.1, given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9, choose, algebra]

5.1 Set $m=2d-1$ and choose distinct real nodes $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. Every $d$-label subfamily is independent by [F8], so the family is full spark by [F3]. Since $m\ge2d-1$, step 4.1 proves it performs phase retrieval. For $d=1$, the same argument uses one node and the one-entry vector $(1)$; for all $d$, step 3.1 rules out any smaller count. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, F8, construct, algebra] ∎

For every $d\ge1$, this count is attained at $m=2d-1$: for any distinct real numbers $t_1,\ldots,t_m$, the vectors $a_i=(1,t_i,t_i^2,\ldots,t_i^{d-1})^{\mathsf T}$ satisfy the stated independence condition and hence the squared measurements determine the signal up to global sign.

[[def-ip-frame-complement-property|Complement property]]

3.1 The lower count is established in step 2.1. For the sufficient count, suppose $m\ge2d-1$ and $\Phi$ is full spark. Since $S$ was arbitrary, the complement property holds, and [F1] gives phase retrieval. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9, choose, algebra]

4.1 Set $m=2d-1$ and choose distinct real nodes $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. Every $d$-label subfamily is independent by [F8], so the family is full spark by [F3]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F8, construct, algebra] ∎

sources:

      url: https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf
    - title: Polyak–Viro Formulas for Coefficients of the Conway Polynomial, §§3.4–4.2
      url: https://math.osu.edu/~chmutov.1/preprints/chmutov-khoury-rossi.pdf
    - title: Elementary proof of existence of the Alexander-Conway polynomial, §§1–4, PDF pp. 1–9
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.03086v1
---

## Definition

For an oriented link type $L$ in $S^3$, the Conway polynomial is the polynomial $\nabla_L(z)\in\mathbb Z[z]$ characterized by the normalization $\nabla_U(z)=1$ for the unknot $U$ and the skein relation
$$\nabla_{L_+}(z)-\nabla_{L_-}(z)=z\,\nabla_{L_0}(z).$$
Here $L_+$ and $L_-$ are identical oriented links outside a ball and have respectively a positive and negative crossing inside it, while $L_0$ is obtained in that ball by the orientation-preserving smoothing. For each integer $k\ge0$, the $k$th Conway coefficient is $c_k(L):=[z^k]\nabla_L(z)$. This carrier records the conventional skein interface; existence and uniqueness of the invariant are a separate well-definedness obligation. The skein characterization is on nonempty oriented links. If the link domain also includes the empty link, extend the invariant by the separate conventional value $\nabla_{\varnothing}(z)=0$; this empty-link value is not determined by the nonempty skein axioms.

## Definition references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Oriented links and ambient-isotopy classes]]

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Positive crossing convention]]

[Chmutov, Duzhin, and Mostovoy, §2.3, printed pp. 35–37](https://www.math.cinvestav.mx/~mostovoy/cdbook/cdbook-as-submitted.pdf)

[Chmutov, Cap Khoury, and Rossi, §§3.4–4.2, PDF pp. 4–8](https://math.osu.edu/~chmutov.1/preprints/chmutov-khoury-rossi.pdf)

[Garaev, “Elementary proof of existence of the Alexander-Conway polynomial,” §§1–4, PDF pp. 1–9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.03086v1)



## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite diagrams of nonempty oriented links, with no ordering of their components, the declared positive/negative crossing convention and oriented smoothing. The link isotopy and diagram conventions are those of the Definition.

[F1] **External input — existence of the Conway coefficient invariants.** T. Garaev, *Elementary proof of existence of the Alexander-Conway polynomial*, arXiv:2012.03086v1 (5 December 2020), Section1, Theorem1, PDF p.2, with the equivalence and skein charts on p.1, supplies a sequence $c_{-1}=0,c_0,c_1,\ldots$ of invariants of oriented link diagrams with unordered components. They are invariant under all oriented Reidemeister moves and planar isotopies, have $c_0(U)=1$ and $c_j(U)=0$ for $j>0$, and satisfy
$$c_j(L_+)-c_j(L_-)=c_{j-1}(L_0),\qquad j\ge0.$$
This is an imported established coefficient-existence result, not a claim to reconstruct its Reidemeister-III argument. The source's crossing sign agrees with the declared convention: it is positive when the ordered over/under tangent pair has positive planar determinant. Its Figure2 is the oriented smoothing in this Definition. Polynomial finiteness, integrality and uniqueness are earned below rather than falsely attributed to the coefficient-sequence statement alone.

[F2] **External input — ambient-link interpretation and conventional normalization.** Chmutov–Duzhin–Mostovoy, *Introduction to Vassiliev Knot Invariants*, §1.2.1, printed p.11/PDF19, gives the Reidemeister diagram criterion with its oriented extension; §2.3.1, printed pp.35–36/PDF43–44, states the Conway invariant of ORIENTED LINKS with values in $\mathbb Z[t]$, normalized to one on the unknot and satisfying its displayed positive-minus-negative skein relation. It uses links with unnumbered components. These are the ambient-link interpretation and the standard skein convention of [F1]; the letter $t$ is renamed $z$. The book's §2.3.2 expressly notes that existence is nontrivial. Here existence is EXTERNALLY supplied, not inferred from that observation or from a formal definition. The empty link, if included in the ambient link domain, is assigned the separate conventional zero value in the Definition; the imported skein characterization is only for nonempty links.

Actual reading limits: the complete Garaev v1 Section1/Theorem1 statement and crossing-sign definitions on PDF pp.1–2, including visual inspection of Figures1–3; the coefficient-extension setup on p.3; CDM's complete §1.2.1 text and its oriented extension on printed p.11, and the complete §2.3.1 definition and displayed skein normalization plus the opening §2.3.2 text on printed pp.35–36. No full Garaev proof, Reidemeister-III reconstruction or full book reading is claimed. These exact established external inputs are used under the run-specific external-source permission.

## Proof

1.1 Form the coefficientwise formal expression $C_D(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(D)z^j$ from [F1]. It is a diagram invariant, has value $1$ on an unknot, and satisfies $C_{D_+}-C_{D_-}=zC_{D_0}$ coefficientwise. A local positive and negative curl on any component of the $r$-component unlink are both that unlink; the oriented smoothing is the $(r+1)$-component unlink. Thus $c_j(U_r)-c_j(U_r)=c_{j-1}(U_{r+1})$ for every $j\ge1$. All coefficients of $U_{r+1}$ vanish. Therefore the unlink values of the formal expression are $1$ for one component and $0$ for more than one. This is also the forced unlink value for ANY polynomial-valued invariant satisfying the Definition. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Here is the finite argument that the expression is actually in $\mathbb Z[z]$. In a diagram choose finitely many component basepoints and an order. Call a crossing bad when its first encounter in this traversal is the underpass. If none is bad, the first component passes over every later component and has a descending self-diagram. Pull its successive arcs above everything they first encounter to isolate a round circle; repeat for the remaining components. Thus a descending diagram is an unlink. At a bad crossing the skein relation writes its value as the value of the switched diagram, plus or minus $z$ times its oriented smoothing. The switched diagram has one fewer bad crossing and the same number $N$ of crossings; the smoothing has $N-1$ crossings. Reset the finite component data on a smoothing if necessary. The nonnegative integer $N(N+1)/2+b$, with $b$ the number of bad crossings, decreases in each branch. Hence this is a FINITE resolution tree. Its leaves have values $0$ or $1$ by step1.1. Working back through the tree uses only integer addition/subtraction and multiplication by $z$, so $C_D\in\mathbb Z[z]$. In fact every branch has at most $N$ smoothing operations, giving degree at most $N$. This proves finiteness and integrality without assuming an integer-valued formal sequence theorem or making an infinite selection. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply the SAME finite tree to any two polynomial-valued invariants satisfying the stated normalization and skein relation. Their unlink leaves agree by step1.1, and each internal skein relation then forces agreement. Their values agree on every diagram. Existence follows from [F1], step1.2 and the ambient-link interpretation [F2], and this argument proves uniqueness. The separately fixed empty-link extension is unique as well, since its prescribed value is zero. Consequently the separate existence/uniqueness obligation mentioned in the Definition is now discharged: the resulting actual link invariant is exactly $\nabla$, and its coefficient $[z^k]\nabla_L$ is well-defined for every $k$. The finite local arguments use no choice axiom; the external constructive coefficient/diagram inputs are explicitly distinguished from them. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

sources:

    - title: "Lisa Piccirillo, The Conway knot is not slice"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923"
      locator: "§2, definition preceding Theorem 2.1, printed pp. 584–585 (PDF pp. 3–4)"
    - title: "Jennifer Hom, Getting a handle on the Conway knot"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171"
      locator: "§3, dualizable-link construction and trace descriptions"
---

## Definition

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, §2, definition preceding Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A three-component link in $S^3$ with the component labels and framing
data in the Definition and countable choice.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is
[[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: each component is
a smooth oriented embedded circle in the standard oriented $S^3$, and
ambient isotopy means an orientation-preserving isotopy of the ambient sphere.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a meridian is the boundary
of a normal disk to the component, oriented by the knot and ambient
orientations, and the preferred longitude is the degree-one peripheral curve
with zero exterior-homology class.

[F3] [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] and
[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: a regular
oriented diagram has finitely many transverse double crossings with over/under
data, each assigned the determinant crossing sign.

[F4] [[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: the half-sum
of mixed crossing signs is an integer independent of the regular oriented
diagram, and it is symmetric in the two components.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The definition specifies $R$ as dotted and $B,G$ as zero-framed attaching circles. Thus $R$ contributes one $1$-handle, while $B$ and $G$ contribute the two $2$-handles in the stated handlebody. [given, construct]

2.1 The two meridional-sublink conditions are invariant under ambient isotopy, and each says that the indicated $2$-handle goes geometrically once over the $1$-handle. The separately stated mixed-crossing condition is a link invariant by [F4], while [F3] fixes the crossing-sign convention; it is not inferred from either meridional-sublink condition. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, §2, definition preceding Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

**Given:** A three-component link in $S^3$ with the component labels and framing
data in the Definition and countable choice.

[A1] Countable choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]: each component is
a smooth oriented embedded circle in the standard oriented $S^3$, and
ambient isotopy means an orientation-preserving isotopy of the ambient sphere.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: a meridian is the boundary
of a normal disk to the component, oriented by the knot and ambient
orientations, and the preferred longitude is the degree-one peripheral curve
with zero exterior-homology class.

[F3] [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]] and
[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]: a regular
oriented diagram has finitely many transverse double crossings with over/under
data, each assigned the determinant crossing sign.

[F4] [[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]]: the half-sum
of mixed crossing signs is an integer independent of the regular oriented
diagram, and it is symmetric in the two components.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The definition specifies $R$ as dotted and $B,G$ as zero-framed attaching
circles. Thus $R$ contributes one $1$-handle, while $B$ and $G$ contribute
the two $2$-handles in the stated handlebody. [given, construct]

1.2 The two meridional-sublink conditions are invariant under ambient isotopy,
and each says that the indicated $2$-handle goes geometrically once over the
$1$-handle. The separately stated mixed-crossing condition is a link
invariant by [F4], while [F3] fixes the crossing-sign convention; it is not
inferred from either meridional-sublink condition. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

[[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity|Schrodinger weak solvability under nonresonance]]

[[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold|Riemannian volume density]]

[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal|Outward unit normal]]

[[def-classical-normal-derivative|Classical normal derivative]]

[[def-riemannian-gradient|Riemannian gradient]]

[[def-riemannian-volume-density|Riemannian density in Green's formula]]

[[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero|Zero trace is equivalent to H-zero]]

[[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain|Sobolev trace]]

[[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace|Boundary extension]]

[[thm-sobolev-gauss-green-formula-on-c-one-domains|Gauss-Green formula]]

[[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem|Smooth boundary-data extension]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact smooth Riemannian domain; positive smooth $\gamma$; a real smooth nonresonant $q$; and the weak solutions in the Definition.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed by the Euclidean trace-kernel and Gauss-Green suppliers [F2, F5].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed by the local weak-solution, trace-lift, and collar suppliers [F3, F4, F6, F8].

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H_0^1(M)$ is the closure of interior compactly supported smooth functions in a fixed finite chartwise $H^1$ norm; the trace is defined chartwise and the fixed finite atlas admits a smooth partition of unity.

[F2] [[thm-kernel-of-the-trace-is-w-one-p-zero]]: on a bounded Euclidean $C^1$ domain, an $H^1$ function has zero trace if and only if it belongs to the $H^1$ closure of compactly supported interior smooth functions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: for each $H^{1/2}$ boundary value, the positive-conductivity weak solution exists uniquely, its weak equation vanishes on every $H_0^1$ test, and smooth boundary data with smooth forcing give a solution smooth up to the boundary.

[F4] [[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity]]: under the stated trivial Dirichlet-kernel condition, the Schrödinger weak solution is unique and smooth for smooth boundary data.

[F5] [[thm-sobolev-gauss-green-formula-on-c-one-domains]]: for smooth functions on a bounded Euclidean $C^1$ domain, integration by parts produces the outward-normal boundary term.

[F6] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: each $H^{1/2}$ boundary datum has an $H^1$ extension in a smooth Euclidean chart; finite chart localization supplies such extensions on $M$.

[F7] [[lem-trace-commutes-with-smooth-boundary-cutoffs-and-charts]]: multiplying by a smooth cutoff multiplies the trace by its boundary restriction, and flattening charts transport the trace to the Euclidean chart trace.

[F8] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: smooth boundary data extend smoothly into a collar by constant normal extension and a cutoff.

[F9] [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]: the trace is a bounded map on $H^1$ and agrees with restriction for smooth functions.

## Verification

**Given:** the data in the Definition and two $H^1$ extensions $V_h^{(1)},V_h^{(2)}$ of the same boundary datum $h$.

1.1 Their difference $W=V_h^{(1)}-V_h^{(2)}$ has zero trace. Localize $W$ by the fixed finite partition in [F1]. On each boundary chart, [F7] shows that the localized function has zero Euclidean trace after flattening; [F2] then approximates it in $H^1$ by compactly supported interior smooth functions. On interior charts, ordinary compactly supported mollification gives the same approximation. Pulling back and summing the finitely many approximations shows $W\in H_0^1(M)$. [A1, F1, F2, F7, given, construct]

2.1 For the conductivity pairing, [F3] gives $\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline W)\,dV_g=0$, since $W\in H_0^1(M)$. Therefore replacing $V_h^{(1)}$ by $V_h^{(2)}$ changes the displayed pairing by zero. For the Schrödinger pairing, the same argument with the weak equation in [F4] gives $\int_M(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline W)+qu_f\overline W)\,dV_g=0$. Thus both definitions are independent of the chosen extension and are well-defined. [A2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F3] and [F4], smooth boundary data yield solutions smooth up to $\partial M$. For smooth test data $h$, choose a smooth collar extension $V_h$ by [F8]. In a boundary chart, write $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv)=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}\partial_jv)$ and $\Delta_gu=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_ju)$. Apply the Euclidean Gauss-Green identity [F5] to the coordinate fluxes; summing over the finite partition gives the Riemannian boundary flux, while artificial chart boundaries cancel and the density transforms to $dS_g$. For the conductivity equation it yields $$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\gamma\,\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$ since $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$. For the Schrödinger equation it yields $$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_{\partial M}\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f\,\overline h\,dS_g,$$ since $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$. The extensions required for the weak pairings exist by [F6], and smooth test extensions exist by [F8]. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $(W,\Sigma,\mathcal A)$ be a decorated knot cobordism from $(Y_0,K_0)$ to $(Y_1,K_1)$, and fix $\mathfrak s\in\operatorname{Spin}^c(W)$. Choose a parametrized Kirby decomposition of $W$, together with admissible Heegaard data and regular almost-complex structures for its elementary pieces. Intermediate pieces may contain links with several components or more than one pair of basepoints. Use the colored multipointed modules with $g+n-1$ attaching curves in $\operatorname{Sym}^{g+n-1}(S)$, and specialize all $w$-colors to $U$ and all $z$-colors to $V$; the displayed doubly pointed formula is the $n=1$ case. For a piece represented by a subordinate Heegaard triple $(S,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma,w,z)$, its triangle-count map has the form
$$
\mathbf x\longmapsto \sum_{\mathbf y}\ \sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\Theta^+_{\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\gamma},\mathbf y)\\ \mu(\phi)=0,\ \mathfrak s(\phi)=\mathfrak s}} \#_2\bigl(\mathcal M(\phi)\bigr)U^{n_w(\phi)}V^{n_z(\phi)}\mathbf y,

Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner

## Definition

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, Definition 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1, Definition 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, a chosen tubular neighborhood,
and its preferred longitude.

[F1] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: the preferred longitude is
the degree-one peripheral curve whose class is zero in the first homology of
the knot exterior.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The attaching framing determines a parallel curve on the boundary torus of the chosen tubular neighborhood. By [F1], the zero framing is the one whose parallel represents the preferred longitude, which is the stated attaching convention. [F1, given, def. preferred-longitude framing]

2.1 The construction uses the supplied preferred-longitude representative as attaching data; it makes no uniqueness claim about such representatives and does not change the chosen attachment. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

## Definition references

[Piccirillo, Definition 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1, Definition 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, a chosen tubular neighborhood,
and its preferred longitude.

[F1] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: the preferred longitude is
the degree-one peripheral curve whose class is zero in the first homology of
the knot exterior.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The attaching framing determines a parallel curve on the boundary torus of
the chosen tubular neighborhood. By [F1], the zero framing is the one whose
parallel represents the preferred longitude, which is the stated attaching
convention. [F1, given, def. preferred-longitude framing]

1.2 The construction uses the supplied preferred-longitude representative as
attaching data; it makes no uniqueness claim about such representatives and
does not change the chosen attachment. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $n\ge3$. On the unit ball $B^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:|x|<1\}$ take the constant matrix conductivity $\gamma(x)=I_n$, the $n\times n$ identity matrix. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, define $F_\varepsilon:\overline{B^n}\to\overline{B^n}$ by $F_\varepsilon(x)=(1+\varepsilon(1-|x|^2))x$ and define $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon=(F_\varepsilon)_*\gamma$ by the anisotropic conductivity pushforward formula. For $\eta=\gamma$ or $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon$, let $\Lambda_\eta$ be the weak energy map on $\mathcal B_{B^n}=H^1(B^n)/H_0^1(B^n)$ given by $\langle\Lambda_\eta f,h\rangle=\int_{B^n}\eta\nabla u_{\eta,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, where $u_{\eta,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$ and $V_h$ is any representative of $h$. Then $F_\varepsilon$ is a smooth diffeomorphism that fixes $\partial B^n$ pointwise, $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon$ is smooth and uniformly positive definite, and $\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon\not\equiv I_n$; nevertheless $\Lambda_{\widetilde\gamma_\varepsilon}=\Lambda_{I_n}$.

## Example

Let the scalar parameter $u$ have prior density
$$p_0(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2},$$
and observe $y=0$ with unit-variance Gaussian noise. The exact forward map is
$G(u)=u$, while a deliberately biased numerical forward/PDE solver reports
$\widetilde G(u)=u+2$. At $y=0$, use likelihoods
$L(u)=\exp(-G(u)^2/2)$ and
$\widetilde L(u)=\exp(-\widetilde G(u)^2/2)$; the common Gaussian density
constant cancels when normalizing. Define each fixed-data posterior by
normalizing the prior times its stated likelihood. The exact posterior is
$N(0,1/2)$ and the solver posterior is $N(-1,1/2)$. For the bounded functional
$f(u)=\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,0]}(u)$, their expectations are respectively
$$\Pi(f)=\tfrac12,\qquad \widetilde\Pi(f)=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)>\tfrac12,$$
where
$$\Phi_0(t):=\int_{-\infty}^{t}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz.$$
The discrepancy is in the forward-solver stage of the posterior error budget;
this toy solver assumption makes no claim about the bias of any general PDE
discretization.

## Example references

[[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget|The model, forward-solver, and discretization stages of the error budget.]]

[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws|The standard normal density and affine normal laws.]]

[[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error|Bounded expectations differ by at most $2\|f\|_\infty$ times library total variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prior density, the exact and solver forward maps, the unit-variance observation noise, and the normalized prior-times-likelihood posterior convention in the Example.

[F1] The error-budget solver term compares the exact-model posterior expectation with the posterior expectation obtained from the declared numerical forward solve. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F2] The standard normal density is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$, and $N(m,s^2)$ is its affine image $m+sZ$ for $s>0$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the library standard-normal law interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F3] For a bounded measurable functional, the expectation difference is at most $2\|f\|_\infty$ times the event-supremum total variation distance. [[prop-ip-bounded-posterior-functional-error]]

## Verification

1.1 With the likelihoods stated in the Example, the exact prior-times-likelihood product is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2}$. The substitution $z=\sqrt2u$ and the normalized standard-normal integral in [F2] give $\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-u^2}\,du=\sqrt\pi$, so this product has normalizing integral $(2\pi)^{-1/2}\sqrt\pi=1/\sqrt2$. Its normalized density is therefore $\pi^{-1/2}e^{-u^2}$, which is $N(0,1/2)$ by [F2]. For the solver output, the prior-times-likelihood product is $$ (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2-(u+2)^2/2}=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-(u+1)^2-1};$$ its normalizing integral is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-1}\sqrt\pi=e^{-1}/\sqrt2$, and its normalized density is $\pi^{-1/2}e^{-(u+1)^2}=N(-1,1/2)$ by [F2]. [A1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The exact density is symmetric about zero, so its mass on $(-\infty,0]$ is $1/2$. Under the solver density, $Z=\sqrt2(U+1)$ is standard normal, and $U\le0$ is equivalent to $Z\le\sqrt2$; hence $\widetilde\Pi(f)=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)$. The standard normal density is positive and symmetric, so $\Phi_0(\sqrt2)>\Phi_0(0)=1/2$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 In the error ledger set $\mu_\star=\mu_{\rm model}=\Pi$ and $\mu_{\rm solver}=\mu_{\rm disc}=\widetilde\Pi$; then the solver-stage term is $\delta_{\rm solver}=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)-1/2$ and the model and discretization terms vanish. Since $\|f\|_\infty=1$, [F3] also gives $\delta_{\rm solver}\le2\|\Pi-\widetilde\Pi\|_{\rm TV}$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

id: ex-ip-boundary-jets-do-not-imply-interior-uniqueness
kind: example
title: "Matching boundary jets without interior equality"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
deps:
  - def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map
  - thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity
dependency_level: 5
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:
  statement: ai-altered
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Mikko Salo, Applications of microlocal analysis to inverse problems (2019)"
      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.03041"
      locator: "Section 5, Theorem 5.1, boundary determination of the full conductivity Taylor series."
---

## Example

On the unit ball $\Omega=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^n$, define
$$\psi(x)= \begin{cases} \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{1}{1-4|x|^2}\right),&|x|<1/2,\\ 0,&|x|\geq1/2. \end{cases}$$
For any $\epsilon\ne0$ with $|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty<1$, the positive conductivities $\gamma_1\equiv1$ and $\gamma_2=1+\epsilon\psi$ agree with all orders of derivatives at $\partial\Omega$ but are unequal in the interior. This example shows that equality of all boundary conductivity jets alone does not imply interior equality; it makes no assertion that the two full DN maps agree.

## Example references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Positive scalar conductivity convention]]

[[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity|Boundary jets are determined by full DN data]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the unit ball and the explicit function $\psi$ in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: an admissible scalar conductivity is smooth and strictly positive on the closure of the domain.

[F2] [[thm-ip-boundary-determination-of-scalar-conductivity]]: equality of full conductivity DN maps implies equality of all boundary-normal jets; the example tests only whether equality of those jets by itself forces interior equality.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 For every integer $m\geq0$, differentiation gives $\frac{d^m}{dt^m}e^{-1/t}=P_m(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_m$, by induction on $m$. For every polynomial $P$, $P(s)e^{-s}\to0$ as $s\to\infty$; for each power $s^N$, this follows from $e^s\geq s^{N+1}/(N+1)!$. Thus every right derivative tends to zero at $t=0$, so extension by zero to $t\leq0$ is smooth and flat there. Composition with $t=1-4|x|^2$ proves $\psi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$, with compact support in $\overline{B(0,1/2)}$. It is nonzero at $x=0$, and $\|\psi\|_\infty<\infty$. [given, induction, construct, algebra]

2.1 The bound $|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty<1$ gives $\gamma_2(x)\geq1-|\epsilon|\|\psi\|_\infty>0$, so [F1] applies. Since $\psi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ agree on that neighborhood and all their boundary derivatives agree. At the origin, $\gamma_2(0)-\gamma_1(0)=\epsilon e^{-1}\ne0$. Thus identical boundary jets do not force interior equality. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Fix $d\ge3$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $x_0=(1/2,\ldots,1/2)$, $a=1/4$, $D=B(x_0,a)\subset(0,1)^d$, and $D'=B(x_0,a/2)$. Choose a nonzero $\psi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ that equals one on $\overline B(0,1/2)$, put $N_\alpha=\|\psi\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R^d)}$, and set $\phi=\psi/\max\{1,N_\alpha\}$. Here the $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm is the maximum of the suprema of the function, its first derivatives, and the $\alpha$-Hölder seminorms of its first derivatives. Let $r=a/4$, $\varepsilon=\min\{1/4,r^{1+\alpha}/8\}$, and $\gamma(x)=1+\varepsilon\phi((x-x_0)/r)$ on $D$. For $m=1/2$, $M=3/2$, and $R=2$, this coefficient belongs to $X_d(2)$.

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)$. 2.1 The costs are equal and $10>2>0$, so strict increase of the logarithm [F2] gives $\operatorname{EIG}(d_1)>\operatorname{EIG}(d_2)$. Thus $d_1$ is the unique maximizer among the two candidates. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

    - title: "David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604"
      url: "https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf"
      locator: "§3.1 and p. 594, information criteria with correlated or design-dependent noise."
---

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N(0,1)$ and take two repeated observations with $A=(1,1)^T$ and noise covariance $\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $-1<\rho<1$. The matrix $\Gamma_\rho$ is positive definite. The expected information gain is $\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}\right)$. In particular, correlation $\rho=\frac12$ gives $\frac12\log(7/3)$, less than the independent-noise value $\frac12\log 3$ at $\rho=0$.

## Example references

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, scalar prior covariance $C=1$, repeated-observation matrix $A=(1,1)^T$, and $-1<\rho<1$.

[A1] AC is inherited from the EIG/KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, linear-Gaussian EIG is the log determinant in the Statement of the cited theorem. [[thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet]]

[F2] The natural logarithm is strictly increasing. [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]

## Verification

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Example.

1.1 The vectors $(1,1)^T$ and $(1,-1)^T$ are eigenvectors of $\Gamma_\rho$ with eigenvalues $1+\rho$ and $1-\rho$. Both are positive for $-1<\rho<1$, so $\Gamma_\rho\succ0$. The predictive covariance is $S_\rho=ACA^T+\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}2&1+\rho\\1+\rho&2\end{pmatrix}$ Thus $\det S_\rho=4-(1+\rho)^2$ and $\det\Gamma_\rho=1-\rho^2$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $\operatorname{EIG}(\rho)=\frac12\log(\det S_\rho/\det\Gamma_\rho)=\frac12\log\left(\frac{4-(1+\rho)^2}{1-\rho^2}\right)$. Factoring numerator and denominator gives $\frac{4-(1+\rho)^2}{1-\rho^2}=\frac{(3+\rho)(1-\rho)}{(1-\rho)(1+\rho)}=1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}$, proving the formula. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 At $\rho=\frac12$, the ratio is $7/3$; at $\rho=0$, it is $3$. Since $7/3<3$, [F2] gives the strict EIG comparison in the Example. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let the target posterior $\pi$ be uniform on $E=\{-1,+1\}$ and define
$$K_\varepsilon(x,\{x\})=1-\varepsilon,\qquad K_\varepsilon(x,\{-x\})=\varepsilon,$$

$$\rho_f(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))}{\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))}.$$
For every $k\ge1$, $\rho_f(k)=(49/50)^k$. Its integrated autocorrelation
time $\tau_f:=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_f(k)$ is therefore $99$, so the
theoretical functional-specific effective sample size of $N=10{,}000$ draws is
$$\operatorname{ESS}_f(10{,}000)=\frac{10{,}000}{99}\approx101.01.$$

only about one percent of the nominal independent-sample size. This is the
theoretical ESS from the stationary autocorrelation sequence, not an empirical
finite-run ESS estimate, and it asserts no central limit theorem.

[F3] A time-homogeneous Markov chain has one-step conditional law given by its transition kernel. [[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

[A1] AC is assumed by the library Markov-chain and invariant-initial-law interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F4] If the initial law is invariant, the chain is strictly stationary. [[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]]

[F5] The theoretical functional ESS is $N/(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_f(k))$ when the process is strictly stationary, has positive finite variance, absolutely summable autocorrelations, and positive integrated autocorrelation time; this definition asserts no CLT. [F2] A point is a strong small-ball MAP when its posterior ball probability divided by the supremum over all centers tends to $1$. [[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator]]

## Example

Let $\Omega=B(0,1)\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\Gamma=\{x\in\partial\Omega:x_3>1/2\}$, a proper nonempty open boundary cap. A measurement protocol that knows only $\Lambda_\gamma f|_\Gamma$ for inputs $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ is a partial-data protocol. It is outside the full-data conductivity uniqueness theorem, whose hypothesis is equality of the DN operators on every boundary input; this example asserts no nonuniqueness for the partial-data protocol.

## Example references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full-data conductivity DN map]]

[[cor-ip-euclidean-cta-conductivity-uniqueness|Full-data conditional conductivity uniqueness]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the unit ball, the open cap $\Gamma$, and the partial input/output restriction in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: full-data equality is equality of the operators on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$.

[F2] [[cor-ip-euclidean-cta-conductivity-uniqueness]]: the full-data theorem's hypothesis is equality of the scalar DN maps on every boundary datum.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 The set $\Gamma$ is nonempty because it contains the north pole and is open in the sphere because it is the inverse image of $(1/2,\infty)$ under the continuous coordinate $x\mapsto x_3$. It is proper because the south pole is not in it. A nonzero smooth bump supported in a small lower cap defines boundary data outside $C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$, so the allowed inputs form a proper subset of the full boundary-data space. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and [F2], the full-data theorem requires the map on every $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ input and the corresponding full boundary output. The stated protocol restricts both input and output to $\Gamma$, so it does not satisfy that hypothesis. This classifies the configuration as outside the theorem's scope and asserts no uniqueness or nonuniqueness conclusion. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Example

Let $H=\mathbb R$, give the unknown parameter $u$ the prior law
$\mu_0=N(0,1)$, and observe one datum $Y=0$ from the model
$Y\mid u\sim N(u,1)$. The Gaussian conjugate update gives posterior
$\mu=N(0,1/2)$. Use the potential $\Phi(u)=u^2/2$ in the pCN algorithm. For
$\beta\in[0,1]$, write $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$, propose
$v=\rho u+\beta\xi$ with $\xi\sim N(0,1)$ independent of the current
state, and accept with probability
$$\alpha(u,v)=\min\{1,\exp((u^2-v^2)/2)\}.$$
The resulting pCN probability kernel leaves $N(0,1/2)$ invariant for every
$\beta\in[0,1]$.

## Example references

[[thm-normal-normal-conjugate-update|A normal prior and one normal observation with known variance give a normal posterior by the precision update.]]

[[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson|The proposal combines the current state with an independent Gaussian reference draw and accepts by the potential ratio.]]

[[thm-ip-pcn-posterior-invariance|A proper pCN posterior target is invariant under its accept-reject kernel.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The one-observation normal model and pCN rule in the Example.

[F1] For prior $N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ and one observation from $N(u,\sigma^2)$, the posterior mean is $(\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2})^{-1}(\mu_0/\tau_0^2+y/\sigma^2)$ and the posterior variance is $(\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2})^{-1}$; evidence is finite and positive. [[thm-normal-normal-conjugate-update]]

[F2] The law $N(m,1)$ has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-(y-m)^2/2)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F3] The pCN rule proposes $v=\rho u+\beta\xi$ and accepts with probability $\min\{1,\exp(\Phi(u)-\Phi(v))\}$ for finite potential values. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]]

[F4] The pCN accept-reject probability kernel leaves its normalized posterior target invariant. [[thm-ip-pcn-posterior-invariance]]

## Proof

**Given:** The model has prior $N(0,1)$, observation variance $1$, datum $y=0$, and potential $\Phi(u)=u^2/2$.

1.1 Apply [F1] with $\mu_0=0$, $\tau_0^2=1$, $\sigma^2=1$, $n=1$, and $y=0$. The posterior variance is $(1+1)^{-1}=1/2$, and its mean is $(1+1)^{-1}(0+0)=0$. The evidence is finite and positive, so the posterior is the proper law $N(0,1/2)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], the likelihood density at $y=0$ is $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$. Its constant factor cancels when the likelihood is normalized against the prior, so the potential $\Phi(u)=u^2/2$ gives exactly the posterior from step 1.1. It is finite on $D=H=\mathbb R$, and the pCN target assumptions are satisfied. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 For the proposal in [F3], $$\Phi(u)-\Phi(v)=\frac{u^2-v^2}{2},$$ so the stated acceptance probability is precisely the algorithm's pCN acceptance rule for this target. [F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Step 1.1 identifies the normalized target, and step 3.1 identifies the kernel as the pCN accept-reject kernel for that target. Applying [F4] proves that $N(0,1/2)$ is invariant for every $\beta\in[0,1]$. [F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X=\mathbb R$ with its usual real Banach norm, let $U=D=\{0,1\}$ with the Borel subspace structure, and let the forward map be $F(u)=u$. Give the parameter the Borel probability $\mu_0(A)=\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}}+\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{1\in A\}}$ for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$. Let the data space be $\mathbb R$ with its usual metric and Borel sigma-algebra. Conditional on $u\in D$, let the observation have law $N(u,1)$, with Lebesgue density
$$
L(u;y)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(y-u)^2}{2}\right),
$$
and likelihood potential $\Phi(u;y)=\tfrac12(y-u)^2+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$. For every $y\in\mathbb R$,
$$
Z(y)=\tfrac12L(0;y)+\tfrac12L(1;y)\in(0,\infty),
$$
and the normalized update on $A\subseteq D$ is
$$
\Pi^y(A)=\frac{L(0;y)\mathbf1_{\{0\in A\}}+L(1;y)\mathbf1_{\{1\in A\}}}{L(0;y)+L(1;y)}.
$$
This is a data-indexed posterior-kernel version for the prior-predictive model; its values on any measurable data-marginal-null set may be changed without changing the conditional-law identities.

[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element|Conditional-kernel values on a measurable data-marginal-null set may be changed.]]

[Dashti and Stuart, §3.2 and §4.1, full lecture notes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.6989)

[Latz, §2.2 and Appendix B.2, full paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1902.10257)

[A1] AC is the assertion that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Under AC, $N(m,\sigma^2)$ is the affine image of $N(0,1)$ and for $\sigma>0$ has Lebesgue density $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F2] AC implies countable choice. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F3] Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite under countable choice. [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]]

[F4] A proper Bayesian model has a probability prior and a parameter-measurable probability sampling kernel. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]

[F1, F14, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

## Example

In $\mathbb R^2$ take $\Phi=(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ with $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(0,1)$, and $a_3=(1,1)$. Its intensity map on classes modulo $x\sim -x$ is $[x]\mapsto(x_1^2,x_2^2,(x_1+x_2)^2)$. Every pair is linearly independent, so every pair spans $\mathbb R^2$; consequently, for every partition one side spans $\mathbb R^2$. Equality of the displayed triples therefore forces two signals to be equal up to a global sign.

## Example references

[[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval|Real intensity map and global-sign quotient]]

[[def-ip-real-full-spark-measurement-family|Full-spark condition]]

[[cor-ip-full-spark-sharp-real-phase-measurement-count|Sharp full-spark measurement count]]

[Radu Balan, Pete Casazza, and Dan Edidin, full-spark threshold, Corollary 2.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412411)

[Radu Balan, full-spark threshold, Corollary 3.3](https://www.norbertwiener.umd.edu/Education/IMA2015/t4/lecture.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The family $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(0,1)$, $a_3=(1,1)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ and the real sign-quotient intensity map.

[F1] [[def-ip-real-full-spark-measurement-family]], [[def-linear-independence]]: a three-vector family in $\mathbb R^2$ is full spark when every two vectors are linearly independent.

[F2] [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], [[def-linear-subspace]]: every span is a subspace containing the listed vectors and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

[F3] [[cor-ip-full-spark-sharp-real-phase-measurement-count]]: a full-spark real family with at least $2d-1$ measurements performs phase retrieval.

## Verification


1.1 For every $(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2$, $$ (u,v)=u a_1+v a_2=(u-v)a_1+v a_3=u a_3+(v-u)a_2,$$ so each pair spans $\mathbb R^2$ by [F2]. For independence, a vanishing combination of $a_1,a_2$ has coordinates $(\alpha,\beta)=(0,0)$; a vanishing combination $\alpha a_1+\beta a_3$ has coordinates $(\alpha+\beta,\beta)=(0,0)$, forcing $\beta=\alpha=0$; and a vanishing combination $\alpha a_2+\beta a_3$ has coordinates $(\beta,\alpha+\beta)=(0,0)$, again forcing $\alpha=\beta=0$. Thus every pair is linearly independent, so [F1] gives full spark. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Here $d=2$ and $m=3=2d-1$. Applying [F3] to step 1.1 proves phase retrieval on the stated global-sign quotient; the intensity coordinates are exactly the three squared inner products displayed in the example. [step 1.1, F3, algebra] ∎
