## Example

Take $q=1$, $\alpha=\beta=1$, $a_j=j$, and $\sigma_j=j$ in the Gaussian sequence detection experiment. Then the sparse boundary parameter is $\lambda=0$, the source-normalized constant is $\Lambda=1$, and a minimax separation rate has order
$$r_\varepsilon^*\asymp\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{1/4}\qquad(\varepsilon\downarrow0).$$

## Example references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, §4.7, Theorem 4.7(d), PDF pp. 18–19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Giné and Nickl, *Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models*, §6.2.3, Gaussian white-noise testing, PDF pp. 506–508](https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), $q=1$, $\alpha=\beta=1$, $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and the Gaussian sequence experiment over $\Theta_1(r)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-minimax-detection-risk-and-separation]]: $\eta\in\Theta_1(r)$ means $\sum_i i^2|\eta_i|\le1$ and $\sum_i i^2\eta_i^2\ge r^2$; the null coordinates are independent $N(0,\varepsilon^2)$.

[F2] [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]] and [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]]: nonnegative functions of finitely many independent coordinates have factorized expectations; finite measures agreeing on the generating finite-coordinate rectangular cylinders and on total mass agree on the sequence sigma-algebra.

[F3] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]]: $Y_i/\varepsilon$ is standard normal under the null, with density $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. This given probability law already supplies $\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(x)\,dx=1$.

[F4] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]]: under countable choice, completing the square and translating the given normalized density in [F3] gives $\mathbb E e^{tG}=e^{t^2/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(x-t)\,dx=e^{t^2/2}$ for every real $t$.

[F5] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]]: Markov's inequality therefore gives $\mathbb P(|G|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}$ for $t>0$.

## Verification

1.1 Substitution gives $\lambda=(1+1)/2-1=0$ and $\Lambda=(2/(1+1))^{1/4}=1$. To prove the rate order, first let $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, set $n=\lfloor1/(4r)\rfloor$, and for each $i\in\{n+1,\ldots,2n\}$ use the two alternatives with sole nonzero coordinate $\eta_i=\pm r/i$. Each lies in $\Theta_1(r)$ because $ri\le1$ and $i^2\eta_i^2=r^2$. Put $\mu_i=r/(\varepsilon i)$; then their standardized means satisfy $|\eta_i|/\varepsilon=\mu_i\le4r^2/\varepsilon$. If $s=r/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $\max_i\mu_i^2\le16\varepsilon^{-2}r^4=16s^4\log(\varepsilon^{-1})=o(\log n)$, because $\log n\ge c\log(\varepsilon^{-1})$ for some $c>0$ when $r\le r_\varepsilon^*$ and $\varepsilon$ is small. For each location $i$, the shifted scalar density divided by the null density is $e^{\pm\mu_iG_i-\mu_i^2/2}$, where $G_i=Y_i/\varepsilon$ under the null; averaging the two signs gives $L_i=e^{-\mu_i^2/2}\cosh(\mu_iG_i)$. Completing the square using [F3] and [F4] gives $\mathbb E_0L_i=1$ and $\mathbb E_0L_i^2=\cosh(\mu_i^2)$. The measure $L_i\,dP_0$ is therefore a probability measure. Finite-coordinate factorization in [F2] identifies its value on every finite-coordinate rectangular cylinder with the sign-mixture sampling law at location $i$: only the $i$th scalar density changes and all other coordinates retain their null law. These cylinders generate the sequence sigma-algebra, so finite-measure uniqueness in [F2] identifies the two measures on all measurable events. For distinct locations, [F2] also gives $\mathbb E_0L_iL_j=1$. Thus the uniform mixture $L=n^{-1}\sum_iL_i$ satisfies $\mathbb E_0(L-1)^2=n^{-2}\sum_i(\cosh(\mu_i^2)-1)\le n^{-1}\exp(\max_i\mu_i^2)=n^{-1}\exp(o(\log n))\to0$. Since $\mathbb E_0(L-1)=0$, its positive and negative parts have equal integrals, so for every event $E$, $|P_\pi(E)-P_0(E)|\le\tfrac12\mathbb E_0|L-1|\le\tfrac12\sqrt{\mathbb E_0(L-1)^2}$. Approximation by averages of event indicators gives the same bound for randomized tests. Therefore the mixture total variation tends to zero, $\gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_1(r))\to1$, and every level-$\alpha$ test has maximal type-II error at least $1-\alpha-o(1)$. The constant randomized test $\psi\equiv\alpha$ gives the matching upper bound $1-\alpha$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 First suppose $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ and $r\to0$. Put $N=\lceil2/r\rceil$, $t_N=4\sqrt{\log N}$, and reject if $\max_{i\le N}|Y_i|/\varepsilon>t_N$. Under the null, [F5] and a union bound give type-I error at most $2N e^{-t_N^2/2}=2N^{-7}\to0$. For any alternative, $|\eta_i|\le i^{-2}$ follows from [F1], so the omitted weighted energy obeys $\sum_{i>N}i^2\eta_i^2\le N^{-2}\sum_{i>N}i^2|\eta_i|\le N^{-2}\le r^2/4$. Hence $\sum_{i\le N}i^2\eta_i^2\ge3r^2/4$. On the event that all $N$ null-noise coordinates satisfy $|\xi_i|\le t_N/2$, nonrejection would imply $|\eta_i|\le(3/2)\varepsilon t_N$ for every $i\le N$, and therefore $\sum_{i\le N}i^2\eta_i^2\le(3/2)\varepsilon t_N\sum_{i\le N}i^2|\eta_i|\le(3/2)\varepsilon t_N$. But $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ makes $r^2/(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log N})\to\infty$, a contradiction for small $\varepsilon$. The probability that the stated noise event fails is at most $2N e^{-(t_N/2)^2/2}=2/N\to0$, so the maximal type-II error tends to zero. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For an arbitrary positive radius sequence with $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$, use the positive representative $r_\varepsilon^*=\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{1/4}$ and put $\bar r_\varepsilon=\min\{r_\varepsilon,\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}$. Then $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$, $\bar r_\varepsilon\le r_\varepsilon$, and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*=\min\{r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*,1/\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}\to\infty$. Apply step 2.1 with $\bar r_\varepsilon$ in place of $r_\varepsilon$. Its cutoff $N=\lceil2/\bar r_\varepsilon\rceil$ now tends to infinity, so both its null-size bound $2N^{-7}$ and its noise-event bound $2/N$ vanish, and the energy-tail and signal-to-threshold estimates in that step apply at $\bar r_\varepsilon$. Since $\Theta_1(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_1(\bar r_\varepsilon)$, the same test has unchanged null size and no larger maximal type-II error on the requested alternative. Its total error therefore tends to zero, and its null size is eventually below any fixed significance level, giving both consistency limits in [F1]. For an empty requested alternative both minimax risks are zero by that definition, with the never-reject test attaining zero total error. This covers the nonvanishing-radius case without using a bounded or nondiverging cutoff. [F1, step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 The impossibility implication in step 1.1 and the all-positive-radius consistency implication in step 3.1 establish the separation-rate order $\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{1/4}$. The parameter and constant were computed in step 1.1, proving the example. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $D=\{x'\in\mathbb R^2:|x'|\leq1\}$ with its Euclidean metric and let
$$M=\{(x_1,x')\in\mathbb R\times D:x_1^2+4|x'|^2\leq1\}$$
with the restricted Euclidean product metric. Then $M$ is a compact smooth three-dimensional product subdomain compactly contained in $\mathbb R\times D^\circ$, and the transversal $D$ is a simple surface whose unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform is injective on real-valued compactly supported smooth functions.

## Example references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product-domain convention]]

[[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform|Simple surface and scalar ray transform]]

[[thm-ip-2d-simple-surface-xray-injectivity|Injectivity on simple surfaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the disk $D$, the ellipsoid $M$, and the Euclidean product metric in the statement.

[F1] [[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain]]: a compact smooth three-dimensional domain compactly contained in a product $\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ with product metric is transversally anisotropic.

[F2] [[def-ip-simple-surface-and-geodesic-xray-transform]]: a compact surface is simple when its boundary is strictly convex, there are no conjugate points, and geodesics exit in finite time.

[F3] [[thm-ip-2d-simple-surface-xray-injectivity]]: for a real $f\in C_c^\infty(D^\circ)$, zero integrals over all nontangential boundary-to-boundary geodesics on a simple surface imply $f=0$.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 The boundary of $M$ is the level set $x_1^2+4|x'|^2=1$. Its defining function has gradient $(2x_1,8x_2,8x_3)$, which cannot vanish on that level set, so $M$ is a compact smooth three-dimensional domain. Every point of $M$ has $|x'|\leq1/2<1$, hence $M\Subset\mathbb R\times D^\circ$; the ambient metric is exactly $dx_1^2\oplus g_D$. By [F1], this is a transversally anisotropic product domain. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 The disk has strictly convex boundary: its outward unit normal is $x'$ on $|x'|=1$ and $g(\nabla_w\nu_{\rm out},w)=|w|^2>0$ for every nonzero tangent $w$. Its curvature is zero, so a normal Jacobi field has scalar coefficient $a+bt$; if it vanishes at two distinct times then $a=b=0$, proving no conjugate points. Every unit-speed straight line exits the bounded disk in finite forward and backward time, and the segment between two points in the disk is unique. Thus $D$ is simple by [F2]. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F3] to this simple surface. Its unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform is injective on the stated compactly supported smooth real functions. This verifies the injective-transversal condition for $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.2] ∎

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. Let $0<a<b$, let $\phi\in C_c^\infty((a,b))$ be nonnegative and not identically zero, define $U(r)=\int_r^b\phi(s)\,ds$ for $r\ge0$, and set $u^\dagger(x)=U(|x|)$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Choose $h\in C_c^\infty((a/2,2b))$ with $0\le h\le1$ and $h=1$ on $\operatorname{supp}\phi$, put $z(x)=h(|x|)x/|x|$ extended by zero at the origin, and let $q=\operatorname{div}z$. On real $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ define the Bessel blur $A=\mathcal F_2^{-1}M_m\mathcal F_2$, where $\mathcal F_2$ is the unitary Fourier transform with phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$ and $M_m$ multiplies by $m(\xi)=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}$. Let $f=Au^\dagger$ and define $p=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\bigl((1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\widehat q(\xi)\bigr)$. Then $A$ is bounded, self-adjoint, and injective, $p\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$, and $A^*p\in\partial TV_2(u^\dagger)$. Thus $u^\dagger$ is the unique minimum-TV exact solution satisfying the full-space source condition; for zero noise the parameter ratio $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n$ is zero.

## Example references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A certificate is an adjoint image in the TV subdifferential at an exact minimum-TV truth.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The full-space regularizer is the extended distributional-TV functional on L².]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §§5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[[thm-plancherel|Plancherel extends the unitary Fourier transform to L².]]

[[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls|A smooth cutoff exists around the compact radial support of $\phi$.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nonzero nonnegative radial profile $\phi$, the radial truth $u^\dagger$, the Fourier multiplier $m$, and full-space $TV_2$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed by the Plancherel supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[thm-plancherel]]: $\mathcal F_2$ is a unitary map on complex $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ and preserves inner products.

[F2] [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]: for integrable $q$, $\widehat q(\xi)=\int q(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx$; integration by parts gives the displayed derivative transform.

[F3] [[lem-schwartz-space-is-dense-in-l-two]]: complex Schwartz functions are dense in complex $L^2$; taking real parts gives density of real Schwartz functions in real $L^2$.

[F4] [[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation]]: $TV_2(v)$ is the supremum of $\int v\operatorname{div}y$ over compactly supported smooth vector fields with $\|y\|_\infty\le1$.

[F5] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]] and [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $q\in\partial TV_2(u)$ when $TV_2(v)\ge TV_2(u)+\langle q,v-u\rangle$ for all $v\in L^2$, using the real Hilbert pairing.

[F6] [[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]: a smooth cutoff can equal one on the compact radial support of $\phi$ and vanish near the origin.

[F7] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: on real-valued functions, the complex $L^2$ inner product equals the real Hilbert pairing.

## Verification

**Proof technique:** Fourier multiplier verification and a calibration field.

The real-valued subspace is closed in complex $L^2$: if $g_j$ are real-valued classes and $g_j\to g$ in complex $L^2$, then $\|\operatorname{Im}g\|_2=\|\operatorname{Im}(g-g_j)\|_2\le\|g-g_j\|_2\to0$, so $g$ is real-valued as an $L^2$ class.

1.1 The multiplier $m$ is real, even, and satisfies $0<m\le1$, so [F1] makes $A$ a contraction on complex $L^2$. For real Schwartz $g$, the integral formula [F2] gives $\widehat g(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}$, and multiplication by $m$ preserves this symmetry. Approximate $m\widehat g$ in $L^2$ by Schwartz functions using [F3], then replace each approximant $s$ by $\tfrac12(s(\xi)+\overline{s(-\xi)})$. These symmetrized approximants remain Schwartz, converge to $m\widehat g$, and have real inverse Fourier transforms by [F2]; [F1] and the closedness observation above pass this property to $Ag$. Density of real Schwartz functions and boundedness of $A$ extend real-valuedness to real $L^2$. By [F7], the complex Plancherel pairing restricts to the real Hilbert pairing. Multiplication by the real function $m$ is self-adjoint, so $\langle Au,v\rangle=\langle u,Av\rangle$ for real $u,v$, and $A^*=A$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7, given, algebra]

1.2 Because $\phi$ is supported away from zero and from $b$, $u^\dagger$ is constant near the origin, smooth across radii $a,b$, and zero for $|x|\ge b$; hence it is a compactly supported smooth real function. Its gradient is $\nabla u^\dagger(x)=-\phi(|x|)x/|x|$ wherever $\phi(|x|)\ne0$ and is zero elsewhere. The cutoff in the Statement exists by [F6] and gives $z\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|z\|_\infty\le1$. Integration by parts gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^2}u^\dagger\operatorname{div}z\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb R^2}z\cdot\nabla u^\dagger\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi(|x|)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|\nabla u^\dagger|\,dx.$$ For every admissible test field $y$, the same integration by parts gives $\int u^\dagger\operatorname{div}y\le\int|\nabla u^\dagger|$, while the field $z$ attains equality. Thus $TV_2(u^\dagger)=\int u^\dagger\operatorname{div}z$. Setting $q=\operatorname{div}z$, [F4] gives $TV_2(v)\ge\int vq=TV_2(u^\dagger)+\langle q,v-u^\dagger\rangle$ for every $v$, so $q\in\partial TV_2(u^\dagger)$. [F4, F5, F6, given, algebra]

2.1 The vector $q$ is smooth and compactly supported, so $q,\partial_1q,\partial_2q\in L^2$. Integration by parts using [F2] gives $\widehat{\partial_jq}=2\pi i\xi_j\widehat q$, and Plancherel [F1] yields $$\int_{\mathbb R^2}(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)|\widehat q(\xi)|^2\,d\xi=\|q\|_2^2+\|\nabla q\|_2^2<\infty.$$ Therefore $\widehat p(\xi):=(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\widehat q(\xi)$ is in $L^2$, defining $p=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\widehat p\in L^2$. The integral formula [F2] gives Hermitian symmetry of $\widehat q$, and the real even multiplier preserves it. As in step 1.1, approximate $\widehat p$ by Schwartz functions, symmetrize them, apply inverse Fourier transformation, and use Plancherel continuity and closedness of the real subspace to conclude that $p$ is real. By construction $A^*p=Ap=q$, so [F5] gives the required source certificate. Injectivity from step 1.1 makes $u^\dagger$ the unique exact solution, hence the unique minimum-TV exact solution. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Step 2.1 provides a certificate at the unique minimum-TV exact truth. For every positive $\alpha_n$ and zero noise $w_n=0$, the parameter ratio is $\|A^*\|\|w_n\|_2/\alpha_n=0$. Thus this example verifies the source condition and the zero-noise parameter side of the full-space deblurring setup without asserting existence of a regularized minimizer. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\Lambda_2=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},t_2^{\pm1}]$, $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and let $\eta:\Lambda_2\to\Lambda_1$ send $t_1,t_2$ to $t$. Choose standard pairwise-disjoint radius-$\epsilon$ tubes with $0<\epsilon<1/\sqrt2$. Let $H$ be the standard Hopf link $\{z=0\}\cup\{w=0\}$ in $S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, orienting its components so the increasing phase meridians are positive, and let $U$ be the standard two-component unlink whose components lie in separate $3$-balls. Choose a common basepoint for the two based positive-meridian loops in the unlink exterior and use it for the unlink cover. For $H$, the complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and the compact exterior is $T^2\times I$; its maximal abelian cover is $\mathbb R^2\times I$, so its absolute multivariable Alexander module is $A_H=0$. Its total-linking cyclic cover is $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$, with trivial $t$-action on first homology, so the one-variable Alexander module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$. For $U$, the compact exterior has free fundamental group on its two positive meridians. The meridian map from $S^1\vee S^1$ induces an isomorphism on first homology of the corresponding maximal abelian covers, whose graph-cover chain complex is $\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}\Lambda_2$; its first homology is free of rank one, so $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$. The total-linking cyclic graph-cover complex computing its first homology is $\Lambda_1^2\xrightarrow{(t-1,\ t-1)}\Lambda_1$, with first homology $\Lambda_1$. These computations distinguish chain specialization from tensoring the multivariable homology module.

The projection below is schematic: the upper crossing has the first component $K_1$ (blue) over, and the lower crossing has the second component $K_2$ (red) over. The calculations use the stated coordinate and meridian graph-cover homology models, not the drawing.

```tikz

  \draw[red,thick] (0.55,0) circle (1);
  \draw[blue,thick] (-0.55,0) circle (1);
  \draw[white,line width=5pt] plot[domain=115:132,samples=20] ({0.55+cos(\x)},{sin(\x)});
  \draw[blue,thick] plot[domain=48:66,samples=20] ({-0.55+cos(\x)},{sin(\x)});
  \draw[white,line width=5pt] plot[domain=-66:-47,samples=20] ({-0.55+cos(\x)},{sin(\x)});
  \draw[red,thick] plot[domain=225:248,samples=20] ({0.55+cos(\x)},{sin(\x)});
  \node[fill=white,inner sep=1pt,font=\scriptsize] at (0,0.835) {blue over};
  \node[fill=white,inner sep=1pt,font=\scriptsize] at (0,-0.835) {red over};
  \node[blue] at (-1.25,0.15) {$K_1$};
  \node[red] at (1.25,-0.15) {$K_2$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Example references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the standard Hopf link $H$ and two-component unlink $U$ specified in the Example; and the maximal-abelian and total-linking covers of their compact exteriors.

[A1] AC is the assumption of the maximal-abelian-cover definition ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The multivariable module is absolute first homology of the maximal abelian cover, with the positive-meridian deck action ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The one-variable module is first homology of the cover classified by total linking, whose defining homomorphism sums the Alexander-dual meridian coordinates ([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]).

[F3] Connected covers are classified by the subgroups they induce ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F4] Cellular homology agrees naturally with singular homology for CW complexes ([[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]).

[F5] $\Lambda_2$ is a domain and UFD, with signed monomials as its units ([[lem-multivariable-laurent-ring-noetherian-ufd]], [[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F6] Diagonal coefficient extension of the maximal-abelian-cover chain complex is the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex ([[lem-multivariable-alexander-order-and-specialization]]).

[F7] The compact-exterior maximal abelian cover and the open-complement maximal abelian cover are deck-equivariantly homotopy equivalent and have the same module ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F8] Homotopies into a covering base lift uniquely after an initial lift is specified ([[thm-homotopy-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F9] A deformation retract induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups at every basepoint in the retract ([[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F10] Seifert--van Kampen applies to the collar-thickened split-sphere union; its overlap is simply connected. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]]

[F11] The degree-one Hurewicz map naturally identifies first homology with the abelianization of fundamental group. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Verification

1.1 Every point of $S^3\setminus H$ has $z\ne0$ and $w\ne0$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto(z/|z|,w/|w|,|z|)$ has inverse $(u,v,s)\mapsto(su,\sqrt{1-s^2}v)$, so the open complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and a compact exterior is $T^2\times I$. The two phase loops are positive meridians of the two coordinate-circle components, hence form the basis of $\pi_1(E_H)=H_1(E_H;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$. By [F3], the maximal abelian cover is the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$, whose first homology vanishes. The compact-exterior/open-complement identification [F7] therefore gives $A_H=0$. [A1, F1, F3, F7, given, construct]

1.2 For the standard unknot $K=\{w=0\}$ in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, the exterior of the tube $|w|\le\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $D^2_{\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}}\times S^1$ by $(z,v)\mapsto(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\,v)$; hence it is a solid torus. For the split unlink use its given separating sphere, with one component and its tube in each ball. The exterior is a collared union along that sphere of two ball-minus-tube pieces. Each piece is a solid-torus unknot exterior with the interior of one disjoint standard ball removed. Reattaching the ball does not change fundamental group, by van Kampen with the simply connected sphere overlap. Thus each piece has group $\mathbb Z$ generated by its positive meridian. Van Kampen on their separating-sphere union gives $\pi_1(E_U)\cong\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z$ with these meridian generators. This does not identify $E_U$ with a handlebody or assert a graph deformation retraction. [A1, F3, F10, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], the two positive meridians form the coordinate basis; the coordinate-sum definition [F2] therefore sends both to $1$, so its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(1,-1)$. Quotienting the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$ by this rank-one translation subgroup gives $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$. Its first homology is $\mathbb Z$ generated by the circle. Every deck transformation is represented by a translation, and the path of translations from the identity to that translation is a homotopy, so $t$ acts as $1$. Thus the cyclic module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)\ne0$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$ because $A_H=0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $G=S^1\vee S^1$ map its two based oriented loops to these meridians in $E_U$. It induces the computed fundamental-group isomorphism and intertwines abelianization to $\mathbb Z^2$. Lift it to the connected maximal abelian covers after fixing the base lift. The induced map on fundamental groups identifies the kernels of abelianization, hence is an isomorphism. Degree-one Hurewicz then makes its map on first homology an isomorphism. This is Laurent-linear: conjugation by each meridian implements its deck action on the kernel abelianization, and the map intertwines those conjugations. The same argument for total linking to $\mathbb Z$ compares the cyclic-cover $H_1$. Only first homology is compared; the separating sphere is not removed by a false homotopy equivalence. The lifted graph cellular boundary is $C_1=\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}C_0=\Lambda_2$, so this graph complex computes the desired first homology. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, F11, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 The quotient $\Lambda_2/(t_1-1)$ is $\mathbb Z[t_2^{\pm1}]$, a domain by [F5], so $t_1-1$ is prime. It does not divide $t_2-1$, whose image under $t_1\mapsto1$ is the nonzero element $t_2-1$. If $(a,b)$ lies in the kernel, $(t_1-1)a=-(t_2-1)b$, so primality forces $t_1-1$ to divide $b$. Write $b=(t_1-1)c$; cancellation in the domain gives $a=-(t_2-1)c$. Thus the kernel is generated by $(-(t_2-1),t_1-1)$; it is free because its second coordinate can vanish only when $c=0$. Hence $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$. [F4, F5, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Under total linking, both loop edges map to $t$, so [F6] gives the cyclic-cover boundary $(t-1,t-1):\Lambda_1^2\to\Lambda_1$. Since $\Lambda_1$ is a domain, its kernel consists of $(a,-a)$ and is free of rank one. This confirms the stated cyclic-cover module and completes the example. [F2, F5, F6, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\Lambda_2=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},t_2^{\pm1}]$, $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, and let $\eta:\Lambda_2\to\Lambda_1$ send $t_1,t_2$ to $t$. Choose standard pairwise-disjoint radius-$\epsilon$ tubes with $0<\epsilon<1/\sqrt2$. Let $H$ be the standard Hopf link $\{z=0\}\cup\{w=0\}$ in $S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, orienting its components so the increasing phase meridians are positive, and let $U$ be the standard two-component unlink whose components lie in separate $3$-balls. Choose a common basepoint for the two based positive-meridian loops in the unlink exterior and use it for the unlink cover. For $H$, the complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and the compact exterior is $T^2\times I$; its maximal abelian cover is $\mathbb R^2\times I$, so its absolute multivariable Alexander module is $A_H=0$. Its total-linking cyclic cover is $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$, with trivial $t$-action on first homology, so the one-variable Alexander module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and suppose its double branched cover bounds a compact simply connected positive-definite smooth four-manifold $W$ whose boundary intersection lattice is isometric to $L_{E_8}$. Then this particular filling lattice has rank eight and has no isometric full-rank embedding into the standard lattice $\mathbb Z^8$. This verifies the algebraic nonembedding input for the conditional KT-26 sliceness obstruction. It does not assert that a specified knot has such a filling, that every slice-disk branched cover satisfies boundary normal generation, or that the conditional obstruction proves any further numerical four-ball-genus bound.

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U$ be the standard unknot, let $T_{2,3}$ be the closure of the positive two-strand braid with three crossings, and let $T_{2,3}^{\dagger}$ be its reverse mirror. In the normalized right-trefoil staircase over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$, generators $a,b,c$ have Maslov gradings $0,-1,-2$, Alexander levels $1,0,-1$, and differential $\partial b=Ua+c$, $\partial a=\partial c=0$; multiplication by $U$ lowers both filtrations by one. Choose the polynomial minus lattice $C^-=\mathbb F_2[U]\langle a,b,c\rangle$ inside this Laurent complex, with each displayed generator at first filtration coordinate zero. Its hat complex is the quotient $C^-/UC^-$; setting $U=0$ refers to this lattice quotient, not to the Laurent complex in which $U$ is invertible. The full reverse-mirror Laurent staircase is the filtered dual, with generators $a^\vee,b^\vee,c^\vee$ at Alexander levels $-1,0,1$ and differential $\partial a^\vee=Ub^\vee$, $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$, $\partial b^\vee=0$. Its chosen polynomial dual lattice has hat quotient with $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$ and $\partial a^\vee=\partial b^\vee=0$. The normalized unknot complex has one generator at level zero and zero differential. These models give
$$\tau(U)=0,\qquad \tau(T_{2,3})=1,\qquad \tau(T_{2,3}^{\dagger})=-1.$$
Both trefoils have smooth four-ball genus one.

## Facts & Assumptions

## Example

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U$ be the standard unknot, let $T_{2,3}$ be the closure of the positive two-strand braid with three crossings, and let $T_{2,3}^{\dagger}$ be its reverse mirror. In the normalized right-trefoil staircase over $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$, generators $a,b,c$ have Maslov gradings $0,-1,-2$, Alexander levels $1,0,-1$, and differential $\partial b=Ua+c$, $\partial a=\partial c=0$; multiplication by $U$ lowers both filtrations by one. Choose the polynomial minus lattice $C^-=\mathbb F_2[U]\langle a,b,c\rangle$ inside this Laurent complex, with each displayed generator at first filtration coordinate zero. Its hat complex is the quotient $C^-/UC^-$; setting $U=0$ refers to this lattice quotient, not to the Laurent complex in which $U$ is invertible. The full reverse-mirror Laurent staircase is the filtered dual, with generators $a^\vee,b^\vee,c^\vee$ at Alexander levels $-1,0,1$ and differential $\partial a^\vee=Ub^\vee$, $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$, $\partial b^\vee=0$. Its chosen polynomial dual lattice has hat quotient with $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$ and $\partial a^\vee=\partial b^\vee=0$. The normalized unknot complex has one generator at level zero and zero differential. These models give
$$\tau(U)=0,\qquad \tau(T_{2,3})=1,\qquad \tau(T_{2,3}^{\dagger})=-1.$$
Both trefoils have smooth four-ball genus one.

## Example

Let $T_{2,3}$ be the right-handed trefoil and $-T_{2,3}$ its reverse mirror. A filtered basis for $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(T_{2,3})$ is $x_0,x_1,x_2$ with $(M,A)(x_0)=(0,1)$, $(M,A)(x_1)=(-1,0)$, $(M,A)(x_2)=(-2,-1)$ and differential $\partial x_1=Ux_0+x_2$, $\partial x_0=\partial x_2=0$. Under the conventions of this page,
$$ \epsilon(T_{2,3})=1,\qquad \Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(t)=\begin{cases}-t,&0\le t\le1,\\ t-2,&1\le t\le2.\end{cases} $$
The graph has its unique interior breakpoint at $t=1$. For the reverse mirror, $\epsilon(-T_{2,3})=-1$ and $\Upsilon_{-T_{2,3}}(t)=-\Upsilon_{T_{2,3}}(t)$.

## Example

Let $T$ be the oriented left-handed trefoil, the closure of the two-strand braid $\sigma_1^{-3}$, and choose a marked point away from its three crossings. Its mirror $\overline T$ is the closure of $\sigma_1^3$, depicted below. Use the smoothing convention in which the zero-resolution of this mirror diagram is the through pairing and the one-resolution is the cap-cup pairing. The reduced Khovanov cohomology of $\overline T$ over $\mathbb F_2$ has total rank $3$. The double branched cover of $T$ is a lens space $L(3,1)$ up to orientation, and the hat Floer group of this lens space over $\mathbb F_2$ has total rank $3$. Thus the two endpoint ranks agree, and any spectral sequence with these finite-dimensional endpoints has no nonzero differential in this example.

~~~tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.55]
\draw (-1,6) .. controls (-3,6) and (-3,0) .. (-1,0);

  \draw (-1,\yt) -- (1,\yb);
  \draw[white,line width=4pt] (1,\yt) -- (-1,\yb);
  \draw[black,line width=1.1pt] (1,\yt) -- (-1,\yb);
}
\node at (0,7) {$\widehat{\sigma_1^3}$};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The drawing depicts the closure of the braid word; the southwest-to-northeast diagonal is drawn over the northwest-to-southeast diagonal, matching the positive-generator convention in the rank calculation. The algebraic calculation uses the smoothing cube and Frobenius maps, not the picture.

## Example

Assume countable choice. Let $U$ be the standard unknot. Its zero-trace is
diffeomorphic to $S^2\times D^2$ and embeds in the standard $S^4$ as a tubular
neighborhood of an unknotted $S^2$. It also has the following dualizable-link
description: take a dotted unknot $R$ and two zero-framed meridian circles
$B,G$ at distinct points of $R$, with their normal spanning disks disjoint.
Then $B\cup R$ and $G\cup R$ are meridional pairs, $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$,
and cancelling either meridional $1$–$2$ pair leaves the zero-framed unknot
trace.

## Statement

Assume full AC. For a knot Seifert surface $F$ with Seifert matrix $V$, the function $q_F(x)=x^TVx\pmod2$ is well-defined on $H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)$ and satisfies
$$q_F(x+y)=q_F(x)+q_F(y)+x\cdot_F y.$$
Its polarization is nondegenerate. For any symplectic basis $(a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_g,b_g)$, the sum $\sum_iq_F(a_i)q_F(b_i)$ is independent of that basis. It is unchanged by either elementary Seifert enlargement, so it depends only on the knot.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form|The quadratic function and Arf convention]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The integral skew part and unimodular intersection form]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot, a connected genus-$g$ spanning surface, and its Seifert matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the chosen integral homology basis and Seifert pairing. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

[F1] $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ is free of rank $2g$, and reduction modulo two identifies $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb F_2$ with $H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)$. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] $V-V^T=J_F$, where $J_F$ is the unimodular integral intersection matrix. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F3] An elementary enlargement adds a symplectic pair whose mod-two Seifert self-values are $(z,0)$ for some integer $z$. [[def-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence]]

## Proof

1.1 If two integral coordinate vectors $x,x'$ represent the same class modulo two, then $x'=x+2y$ for an integral vector $y$, and $$(x+2y)^TV(x+2y)-x^TVx=2x^TVy+2y^TVx+4y^TVy$$ is even. Thus $x^TVx\pmod2$ is well-defined. Expanding the quadratic expression gives $$q_F(x+y)-q_F(x)-q_F(y)=x^T(V+V^T)y\pmod2=x^T(V-V^T)y=x\cdot_Fy,$$ where plus and minus agree in $\mathbb F_2$. By [F2], this alternating form is nondegenerate. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In a symplectic basis, every vector is uniquely $x=\sum_i(a_i a_i+b_i b_i)$ with $a_i,b_i\in\mathbb F_2$. The refinement identity gives $$q_F(x)=\sum_i\bigl(a_iq_F(a_i)+b_iq_F(b_i)+a_ib_i\bigr).$$ Therefore the finite Gauss sum factors as $$\sum_{x\in H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)}(-1)^{q_F(x)}=\prod_i\sum_{a,b\in\mathbb F_2}(-1)^{a q_F(a_i)+b q_F(b_i)+ab}=2^g(-1)^{\sum_iq_F(a_i)q_F(b_i)}.$$ The left side depends only on $q_F$, not on a basis, so the exponent defining the Arf value is basis-independent. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Under either enlargement in [F3], the new basis vectors $u,v$ have $u\cdot v=1$, $q(u)=z\pmod2$, and $q(v)=0$; moreover $v$ is orthogonal to all old basis vectors because its encircling disk misses them. If $u$ pairs nontrivially with old basis vectors, add a linear combination of the old symplectic basis to $u$ to obtain $u'$ orthogonal to all of them; the nondegenerate old intersection matrix gives the required coefficients, and $u'\cdot v=1$ remains unchanged. The old basis together with $u',v$ is symplectic; its new Arf contribution is $q(u')q(v)=0$, while the old $q$-values are unchanged. More precisely, put $u''=u'+q(u')v$. The refinement identity and $q(v)=0$, $u'\cdot v=1$ give $q(u'')=q(u')+q(u')=0$, while $u''\cdot v=1$ and both $u'',v$ remain orthogonal to the old subspace. Thus the enlarged quadratic space is isometric to the old one orthogonally summed with the hyperbolic plane $q_H(s,t)=st$: on $su''+tv$ the value is $st$. An integral congruence reduces to an invertible mod-two coordinate change and hence an isometry of quadratic spaces. Consequently, the stable isometry class is invariant under congruences, enlargements and their reverses. Here stable isometry means isometry after adjoining finitely many copies of $q_H$ on either side. Thus the Gauss-sum Arf value is unchanged by enlargement or reduction. By the knot-matrix S-equivalence lemma, all spanning surfaces give the same value. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot of genus $g$, let $V$ be a Seifert matrix in an integral symplectic basis, and let $\Delta_K^\#(t)$ be the unique symmetric Alexander normalization with $\Delta_K^\#(1)=1$. In the quotient ring $\mathbb F_2[t,t^{-1}]/(1+t)^4$,
$$\Delta_K^\#(t)=1+\operatorname{Arf}(K)\frac{(1+t)^2}{t}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form|The Seifert quadratic Arf invariant]]

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix convention]]

[[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization|The symmetric Alexander and Conway normalization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot, a genus-$g$ Seifert surface, and its positive-push Seifert matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the Seifert pairing and Alexander conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $V-V^T$ is the standard integral symplectic intersection matrix in a handle basis, and changes of integral symplectic basis preserve the Arf value. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]], [[lem-arf-quadratic-enhancement-from-seifert-form]]

[F2] In a symplectic basis, $\operatorname{Arf}(K)=\sum_i v_{2i-1,2i-1}v_{2i,2i}\pmod2$, equivalently $\sum_{x\in H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)}(-1)^{q_F(x)}=2^g(-1)^{\operatorname{Arf}(K)}$. [[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form]], [[lem-arf-quadratic-enhancement-from-seifert-form]]

[F3] The determinant $\det(uV-u^{-1}V^T)$ is $\nabla_K(u-u^{-1})=\Delta_K^\#(u^2)$. [[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant]], [[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization]]

[F4] $\det(V-V^T)=1$ in a positively oriented symplectic basis, so the centered determinant is the unique normalized symmetric Alexander generator. [[thm-seifert-determinant-is-the-knot-alexander-polynomial]], [[cor-knot-alexander-normalization-symmetry-and-genus-bound]]

## Proof

1.1 If $g=0$, the matrix and homology group are empty, $\Delta_K^\#=1$, and $\operatorname{Arf}(K)=0$, so the congruence holds. Assume $g\ge1$. Choose a symplectic integral basis and, in each pair, arrange $v_{2i-1,2i}\equiv1$ and $v_{2i,2i-1}\equiv0\pmod2$. This is possible because their difference is $1$; if the odd entry is in the reverse position, replace $(a_i,b_i)$ by $(b_i,-a_i)$, which keeps $a_i\cdot b_i=1$. Let $A(t)=V^T-tV$. For indices $r,s$ in a paired position, its entries modulo two are $a_{2i,2i-1}=1$ and $a_{2i-1,2i}=t$; for every other position $a_{rs}=(1+t)v_{rs}$. The diagonal case is included, as $(1-t)v_{rr}=(1+t)v_{rr}$ modulo two. [A1, F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Let $B$ be the symmetric matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ with $B_{2i-1,2i}=B_{2i,2i-1}=1$ and all other entries $B_{rs}=v_{rs}$. For a permutation $\phi$ of $\{1,\ldots,2g\}$, let $\alpha$ count the indices $i$ for which $\phi(2i)=2i-1$, and let $\beta$ count those for which $\phi(2i-1)=2i$. Grouping the determinant expansion by these two counts gives $$\det A(t)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=0}^{g}\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}(1+t)^{2g-\alpha-\beta}t^\beta\pmod2,$$ where $\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}$ is the sum of $\prod_r B_{r,\phi(r)}$ over permutations with those counts. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^3$
be an oriented smooth embedded knot with regular oriented diagram $D$ in the
$(x_1,x_2)$-plane, and write $\gamma=\pi\circ K$ for its projected immersion.
Let $\widehat T_\gamma(t)$ be the unit tangent following the projected
orientation, and let $R(u,v)=(-v,u)$ be the positive quarter-turn in the
oriented projection plane. Define
$$b_D(t):=(R\widehat T_\gamma(t),0)\in\mathbb R^3.$$
This smooth nonzero vector is perpendicular to the spatial tangent of $K$ and
represents the blackboard normal section. Let $\Phi$ be a tubular chart of $K$
whose vertical differential at each zero vector induces the identity on the
ambient normal quotient. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ put
$$K_\varepsilon(t):=\Phi\bigl(K(t),\varepsilon[b_D(t)]\bigr),$$
oriented by the parameter orientation of $K$. Then $K_\varepsilon$ is embedded
and disjoint from $K$, and the mixed crossings in the projected diagram of
$K\cup K_\varepsilon$ consist of exactly two crossings for each crossing $c$
of $D$, both with sign $\operatorname{sgn}(c)$. There are no other mixed
crossings.

```tikz

  \def\e{0.22}
  \draw[->] (-0.8,0) -- (0.8,0) node[right] {$O$};
  \draw[->] (-0.8,\e) -- (0.8,\e) node[right] {$O'$};

  \draw (0,0.08) -- (0,0.14);
  \draw[->] (0,0.30) -- (0,0.8) node[above] {$U$};
  \draw[->] (-\e,-0.8) -- (-\e,-0.08);
  \draw (-\e,0.08) -- (-\e,0.14);
  \draw[->] (-\e,0.30) -- (-\e,0.8) node[above] {$U'$};
  \node[below right] at (0,0) {$c$};
  \node[below left] at (-\e,0) {$m_1$};
  \node[above right] at (0,\e) {$m_2$};
  \node[above left] at (-\e,\e) {$c'$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In this positive local chart, $O$ and $U$ are the original over and under
branches, and $O'$ and $U'$ are their first-order blackboard offsets in a
normalized tubular chart. The
crossings $m_1,m_2$ are mixed and positive; $c'$ is a self-crossing of the
push-off. The diagram is schematic and is not used in the proof.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing|Crossing signs and blackboard vectors]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, an oriented smooth embedded knot in
$\mathbb R^3$, and its regular oriented diagram $D$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] A regular diagram is an immersion with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and finitely many component arcs ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]).

[F2] Each crossing sign is the determinant sign of its oriented over and under projected tangents in the oriented projection plane ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] The blackboard vector is the nonzero normal section given by the positive quarter-turn of the projected oriented tangent ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F4] A smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension with invertible differential at a point is a diffeomorphism on suitable neighborhoods of that point ([[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]]).

[F5] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the normal quotient has its smooth vector-bundle structure; a tubular chart is a diffeomorphism fixed on the zero section, and its normalization makes the vertical differential the identity on the normal quotient ([[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]], [[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[cor-tubular-neighbourhoods-are-unique-up-to-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F6] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every sufficiently small push-off along a smooth nowhere-zero normal section is an embedded circle disjoint from the original knot ([[lem-framed-knot-push-off-self-linking-well-defined]]).

[F7] Every open cover of a compact metric space has a positive Lebesgue number, so sufficiently close parameters lie together in one member of a finite cover ([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

## Proof

1.1 The zero section of $\nu K$ is compact, so after shrinking the parameter interval there is a $\delta>0$ such that $\rho(t,\varepsilon):=\pi\Phi(K(t),\varepsilon[b_D(t)])$ is smooth on $S^1\times(-\delta,\delta)$, with $\rho(t,0)=\gamma(t)$. The normalized-chart condition says that $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ represents $R\widehat T_\gamma(t)$ modulo the tangent line spanned by $\gamma'(t)$. Therefore $\gamma'(t)$ and $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ are linearly independent at every $t$. By [F4], $(t,\varepsilon)\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective near every $(t,0)$. Compactness of $S^1$ and [F7] give an open diagonal neighbourhood $V_\Delta\subseteq S^1\times S^1$ and a uniform $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that, for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, whenever $(s,t)\in V_\Delta$, the points $\rho(s,0)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, and the points $\rho(s,\varepsilon)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, lie in one common injectivity chart. Shrink $V_\Delta$, if necessary, so that it contains no off-diagonal crossing pair; this is possible because there are finitely many such pairs. Hence there are no projected coincidences between the original and offset branches with close parameters, and $t\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective. Choose disjoint small open neighbourhoods of the finitely many ordered crossing pairs of $\gamma$ outside $V_\Delta$; by [F1], these are the only off-diagonal equalities $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$. The compact complement of $V_\Delta$ and those crossing neighbourhoods contains no such equality, so $\lVert\gamma(s)-\gamma(t)\rVert$ has a positive minimum there. Smoothness gives uniform convergence $\rho(\cdot,\varepsilon)\to\gamma$, excluding original/offset and offset/offset projected coincidences on this compact complement for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Thus every projected coincidence lies in one of the chosen crossing neighbourhoods. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, choose]

2.1 Fix one crossing disk with disjoint parameter intervals around the over branch $\alpha$ and under branch $\beta$, and with no other branch entering. For $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, the map $$G_{ij}(s,t,\varepsilon):=\bigl(\rho(s,i\varepsilon)-\rho(t,j\varepsilon),\varepsilon\bigr)$$ has invertible derivative at the original crossing and $\varepsilon=0$: its first two columns are $\alpha'(0)$ and $-\beta'(0)$, which are linearly independent by transversality, and its last coordinate is $\varepsilon$. By [F4], each of the four branch pairs has exactly one transverse projected intersection near this crossing for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. They are, respectively, the original crossing, the two mixed crossings, and the crossing of the two offset branches. The local injectivity from step 1.1 excludes intersections between an original branch and its own offset; it also implies that the four listed crossing points are distinct, since a coincidence between any two would place an original branch and its own offset at the same projected point. Thus there are no triple points in this crossing disk. The strict height order of $\alpha$ over $\beta$ at the original crossing persists for all four nearby crossings when $\varepsilon$ is small. The projected tangent determinants are nonzero and vary continuously, so both mixed crossings have sign $\operatorname{sgn}(c)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 There are finitely many crossing disks, so choose $\varepsilon$ below all local bounds from steps 1.1 and 2.1. By [F6], the spatial push-off is an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. The projection of $K\cup K_\varepsilon$ has only the finitely many transverse double points described above and no triple points, so it is a regular diagram. Each original crossing disk contributes exactly two mixed crossings, both with the original sign, and step 1.1 excludes all other mixed crossings. Countable Choice is used only through [F6] for the tubular push-off; the finite projected-crossing argument uses no choice. [A1, F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

[F3] The blackboard vector is the nonzero normal section given by the positive quarter-turn of the projected oriented tangent ([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F4] A smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension with invertible differential at a point is a diffeomorphism on suitable neighborhoods of that point ([[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]]).

[F5] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the normal quotient has its smooth vector-bundle structure; a tubular chart is a diffeomorphism fixed on the zero section, and its normalization makes the vertical differential the identity on the normal quotient ([[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]], [[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[cor-tubular-neighbourhoods-are-unique-up-to-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F6] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every sufficiently small push-off along a smooth nowhere-zero normal section is an embedded circle disjoint from the original knot ([[lem-framed-knot-push-off-self-linking-well-defined]]).

[F7] Every open cover of a compact metric space has a positive Lebesgue number, so sufficiently close parameters lie together in one member of a finite cover ([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

## Proof

1.1 The zero section of $\nu K$ is compact, so after shrinking the parameter interval there is a $\delta>0$ such that $\rho(t,\varepsilon):=\pi\Phi(K(t),\varepsilon[b_D(t)])$ is smooth on $S^1\times(-\delta,\delta)$, with $\rho(t,0)=\gamma(t)$. The normalized-chart condition says that $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ represents $R\widehat T_\gamma(t)$ modulo the tangent line spanned by $\gamma'(t)$. Therefore $\gamma'(t)$ and $\partial_\varepsilon\rho(t,0)$ are linearly independent at every $t$. By [F4], $(t,\varepsilon)\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective near every $(t,0)$. Compactness of $S^1$ and [F7] give an open diagonal neighbourhood $V_\Delta\subseteq S^1\times S^1$ and a uniform $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that, for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, whenever $(s,t)\in V_\Delta$, the points $\rho(s,0)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, and the points $\rho(s,\varepsilon)$ and $\rho(t,\varepsilon)$, lie in one common injectivity chart. Shrink $V_\Delta$, if necessary, so that it contains no off-diagonal crossing pair; this is possible because there are finitely many such pairs. Hence there are no projected coincidences between the original and offset branches with close parameters, and $t\mapsto\rho(t,\varepsilon)$ is locally injective. Choose disjoint small open neighbourhoods of the finitely many ordered crossing pairs of $\gamma$ outside $V_\Delta$; by [F1], these are the only off-diagonal equalities $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$. The compact complement of $V_\Delta$ and those crossing neighbourhoods contains no such equality, so $\lVert\gamma(s)-\gamma(t)\rVert$ has a positive minimum there. Smoothness gives uniform convergence $\rho(\cdot,\varepsilon)\to\gamma$, excluding original/offset and offset/offset projected coincidences on this compact complement for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Thus every projected coincidence lies in one of the chosen crossing neighbourhoods. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, choose]

2.1 Fix one crossing disk with disjoint parameter intervals around the over branch $\alpha$ and under branch $\beta$, and with no other branch entering. For $i,j\in\{0,1\}$, the map
$$G_{ij}(s,t,\varepsilon):=\bigl(\rho(s,i\varepsilon)-\rho(t,j\varepsilon),\varepsilon\bigr)$$
has invertible derivative at the original crossing and $\varepsilon=0$: its first two columns are $\alpha'(0)$ and $-\beta'(0)$, which are linearly independent by transversality, and its last coordinate is $\varepsilon$. By [F4], each of the four branch pairs has exactly one transverse projected intersection near this crossing for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. They are, respectively, the original crossing, the two mixed crossings, and the crossing of the two offset branches. The local injectivity from step 1.1 excludes intersections between an original branch and its own offset; it also implies that the four listed crossing points are distinct, since a coincidence between any two would place an original branch and its own offset at the same projected point. Thus there are no triple points in this crossing disk. The strict height order of $\alpha$ over $\beta$ at the original crossing persists for all four nearby crossings when $\varepsilon$ is small. The projected tangent determinants are nonzero and vary continuously, so both mixed crossings have sign $\operatorname{sgn}(c)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 There are finitely many crossing disks, so choose $\varepsilon$ below all local bounds from steps 1.1 and 2.1. By [F6], the spatial push-off is an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. The projection of $K\cup K_\varepsilon$ has only the finitely many transverse double points described above and no triple points, so it is a regular diagram. Each original crossing disk contributes exactly two mixed crossings, both with the original sign, and step 1.1 excludes all other mixed crossings. Countable Choice is used only through [F6] for the tubular push-off; the finite projected-crossing argument uses no choice. [A1, F1, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with rational-homology-sphere boundary $M$. The signed intersection pairing on interior two-cycles descends to a symmetric integer-valued bilinear form on $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)/\operatorname{Tor}$, this group is free of finite rank, and the form is nondegenerate after extending scalars to $\mathbb Q$. The form need not be unimodular.

## Statement references

[[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary|Boundary intersection lattice and rational-homology-sphere convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M$ and $H_*(M;\mathbb Q)\cong H_*(S^3;\mathbb Q)$.

[F1] The long exact sequence of the pair contains $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(M;\mathbb Q)$. Both end groups vanish by the boundary hypothesis. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]

[F2] Poincaré–Lefschetz duality identifies $H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)$ with $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F3] Over the field $\mathbb Q$, the universal-coefficient theorem identifies $H^2(W;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_2(W;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

[F4] Double $W$ along a boundary collar; the resulting closed smooth manifold has finite CW homotopy type under full AC. Folding the second copy into the first makes $W$ a homotopy retract of the double, so $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is a direct summand of a finitely generated group. [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]] [[lem-a-closed-smooth-manifold-has-the-homotopy-type-of-a-finite-cw-complex]]

[F5] The boundary intersection form is the signed intersection pairing on interior representatives. [[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary]]

[A1] Full AC is assumed for the finite-CW homotopy-type supplier [F4].

## Proof

**Given:** The data and suppliers [F1]–[F5].

1.1 The collar of $M$ lets every absolute two-cycle be moved into $\operatorname{int}W$. The signed transverse intersection number is integer-valued and bilinear. Since $H_2(M;\mathbb Q)=0$, [F1] shows that $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism. [given, F1, F5, construct]

2.1 The pairing map over $\mathbb Q$ is the composite $H_2(W;\mathbb Q)\to H_2(W,M;\mathbb Q)\xrightarrow{\operatorname{PD}^{-1}}H^2(W;\mathbb Q)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_2(W;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$. Every map in this composite is an isomorphism by step 1.1, [F2], and [F3], so the form is rationally nondegenerate. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F4] and [A1], $H_2(W;\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated, so its torsion-free quotient is a finite-rank free abelian group. If $x$ has finite order $m$, bilinearity gives $mQ_W(x,y)=Q_W(mx,y)=0$ in $\mathbb Z$, hence $Q_W(x,y)=0$; the same argument applies in the other variable. Thus the form descends to the torsion-free quotient. The four-dimensional cup-product sign is $(-1)^{2\cdot2}=+1$, so the form is symmetric. [F4, F5, A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|The fixed height and bridge-position convention]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|Connected-sum decomposition and nontrivial factors]]

[[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum|A sphere transverse to the knot determines the oriented factors]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated countable-choice hypothesis, fixed bridge pair $(K,S)$ and initial spanning disks, the specified two-puncture sphere $P$, and the two essential-annulus hypotheses.

[F1] A knot exterior is irreducible under countable choice. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]]

[F2] Smooth Schoenflies identifies both sides of a smooth sphere simultaneously with balls, by an ambient isotopy. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]]

[F3] Supplied smooth ball windows admit collar-compatible attachment and removal. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F4] A compact smooth embedding isotopy extends ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F5] The oriented factors obtained from a two-puncture sphere by boundary caps are the connected-sum factors, independently of the cap choices. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $B_+,B_-$ for the fixed bridge balls, $D_i^\pm$ for their spanning disks, and $T_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$. Arrange finite transverse intersections, with $P\cap S\cap K=\varnothing$, and take the knot tube sufficiently small and adapted to these intersections. A product neighborhood of each $D_i^\pm$ identifies a neighborhood of its bridge with the usual boundary-parallel ball-arc. Cutting $B_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ along the disks $D_i^\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ gives a ball: successively slide each bridge along its displayed disk into a boundary collar, and remove its displayed half-tube; each cut opens that collar tunnel. These moves use disjoint same-side disk neighborhoods. In particular this is a *complete* meridian-disk system, not merely a collection of compressing disks. Throughout the proof the knot and $S$ themselves stay fixed; a puncture of $P$ is allowed to travel along the fixed knot. [given, F3, construct]

1.2 First remove compressions of $T_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ in its bridge exterior. A compressing circle is nullhomotopic in $E$, hence in $A$ by the assumed injection; in an annulus it bounds a disk $E_0\subset A$. This disk must cross $S$, since otherwise the proposed compression was inessential on the relevant $T_\pm\setminus N(K)$. The compression disk and $E_0$ form a sphere in $E$ after rounding. Its ball from [F1] has no other part of $A$ inside: $A\setminus E_0$ is connected and reaches $\partial E$, whereas the ball is in the interior. Push $E_0$ across this ball to a parallel copy of the compression disk. This is an isotopy of $P$ supported off $K$, removes all the intersection circles lying inside $E_0$, and creates none. Thus each such operation strictly reduces $|P\cap S|$. After finitely many operations both punctured $T_\pm$ are incompressible. The same preparation can be repeated after a later pass. These are isotopies of the given sphere, so its oriented factors are preserved. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 Fix one side, temporarily written $B,T,\mathcal D$. Remove circle components of $T\cap\mathcal D$ by disk exchange: a circle innermost on a spanning disk bounds a disk on the punctured $T$ by its incompressibility; take one innermost among the disk-bounding circles on $T$. Its interior contains no intersection arcs, since those have endpoints on $\partial T$ or $K$, and contains no intersection circles by this choice. Replace the disk of the spanning disk bounded by that circle by a nearby copy of this disk on $T$. The replacement is embedded, misses every other spanning disk, keeps the bridge boundary arc fixed and reduces the total number of circles. Repeat finitely. Intersection arcs now have either one endpoint on $K$ and one on the disk's foot in $S$ (type I), or both endpoints on the foot (type II). An arc with both endpoints on $K$ would join the two punctures of $A$: choose the subdisk next to the segment of the bridge between those endpoints. It has no other intersection arcs, since that segment has no further punctures and its interior foot-free subdisk cannot contain an arc ending on $S$. After deleting circles, its part in $E$ would be a boundary compression along a spanning arc of $A$, contrary to hypothesis. This also shows $P\cap S\ne\varnothing$: if it were empty, after circle removal the two punctures would have to be joined by just such an arc. Thus every component of either unpunctured planar $T_\pm$ has nonempty boundary. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Here are the three disk moves, including their supports. For an arc innermost next to a disk's foot, let $\Delta$ be its cut-off subdisk containing no other intersection arcs. A neighborhood of $\Delta$, with collars on its boundary intervals, is a standard disk times an interval. Pushing the surface band across $\Delta$ and a little through $S$ is a smooth embedding isotopy: in these coordinates translate the band in the interval direction, with a bump zero at the ends of the retained intervals, and round the two moving corners. The support can avoid the other same-side spanning disks. For a type-I arc this slides its puncture along the bridge through the adjacent endpoint on $S$; the velocity along $K$ is tangent to $K$, so the isotopy extends preserving $K$ setwise. It removes this puncture from the treated side and does not change the homeomorphism type of the **unpunctured** $T$. Call this move I. For a type-II arc essential in unpunctured $T$, the same band push cuts $T$ along that arc; call this move II. Both remove their chosen intersection arc and create no new intersections with the treated disk system. Their punctured-surface operations are boundary cuts. All isotopies can be stationary at their time endpoints and extended using [F4]. [given, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 The remaining move changes a spanning disk, not $P$. Suppose a type-II arc $\gamma$ cuts off a disk $E_0$ from $T\setminus N(K)$ with no other intersection arcs in its interior. On its spanning disk, retain the component of the cut along $\gamma$ containing the bridge, and replace the other component by a nearby copy of $E_0$. The union along $\gamma$ is a disk: two disks glued along one boundary interval. Its new foot is the old retained foot together with $\partial E_0\setminus\gamma$, pushed a little on $S$. Push its interior off $T$ on the retained disk's side and round the seam. Since $E_0$ has no punctures or other intersection arcs, the replacement misses $K$ except on its original bridge, is disjoint from all other same-side spanning disks, and deletes $\gamma$ and any intersections on the discarded part without adding any. This move III is valid even when $\gamma$ is not innermost on its spanning disk. In particular it is a disk replacement, not an unproved assertion that two disks in a knotted region are isotopic. [given, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 If the treated disk system is still met, one of these moves is available. Here is the finite innermost argument for the only obstructed case. If neither I nor II is available, every arc innermost next to a foot is type II and cuts off a disk $E_0$ of the unpunctured surface $T$. Choose one such arc $\gamma$ and its foot-adjacent disk $\Delta$. If $E_0$ has no punctures, take an innermost subdisk of $E_0$ cut off by intersection arcs; it is empty and gives III. Otherwise a puncture of $E_0$ starts a type-I arc. The disk $Q=E_0\cup\Delta$, rounded at $\gamma$, is a proper disk in the bridge ball. It separates it into two balls: cap by either boundary disk on $\partial B$ and apply [F2], retaining the actual collars. Call the side away from the bridge on the spanning disk of $\gamma$ the inside. Follow the type-I arc's spanning disk from its puncture towards its foot. If this arc were foot-innermost, I would be available. The arcs between it and the foot therefore contain an innermost type-II arc on the inside. Its disk cut off on $T$ is also on the inside: $T$ misses the interior of $\Delta$, and its only portion on $Q$ is $E_0$, so an arc or cut-off disk cannot leave the inside without crossing $E_0$ or $\Delta$; if it lies on $E_0$, use its subdisk there and push its collar inward. Its own foot-adjacent disk together with that cut-off disk now cuts off an inside ball contained in the previous one. The bridge-containing side is again discarded. This is a strict descent in the finite set of intersection arcs contained on or inside these disks: the previous delimiting arc is outside the next inside ball. Repeat if its cut-off disk has a puncture. A strict descent cannot continue indefinitely. It ends with a puncture-free disk, and an innermost subdisk in it is the empty disk required for III. This proves availability without assuming an arbitrary boundary compression has the required foot. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct]

5.1 Perform available moves on this one side. Each deletes at least one arc of the treated system, and creates none there, so this inner process is finite. If necessary remove circles as in step 2.1. The punctured surface remains incompressible after a move I or II. To verify the usual boundary-cut assertion here, reverse its band in the empty disk-product neighborhood of step 3.1. Put a proposed compression disk transverse to the band cocore and remove its outermost intersections in that product; a surviving essential compression would give a compression of the old surface. If its boundary bounds a disk on the old surface, that disk is disjoint from the cut arc: a proper arc cannot enter the interior of a disk bounded by a disjoint interior circle without crossing that circle. It is therefore also a disk on the cut surface. Any sphere produced in removing the outermost intersections bounds a ball, since a bridge exterior cut from a ball along trivial-arc tubes is a handlebody; its sphere bounds a ball on the side not meeting the boundary by the same [F2] argument as in [F1]. Thus it cannot supply an exceptional compression. Move III does not change the surface. At termination $T$ misses both $K$ and the complete disk system. It lies in the cut-open ball of step 1.1 and is a union of disks: for a nondisk planar component an innermost boundary curve on that ball's sphere gives, by a small boundary-collar push, a compression, contrary to incompressibility. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 We give the strict count rather than infer it from the number of punctured boundary curves. For an unpunctured planar surface with $b$ boundary curves and $c$ components, set $z$ equal to its number of nondisk components. Moves I and III do not change this surface's topology. Every move II cuts an essential proper arc. A nonseparating such cut reduces the total $\sum(b_j-1)=b-c$ by one; a separating cut leaves this total unchanged and creates no disk, since the arc was essential. At the end this total is zero, so there were exactly $b-c$ nonseparating cuts. Each creates at most one new disk; initially there were $c-z$ disks. Punctures do not occur in $b$. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Repeat the compression cleanup of step 1.2 and then a complete pass on either side that has a nondisk component. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

[F1] A knot exterior is irreducible under countable choice. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]]

[F2] Smooth Schoenflies identifies both sides of a smooth sphere simultaneously with balls, by an ambient isotopy. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]]

[F3] Supplied smooth ball windows admit collar-compatible attachment and removal. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F4] A compact smooth embedding isotopy extends ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F5] The oriented factors obtained from a two-puncture sphere by boundary caps are the connected-sum factors, independently of the cap choices. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

Arrange finite transverse intersections, with $P\cap S\cap K=\varnothing$, and take the knot tube sufficiently small and adapted to these intersections. A product neighborhood of each $D_i^\pm$ identifies a neighborhood of its bridge with the usual boundary-parallel ball-arc. Cutting $B_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ along the disks $D_i^\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ gives a ball: successively slide each bridge along its displayed disk into a boundary collar, and remove its displayed half-tube; each cut opens that collar tunnel. These moves use disjoint same-side disk neighborhoods. In particular this is a *complete* meridian-disk system, not merely a collection of compressing disks. Throughout the proof the knot and $S$ themselves stay fixed; a puncture of $P$ is allowed to travel along the fixed knot. [given, F3, construct]

1.2 First remove compressions of $T_\pm\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ in its bridge exterior. A compressing circle is nullhomotopic in $E$, hence in $A$ by the assumed injection; in an annulus it bounds a disk $E_0\subset A$. This disk must cross $S$, since otherwise the proposed compression was inessential on the relevant $T_\pm\setminus N(K)$. The compression disk and $E_0$ form a sphere in $E$ after rounding. Its ball from [F1] has no other part of $A$ inside: $A\setminus E_0$ is connected and reaches $\partial E$, whereas the ball is in the interior. Push $E_0$ across this ball to a parallel copy of the compression disk. This is an isotopy of $P$ supported off $K$, removes all the intersection circles lying inside $E_0$, and creates none. Thus each such operation strictly reduces $|P\cap S|$. After finitely many operations both punctured $T_\pm$ are incompressible. The same preparation can be repeated after a later pass. The union along $\gamma$ is a disk: two disks glued along one boundary interval. Its new foot is the old retained foot together with $\partial E_0\setminus\gamma$, pushed a little on $S$. Push its interior off $T$ on the retained disk's side and round the seam. Since $E_0$ has no punctures or other intersection arcs, the replacement misses $K$ except on its original bridge, is disjoint from all other same-side spanning disks, and deletes $\gamma$ and any intersections on the discarded part without adding any. If its boundary bounds a disk on the old surface, that disk is disjoint from the cut arc: a proper arc cannot enter the interior of a disk bounded by a disjoint interior circle without crossing that circle. It is therefore also a disk on the cut surface. Any sphere produced in removing the outermost intersections bounds a ball, since a bridge exterior cut from a ball along trivial-arc tubes is a handlebody; its sphere bounds a ball on the side not meeting the boundary by the same [F2] argument as in [F1]. Thus it cannot supply an exceptional compression. Move III does not change the surface. At termination $T$ misses both $K$ and the complete disk system. It lies in the cut-open ball of step 1.1 and is a union of disks: for a nondisk planar component an innermost boundary curve on that ball's sphere gives, by a small boundary-collar push, a compression, contrary to incompressibility. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, construct]

4.1 We give the strict count rather than infer it from the number of punctured boundary curves. For an unpunctured planar surface with $b$ boundary curves and $c$ components, set $z$ equal to its number of nondisk components. Moves I and III do not change this surface's topology. Every move II cuts an essential proper arc. A nonseparating such cut reduces the total $\sum(b_j-1)=b-c$ by one; a separating cut leaves this total unchanged and creates no disk, since the arc was essential. Punctures do not occur in $b$. [step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.2, algebra]

Cleanup and every such pass strictly decrease the positive integer $|P\cap S|$, so the outer process is finite. At its end every component of both $T_+$ and $T_-$ is a disk. Each operation on $P$ was an embedding isotopy through spheres meeting $K$ in exactly two points, preserving $K$ setwise; each other operation changed only a spanning disk. The specified oriented factors are therefore still the same by [F5]. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.1 Each $T_\pm$ is now a single disk. Apply I and III on the upper side until it has no punctures or disk intersections; II is unavailable on a disk. The two punctures then lie in the lower disk. Apply I and III below only until one of its punctures has passed to the upper disk. There is now one puncture in each disk, and the intersection circle has not changed. Each remaining puncture is on exactly one spanning disk on its own side, and a type-I arc has just one puncture endpoint. There are therefore exactly two type-I arcs in total. Their other endpoints are on $P\cap S$, away from $K$, and can be taken distinct by a small foot perturbation on $S$. Thus their union consists of two disjoint embedded arcs, as asserted. All choices and all moves after the stated smooth suppliers were finite. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 4.2, construct] ∎
