## Statement

Let P be a pattern of nonzero winding n. If P(U) is smoothly slice in an R_n-homology 4-ball, then P is weakly injective on C^{1/n}, meaning P(K)=P(U) implies K=U in that category. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then P is weakly injective on C_ex (respectively C_top). In ordinary smooth concordance, if P(U) is smoothly slice in standard B⁴ and P has strong winding number ±1, then P is weakly injective on C_sm provided the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture holds.

For any pattern P and knots K,J with P(K)=P(J) in one of these concordance groups, the connected-sum reduction constructs a pattern R for which R(−K#J) is concordant to U, whose closure R(U)=−P(K)#P(K) is ribbon, and whose winding w(R)=w(P). If P is strong winding ±1, then R is strong winding ±1. This reduction turns injectivity of P into weak injectivity of R; it does not assert that P itself is weakly injective without the closure hypotheses above.

## Statement references

[[lem-satellite-operator-preserves-concordance|Concordance preservation for the satellite function]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|Smooth and locally flat topological slice disks]]

[CDR, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 5.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1205.5058v3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A pattern P, knots K,J, and the exact category and closure-slice hypotheses stated above.

[F1] The solid-torus meridian is strong winding when it normally generates the closure-complement group ([[def-satellite-induced-concordance-operator]]).

[F2] The zero-surgery comparison has a smooth R_n branch and category-specific exotic/topological branches with their closure hypotheses ([[lem-cdr-zero-surgery-pattern-homology-cobordism]]).

[F3] The definitions of C_ex, C_top and C^{1/n} specify the ambient 4-manifold and coefficient conditions ([[def-cdr-satellite-concordance-categories]]).

[F4] Only finite connected-sum, inverse and compatibility instances for the actual supplied knots and concordances are used here. Their choice-free compact-input specialization is established in step0.1. The general AC_omega group theorem records the same operations ([[thm-cdr-concordance-categories-form-abelian-groups]]); its stronger choice premise is not invoked in $V$ for this unqualified Statement.

[F5] The ordinary smooth branch uses the special smooth S⁴-complement assertion ([[lem-cdr-smooth-s4-complement-is-standard-ball]]).

[F6] Satellite insertion rewrites P(K#J) as P_K(J) for the simultaneous companion-insertion pattern P_K ([[lem-satellite-connected-sum-substitution]]).

[F7] The satellite rule descends to the specified concordance classes only after concordance preservation ([[lem-satellite-operator-preserves-concordance]]).

[F8] A concordance annulus with a compatible zero-framed normal neighborhood gives a zero-surgery cobordism ([[lem-concordance-annulus-induces-zero-surgery-cobordism]]).

[F9] Strong winding survives companion insertion and local connected sum ([[lem-strong-winding-stable-under-companion-insertion]]).

[F10] The reverse-mirror connected sum −J#J bounds a ribbon disk ([[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]]).

[F11] **External TOP input.** A compact contractible topological four-manifold with boundary homeomorphic to the standard $S^3$ is homeomorphic to $B^4$. This is the Freedman consequence invoked explicitly in Cochran–Davis–Ray, Proposition3.2 and its proof, printed7–8; it is imported, not locally reconstructed. A supplied boundary marking is respected: if $h:B\to B^4$ is any such homeomorphism and $k:\partial B\to S^3$ is the required marking, extend $k\circ(h|_{\partial B})^{-1}$ radially over $B^4$ by the Alexander extension and postcompose $h$. Thus the co-core boundary knot retains its actual endpoint marking. This fact applies to the underlying TOP manifold of a smooth contractible $B$ as well; it asserts no smooth standardness. The cited application in CDR printed7–8 was read directly; the original Freedman paper is cited as its authoritative source, not claimed read in full here.

[F12] **External remaining concordance input.** Zero-framed surgery on a concordance annulus descends to a homology cobordism of the zero-surgery manifolds in the same category; the coefficient ring is $R_n$ for localized concordance, and in the TOP/exotic categories the fundamental group is normally generated by either boundary knot-group image. The meridians are the normal-circle factors along the framed annulus and are identified by its product coordinate. This is the zero-surgery descent in CDR Section3, printed7, paragraph preceding Definition3.1 and diagram3.1, read directly. The local normal-GIVEN construction [F8] is retained; this explicit external input supplies its needed conclusion where an unresolved general annulus-neighborhood/descent interface would otherwise be required. No local reconstruction of that missing interface is asserted.

[F13] **Compact finite-input convention.** The classical external results are initially used in ordinary ZFC, not assumed choice-free from their citations. For this one application take finitely many charts covering the given compact manifolds and finitely many pair charts covering each given compact disk or annulus, shrinking to closed inner charts inside open outer charts. Such finite subcovers exist by compactness; selecting this finite list uses no axiom of choice. Include the actual boundary/product collars and all supplied homeomorphisms in the list. Encode chart domains and overlaps by their rational balls, continuous maps and their inverses by dense rational data with moduli on the closed inner charts, and smooth maps by all finite-order derivative and Taylor-remainder data. The modulus at each integer scale is the least integer satisfying its uniform-continuity bound; restrictions to rational compact boxes use the least box index. These are uniquely defined choices from subsets of $\mathbb N$, not a countable family of freely selected charts. Include positive open-image and overlap margins, inverse identities, finite cover/Lebesgue bounds, and the pair-section identities with positive separation from the compact outside-patch remainder. On the standard disk/annulus parameters the latter certify the actual plane section, not merely a continuous embedding. One real $r$ codes these finitely many maps and their canonical countable data. The external relative-constructibility input is that $L[r]$ is an inner model of ZFC containing $r$ (Karagila, §8.3, p.42); no ambient choice hypothesis is required. All compact maps are decoded using these same moduli, so the inverse identities, covers, pair sections and collar equalities are checked on dense rational sets with their displayed buffers and remain valid in the ambient universe $V$. An internally produced compact witness is exported with the same certificates, and hence is an actual ambient compact witness. This uses the peer-checked compact annulus coding pattern of the standard connected-sum compatibility supplier only at its geometric scope; it does not assert that arbitrary homology or fundamental-group hypotheses are absolute.

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F13] to the finite compact input for the branch at hand. For TOP the ambient product or ball is already standard; for the exotic branch its actual marked product/ball homeomorphism is given and is encoded in both directions. Use two coding passes. First encode only this finite compact geometry by a real $r_0$. In $L[r_0]$, before imposing any localized homology or strong-winding condition, use the ordinary finite smooth Morse construction to obtain finite handle/CW presentations of the supplied smooth ambient manifolds and finite presentations of the relevant knot exteriors, with their comparison maps, homotopies and peripheral markings. Export these purely geometric presentations and compact comparison certificates by [F13]. No choice-free generic-Morse theorem in $V$ is being assumed. Now work in $V$: its given localized homology hypothesis applies to these actual exported presentations. Let P be an oriented pattern of winding n≠0 and K an oriented knot. ## Statement

Assume AC. Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a based map of path-connected CW
complexes, let $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$ and $H=\pi_1(Y,y_0)$, and put
$\phi=f_*:G\to H$. Let $c_X:X\to BG$ and $c_Y:Y\to BH$ be based classifying
maps inducing the identity on the identified fundamental groups. There is a
based map $B\phi:BG\to BH$ inducing $\phi$, and
$$
B\phi\circ c_X\simeq c_Y\circ f
$$
by a based homotopy. Consequently the induced maps on singular homology commute.

## Statement references

[Davis and Kirk, Theorem 7.20 and Corollary 7.24](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Davis_Kirk_Lecture%20notes%20in%20algebraic%20topology.pdf)

[Miller, Lectures 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-906-algebraic-topology-ii-spring-2020/e8a061a73ca1a451df8809c7a7fbc846_MIT18_906S20_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the based map $f$, the classifying maps $c_X,c_Y$, and the CW models in the statement.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A classifying CW model is connected, has its specified fundamental group, and has zero higher homotopy groups. [[cor-classifying-space-of-a-discrete-group-is-a-k-g-one]]

[F2] Under AC, connected CW models $K(G,1)$ exist for every group and the classifying-space construction is available for the stated groups. [[thm-existence-and-homotopy-uniqueness-of-eilenberg-maclane-spaces]]

[F3] Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on singular homology. [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data above and [A1].

1.1 Construct $B\phi$ on the one-skeleton of $BG$ by sending each based loop representing $g\in G$ to a based loop representing $\phi(g)\in H$. Every two-cell attaching loop represents the identity in $G$, so its image represents the identity in $H$ and extends over the two-cell. For a cell of dimension $k\geq3$, the attaching map is a sphere map into $BH$ and extends over the disk because $\pi_{k-1}(BH)=0$ by [F1]. AC chooses the extensions over the set of cells. This gives a based map inducing $\phi$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 The maps $B\phi\circ c_X$ and $c_Y\circ f$ induce the same homomorphism $\phi$ on fundamental groups. On the vertices choose based paths joining their values, and on each one-cell fill the resulting boundary loop; that loop is null because the two induced fundamental-group maps agree. Inductively, the obstruction to extending the homotopy across each $k$-cell is a map $S^k\to BH$, and it is null for $k\geq2$ by [F1]. AC supplies the cell extensions. Hence the maps are based homotopic. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 By [F3], the homotopy of step 2.1 gives $(B\phi)_*\circ(c_X)_*=(c_Y)_*\circ f_*$. This is the asserted naturality, including degree two. [F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a based map of path-connected CW
complexes, let $G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$ and $H=\pi_1(Y,y_0)$, and put
$\phi=f_*:G\to H$. Let $c_X:X\to BG$ and $c_Y:Y\to BH$ be based classifying
maps inducing the identity on the identified fundamental groups. There is a
based map $B\phi:BG\to BH$ inducing $\phi$, and
$$
B\phi\circ c_X\simeq c_Y\circ f
$$
by a based homotopy. Consequently the induced maps on singular homology commute.

## Statement references

[Davis and Kirk, Theorem 7.20 and Corollary 7.24](https://www.maths.gla.ac.uk/~mpowell/Davis_Kirk_Lecture%20notes%20in%20algebraic%20topology.pdf)

[Miller, Lectures 13–14](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-906-algebraic-topology-ii-spring-2020/e8a061a73ca1a451df8809c7a7fbc846_MIT18_906S20_notes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the based map $f$, the classifying maps $c_X,c_Y$, and the CW models in the statement.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A classifying CW model is connected, has its specified fundamental group, and has zero higher homotopy groups. [[cor-classifying-space-of-a-discrete-group-is-a-k-g-one]]

[F2] Under AC, connected CW models $K(G,1)$ exist for every group and the classifying-space construction is available for the stated groups. [[thm-existence-and-homotopy-uniqueness-of-eilenberg-maclane-spaces]]

[F3] Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on singular homology. [[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data above and [A1].

1.1 Construct $B\phi$ on the one-skeleton of $BG$ by sending each based loop representing $g\in G$ to a based loop representing $\phi(g)\in H$. Every two-cell attaching loop represents the identity in $G$, so its image represents the identity in $H$ and extends over the two-cell. For a cell of dimension $k\geq3$, the attaching map is a sphere map into $BH$ and extends over the disk because $\pi_{k-1}(BH)=0$ by [F1]. AC chooses the extensions over the set of cells. This gives a based map inducing $\phi$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 The maps $B\phi\circ c_X$ and $c_Y\circ f$ induce the same homomorphism $\phi$ on fundamental groups. On the vertices choose based paths joining their values, and on each one-cell fill the resulting boundary loop; that loop is null because the two induced fundamental-group maps agree. Inductively, the obstruction to extending the homotopy across each $k$-cell is a map $S^k\to BH$, and it is null for $k\geq2$ by [F1]. AC supplies the cell extensions. Hence the maps are based homotopic. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F3], the homotopy of step 1.2 gives $(B\phi)_*\circ(c_X)_*=(c_Y)_*\circ f_*$. This is the asserted naturality, including degree two. [F3, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots, and use the epsilon sign convention from the preceding definition. If their knot Floer complexes are stably filtered equivalent, meaning that there are totally acyclic bifiltered complexes $A$ and $B$ with $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A$ filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(J)\oplus B$, then $\epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)$. The acyclic summands here need not be acyclic after taking either associated-graded filtration.

The invariant satisfies $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$, $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$, and the tensor rules
$$ \epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(K),\qquad \epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(J). $$
The converse of $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$ fails: the knot $T_{2,5}\#-T_{4,5}\#T_{2,3;2,5}$ has $\tau=0$ and $\epsilon=1$, where $T_{p,q}$ is the positive $(p,q)$ torus knot and $T_{2,3;2,5}$ is the $(2,5)$ cable of the right-handed trefoil with longitudinal winding two. Epsilon is not an integer-valued homomorphism on the smooth concordance group: the right-handed trefoil has $\epsilon=1$ and its connected sum with itself also has $\epsilon=1$, not $2$.

## Statement references

[[def-epsilon-from-filtered-knot-floer-complex|Epsilon sign convention and map definition]]

[[def-knot-floer-filtration-and-tau|Normalized knot Floer filtration and tau]]

[Hom, *The knot Floer complex and the smooth concordance group*, §§3 and 6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635)

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383)

[Hom, *A note on the concordance invariants epsilon and upsilon*, §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.8200)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual normalized finite free Maslov-graded bifiltered complexes of the knots, with the supplied geometric tensor and duality identifications. Every newly used finite operation below is over $\mathbb F_2$.

[F1] [[def-epsilon-from-filtered-knot-floer-complex]] defines $F_s,G_s$ and epsilon. Its supplied two-hook argument proves the three cases are exhaustive and the two maps cannot both vanish.

[F2] [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]] supplies actual reverse-mirror duality, conjugation and normalized horizontal homology. The vertical and horizontal homologies at level zero are each one-dimensional, in Maslov degree zero.

[F3] [[lem-tau-connected-sum-filtered-tensor-product]] supplies the actual normalized filtered tensor identification and additive vertical threshold; the finite field-complex Kunneth calculation also follows by splitting boundary pairs.

[F4] [[lem-epsilon-stable-core-from-finite-filtered-splittings]] supplies stable-core invariance of the vertical threshold and both hook-map zero patterns, allowing arbitrary totally acyclic stabilizers without assuming their vertical or associated-graded complexes acyclic.

[F5] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] supplies the actual normalized grid comparison. In particular tilde homology is hat knot Floer homology tensored with $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$, where $V$ has degrees $(0,0),(-1,-1)$. Its grid, differential, scalar and analytic suppliers are reused as proved interfaces.

[F6] [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] identifies oriented decorated diagrams with the same signed rotation/strand code and selected outer face. [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] fixes the positive Clifford-torus convention. The five-grid with $O=[4,3,2,1,0]$ and $X=[2,1,0,4,3]$ is identified with the positively oriented right-handed trefoil in step 1.4 below; its three crossing signs are all positive.

[F7] The grid coordinate and orientation conventions are [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]; the finite signed visit, crossing-rotation and face-selector data are [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]].

## Proof

1.1 In the finite-rank free Maslov-graded knot Floer category, [F4] proves the stable-equivalence conclusion directly. Its finite endomorphism matrices strictify homotopy idempotents and give a unique non-acyclic indecomposable core up to filtered homotopy. The rank-one vertical homology of each original knot complex forces its internal acyclic complementary summands to have acyclic vertical complexes. Consequently its vertical threshold and the zero/nonzero patterns of $F_\tau,G_\tau$ are precisely those of that core. Stable equivalence identifies the two cores even if the externally added acyclic summands have nonzero vertical or associated-graded homology. Thus the three-case epsilon values in [F1] agree. This argument does not apply the epsilon definition to the stabilized complexes themselves. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 First reduce a finite based Laurent complex by explicit filtered contractions. If a differential coefficient preserves both coordinates, homogeneity makes it a single Laurent monomial; translate its target so that it is $1$. Write $da=b+r$ with $a,b$ at the same bifiltration and replace $b$ by $b'=da$. This is a filtered homogeneous basis change with inverse $b=b'+r$. For every other basis element $c$, subtract the coefficient of $b'$ in $dc$ times $a$ from $c$; this is filtered since the relevant copy of $a$ has the coordinates of the corresponding copy of $b'$. The new differentials contain no $b'$, and their $a$ coefficients vanish by $d^2=0$. Thus the pair $a\to b'$ splits off. Inclusion $I$, projection $P$ and $H(b')=a$, zero on all other generators, satisfy $PI=1$ and $IP+1=dH+Hd$, with $H$ preserving both filtrations and of Maslov degree $+1$. Finitely many repetitions give a reduced complex with no equal-bifiltration arrow. Tensoring these identities with another complex preserves them: the extra differential terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Dualizing likewise preserves them. This supplies all reduction inverse maps and homotopies used below, including their tensor compatibility. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.3 We next admit the actual complexes used for the geometric examples. Use the following marking-cell arrays, rows ordered bottom to top: for positive $T_{2,5}$ take $n=7$, $O=[6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,6,5]$; for positive $T_{4,5}$ take $n=9$, $O=[8,7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,8,7,6,5]$. The first has five positive crossings and oriented over/under word $A^+B^-C^+D^-E^+A^-B^+C^-D^+E^-$, where superscripts indicate over/under and all crossing signs are positive. The explicit positive torus curve $(r e^{2it},s e^{5it})$, $r=s=1/\sqrt2$, has this identical code in stereographic projection: its planar angle is $2t$, radius $r/(1-s\sin5t)$, height $s\cos5t/(1-s\sin5t)$, and crossing parameters $t/(2\pi)=0,1/10,\ldots,9/10$. Equal projections force parameter difference $\pi$ and $\sin5t=0$. At the overparameter the radial derivative is positive and at the underpartner negative, so the oriented crossing determinant is positive. The angular derivative is nonzero, and there are no triple points. Thus [F6] admits this grid as the actual positive $T_{2,5}$. [F6, given, construct, algebra]

1.4 Verify the trefoil grid in [F6] directly. Use row indices $0,1,2,3,4$ from bottom to top and column indices from left to right, as in [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]], and draw the standard planar grid realization using the in-square mark-to-mark intervals. Following the grid orientation gives the single cycle $$O_{0,4}\to X_{0,2}\to O_{2,2}\to X_{2,0}\to O_{4,0}\to X_{4,3}\to O_{1,3}\to X_{1,1}\to O_{3,1}\to X_{3,4}\to O_{0,4}.$$ The horizontal and vertical intervals meet away from their endpoints at exactly three crossings: $c_1=(\text{row }1,\text{column }2)$, $c_2=(\text{row }2,\text{column }1)$, and $c_3=(\text{row }3,\text{column }3)$. Traversing the component from $O_{0,4}$ encounters $c_1$ over, $c_2$ under, $c_3$ over, $c_1$ under, $c_2$ over, and $c_3$ under. At $c_1$ and $c_2$ the oriented projected tangents $(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ are $((0,1),(-1,0))$; at $c_3$ they are $((0,-1),(1,0))$. Each determinant is $+1$ by [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]. Thus its signed oriented Gauss code is $1_O,2_U,3_O,1_U,2_O,3_U$ with crossing-sign vector $(+1,+1,+1)$. This code is also obtained by traversing the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$: its first braid strand encounters the three positive half twists over, under, over, and the returning strand encounters them under, over, under. The signed visit data determine the same crossing rotation and strand code, hence identify the face-permutation cycles. Retain the grid diagram's outer-face cycle and choose the corresponding face of the braid-closure diagram. To make this chosen face outer, compactify the projection plane to the oriented sphere $S^2$ and choose a point $q$ in that face, away from the diagram. An orientation-preserving rotation of $S^2$ sending $q$ to the projection point at infinity makes precisely this face outer. Realize the diagram lift in a product collar of the equatorial $S^2$ in $S^3$; the rotation extends by the same rotation on the first three coordinates and the identity on the normal coordinate. Its path of rotations is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of $S^3$ preserving the crossing heights and oriented strand data. The two resulting plane codes now have the same selected outer face, so [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] identifies their diagrams up to planar isotopy. Thus the original grid and braid closure represent the same oriented knot even if their initially chosen planar outer faces differ. The braid closure lies on the standard unknotted torus with slope $2\alpha+3\beta$ (equivalently the swapped slope $3\alpha+2\beta$ under the orientation-preserving torus-coordinate swap), so it is $T(2,3)$ by [[def-coprime-torus-knot]]. The grid therefore represents the right-handed trefoil with its positive orientation, and its writhe is $+3$. [F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 Let $s=\tau(C)$ and choose a Maslov-zero vertical cycle $z$ at $j\le s$ representing its distinguished class. Its corner part $z_c$ is nonzero, or the threshold would be smaller. If $F_s=0$, choose a Maslov-one northeast-hook chain $b$ with $d_Nb=z_c$ and split it into strictly upper, corner and strictly right parts $b_+,b_0,b_r$. The strictly upper part of $d_vb_+$ is zero, since the other parts cannot reach it. Hence $z'=z+d_vb_+$ is another distinguished vertical cycle supported at $j\le s$. Put $q=b_0+b_r$. Its horizontal boundary $h=d_hq$ has no strictly right component, and its corner is $z'_c$, by the corner equation of $d_Nb=z_c$. Then $x=z'+h_{\mathrm{left}}$ is supported in $i\le0,j\le s$, its vertical projection represents the distinguished class, and its horizontal projection is the boundary $h$. Conversely, if such an $x$ has horizontal part $d_hq$, project $q$ to the northeast hook: its strictly left part cannot reach the corner or right ray, and the remaining boundary is precisely $x_c$, with no upper component. Thus $F_s=0$. This proves the exact boundary-representative alternative, rather than assuming a simultaneous simplification theorem. [F1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.2 The dual vertical threshold is $-s$. Indeed, if $B$ is the vertical boundary space, the distinguished cycle $z$ is not in $B+V^{\le s-1}$, since such an expression would give a lower-level cycle representing it. Finite-dimensional basis extension gives a cocycle functional annihilating that subspace and taking $z$ to $1$; its dual filtration is at most $-s$. A dual cocycle at level at most $-s-1$ vanishes on every cycle at level $s$ and hence on the one-dimensional vertical homology, so it is a dual boundary. The finite perfect pairing identifies the dual of the northeast hook at $s$ with the southwest hook of $C^*$ at $-s$. The transpose of $F_s(C)$ is $G_{-s}(C^*)$, and the transpose of $G_s(C)$ is $F_{-s}(C^*)$: quotient/inclusion maps reverse under this pairing. Duality of finite-dimensional homology preserves zero/nonzero. Thus $\epsilon(C^*)=-\epsilon(C)$; [F2] identifies this with $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.3 Following oriented strands in the nine-grid gives fifteen positive crossings and the full signed rotation/strand code of the closure of the four-strand positive word $121321321121321$, after a cyclic starting-point change and reversal of the knot orientation. This is an explicit finite code equality: enumerate crossings in each row and column interval, then follow each row $O\to X$ and column $X\to O$; on the braid follow the strand permutation through each listed crossing, taking the top-right strand over to bottom-left. The exact words and crossing correspondence are recorded in the finite certificate named in Remarks. Commutations $13=31$ and braid relations $121=212$, $232=323$ give the successive words $123121321121321$, $123123121121321$, $123123121212321$, $123123121213231$, $123123121231231$, $123123121231213$, $123123121232123$, $123123121323123$, $123123123123123$. Each is a local disjoint-strand isotopy or oriented R3, so their closures are equivalent. The last is $(123)^5$. To identify its torus embedding, cut the Clifford curve $(r e^{4it},s e^{5it})$ by the disk coordinate $\arg(z_1)=\theta$: its four disk points have arguments $5(\theta+2\pi k)/4$. A generic phase makes one quarter-turn's braid $132$, which becomes $321$ by moving the first generator past the closure cut, and then $123$ by reversing the four disk positions via the half-turn conjugation. Five quarter-turns give the last closure. Finally simultaneous complex conjugation is an ambient SO(4) isotopy endpoint and sends this curve to its orientation reverse: rotate its two imaginary axes through $\pi$. Thus the code reversal preserves oriented knot type, and [F6] proves the actual positive $T_{4,5}$ admission. [F6, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

2.4 For the cable take $n=10$, $O=[8,9,7,6,4,5,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,5,2,3,0,1,8,9,6,7]$. Here is an explicit preferred-framing admission independent of any Floer calculation. Double each row and column of the admitted positive trefoil five-grid in [F6]. At an old corner let $h,v\in\{\pm1\}$ be the directions toward its horizontal and vertical partner. A diagonal two-mark block for $hv=1$ and an antidiagonal block for $hv=-1$ give exactly two crossing-free parallel corners; checking the four quadrants verifies this and the oriented attachments. Only at the $O$ corner $(\text{row }0,\text{column }4)$, where $h=-1,v=1$, use the opposite diagonal block. It introduces one crossing of sign $hv=-1$. The listed ten-grid is precisely these ten corner blocks, and its component cycle visits rows $0,4,9,2,7,1,5,8,3,6,0$, hence it is one knot. Away from the exceptional block it follows two blackboard parallel copies of the trefoil. The blackboard longitude has linking number equal to writhe $+3$, so $\lambda_{\mathrm{bb}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}+3\mu$. The one negative half-twist therefore gives slope $2\lambda_{\mathrm{bb}}-\mu=2\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}+5\mu$, with longitudinal orientation inherited from the original trefoil. This is exactly $T_{2,3;2,5}$ in the Statement; it is not identified from a polynomial or a candidate matrix. [F6, step 1.4, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $G_s\ne0$, choose a Maslov-zero southwest-hook cycle mapping to the distinguished vertical class. In the reduced complex it is $x=z+\ell$, with $z$ on the lower vertical ray, including the corner, and $\ell$ strictly left at $j=s$. The two retained boundary equations are exactly $d_vz=0$ and $d_h(z_c+\ell)=0$: a lower ray cannot reach the other ray, and the corner has no equal-bifiltration differential. Conversely these two equations give a southwest-hook cycle mapping to the vertical class. Therefore $G_s\ne0$ is exactly the existence of this simultaneous vertical/horizontal cycle representative. If also $F_s\ne0$, its horizontal cycle is not a boundary, by step 2.1. Each constructed $x$ extends to a homogeneous filtered Laurent basis: choose a nonzero original corner coordinate $e$, whose coefficient is $1$, and replace $e$ by $x$. Homogeneity excludes any other power of that same basis element, and all other terms are no higher in either filtration, so the inverse is the same filtered elementary substitution. These are the needed distinguished representative normal forms. A chosen horizontal noncycle alone is not used as an epsilon test. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 Compute the tilde groups of these three new grids by the following finite exact procedure. Enumerate the $n!$ state permutations $p$. For each ordered pair $a\ne b$, take the positive cyclic row interval $a\to b$ and column interval $p(a)\to p(b)$. Its initial corners are southwest and northeast, and the two row orders give the two directed rectangles for each unordered pair. Retain the rectangle exactly when its cell support contains no $O$ or $X$, and no state point lies in the product of its strict interior intervals. Its target swaps $p(a),p(b)$; equal targets cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Compute each state's degrees directly from $M_O=I(p,p)+I(O,O)-I(p,O)-I(O,p)+1$ and $A=(M_O-M_X-(n-1))/2$. In a column, use the largest target permutation index as pivot. If that pivot has an existing stored column, take symmetric difference with it; otherwise store the column there. A replacement is an invertible field-column operation and strictly lowers the pivot, so distinct stored pivots give precisely the rank. For each grade, homology dimension is basis count minus outgoing rank minus incoming rank. The completed exact computation over all $5040$, $362880$, $3628800$ states respectively gives tilde dimensions $320$, $1792$, $2560$ and the graded polynomials recorded in Remarks. The implementation and full pivot checkpoints are finite arithmetic certificates of this explicit calculation; its square-zero input is the already supplied grid differential, not an unproved reconstruction theorem. [F5, step 1.3, step 2.3, step 1.4, step 2.4, construct, algebra]

4.1 Normalize Laurent bases at $i=0$. The vertical slice of $C\otimes D$ is the ordinary field tensor of the vertical slices, with differential $d_v\otimes1+1\otimes d_v$; no term lowering algebraic level can survive there. Similarly horizontal slices at levels $s,t$ tensor to the horizontal slice at $s+t$. Splitting a finite field complex into boundary pairs and homology representatives proves the field Kunneth assertion directly: a boundary pair tensored with anything is contractible by its pair homotopy. In particular the tensor of distinguished vertical cycles represents the distinguished tensor class. Its threshold is $s+t$ by [F3]. All representatives used in steps 2.1, 3.1 are supported southwest, so their vertical and horizontal projections tensor exactly to the projections of their tensor. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 By [F5], divide only the tilde HOMOLOGY dimension polynomial by $(1+m^{-1}a^{-1})^{n-1}$. Its quotient is unique by successively subtracting the largest-Maslov nonzero monomial times this factor. For $T_{2,5}$ the normalized hat degrees, each of rank one, are $(M,A)=(0,2),(-1,1),(-2,0),(-3,-1),(-4,-2)$; for $T_{4,5}$ they are $(0,6),(-1,5),(-2,2),(-5,0),(-6,-2),(-11,-5),(-12,-6)$; for the cable they are $(0,4),(-1,3),(-2,0),(-7,-3),(-8,-4)$. Now reduce the actual singly pointed CFK-infinity model supplied by [F5] using the contractions in step 1.2. Its Laurent basis at $i=0$ has exactly these reduced hat groups: every canceled equal-bifiltration pair is a graded boundary pair, and the reduced corner differential is zero. This step does not cancel $V$ in a chain category or tensor homology through a nonflat quotient. [F5, step 1.2, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 If both epsilon values are $1$, choose the boundary representatives of step 2.1. Both horizontal parts are cycles; if $x_h=d_ha$, then $(x\otimes y)_h=d_h(a\otimes y_h)$. Its vertical part is the distinguished tensor class, so the converse in step 2.1 gives $F_{s+t}=0$, and epsilon of the tensor is $1$. The same proof works when one factor has epsilon zero and the other has epsilon $1$, using a cycle representative from step 3.1 for the zero factor. If both factors have epsilon zero, tensor their southwest-hook lifts to obtain $G_{s+t}\ne0$. Their duals also have epsilon zero by step 2.2; applying the same lift construction to the dual tensor gives its $G_{-(s+t)}\ne0$, hence $F_{s+t}\ne0$ on the original tensor. Its epsilon is therefore zero. Dualizing the already proved positive cases proves the negative/negative and zero/negative cases. Together with [F3], these are exactly both tensor rules in the Statement, with actual representatives and compatible homotopies. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

5.2 These exact degree profiles determine the full differential; no general inference from hat ranks to a full staircase is needed. List their generators in the displayed order as $e_0,e_1,\ldots$. ## Statement

Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots, and use the epsilon sign convention from the preceding definition. If their knot Floer complexes are stably filtered equivalent, meaning that there are totally acyclic bifiltered complexes $A$ and $B$ with $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A$ filtered-chain-homotopy equivalent to $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(J)\oplus B$, then $\epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)$. The acyclic summands here need not be acyclic after taking either associated-graded filtration.

The invariant satisfies $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$, $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$, and the tensor rules
$$ \epsilon(K)=\epsilon(J)\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(K),\qquad \epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\epsilon(K\#J)=\epsilon(J). $$
The converse of $\epsilon(K)=0\Rightarrow\tau(K)=0$ fails: the knot $T_{2,5}\#-T_{4,5}\#T_{2,3;2,5}$ has $\tau=0$ and $\epsilon=1$, where $T_{p,q}$ is the positive $(p,q)$ torus knot and $T_{2,3;2,5}$ is the $(2,5)$ cable of the right-handed trefoil with longitudinal winding two. Epsilon is not an integer-valued homomorphism on the smooth concordance group: the right-handed trefoil has $\epsilon=1$ and its connected sum with itself also has $\epsilon=1$, not $2$.

## Proof

1.1 In the finite-rank free Maslov-graded knot Floer category, [F4] proves the stable-equivalence conclusion directly. Its finite endomorphism matrices strictify homotopy idempotents and give a unique non-acyclic indecomposable core up to filtered homotopy. The rank-one vertical homology of each original knot complex forces its internal acyclic complementary summands to have acyclic vertical complexes. Consequently its vertical threshold and the zero/nonzero patterns of $F_\tau,G_\tau$ are precisely those of that core. Stable equivalence identifies the two cores even if the externally added acyclic summands have nonzero vertical or associated-graded homology. Thus the three-case epsilon values in [F1] agree. This argument does not apply the epsilon definition to the stabilized complexes themselves. [given, F1, F4, algebra]

2.1 First reduce a finite based Laurent complex by explicit filtered contractions. If a differential coefficient preserves both coordinates, homogeneity makes it a single Laurent monomial; translate its target so that it is $1$. Write $da=b+r$ with $a,b$ at the same bifiltration and replace $b$ by $b'=da$. This is a filtered homogeneous basis change with inverse $b=b'+r$. For every other basis element $c$, subtract the coefficient of $b'$ in $dc$ times $a$ from $c$; this is filtered since the relevant copy of $a$ has the coordinates of the corresponding copy of $b'$. The new differentials contain no $b'$, and their $a$ coefficients vanish by $d^2=0$. Thus the pair $a\to b'$ splits off. Inclusion $I$, projection $P$ and $H(b')=a$, zero on all other generators, satisfy $PI=1$ and $IP+1=dH+Hd$, with $H$ preserving both filtrations and of Maslov degree $+1$. Finitely many repetitions give a reduced complex with no equal-bifiltration arrow. Tensoring these identities with another complex preserves them: the extra differential terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Dualizing likewise preserves them. This supplies all reduction inverse maps and homotopies used below, including their tensor compatibility. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Let $s=\tau(C)$ and choose a Maslov-zero vertical cycle $z$ at $j\le s$ representing its distinguished class. Its corner part $z_c$ is nonzero, or the threshold would be smaller. If $F_s=0$, choose a Maslov-one northeast-hook chain $b$ with $d_Nb=z_c$ and split it into strictly upper, corner and strictly right parts $b_+,b_0,b_r$. The strictly upper part of $d_vb_+$ is zero, since the other parts cannot reach it. Hence $z'=z+d_vb_+$ is another distinguished vertical cycle supported at $j\le s$. Put $q=b_0+b_r$. Its horizontal boundary $h=d_hq$ has no strictly right component, and its corner is $z'_c$, by the corner equation of $d_Nb=z_c$. Then $x=z'+h_{\mathrm{left}}$ is supported in $i\le0,j\le s$, its vertical projection represents the distinguished class, and its horizontal projection is the boundary $h$. Conversely, if such an $x$ has horizontal part $d_hq$, project $q$ to the northeast hook: its strictly left part cannot reach the corner or right ray, and the remaining boundary is precisely $x_c$, with no upper component. Thus $F_s=0$. This proves the exact boundary-representative alternative, rather than assuming a simultaneous simplification theorem. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 If $G_s\ne0$, choose a Maslov-zero southwest-hook cycle mapping to the distinguished vertical class. In the reduced complex it is $x=z+\ell$, with $z$ on the lower vertical ray, including the corner, and $\ell$ strictly left at $j=s$. The two retained boundary equations are exactly $d_vz=0$ and $d_h(z_c+\ell)=0$: a lower ray cannot reach the other ray, and the corner has no equal-bifiltration differential. Conversely these two equations give a southwest-hook cycle mapping to the vertical class. Therefore $G_s\ne0$ is exactly the existence of this simultaneous vertical/horizontal cycle representative. If also $F_s\ne0$, its horizontal cycle is not a boundary, by step 2.2. Each constructed $x$ extends to a homogeneous filtered Laurent basis: choose a nonzero original corner coordinate $e$, whose coefficient is $1$, and replace $e$ by $x$. Homogeneity excludes any other power of that same basis element, and all other terms are no higher in either filtration, so the inverse is the same filtered elementary substitution. These are the needed distinguished representative normal forms. A chosen horizontal noncycle alone is not used as an epsilon test. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

2.4 The dual vertical threshold is $-s$. Indeed, if $B$ is the vertical boundary space, the distinguished cycle $z$ is not in $B+V^{\le s-1}$, since such an expression would give a lower-level cycle representing it. Finite-dimensional basis extension gives a cocycle functional annihilating that subspace and taking $z$ to $1$; its dual filtration is at most $-s$. A dual cocycle at level at most $-s-1$ vanishes on every cycle at level $s$ and hence on the one-dimensional vertical homology, so it is a dual boundary. The finite perfect pairing identifies the dual of the northeast hook at $s$ with the southwest hook of $C^*$ at $-s$. The transpose of $F_s(C)$ is $G_{-s}(C^*)$, and the transpose of $G_s(C)$ is $F_{-s}(C^*)$: quotient/inclusion maps reverse under this pairing. Duality of finite-dimensional homology preserves zero/nonzero. Thus $\epsilon(C^*)=-\epsilon(C)$; [F2] identifies this with $\epsilon(-K)=-\epsilon(K)$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Normalize Laurent bases at $i=0$. The vertical slice of $C\otimes D$ is the ordinary field tensor of the vertical slices, with differential $d_v\otimes1+1\otimes d_v$; no term lowering algebraic level can survive there. Similarly horizontal slices at levels $s,t$ tensor to the horizontal slice at $s+t$. Splitting a finite field complex into boundary pairs and homology representatives proves the field Kunneth assertion directly: a boundary pair tensored with anything is contractible by its pair homotopy. In particular the tensor of distinguished vertical cycles represents the distinguished tensor class. Its threshold is $s+t$ by [F3]. All representatives used in steps 2.2–2.3 are supported southwest, so their vertical and horizontal projections tensor exactly to the projections of their tensor. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

3.2 If both epsilon values are $1$, choose the boundary representatives of step 2.2. Both horizontal parts are cycles; if $x_h=d_ha$, then $(x\otimes y)_h=d_h(a\otimes y_h)$. Its vertical part is the distinguished tensor class, so the converse in step 2.2 gives $F_{s+t}=0$, and epsilon of the tensor is $1$. The same proof works when one factor has epsilon zero and the other has epsilon $1$, using a cycle representative from step 2.3 for the zero factor. If both factors have epsilon zero, tensor their southwest-hook lifts to obtain $G_{s+t}\ne0$. Their duals also have epsilon zero by step 2.4; applying the same lift construction to the dual tensor gives its $G_{-(s+t)}\ne0$, hence $F_{s+t}\ne0$ on the original tensor. Its epsilon is therefore zero. Dualizing the already proved positive cases proves the negative/negative and zero/negative cases. Together with [F3], these are exactly both tensor rules in the Statement, with actual representatives and compatible homotopies. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 We next admit the actual complexes used for the geometric examples. Use the following marking-cell arrays, rows ordered bottom to top: for positive $T_{2,5}$ take $n=7$, $O=[6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,6,5]$; for positive $T_{4,5}$ take $n=9$, $O=[8,7,6,5,4,3,2,1,0]$, $X=[4,3,2,1,0,8,7,6,5]$. The first has five positive crossings and oriented over/under word $A^+B^-C^+D^-E^+A^-B^+C^-D^+E^-$, where superscripts indicate over/under and all crossing signs are positive. The explicit positive torus curve $(r e^{2it},s e^{5it})$, $r=s=1/\sqrt2$, has this identical code in stereographic projection: its planar angle is $2t$, radius $r/(1-s\sin5t)$, height $s\cos5t/(1-s\sin5t)$, and crossing parameters $t/(2\pi)=0,1/10,\ldots,9/10$. Equal projections force parameter difference $\pi$ and $\sin5t=0$. At the overparameter the radial derivative is positive and at the underpartner negative, so the oriented crossing determinant is positive. The angular derivative is nonzero, and there are no triple points. Thus [F6] admits this grid as the actual positive $T_{2,5}$. [F6, given, construct, algebra]

4.2 Following oriented strands in the nine-grid gives fifteen positive crossings and the full signed rotation/strand code of the closure of the four-strand positive word $121321321121321$, after a cyclic starting-point change and reversal of the knot orientation. This is an explicit finite code equality: enumerate crossings in each row and column interval, then follow each row $O\to X$ and column $X\to O$; on the braid follow the strand permutation through each listed crossing, taking the top-right strand over to bottom-left. The exact words and crossing correspondence are recorded in the finite certificate named in Remarks. Commutations $13=31$ and braid relations $121=212$, $232=323$ give the successive words $123121321121321$, $123123121121321$, $123123121212321$, $123123121213231$, $123123121231231$, $123123121231213$, $123123121232123$, $123123121323123$, $123123123123123$. Each is a local disjoint-strand isotopy or oriented R3, so their closures are equivalent. The last is $(123)^5$. To identify its torus embedding, cut the Clifford curve $(r e^{4it},s e^{5it})$ by the disk coordinate $\arg(z_1)=\theta$: its four disk points have arguments $5(\theta+2\pi k)/4$. A generic phase makes one quarter-turn's braid $132$, which becomes $321$ by moving the first generator past the closure cut, and then $123$ by reversing the four disk positions via the half-turn conjugation. Five quarter-turns give the last closure. Finally simultaneous complex conjugation is an ambient SO(4) isotopy endpoint and sends this curve to its orientation reverse: rotate its two imaginary axes through $\pi$. Thus the code reversal preserves oriented knot type, and [F6] proves the actual positive $T_{4,5}$ admission. [F6, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

4.3 Verify the trefoil grid in [F6] directly. Use row indices $0,1,2,3,4$ from bottom to top and column indices from left to right, as in [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]], and draw the standard planar grid realization using the in-square mark-to-mark intervals. Following the grid orientation gives the single cycle
$$O_{0,4}\to X_{0,2}\to O_{2,2}\to X_{2,0}\to O_{4,0}\to X_{4,3}\to O_{1,3}\to X_{1,1}\to O_{3,1}\to X_{3,4}\to O_{0,4}.$$
The horizontal and vertical intervals meet away from their endpoints at exactly three crossings: $c_1=(\text{row }1,\text{column }2)$, $c_2=(\text{row }2,\text{column }1)$, and $c_3=(\text{row }3,\text{column }3)$. Traversing the component from $O_{0,4}$ encounters $c_1$ over, $c_2$ under, $c_3$ over, $c_1$ under, $c_2$ over, and $c_3$ under. At $c_1$ and $c_2$ the oriented projected tangents $(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$ are $((0,1),(-1,0))$; at $c_3$ they are $((0,-1),(1,0))$. Each determinant is $+1$ by [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]. Thus its signed oriented Gauss code is $1_O,2_U,3_O,1_U,2_O,3_U$ with crossing-sign vector $(+1,+1,+1)$. This code is also obtained by traversing the closure of the positive two-strand braid $\sigma_1^3$: its first braid strand encounters the three positive half twists over, under, over, and the returning strand encounters them under, over, under. The signed visit data determine the same crossing rotation and strand code, hence identify the face-permutation cycles. Retain the grid diagram's outer-face cycle and choose the corresponding face of the braid-closure diagram. To make this chosen face outer, compactify the projection plane to the oriented sphere $S^2$ and choose a point $q$ in that face, away from the diagram. An orientation-preserving rotation of $S^2$ sending $q$ to the projection point at infinity makes precisely this face outer. Realize the diagram lift in a product collar of the equatorial $S^2$ in $S^3$; the rotation extends by the same rotation on the first three coordinates and the identity on the normal coordinate. Its path of rotations is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy of $S^3$ preserving the crossing heights and oriented strand data. The two resulting plane codes now have the same selected outer face, so [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] identifies their diagrams up to planar isotopy. Thus the original grid and braid closure represent the same oriented knot even if their initially chosen planar outer faces differ. status: draft

sources:

      url: "https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf"
      locator: "§4.4, Lemma 4.4.1 and Exercise 4.4.2; §5.1.1, printed p. 27, uniqueness up to isotopy of a simple closed curve of fixed primitive coordinates on a torus."
---

## Statement

Let $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ be oriented by $dx\wedge dy$, and identify $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ in the standard basis, so the algebraic intersection of classes $v,w$ is $\det(v,w)$. Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\subset T$ be smooth embedded circles that are not null-homotopic. Orient them so that their homology classes agree, and suppose their common class $v\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is primitive, meaning it is not an integer multiple $m u$ with $|m|>1$. Then $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are isotopic through embedded circles in $T$.

## Statement references

[Cattabriga–Francaviglia, *Knot Theory and Applications: Lecture Notes*, §4.4 and §5.1.1](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The torus and two oriented essential smooth embedded circles with common primitive class $v$.

## Proof

1.1 Since $v$ is primitive, Bezout's identity gives $w\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\det(v,w)=1$. The linear torus diffeomorphism taking the basis $(v,w)$ to the standard basis takes both curves to curves of class $(1,0)$. It is enough to prove the claim for that class. [given, algebra, construct]

2.1 Put the two curves in transverse position. If they intersect, lift them to the annular cover $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle(1,0)\rangle$. Each lift is an essential embedded circle, and the deck translates of each one are disjoint. In the universal cover of $A$, a lift of either circle is a proper line invariant under horizontal unit translation and contained in a bounded horizontal strip; all such lines have the same two ends. The signed intersection sum in a fundamental period is zero because both curves have class $(1,0)$. Thus intersections have both signs. Two successive intersections of opposite sign cut off a bounded region between subarcs of the two lines. Choose among such regions one with the least number of interior intersections and, among those, least horizontal width modulo deck translation. If a lifted arc entered the region, its first entry and exit would cut off a region with fewer interior intersections; if a nontrivial deck translate met it, the overlap would yield a region of smaller horizontal width. Hence its interior is disjoint from all lifted arcs and translates, and its projection is an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one arc across the bigon removes two intersections and creates none. Compactness and transversality give finitely many intersections, so finitely many such isotopies make the curves disjoint. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The disjoint curves still have primitive class $(1,0)$, so neither bounds a disk. Cutting the torus along the second curve gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. The first curve remains essential in that annulus. Cutting the annulus along it gives two annuli, so it is parallel to the second curve and isotopic to it. Composing this isotopy with the finite bigon-removal isotopies in step 2.1 proves the assertion for the original pair; undoing the linear diffeomorphism proves it for $v$. [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The subfield of $\mathbb C$ fixed by every field automorphism $\sigma:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ with $\sigma(q)=q$ for all $q\in\mathbb Q$ is exactly $\mathbb Q$.

## Statement references

[Milne, *Fields and Galois Theory*, §§3 and 9](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/FT.pdf)

[The Stacks Project, Section 9.26, Lemma 9.26.3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030F)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the field inclusion $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb C$, and an element $z\in\mathbb C$.

[F1] Under full AC, every algebraically independent subset extends to a maximal algebraically independent set, and a maximal set is a transcendence basis ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[lem-maximal-algebraically-independent-subset-is-a-transcendence-basis]]).

[F2] The algebraic numbers $\overline{\mathbb Q}=\{z\in\mathbb C:z\text{ is algebraic over }\mathbb Q\}$ form an algebraically closed algebraic extension of $\mathbb Q$: roots exist in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]) and remain algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ by transitivity ([[thm-transitivity-of-algebraicity]]).

[F3] Full AC is equivalent over ZF to Zorn's lemma ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]; [[cor-ac-iff-zorn]]).

## Proof

1.1 Let $F\subset\Omega$ be a field extension with $\Omega$ algebraic over $F$, let $F_0$ be an intermediate field, and let $\phi_0:F_0\to\Omega'$ be an embedding into an algebraically closed field $\Omega'$. Order all extensions $\phi:E\to\Omega'$ with $F_0\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$ by extension. A chain has the union embedding, so Zorn's lemma from [F3] gives a maximal one. If $E\ne\Omega$, choose $\alpha\in\Omega\setminus E$; it is algebraic over $E$. Apply $\phi$ to its minimal polynomial and choose a root $\beta\in\Omega'$. The transported minimal polynomial is irreducible over $\phi(E)$ because $\phi$ is an isomorphism onto its image, so sending $\alpha$ to $\beta$ extends $\phi$ to an embedding of $E(\alpha)$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\phi$ extends to $\Omega$. If $\phi_0$ maps $F$ onto $F$ and both source and target are algebraic closures of $F$, this extension is onto: its image is algebraically closed and contains $F$, so it contains every root of every polynomial over $F$, hence all of $\Omega$. [F3, given, algebra, choose]

1.2 Use [F2] to view $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ as a subfield of $\mathbb C$. By [F1], choose a transcendence basis $B$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$. Then $\mathbb C$ is algebraic over $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ and, being algebraically closed, is an algebraic closure of that field. [F1, F2, given, choose]

2.1 If $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ but $z\notin\mathbb Q$, its irreducible minimal polynomial has degree at least two and has distinct roots because its derivative is nonzero and relatively prime to it. Choose another root $z'\in\overline{\mathbb Q}$. By step 1.1, the embedding $\mathbb Q(z)\to\overline{\mathbb Q}$ sending $z$ to $z'$ extends to an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ over $\mathbb Q$. Extend it coefficientwise to $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ while fixing $B$, then apply step 1.1 to extend it to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$. This automorphism moves $z$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra, choose]

2.2 If $z$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, it is transcendental over the algebraic extension $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ by transitivity in [F2]. Extend $\{z\}$ to a transcendence basis $B$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ using [F1]. The assignment fixing $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ and every element of $B\setminus\{z\}$ while sending $z$ to $z+1$ defines an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$; its inverse sends $z$ to $z-1$. By step 1.1 it extends to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$, and it moves $z$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, choose]

3.1 Every complex number outside $\mathbb Q$ is either algebraic nonrational or transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, and steps 2.1, 2.2 exhibit an automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ that moves it. Every element of $\mathbb Q$ is fixed by definition. Thus the common fixed field is exactly $\mathbb Q$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, given] ∎

[F2] The algebraic numbers $\overline{\mathbb Q}=\{z\in\mathbb C:z\text{ is algebraic over }\mathbb Q\}$ form an algebraically closed algebraic extension of $\mathbb Q$: roots exist in $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]) and remain algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ by transitivity ([[thm-transitivity-of-algebraicity]]).

Order all extensions $\phi:E\to\Omega'$ with $F_0\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$ by extension. A chain has the union embedding, so Zorn's lemma from [F3] gives a maximal one. If $E\ne\Omega$, choose $\alpha\in\Omega\setminus E$; it is algebraic over $E$. Apply $\phi$ to its minimal polynomial and choose a root $\beta\in\Omega'$. The transported minimal polynomial is irreducible over $\phi(E)$ because $\phi$ is an isomorphism onto its image, so sending $\alpha$ to $\beta$ extends $\phi$ to an embedding of $E(\alpha)$, contradicting maximality. Hence $\phi$ extends to $\Omega$. If $\phi_0$ maps $F$ onto $F$ and both source and target are algebraic closures of $F$, this extension is onto: its image is algebraically closed and contains $F$, so it contains every root of every polynomial over $F$, hence all of $\Omega$. [F3, given, algebra, choose]

1.2 Use [F2] to view $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ as a subfield of $\mathbb C$. By [F1], choose a transcendence basis $B$ of $\mathbb C$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$. 1.3 If $z$ is algebraic over $\mathbb Q$ but $z\notin\mathbb Q$, its irreducible minimal polynomial has degree at least two and has distinct roots because its derivative is nonzero and relatively prime to it. Choose another root $z'\in\overline{\mathbb Q}$. By step 1.1, the embedding $\mathbb Q(z)\to\overline{\mathbb Q}$ sending $z$ to $z'$ extends to an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ over $\mathbb Q$. Extend it coefficientwise to $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$ while fixing $B$, then apply step 1.1 to extend it to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$. This automorphism moves $z$. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra, choose]

1.4 If $z$ is transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, it is transcendental over the algebraic extension $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ by transitivity in [F2]. Extend $\{z\}$ to a transcendence basis $B$ over $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ using [F1]. The assignment fixing $\overline{\mathbb Q}$ and every element of $B\setminus\{z\}$ while sending $z$ to $z+1$ defines an automorphism of $\overline{\mathbb Q}(B)$; its inverse sends $z$ to $z-1$. By step 1.1 it extends to an automorphism of $\mathbb C$, and it moves $z$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, choose]

2.1 Every complex number outside $\mathbb Q$ is either algebraic nonrational or transcendental over $\mathbb Q$, and steps 1.3–1.4 exhibit an automorphism fixing $\mathbb Q$ that moves it. Every element of $\mathbb Q$ is fixed by definition. Thus the common fixed field is exactly $\mathbb Q$. [step 1.3, step 1.4, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be an
oriented smooth embedded circle and let $s$ be a smooth nowhere-zero section of
its normal bundle. For any tubular neighbourhood chart that is the inclusion
on the zero section and identifies each vertical normal fibre with the ambient
normal quotient by the identity, the curve $K_{\varepsilon s}$ obtained by
mapping the graph of $\varepsilon s$ into $S^3$ is an embedded oriented circle
disjoint from $K$ for every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. The integer
linking number of $K$ with $K_{\varepsilon s}$ is independent of the sufficiently
small radius, of the representative section in its homotopy class, and of the
normalized tubular chart. It therefore defines a self-linking integer of the
framing class $[s]$.

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy|Smooth oriented knots]]

[[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold|Normal bundle as quotient by the tangent bundle]]

[[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold|Tubular neighbourhood existence]]

[[cor-tubular-neighbourhoods-are-unique-up-to-ambient-isotopy|Normalized tubular neighbourhood uniqueness]]

[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-compact-embedded-submanifolds-extends-to-an-ambient-isotopy|Ambient isotopy extension for compact embedded families]]

[[def-smooth-bundle-metric|Smooth bundle metric]]

[[thm-every-smooth-vector-bundle-admits-a-smooth-bundle-metric|Existence of a smooth bundle metric]]

[[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function|Smooth endpoint reparameterization]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable-choice hypothesis]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, an oriented smooth embedded circle
$K\subset S^3$, and a smooth nowhere-zero normal section $s$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The normal bundle is the quotient $TS^3|_K/TK$; under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ it is a smooth vector bundle, and a tubular neighbourhood is a diffeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of its zero section onto an ambient neighbourhood of $K$ ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[prop-normal-and-conormal-bundles-are-smooth-vector-bundles]], [[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]], [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]]).

[F2] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the smooth normal bundle admits a smooth bundle metric ([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]], [[thm-every-smooth-vector-bundle-admits-a-smooth-bundle-metric]]).

[F3] Two normalized tubular embeddings of the same closed submanifold, when defined on the same open disk bundle and inducing the same vertical normal-quotient identification, are ambient isotopic near the compact zero section after shrinking ([[cor-tubular-neighbourhoods-are-unique-up-to-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F4] If $P$ is a compact smooth manifold without boundary and $F:P\times I\to S^3$ is a smooth family of embeddings constant near both ends, then $F$ extends to an ambient isotopy of $S^3$ ([[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-compact-embedded-submanifolds-extends-to-an-ambient-isotopy]]).

[F5] The integer half-sum of mixed crossing signs is invariant under ambient isotopy of two-component oriented links ([[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]], [[thm-oriented-linking-number-scan-terminates-and-is-correct]]).

[F6] The supplied smooth step function has values in $[0,1]$, satisfies $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge1$, and is smooth; for any $0<a<1/2$, $\chi_a(u):=\sigma((u-a)/(1-2a))$ is a smooth map $[0,1]\to[0,1]$, equals $0$ on $u\le a$, and equals $1$ on $u\ge1-a$ ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]]).

## Proof

1.1 Choose a tubular chart $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ as in [F1]. The graph map $x\mapsto(x,\varepsilon s(x))$ is an embedding because its projection to the base $K$ is the identity; it is disjoint from the zero section because $s(x)\ne0$. Since $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism on $\Omega$, its image $K_{\varepsilon s}$ is embedded and disjoint from $K$ whenever the graph is contained in $\Omega$. The zero section is compact, so an open neighbourhood of it contains all sufficiently small scalar multiples of $s$ over $K$; hence such $\varepsilon$ exist. The orientation of $K_{\varepsilon s}$ is transported from the base orientation by its projection to $K$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $a\in(0,1/2)$ and use the smooth plateau $\chi_a$ of [F6]. For two sufficiently small radii $\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1>0$ in the same chart, define $\varepsilon(u)=(1-\chi_a(u))\varepsilon_0+\chi_a(u)\varepsilon_1$. The family of embeddings of $P:=S^1\sqcup S^1$ whose first component is $K$ and whose second is $K_{\varepsilon(u)s}$ is smooth, stays embedded and disjoint by step 1.1, and is constant on endpoint collars. Here $P$ is compact and boundaryless, so [F4] extends this family to an ambient isotopy; [F5] shows that the linking number is unchanged. If $s_v$ is a smooth homotopy through nonzero sections, compactness of $K\times[0,1]$ gives one small scalar $\varepsilon$ for which all graphs lie in $\Omega$. Replacing $v$ by $\chi_a(u)$ in the family $K\cup K_{\varepsilon s_v}$ again gives a smooth family of embeddings of the same compact boundaryless source, stationary near its endpoints; [F4] and [F5] show that the linking number is independent of the representative section. [A1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\Phi_0:\Omega_0\to S^3$ and $\Phi_1:\Omega_1\to S^3$ be two normalized tubular charts. By [F2], choose a smooth bundle metric on $\nu K$. Since $K$ is compact and $\Omega_0\cap\Omega_1$ is an open neighbourhood of the zero section, finitely many bundle trivializations give a common radius $r>0$ such that the open metric disk bundle $\Omega_r=\{v\in\nu K:\lVert v\rVert<r\}$ is contained in both domains. Restrict both charts to this same $\Omega_r$. They now satisfy the common-domain hypothesis of [F3]. After its permitted shrinking, [F3] gives an ambient isotopy $H_t$ with $H_1\circ\Phi_0=\Phi_1$ on a neighbourhood of the compact zero section. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that the graph of $\varepsilon s$ lies in this neighbourhood. Then $H_1$ carries the oriented pair formed from $K$ and its $\Phi_0$-push-off to the corresponding pair for $\Phi_1$, so [F5] makes their linking numbers equal. Steps 1.1–2.1 prove independence of chart, sufficiently small radius and representative section. Countable Choice is used through the metric and tubular-neighbourhood suppliers; the finite linking computations are choice-free. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a compact smooth
planar annulus and set
$X=\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)\times(-1,1)
=\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A\times[-1,1])$, the interior of a solid torus.
A regular annular diagram is a finite immersed union of circles in
$\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)$ with only finitely many transverse double
points, no triple points, and over/under data from the interval coordinate.
The **blackboard framing** is the normal strip lying in the annulus. A specified
framing differs from it on each component by an integer full-twist correction,
measured by the winding number of its normal direction relative to the
blackboard normal. Count the correction positively for an A-type full twist,
whose local curl has A-smoothing equal to the straight strip with one
contractible circle; count the opposite B-type twist negatively. Every framed
link in $X$ admits a regular annular diagram. The correction may be recorded
as signed full-twist marks on diagram arcs; its total is additive when arcs
are concatenated.

If two framed links in $X$ are ambient isotopic through links in $X$, their
regular annular diagrams are related by finitely many annular planar isotopies
and local oriented Reidemeister I, II, and III moves in disks contained in
$\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)$. Reidemeister II and III and planar isotopy
preserve the blackboard framing; an A-type or B-type Reidemeister I move
changes it by one corresponding full twist, so the correction integer changes
by the opposite twist. For framed links in $S^3$, every link also admits a
regular planar diagram, and any two diagrams of ambient-isotopic framed links
are related by a finite planar-isotopy/Reidemeister sequence with the same
framing-correction rule.

## Statement references

[Józef H. Przytycki, *Fundamentals of Kauffman Bracket Skein Modules* (1998), §3, Lemma 3.5 and Proposition 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9809113)

[Daniel Queffelec, *Reidemeister's theorem using transversality* (2024), arXiv:2406.18203v1, §§2–3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.18203v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, a framed link in $S^3$ or $X$, and a framed ambient isotopy between two such links.

[A1] Countable choice is the assertion that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] A regular oriented link diagram is an immersion with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and over/under and orientation data; every oriented link in $S^3$ has a regular projection under countable choice ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]).

[F2] Under countable choice, two regular oriented diagrams in $S^3$ represent equivalent oriented links exactly when a finite sequence of planar isotopies and oriented Reidemeister I, II, and III moves connects them ([[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]).

[F3] Under countable choice, a smooth isotopy in $\mathbb R^3$ with regular endpoint projections can be perturbed, fixed near its endpoints, so its projection has finitely many isolated cusps, quadratic double tangencies, and transverse triple events; each event time is distinct ([[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], [[lem-a-generic-isotopy-of-links-has-only-reidemeister-singular-times]]).

[F4] Parametric transversality gives generic parameter slices transverse to any fixed finite list of smooth strata, and a transverse preimage of codimension $c$ in a source of dimension $m<c$ is empty ([[thm-parametric-transversality]], [[thm-transverse-preimage-theorem]]).

[F5] R1, R2, and R3 are the local kink, two-strand cancellation, and strand-past-crossing replacements, with all sign and orientation variants; planar isotopy transports the diagram without creating or deleting a crossing ([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]], [[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]).

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal A$ be a compact smooth
planar annulus and set
$X=\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)\times(-1,1)
=\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A\times[-1,1])$, the interior of a solid torus.
A regular annular diagram is a finite immersed union of circles in
$\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)$ with only finitely many transverse double
points, no triple points, and over/under data from the interval coordinate.
The **blackboard framing** is the normal strip lying in the annulus. A specified
framing differs from it on each component by an integer full-twist correction,
measured by the winding number of its normal direction relative to the
blackboard normal. Count the correction positively for an A-type full twist,
whose local curl has A-smoothing equal to the straight strip with one
contractible circle; count the opposite B-type twist negatively. Every framed
link in $X$ admits a regular annular diagram. The correction may be recorded
as signed full-twist marks on diagram arcs; its total is additive when arcs
are concatenated.

If two framed links in $X$ are ambient isotopic through links in $X$, their
regular annular diagrams are related by finitely many annular planar isotopies
and local oriented Reidemeister I, II, and III moves in disks contained in
$\operatorname{int}(\mathcal A)$. Reidemeister II and III and planar isotopy
preserve the blackboard framing; an A-type or B-type Reidemeister I move
changes it by one corresponding full twist, so the correction integer changes
by the opposite twist. For framed links in $S^3$, every link also admits a
regular planar diagram, and any two diagrams of ambient-isotopic framed links
are related by a finite planar-isotopy/Reidemeister sequence with the same
framing-correction rule.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $L$ be a free abelian group of rank $n$ with an integer-valued symmetric bilinear form whose Gram determinant is $1$ or $-1$, and let $f:L\to\mathbb Z^n$ be an isometric homomorphism, where $\mathbb Z^n$ has its standard dot product. Then $f(L)=\mathbb Z^n$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rank-$n$ free abelian group $L$, a unimodular integral symmetric form on $L$, and an isometric homomorphism $f$ to the standard dot-product lattice $\mathbb Z^n$.

[A1] The stated Gram determinant has absolute value one; the argument is finite integral linear algebra and uses no choice axiom.

[F1] If $A\in M_n(\mathbb Z)$ has nonzero determinant, then the subgroup $A\mathbb Z^n$ has index $|\det A|$ in $\mathbb Z^n$. [[cor-index-of-a-full-rank-integer-sublattice-is-the-absolute-determinant]]

## Proof

1.1 Choose an integral basis of $L$ and let $B$ be the integer $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are the images of that basis under $f$. Since $f$ is isometric, the Gram matrix of $L$ is $B^{\mathsf T}B$. [given, A1, choose, construct]

2.1 Taking determinants gives $1=|\det(B^{\mathsf T}B)|=|\det B|^2$, hence $\det B=1$ or $-1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1] and step 2.1, the image subgroup $B\mathbb Z^n=f(L)$ has index $|\det B|=1$ in $\mathbb Z^n$. The quotient therefore has one element, which means $B\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n$ and $f(L)=\mathbb Z^n$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For any based classifying map $c:X\to BG$ inducing the identity on fundamental
groups, the induced homomorphism
$$c_*:H_2(X;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(BG;\mathbb Z)=H_2(G;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective.

## Statement references

[McCleary, §8bis.2](https://pages.vassar.edu/mccleary/files/2011/04/MC08bis.fin_.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a path-connected CW complex $X$, a basepoint $x_0$, and
$G=\pi_1(X,x_0)$.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[L1] Full AC implies DC: apply AC to the family of nonempty successor sets of a serial relation, choose an initial element, and iterate the resulting choice function. [[def-dependent-choice]]

[F1] Under AC, $BG$ is a connected CW model with $\pi_1(BG)\cong G$ and
$\pi_k(BG)=0$ for $k>1$. [[cor-classifying-space-of-a-discrete-group-is-a-k-g-one]]

[F2] The long exact sequence of a Serre fibration computes the homotopy groups
of its fiber. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-homotopy-groups-of-a-fibration]]

[F3] The homological Serre spectral sequence gives the exact five-term sequence
for the homology of a fibration. [[thm-homological-serre-spectral-sequence]],
[[thm-five-term-exact-sequence-of-a-first-quadrant-homological-spectral-sequence]]

[F4] A simply connected path-connected space has zero first homology by the
degree-one Hurewicz theorem. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F5] Under AC there is a connected CW model $K(G,1)$, and under DC its homology with trivial coefficients is the bar-model group homology. [[thm-existence-and-homotopy-uniqueness-of-eilenberg-maclane-spaces]], [[lem-diagonal-bar-coinvariants-compute-group-homology]], [[def-dependent-choice]]

**Given:** The data above and [A1].

For every cell of dimension at least three, its attaching sphere extends because the corresponding higher homotopy group of $BG$ vanishes. AC supplies the simultaneous cellwise extensions. The resulting based map $c:X\to BG$ induces the identity on $\pi_1$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

## Statement

For every closed connected oriented rational homology three-sphere $Y$ and Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, the standard Heegaard Floer groups $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$ and $HF^+(Y,\mathfrak t)$ constructed from admissible pointed Heegaard diagrams are independent, up to grading-preserving isomorphism, of the diagram and regular auxiliary data. The image of $HF^\infty\to HF^+$ is a graded plus tower, isomorphic as an $\mathbb F_2[U]$-module to $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ with an absolute rational grading shift and with $U$ of degree $-2$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have a least grading; this least grading $d(Y,\mathfrak t)$ exists and is independent of choices. Every tower element is $U$-torsion and is divisible by every power of $U$. The normalization is $d(S^3,\mathfrak t_0)=0$.

## Statement references

[[def-heegaard-floer-plus-infinity-absolute-grading|The disk-count complex and grading conventions]]

[[def-heegaard-floer-correction-term|The correction-term definition]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Holomorphic Disks and Topological Invariants for Closed Three-Manifolds*, Sections 3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0101206v1)

[Hom, *Lecture Notes on Heegaard Floer Homology*, Sections 2.1–2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.01836v1)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-absolute-grading-and-cobordism-maps]] constructs the absolute grading and its compatibility with pointed moves and the minus/infinity/plus sequence.

[F2] [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-infinity-standardness-and-rational-cobordism-isomorphism]] proves that the infinity group of each rational-sphere Spin$^c$ structure is a single Laurent tower.

## Proof

**Given:** A rational homology sphere $Y$, a Spin$^c$ structure $\mathfrak t$, and a finite admissible pointed diagram. Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ and choose a homogeneous Laurent generator $\rho$ of $HF^\infty(Y,\mathfrak t)$.

1.1 The minus chain complex is finite free over $\mathbb F_2[U]$, with generators $[\mathbf x,-1]$ for the finitely many intersection points in $\mathfrak t$. Its homology is finitely generated and its localization is the infinity homology, since localization is exact and the localized differentials are identical. Thus the graded image $L$ of $HF^-\to R\rho$ is nonzero. Its degrees are bounded above by the largest degree of a minus-chain generator. The set of integers $j$ with $U^j\rho\in L$ is consequently nonempty, bounded below, and closed under addition of nonnegative integers. If $a$ is its minimum, that set is exactly $\{a,a+1,\ldots\}$. Every homogeneous element of the Laurent tower is a monomial multiple of $\rho$, and the image is graded; hence $L=U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$. [F1, F2]

2.1 The long exact sequence of the actual short exact sequence $CF^-\to CF^\infty\to CF^+$ identifies the image in plus homology, with its grading, as $R\rho/U^a\mathbb F_2[U]\rho$. Its nonzero homogeneous elements have exponents $j<a$, so their least degree is $\deg\rho-2(a-1)$, attained at $U^{a-1}\rho$. Sending the standard tower element $U^k$ to $U^{k+a-1}\rho$ identifies the image with $R/U\mathbb F_2[U]$ shifted by this least degree. Multiplying any individual element sufficiently many times by $U$ kills it, while decreasing exponents supplies a preimage under any power of $U$. This proves all the tower assertions. [step 1.1]

3.1 The pointed-move maps preserve absolute grading and the minus/infinity/plus exact sequence, so they carry $L$ onto the corresponding image lattice and induce grading-preserving tower isomorphisms. Therefore the least degree is independent of the diagram and auxiliary data. Choosing $U^b\rho$ instead changes $a$ to $a-b$ and $\deg\rho$ to $\deg\rho-2b$, leaving that degree unchanged. In the genus-zero diagram of $S^3$ there is one generator $[\mathbf x_0,0]$ of degree zero, no nonconstant disks, and minus lattice $U\mathbb F_2[U][\mathbf x_0,0]$. Here $a=1$, giving $d(S^3)=0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
