## Statement

Use the Ozsvath–Szabo orientation convention $L(p,1)$ given by positive $p$-surgery on the unknot and label its Spin$^c$ structures by $i\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, represented by $0\le i<p$. For every integer $p\ge1$,
$$d(L(p,1),i)=\frac{(2i-p)^2-p}{4p}.$$
For the opposite orientation the correction terms are negated, with the conjugate Spin$^c$ label understood.

## Statement references

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|The lens-space surgery orientation]]

[[def-heegaard-floer-correction-term|The correction-term convention]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Absolutely Graded Floer Homologies and Intersection Forms for Four-Manifolds with Boundary*, Propositions 4.2 and 4.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110170v1)

[Aceto and Golla, *Dehn Surgeries and Rational Homology Balls*, Proposition 3.5 and Remark 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.07559v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-lens-space-q-one-triangles-and-cyclic-handle-maps]] supplies the explicit individual index-zero, basepoint-zero count-one triangles, their cyclic maps and Chern evaluation $k=2i-p$ on a generator of square $-p$.

[F2] [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-absolute-grading-and-cobordism-maps]] constructs the absolute grading, with the sphere generator at degree zero, and proves the degree formula for these actual fixed-Spin$^c$ handle maps.

[F3] [[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-term-heegaard-invariance]] identifies the correction term as the bottom degree of the infinity image. The convention in the statement is [[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]].

## Proof

**Given:** $p\ge1$ and a label $0\le i<p$, with the torus diagrams and fixed triangle structures of [F1].

1.1 The alpha-gamma diagram, and the diagram with those two attaching curves reversed, each have one intersection in each Spin$^c$ structure. Their infinity differentials are zero: the Maslov index of a self-disk in a torsion Spin$^c$ structure is $2n_z$, so cannot be one. The minus lattice in each summand is therefore exactly $U\mathbb F_2[U][x_i,0]$, and its plus image has bottom $[x_i,0]$. Its correction term is the absolute grading of that generator, with no unknown exponent shift. [F1, F3]

2.1 For the negative-trace map from $S^3$ to $-L(p,1)$, the fixed triangle has index and basepoint multiplicity zero and count one. It sends the sphere generator at exponent zero to $[x_i,0]$. The four-dimensional data are $c_1^2=-k^2/p$, $\chi=1$ and $\sigma=-1$. Hence its degree is $D_i=(1-k^2/p)/4$, and $d(-L(p,1),i)=D_i$. This computes the negative orientation directly. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The cyclically reordered triangle gives the actual fixed-structure map from $L(p,1)$ to $S^3$ and sends $[x_i,0]$ to the sphere generator at exponent zero. It is the same oriented triple four-manifold with the other sphere input filled, so it has the same degree $D_i$. Consequently $0=\operatorname{gr}[x_i,0]+D_i$, and $d(L(p,1),i)=-D_i=((2i-p)^2-p)/(4p)$. This argument uses an actual turned-around triangle map rather than a general grading-duality assertion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The characteristic labels under orientation reversal or conjugation are paired by $k\mapsto-k$, equivalently $i\mapsto p-i$ modulo $p$. Their squares agree, so the two computations give exactly the asserted negation for the opposite orientation with the conjugate label. For $p=1$ the same computation has $k=-1$ and both correction terms zero. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Use the Ozsvath–Szabo orientation convention $L(p,1)$ given by positive $p$-surgery on the unknot and label its Spin$^c$ structures by $i\in\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, represented by $0\le i<p$. For every integer $p\ge1$,
$$d(L(p,1),i)=\frac{(2i-p)^2-p}{4p}.$$
For the opposite orientation the correction terms are negated, with the conjugate Spin$^c$ label understood.

## Statement references

[[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention|The lens-space surgery orientation]]

[[def-heegaard-floer-correction-term|The correction-term convention]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Absolutely Graded Floer Homologies and Intersection Forms for Four-Manifolds with Boundary*, Propositions 4.2 and 4.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0110170v1)

[Aceto and Golla, *Dehn Surgeries and Rational Homology Balls*, Proposition 3.5 and Remark 3.6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.07559v2)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-lens-space-q-one-triangles-and-cyclic-handle-maps]] supplies the explicit individual index-zero, basepoint-zero count-one triangles, their cyclic maps and Chern evaluation $k=2i-p$ on a generator of square $-p$.

[F2] [[lem-rational-heegaard-floer-absolute-grading-and-cobordism-maps]] constructs the absolute grading, with the sphere generator at degree zero, and proves the degree formula for these actual fixed-Spin$^c$ handle maps.

[F3] [[lem-heegaard-floer-correction-term-heegaard-invariance]] identifies the correction term as the bottom degree of the infinity image. The convention in the statement is [[def-lens-space-surgery-orientation-convention]].

## Proof

**Given:** $p\ge1$ and a label $0\le i<p$, with the torus diagrams and fixed triangle structures of [F1].

1.1 The alpha-gamma diagram, and the diagram with those two attaching curves reversed, each have one intersection in each Spin$^c$ structure. Their infinity differentials are zero: the Maslov index of a self-disk in a torsion Spin$^c$ structure is $2n_z$, so cannot be one. The minus lattice in each summand is therefore exactly $U\mathbb F_2[U][x_i,0]$, and its plus image has bottom $[x_i,0]$. Its correction term is the absolute grading of that generator, with no unknown exponent shift. [F1, F3]

1.2 For the negative-trace map from $S^3$ to $-L(p,1)$, the fixed triangle has index and basepoint multiplicity zero and count one. It sends the sphere generator at exponent zero to $[x_i,0]$. The four-dimensional data are $c_1^2=-k^2/p$, $\chi=1$ and $\sigma=-1$. Hence its degree is $D_i=(1-k^2/p)/4$, and $d(-L(p,1),i)=D_i$. This computes the negative orientation directly. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

1.3 The cyclically reordered triangle gives the actual fixed-structure map from $L(p,1)$ to $S^3$ and sends $[x_i,0]$ to the sphere generator at exponent zero. It is the same oriented triple four-manifold with the other sphere input filled, so it has the same degree $D_i$. Consequently $0=\operatorname{gr}[x_i,0]+D_i$, and $d(L(p,1),i)=-D_i=((2i-p)^2-p)/(4p)$. This argument uses an actual turned-around triangle map rather than a general grading-duality assertion. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

1.4 The characteristic labels under orientation reversal or conjugation are paired by $k\mapsto-k$, equivalently $i\mapsto p-i$ modulo $p$. Their squares agree, so the two computations give exactly the asserted negation for the opposite orientation with the conjugate label. For $p=1$ the same computation has $k=-1$ and both correction terms zero. [F1, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

## Statement

Let an oriented finite ideal triangulation of the interior of a compact connected orientable three-manifold have $k\ge1$ ideal vertices, each with torus link. Assign a positive ideal-tetrahedron shape to every tetrahedron. Suppose that around every finite edge the product of its incident complex shape parameters is $1$ and the sum of its dihedral angles is $2\pi$. For each ideal vertex $v$, choose a basis $(\alpha_v,\beta_v)$ of the fundamental group of its torus link and suppose the cusp multipliers satisfy $H(\alpha_v)=H(\beta_v)=1$. Then the face gluings define a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric on the manifold interior, with one rank-two cusp for each ideal vertex.

## Statement references

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, Theorem 0.1 and §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Diagram

Opposite edges of a normalized ideal tetrahedron carry the same shape parameter. The wire drawing records that convention only; all edge classes, products and angle sums in the proof are computed from the given face pairings, not from the drawing.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.0,line cap=round,line join=round]
  \coordinate (a) at (0,0);
  \coordinate (b) at (2,0);
  \coordinate (c) at (1,1.7);
  \coordinate (d) at (1,0.65);
  \draw[thick] (a)--(b)--(c)--cycle;
  \draw[thick,dashed] (d)--(a) (d)--(b) (d)--(c);
  \node[below left] at (a) {$0$};
  \node[below right] at (b) {$1$};
  \node[above] at (c) {$\infty$};
  \node[right] at (d) {$z$};
  \node at (1,-0.35) {$z$ on $01,\infty z$};
  \node at (2.9,0.95) {$z'$ on $0\infty,1z$};
  \node at (1.0,2.05) {$z''$ on $1\infty,0z$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite face-paired ideal triangulation, its positive shapes, all edge equations and angle sums, and a homology basis on each torus vertex link.

[F1] [[def-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-and-cusp-holonomy]]: a positive shape determines a nondegenerate ideal tetrahedron in $\mathbb H^3$, its corner factors, and the cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ along a path in a torus vertex link.

[F2] [[lem-ideal-tetrahedron-shape-parameter-relations]]: the argument of each positive shape parameter is the corresponding dihedral angle.

[F3] [[lem-ideal-torus-cusp-holonomy-criterion]]: for one torus vertex, edge products $1$, angle sums $2\pi$, and cusp multipliers $1$ on a fundamental-group basis imply a complete hyperbolic cusp.

[F4] [[lem-horocusp-truncation-has-finite-volume]]: a rank-two translation-lattice horocusp with Euclidean cross-section area $A$ has volume $A/2$.

[F5] [[def-pared-hyperbolic-structures-and-volume]]: a hyperbolic structure is a curvature $-1$ metric on the manifold interior, and a torus cusp is a horoball quotient by its peripheral subgroup.

## Proof

1.1 For each tetrahedron, [F1] supplies a nondegenerate ideal simplex, and the assigned face maps are hyperbolic isometries because their three corresponding ideal vertices have the same cross-ratio shape. Around a finite edge, the product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity the identity, while the angle sum $2\pi$ makes the total rotation one full turn. Thus the simplices glue to a smooth curvature $-1$ metric away from the ideal vertices. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Fix an ideal vertex $v$ and let $T_v$ be its torus link. Truncate the corners at $v$ by small horospheres. The resulting finite collection of Euclidean corner triangles triangulates $T_v$, and the face identifications restrict to Euclidean similarities. At a vertex of this link triangulation, corresponding to an incident edge of the ideal triangulation, the edge-shape product equation makes the accumulated complex similarity equal to $1$, while the $2\pi$ angle sum makes the total cone angle exactly $2\pi$. Thus the link similarity structure has no cone singularities. For a loop $\gamma$ on $T_v$, the linear part of its similarity holonomy is the multiplier $H_v(\gamma)$: crossing a corner contributes its shape factor or reciprocal according to the side traversed. The two assumed basis multipliers are $1$, so this linear part is the identity for every loop in $\pi_1(T_v)$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. This is the local cusp argument underlying [F3], carried out separately on every link; the one-vertex Statement of [F3] is not applied to the full triangulation. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 A horospherical truncation of each ideal tetrahedron is compact and has finite volume because its smooth hyperbolic volume density is bounded on that compact region. Each removed vertex tail is contained in a rank-two horocusp and has finite volume by [F4]. There are finitely many tetrahedra and vertices, so the glued manifold has finite total volume. [given, F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The part remaining after all cusp neighborhoods are removed is a compact union of truncated tetrahedra. Let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence. If infinitely many terms lie in that compact part, a subsequence converges there and the Cauchy property forces the whole sequence to the same limit. Otherwise the sequence eventually lies in the union of the finitely many disjoint cusp ends; sufficiently deep points in distinct ends have positive separation through the compact core, so the Cauchy property forces it eventually into one end, where it converges by step 2.1. Thus the full metric is complete. Together with step 3.2 and the curvature $-1$ charts from step 1.1, this is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic structure as defined in [F5]. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.2, construct] ∎

## Sources

[William P. Thurston, *The Geometry and Topology of Three-Manifolds*, Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.5](https://library.slmath.org/nonmsri/gt3m/PDF/4.pdf)

[Petronio and Porti, *Negatively Oriented Ideal Triangulations and a Proof of Thurston’s Hyperbolic Dehn Filling Theorem*, Theorem 0.1 and §§1–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9901045)

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be a solid torus. Every connected, two-sided, properly embedded incompressible and boundary-incompressible surface $F\subset V$ with nonempty boundary is a disk, either a meridian disk or a boundary-parallel disk. In particular, if $F$ is not boundary-parallel, it is a meridian disk. Any two smooth meridian disks with the same boundary admit a smooth isotopy of embeddings relative to that boundary, with a boundary-fixing topological ambient extension. If both disks are neat, this can be a smooth ambient isotopy relative to the boundary. In addition, every two-sided embedded torus $T\subset\operatorname{int}V$ has a compressing disk in $V$.

## Statement references

[Allen Hatcher, *Notes on Basic 3-Manifold Topology*, Example preceding Lemma 1.10](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/3M/3M.pdf)

[Walter Neumann and Gadde Swarup, *Canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9712227)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the standard smooth solid torus $V$, the connected two-sided proper surface $F$ with nonempty boundary and the two disk-obstruction hypotheses; and, for the last assertion, an embedded two-sided torus $T$ in its interior.

[A1] Full AC is [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and implies countable choice ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], Statement; [[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] The disk obstructions and product definition of boundary-parallelity are [[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition.

[F2] Every smooth sphere in $S^3$ bounds smooth balls on both sides ([[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], Statement).

[F3] A smooth sphere boundary map extends over parametrized balls, as a product in their smaller boundary collars ([[lem-smooth-sphere-diffeomorphisms-extend-over-balls]], Statement). Smooth disk boundary maps extend retaining prescribed collars ([[lem-smooth-jordan-disk-boundary-maps-extend-to-diffeomorphisms]], Statement).

[F4] Essential torus circles in the same primitive class admit smooth finite bigon reductions and parallel-strip parameters ([[lem-relative-smooth-mapping-classes-of-annulus-and-torus]], Proof 1.1–2.1). Disk pushes across a ball have a smooth cap sweep with fixed boundary circle, explicitly parametrized in [[lem-gluing-irreducible-smooth-three-manifolds-across-injective-annuli]], Proof 3.1.

[F5] Finite relative general position and smooth ambient extension are [[lem-relative-transversality-for-embedded-surfaces]] and [[thm-isotopy-extension]], Statements.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $V=S^1\times D^2$ be a solid torus. Every connected, two-sided, properly embedded incompressible and boundary-incompressible surface $F\subset V$ with nonempty boundary is a disk, either a meridian disk or a boundary-parallel disk. In particular, if $F$ is not boundary-parallel, it is a meridian disk. Any two smooth meridian disks with the same boundary admit a smooth isotopy of embeddings relative to that boundary, with a boundary-fixing topological ambient extension. If both disks are neat, this can be a smooth ambient isotopy relative to the boundary. In addition, every two-sided embedded torus $T\subset\operatorname{int}V$ has a compressing disk in $V$.

## Statement

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $g\geq0$ and let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ satisfy $\det(V-V^T)=\pm1$, where the empty skew matrix has determinant $1$. There is a connected compact smooth oriented surface $F\subset S^3$ with one boundary component and an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ whose positive-push Seifert matrix is exactly $V$.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix of a chosen oriented surface and basis]]

[[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection|The skew part of a Seifert matrix is its surface intersection form]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an integer $2g\times2g$ matrix $V$ with unimodular alternating part $J=V-V^T$.

[A1] Full AC is the choice-function axiom assumed by the knot Seifert-pairing convention and the supplied transversality interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For a knot Seifert matrix, $V-V^T$ is the unimodular oriented intersection matrix of the chosen surface. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F2] For disjoint oriented curves in a regular diagram, linking is one half the signed mixed-crossing sum. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F3] The positive-push entry is $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]]

## Proof

1.1 If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$. [given, construct, induction]

2.1 Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$. [F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot. [F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The diagram records the positive oriented clasp between the positive push-off of one band core and the other core. At the left crossing the blue strand is over; at the right crossing the red strand is over. With both arrows oriented as shown, the two mixed crossing signs are positive, so their half-sum changes the linking number by $+1$; reversing both local crossing conventions gives $-1$. The proof uses the crossing formula and finite local modifications, not the drawing.

  \draw[thick,blue,->] (0.92,0) -- (2,0);
  \draw[thick,red,->] (-1.2,-1) -- (-0.72,-0.16);
  \draw[thick,red] (-0.68,0.16) .. controls (-0.35,0.9) and (0.25,0.9) .. (0.7,0);
  \draw[thick,red,->] (0.7,0) .. controls (0.92,-0.4) .. (1.2,-1);
  \node[blue] at (-1.35,0.28) {$a_i^+$};
  \node[red] at (-1.45,-0.78) {$a_j$};
  \node at (-0.7,0.48) {$+$};
  \node at (0.7,0.48) {$+$};
  \node at (0,-1.35) {oriented clasp};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Statement

Assume full AC for the knot Seifert-pairing convention. Let $V\in M_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be an invertible Seifert matrix and put $B=V+V^T$ and $T=V^{-1}V^T$ on $\mathbb Q^{2g}$. Then $B$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T$ is an invertible $B$-isometry, and $I-T$ is invertible; hence $(\mathbb Q^{2g},B,T)$ is a rational Seifert isometric structure.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push integral Seifert matrix]]

[[def-integral-witt-and-seifert-isometric-structures|The definition of a rational Seifert isometric structure]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and an invertible integral Seifert matrix $V$.

[A1] Full AC is the stated hypothesis of the Seifert-pairing interface. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For a knot Seifert matrix, $V-V^T$ is the unimodular surface intersection matrix. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F2] A rational Seifert isometric structure has a nonsingular symmetric form $B$, an invertible $B$-isometry $T$, and invertible $I-T$. [[def-integral-witt-and-seifert-isometric-structures]]

## Proof

1.1 The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives $$ T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B, $$ because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full-data conductivity and Schrödinger DN maps]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

[[lem-ip-smooth-manifold-elliptic-nonresonant-regularity|Nonresonant Schrödinger solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the weak DN-map well-posedness suppliers [F2]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the weak DN-map well-posedness suppliers [F2]--[F3].

**Given:** the compact smooth Riemannian domain, two positive conductivities or two real nonresonant potentials, and arbitrary smooth complex boundary values $f_1,f_2$.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the conductivity DN map is the weak boundary form of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_g)$, and the Schrödinger DN map is the weak boundary form of $-\Delta_g+q$; their smooth-data fluxes use $\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$ and $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$, respectively.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected open set with smooth boundary, let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ satisfy $c|\xi|^2\le\xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\le C|\xi|^2$ for fixed $0<c\le C<\infty$, and let $f\in\mathcal B_\Omega=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the boundary trace-data class defined by the anisotropic weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. Then there is a unique $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and $\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla v\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. The energy formula defining $\Lambda_\gamma$ is independent of the chosen representative of its second boundary argument and is a bounded bilinear form on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-anisotropic-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]

[[thm-lax-milgram]]

[[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

[[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]]

[[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration|Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice]]

[Salo, §1, pp. 170–171](https://library.slmath.org/books/Book60/files/30salo.pdf)

[Daudé, Kamran, and Nicoleau, §1, PDF pp. 1–2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.00910)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice; a bounded connected smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$; a symmetric coefficient $\gamma$ with constants $0<c\le C$ as in the statement; the boundary quotient $\mathcal B_\Omega=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$; and a class $f\in\mathcal B_\Omega$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice; it supplies the Choice assumption of the published Sobolev completeness and trace interfaces used in the boundary-data definition. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] $\mathcal B_\Omega$ is $H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$, where $H^1=W^{1,2}$ and $H_0^1$ is the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; the map $\Lambda_\gamma$ uses the weak solution and the energy pairing in the definition. ([[def-ip-anisotropic-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]])

[F2] If $\Omega$ is bounded in one direction and $w\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, then $\|w\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)(b-a)\|Dw\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for a slab $a<x\cdot e<b$ containing $\Omega$. ([[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]])

[F3] Under the Axiom of Choice, $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ with its Sobolev norm is a complete normed space; in particular $H^1(\Omega)$ is complete, and its closed subspace $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is complete. ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]])

[F4] Under Countable Choice, a bounded coercive real bilinear form on a real Hilbert space has a unique solution to each bounded linear functional equation. ([[thm-lax-milgram]])

[F5] The Axiom of Choice implies Countable Choice. ([[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

[F6] The coefficient inequalities give $|\gamma(x)\xi|\le C|\xi|$ and $\xi^T\gamma(x)\xi\ge c|\xi|^2$ for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$.

**Choice use:** Countable Choice is used by [F4]. The Axiom of Choice is also carried by [F3] and the trace-data interface [F1]; no family of representatives is selected in the proof.

## Proof

1.1 The space $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a closed linear subspace of the complete space $H^1(\Omega)$ by [F1] and [F3]. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, it lies in a slab $a<x\cdot e<b$ for some unit vector $e$ and finite $a<b$; applying [F2] with $p=2$ gives $\|v\|_{L^2}\le C(2)(b-a)\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Thus $\|v\|_H:=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is a norm equivalent to the inherited $H^1$ norm, and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a real Hilbert space for $(v,w)_H=\int_\Omega\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\,dx$. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Fix any representative $U\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $f$; the existence argument below is independent of which representative is fixed. On $H_0^1(\Omega)$ define $a_\gamma(z,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla z\cdot\nabla v\,dx$ and $F_U(v)=-\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla U\cdot\nabla v\,dx$. By [F6], $a_\gamma$ is bounded by $C\|z\|_H\|v\|_H$, coercive by $c\|z\|_H^2$, and $F_U$ is bounded by $C\|\nabla U\|_{L^2}\|v\|_H$. Countable Choice follows from [F5], so [F4] gives a unique $z\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $a_\gamma(z,v)=F_U(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Then $u_{\gamma,f}:=U+z$ has quotient class $f$ and satisfies the stated weak equation. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u_1,u_2$ are two weak solutions with boundary class $f$, then $w=u_1-u_2\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla w\cdot\nabla v\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Taking $v=w$ and using [F6] gives $c\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}^2\le0$, so $\|w\|_H=0$ and hence $w=0$ by the norm property in step 1.1. [F6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Let $h\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and let $V,V'$ be any two representatives of $h$. Their difference lies in $H_0^1(\Omega)$ by [F1], so the weak equation for $u_{\gamma,f}$ gives $\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla(V-V')\,dx=0$. Therefore the energy pairing is independent of the representative of $h$. [F1, step 2.1]

4.1 The weak solution minimizes the quadratic energy in its boundary class: if $W$ is any representative of $f$, then $W-u_{\gamma,f}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, and expanding the square with the weak equation gives $\int_\Omega\gamma|\nabla W|^2\,dx=\int_\Omega\gamma|\nabla u_{\gamma,f}|^2\,dx+\int_\Omega\gamma|\nabla(W-u_{\gamma,f})|^2\,dx$. Using [F6] and taking the infimum over representatives yields $\|\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{C/c}\,\|f\|_{\mathcal B_\Omega}$. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra] To prove bilinearity, for $f_1,f_2\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, the function $a u_{\gamma,f_1}+b u_{\gamma,f_2}$ has boundary class $af_1+bf_2$ and satisfies the weak equation by linearity of the quotient map and of the integral. Uniqueness from step 3.1 therefore gives $u_{\gamma,af_1+bf_2}=a u_{\gamma,f_1}+b u_{\gamma,f_2}$. For $h_1,h_2\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, representatives $V_{h_1},V_{h_2}$ give $aV_{h_1}+bV_{h_2}$ as a representative of $ah_1+bh_2$; representative independence from step 3.2 and linearity of the integral show that the energy pairing is linear in its second argument as well. Thus the energy form is bilinear, and the bound just proved makes it a bounded bilinear form on $\mathcal B_\Omega\times\mathcal B_\Omega$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element with Borel law $\mu$. Let $C:B^*\to B$ be its covariance operator, let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/\ker C$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=m(C\ell)$, and let $i:E\to B$ be the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. For every $h\in E$ and $r>0$,
$$ \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x-ih\|_B\le r\}\bigr)\le \mu\bigl(\{x\in B:\|x\|_B\le r\}\bigr). $$

## Statement references

[[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space|a centered Borel Gaussian is Borel measurable and has centered normal continuous-linear projections]]

[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs|the covariance operator and covariance-induced Hilbert space]]

[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined|the canonical Cameron–Martin injection is continuous and injective]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, HB, countable choice, a real separable Banach space $B$, a centered Borel Gaussian random element $W$, its covariance operator $C$, and its covariance-induced Hilbert space $E$ with canonical injection $i$.

[A1] AC is assumed by the finite-dimensional Gaussian-centering result used below. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] HB and countable choice supply the countable norming family used to recover the Banach norm from scalar coordinates. [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] $W$ is Borel measurable, each $\ell(W)$ is centered normal, and every finite vector of continuous-linear coordinates is a possibly degenerate multivariate normal vector. [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]], [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F2] $E$ is the completion of $B^*/\ker C$, the map $i$ extends $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$, and $\ell(ih)=\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E$. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F3] There are $\ell_j\in B^*$ with $\|x\|_B=\sup_j|\ell_j(x)|$ for every $x\in B$. [[lem-separable-banach-has-countable-norming-family]]

[F4] For a nondegenerate finite-dimensional centered Gaussian vector, every bounded symmetric loss with convex sublevel sets has minimum expectation at the center. Applying this to the indicator of the complement of a closed symmetric convex set gives the Gaussian shift inequality for that set. [[lem-gaussian-centering-for-bounded-symmetric-quasiconvex-loss]]

[F5] For a finite measure, probabilities of a decreasing sequence of measurable sets converge to the probability of their intersection. [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** compare finite collections of norming coordinates by finite-dimensional Gaussian centering, then pass to the norm ball by continuity from above.

1.1 Choose the norming family from [F3]. Fix $r>0$, $h\in E$, and $n\ge1$. Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, choose]

2.1 In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields $$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$ If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality. [A1, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound. [F3, F5, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, let $\gamma,\widetilde\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, let $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, and let $\xi_0\in T_{x_0}^*\partial\Omega$ have unit norm in the induced boundary metric. Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$
have boundary values $\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\phi}\chi$, where $\phi$ is real with $|d\phi|=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, have $H^1(\Omega)$ norms bounded above and below by positive constants, and satisfy
$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$
The same limit holds with $v_{\lambda,\gamma},v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ replaced by their exact corrections.

## Statement references

[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts|Smooth Euclidean boundary charts]]

[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal|Outward normal and boundary distance]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

**Given:** the smooth bounded domain, positive smooth conductivities, a boundary point and unit tangential covector, and a cutoff equal to one near that point.

[F1] [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: a smooth boundary has local smooth charts flattening it, and a neighborhood of the compact boundary is smoothly parametrized by inward normal distance.

[F2] [[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds-with-boundary]]: a finite smooth partition of unity can localize and patch the chartwise constructions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: a positive smooth conductivity has a unique weak Dirichlet solution for each $H^{1/2}$ boundary value, and its zero-trace Poincare inequality holds.

[F4] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: the exact corrections are measured in the chartwise $H^1$ norm and the zero-trace space is the closure of compactly supported smooth functions.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set $$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$ For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives $$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$ where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and $L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$. The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 2.1. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 2.1 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 3.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives $$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$ Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$. [F1, F2, given, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]: $$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$ If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives $$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$ uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, let $\gamma,\widetilde\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, let $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, and let $\xi_0\in T_{x_0}^*\partial\Omega$ have unit norm in the induced boundary metric. Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$
have boundary values $\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\phi}\chi$, where $\phi$ is real with $|d\phi|=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, have $H^1(\Omega)$ norms bounded above and below by positive constants, and satisfy
$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$
The same limit holds with $v_{\lambda,\gamma},v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ replaced by their exact corrections.

## Statement references

[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal|Outward normal and boundary distance]]

[[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness|Positive conductivity weak solvability]]

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is a hypothesis of the positive-conductivity solvability supplier [F3]; it is used only for the exact correction.

**Given:** the smooth bounded domain, positive smooth conductivities, a boundary point and unit tangential covector, and a cutoff equal to one near that point.

[F1] [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] and [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]: a smooth boundary has local smooth charts flattening it, and a neighborhood of the compact boundary is smoothly parametrized by inward normal distance.

[F2] [[thm-smooth-partitions-of-unity-exist-on-manifolds-with-boundary]]: a finite smooth partition of unity can localize and patch the chartwise constructions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-conductivity-map-wellposedness]]: a positive smooth conductivity has a unique weak Dirichlet solution for each $H^{1/2}$ boundary value, and its zero-trace Poincare inequality holds.

[F4] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: the exact corrections are measured in the chartwise $H^1$ norm and the zero-trace space is the closure of compactly supported smooth functions.

Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it. [F1, given, construct]

1.2 In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set
$$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$
For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$. $$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$

$$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$
Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. 2.3 Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]:
$$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$
If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, step 2.2, algebra]

3.1 In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives
$$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$
uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. $$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$
whose constant is strictly positive. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. 3.3 The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 2.3, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 2.2. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $d=2$ with the conductivity class $X_2(R)$ of the Calderón admissible class. For $\gamma\in X_2(R)$ let $\widetilde{\gamma-1}$ be the zero extension of $\gamma-1$ from $\Omega$ to $\mathbb R^2$ and set $\gamma_e:=1+\widetilde{\gamma-1}$. Define $B:=\max\{1,M,m^{-1}\}$. There is a constant $C_1$ depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R$ such that
$$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_1|h|\qquad(h\in\mathbb R^2).$$
For every finite $p>2B$ there is $C_p<\infty$, depending only on $\Omega,m,M,R,p$, such that
$$\sup_{\gamma\in X_2(R)}\ \sup_{|h|\le t}\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_p t^{1/p}\qquad(t\ge0).$$
The extension is an almost-everywhere measurable class; no pointwise continuity is asserted.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class|The BV class, bounds and measurable background extension.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|The distributional total-variation convention.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-extension-and-translation|The zero-extension variation bound and full-space translation inequality.]]

[[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn|The translation operator on almost-everywhere function classes.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; $\gamma\in X_2(R)$; $h\in\mathbb R^2$; and $p>2B$.

[F1] $m\le\gamma\le M$ almost everywhere, $\gamma=1$ almost everywhere on $\Omega\setminus\Omega'$, and $TV(\gamma;\Omega)\le R$. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]], [[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv]])

[F2] If $u\in BV(\Omega)$ on a bounded Lipschitz domain, then its zero extension lies in $BV(\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|\widetilde u\|_1+TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)\le C_\Omega(\|u\|_1+TV(u;\Omega))$, and $\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_1\le |h|TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$ for $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$. ([[lem-ip-bv-extension-and-translation]])

[F3] Translation preserves almost-everywhere classes and constants. ([[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed for the BV extension and translation supplier. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and $\gamma\in X_2(R)$.

1.1 Set $u:=\gamma-1$ on $\Omega$. Since constants have zero distributional derivative, [F1] gives $u\in BV(\Omega)$, $TV(u;\Omega)=TV(\gamma;\Omega)\le R$, and $\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\le |\Omega|(M+1)$. The smooth bounded domain $\Omega$ is Lipschitz, so [F2] applies. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 By the zero-extension part of [F2], $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and $$TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)\le C_\Omega\bigl(|\Omega|(M+1)+R\bigr)=:V_0.$$ Since $\gamma_e=1+\widetilde u$, [F3] gives $\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_1=\|\widetilde u(\cdot+h)-\widetilde u\|_1\le V_0|h|$. Thus the first inequality holds with $C_1=V_0$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The bound $m\le\gamma\le M$ inside $\Omega$ and the background value $1$ outside show $|\gamma_e|\le B$ almost everywhere; hence $|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e|\le2B$ almost everywhere. Applying [F3] and step 2.1 yields $$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_p^p\le(2B)^{p-1}V_0|h|.$$ Taking $p$-th roots and then the supremum over $|h|\le t$ gives the second inequality with $C_p=((2B)^{p-1}V_0)^{1/p}$. At $t=0$ both sides vanish. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected smooth domain, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$ and $R>0$. For every $\gamma,\gamma_0\in X_d(R)$ there exist constants $C>0$, $\rho>0$ and $t_0\in(0,1)$, depending only on $d,\alpha,\Omega,\Omega',m,M,R$, such that
$$\|\gamma-\gamma_0\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\,\omega\!\left(\|\dot{\Lambda}_\gamma-\dot{\Lambda}_{\gamma_0}\|_{\mathcal L(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1,(\mathcal D(\Omega)/\mathbb C\mathbf1)^*)}\right),$$
where $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the trace quotient and $\dot\Lambda_\gamma$ is the induced weak Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on the constant quotient, and
$$\omega(0):=0,\qquad \omega(t):=\left[\log\!\left(\frac1{\min\{t,t_0\}}\right)\right]^{-\rho}\quad(t>0).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice, the fixed parameters in the statement, and $\gamma_1=\gamma$, $\gamma_2=\gamma_0$ in $X_d(R)$.

[F1] Fixed-collar extension preserves global $C^{1,\alpha}$ bounds, ellipticity, and support of $\gamma_j-1$ in $\overline{\Omega'}$. ([[def-ip-calderon-admissible-conductivity-class]], [[lem-ip-calderon-fixed-collar-c1alpha-extension]])

[F2] Weak conductivity solutions and their energy-form DN maps are well-defined, and the full trace-space norm of their difference equals its constant-quotient norm. The rough Alessandrini identity holds. ([[def-ip-calderon-weak-dn-map-for-bounded-conductivities]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-dn-map-wellposedness]], [[lem-ip-calderon-rough-alessandrini-and-quotient-norm]])

[F3] The cutoff estimates give local $L^2$ and gradient bounds $Cs^{-1/2}$ and $Cs^{1/2}$ from the homogeneous positive-half norm, and bounded cutoff maps between the negative-half norms. ([[lem-ip-calderon-bourgain-cutoff-estimates]])

[F4] For a compactly supported $C^{0,\alpha}$ vector field $a=\nabla\log\gamma$, the potential $q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}a+\tfrac14|a|^2$ admits null-phase CGO solutions $U_\zeta=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta)$ with $\|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. If $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$, the circle-and-scale average of either squared norm is at most $C(1+(1+|k|^2)/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$. ([[lem-ip-calderon-rough-potential-cgo-construction]], [[lem-ip-calderon-averaged-negative-bourgain-estimate]])

[F5] Plancherel identifies the $H^1(\mathbb R^d)$ norm with $\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{1/2}\widehat v\|_2$ in the unitary angular-frequency convention; zero-boundary functions on a bounded ball satisfy Poincaré. Smooth compactly supported functions are dense in $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d)$. ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-poincare-inequality-for-w-one-p-zero]], [[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed at the stated Sobolev, weak-solution and Fourier interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $\nabla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-\nabla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vw\rangle=-\int\nabla g_j\cdot\nabla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},\nabla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. A solution $U_j$ of the Schrödinger form equation therefore gives a weak conductivity solution $u_j$: test the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density. Subtracting the two Schrödinger forms for solutions $U_1,U_2$, or repeating the weak-solution subtraction in [F2], gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2\rangle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. Here $f_j$ is the trace class of $u_j$, and the conjugation converts the sesquilinear DN convention to the bilinear interior form. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2\rangle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. We first prove the modulated cutoff bound used for each linear remainder term. Let $u$ be Schwartz and write the Fourier convolution for $\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u$ with $h=\xi-\eta-k$. The symbol comparison and characteristic-sphere estimate proved in [F3] give, uniformly in the center $y$, $\int\langle\xi-y\rangle^{-L}(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})\,d\xi\le C_L$ for sufficiently large $L$, and $s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$, where $D_\zeta$ is distance to the characteristic sphere of $p_\zeta$. Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$. Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. 6.1 Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$. [step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $\nabla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H\nabla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $\nabla\log H\cdot\nabla w$. 9.1 Combine steps 7.1–8.1 for $0\le\delta<t_0$, reducing $t_0$ below $1/2$ if necessary. For $\delta\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. This is precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. Every bound used only the fixed class parameters, the geometry and $d,\alpha$, and the zero-data case was proved in step 8.1. [F1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply
 $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$.
Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention. [F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. For the divergence field $f=a_1-a_2$, split $f=\rho_h*f+(f-\rho_h*f)$ with a fixed nonnegative unit-mass mollifier. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. Substituting step 5.1 in step 6.1 therefore gives $\mathcal Q\le C[\delta e^{D t^A}+t^{-\beta}]$ for a fixed $D>0$, after absorbing the polynomial factor $t^{d/2}\lambda^2$ into the exponential. For sufficiently small $0<\delta<t_0$, take $t=(\log(1/\delta)/(2D))^{1/A}\ge1$. The first term becomes $\sqrt\delta$, and the second is $C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\beta/A}$. The former is bounded by a constant times the latter, since $e^{-x/2}x^{\beta/A}$ is bounded for $x\ge1$. Hence $\mathcal Q\le C[\log(1/\delta)]^{-\rho}$ with $\rho=\beta/A>0$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$. [step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $\nabla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H\nabla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $\nabla\log H\cdot\nabla w$. Test this identity with $w$ to obtain $\int H|\nabla w|^2=-\langle Q,Hw\rangle$. The test is legitimate by $H^1$ approximation, since $Q$ is an $L^2$ field plus a divergence of an $L^2$ field and $Hw\in H_0^1(B)$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle Q,Hw\rangle|\le\mathcal Q\|Hw\|_{H^1(\mathbb R^d)}\le C\mathcal Q\|w\|_{H^1(B)}$. Since $H\ge m_*>0$, Poincaré in [F5] implies $\|w\|_{H^1(B)}\le C\mathcal Q$; if this norm is zero the estimate is immediate, otherwise divide the resulting quadratic inequality by it. Finally the mean value theorem on the bounded interval of possible $\log g_j$ gives $|\gamma_1-\gamma_2|=|e^{2\log g_1}-e^{2\log g_2}|\le2\max\{M,1\}|w|$. Thus $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C\mathcal Q$. In particular $\delta=0$ forces equality of the coefficients. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 Combine steps 7.1–8.1 for $0\le\delta<t_0$, reducing $t_0$ below $1/2$ if necessary. For $\delta\ge t_0$, use $\|\gamma_1-\gamma_2\|_2\le2M|\Omega|^{1/2}$ and enlarge $C$ to at least $2M|\Omega|^{1/2}[\log(1/t_0)]^\rho$. This is precisely the saturated modulus in the statement. Every bound used only the fixed class parameters, the geometry and $d,\alpha$, and the zero-data case was proved in step 8.1. [F1, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎
