## Statement

Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$ and $1\le s\le n$, and let $h\in\mathbb R^n$ use one-based coordinate labels $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with label $j$ corresponding to library coordinate $j-1$. In real scalar expressions, a natural number denotes its canonical real image. Order the coordinates by decreasing $|h_j|$, breaking ties by increasing $j$. Let $S$ consist of the first $s$ indices, and partition $S^c$ in this same order into consecutive nonempty blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$ of size $s$, with only the last block possibly smaller; if $S^c=\varnothing$, take $q=0$. Then
$$\|h_{S^c}\|_2\le \|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-nullspace-property|One-based finite coordinate restrictions]]

[[def-p-norms-on-rn|Finite-dimensional one- and two-norms]]

[[def-canonical-natural|Canonical real image of the natural scalar $s$]]

[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics|Triangle inequality for the finite-dimensional two-norm]]

[[lem-of-naturals-positive|Positivity and strict increase of canonical natural scalars]]

[Foucart and Rauhut, *A Mathematical Introduction to Compressive Sensing*, §4.3, proof of Theorem 4.25, printed pp. 89–90](https://www.mat.uniroma2.it/~speleers/cime2024/material/book_rauhut.pdf)

[Mendelson, Rauhut, and Ward, *Improved Bounds for Sparse Recovery from Subsampled Random Convolutions*, §2.1, Theorem 2.2, printed p. 5](https://www.mathc.rwth-aachen.de/~rauhut/files/circulant-independent.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Integers $n\ge1$, $1\le s\le n$, a vector $h\in\mathbb R^n$, the deterministic ordered coordinate list $j_1,\ldots,j_n$, its first-$s$ set $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, and the finite successive tail blocks $T_1,\ldots,T_q$.

[F1] [[def-ip-nullspace-property]]: $h_S$ agrees with $h$ on $S$ and is zero on $S^c$; the coordinate labels are one-based with label $j$ identified with library coordinate $j-1$.

[F2] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: $\|v\|_1=\sum_j|v_j|$ and $\|v\|_2=(\sum_j|v_j|^2)^{1/2}$ on finite-dimensional real coordinate spaces.

[F3] [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]: $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm and obeys the triangle inequality.

[F4] [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]: finite sums preserve termwise inequalities and a sum of nonnegative terms is nonnegative.

[F5] [[lem-of-square-monotone]]: for nonnegative $a,b$, $a^2\le b^2$ implies $a\le b$.

[F6] [[def-canonical-natural]]: a natural number used as a real scalar denotes its canonical real image.

[F7] [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: the canonical real image of $s$ is positive for $s\ge1$; if $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers, then their canonical real images satisfy $k_r\le s$.

## Proof
1.1 If $q=0$, then $S^c=\varnothing$ and the conclusion is $0\le\|h_S\|_2$. If $q\ge1$, write $r=|T_1|\le s$. The order gives $T_1=\{j_{s+1},\ldots,j_{s+r}\}$ and $S=\{j_1,\ldots,j_s\}$, with $|h_{j_{s+k}}|\le|h_{j_k}|$ for every $1\le k\le r$. Termwise squaring and finite-sum monotonicity therefore give $\|h_{T_1}\|_2^2=\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_{s+k}}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^r|h_{j_k}|^2\le\sum_{k=1}^s|h_{j_k}|^2=\|h_S\|_2^2.$ Both norms are nonnegative, so [F5] gives $\|h_{T_1}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2$. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 For each $2\le r\le q$, the preceding block $T_{r-1}$ has size $s$. Its last ordered coordinate has magnitude no greater than any earlier entry, hence no greater than the average magnitude on $T_{r-1}$. Every entry of $T_r$ is no greater than that last entry. Put $c=\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1/s$. Then each entry of $T_r$ has magnitude at most $c$. If $k_r=|T_r|$, termwise comparison gives $$\|h_{T_r}\|_2^2=\sum_{j\in T_r}|h_j|^2\le k_r c^2\le s c^2=\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1^2}{s},$$ using $k_r\le s$ as natural numbers: padding the sum of $k_r$ copies of the nonnegative number $c^2$ by the remaining nonnegative copies gives the sum of $s$ copies, by [F4]; [F6,F7] interpret these counts as real scalars. Since both sides are nonnegative, [F5] gives $\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\frac{\|h_{T_{r-1}}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ The blocks are disjoint and finite. By [F6], [F7], the triangle inequality, step 1.1, and this block bound, $\|h_{S^c}\|_2=\Big\|\sum_{r=1}^q h_{T_r}\Big\|_2\le\sum_{r=1}^q\|h_{T_r}\|_2\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac1{\sqrt{s}}\sum_{r=1}^{q-1}\|h_{T_r}\|_1\le\|h_S\|_2+\frac{\|h_{S^c}\|_1}{\sqrt{s}}.$ This proves the claimed estimate, including a final block smaller than $s$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The tie-breaking rule makes the block partition deterministic. The proof uses only finite coordinate comparisons and the Euclidean triangle inequality; no choice axiom is used.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a
finite or countable complete orthonormal basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$. For each finite
$F\subseteq J$, define the coordinate map
$\pi_F:H\to\mathbb R^F$ by
$\pi_F(x)=(\langle x,e_j\rangle)_{j\in F}$. If $\nu$ and $\nu'$ are Borel

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain|Fixed-atlas Sobolev and trace spaces]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Rellich compactness and abstract Fredholm suppliers used in steps 2.1 and 3.1.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function; this is assumed by the Lax--Milgram, partition, and trace suppliers used in steps 1.1 and 4.1.

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact smooth Riemannian domain; a real smooth potential with trivial Dirichlet kernel; $F\in L^2(M)$; and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H_0^1(M)$ is the closure of compactly supported interior smooth functions in $H^1(M)$; the boundary space $H^{1/2}$ is defined by finite chartwise Euclidean $W^{1/2,2}$ norms.

[F2] [[thm-lax-milgram]]: a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space has a unique weak solution.

[F3] [[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-zero-to-lp]]: on a bounded Euclidean open set, $W_0^{1,2}$ is compactly embedded in $L^2$.

[F4] [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]]: for compact $K$ on a Banach space, $I-K$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and then it is boundedly invertible.

[F5] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: a smooth bounded Euclidean domain has a bounded right inverse from its $H^{1/2}$ boundary space to $H^1$.

[F6] [[thm-higher-order-boundary-regularity-for-dirichlet-problems]]: a zero-trace weak solution of a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain gains two derivatives, with the stated $H^{m+2}$ estimate.

## Proof

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 Choose a real constant $Q>1+\|q\|_{L^\infty(M)}$ and let $A=-\Delta_g+Q$ on $H_0^1(M)$, with form $a(w,z)=\int_M(g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)+Qw\bar z)\,dV_g$. The form is bounded and coercive in the chartwise $H^1$ norm, so [F2] gives a bounded inverse $A_D^{-1}:(H_0^1(M))^*\to H_0^1(M)$. [A2, given, F1, F2]

2.1 Multiplication by $Q-q$ maps $H_0^1(M)$ boundedly to $L^2(M)$, and the inclusion $H_0^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: localize with the finite atlas and partition, apply [F3] on each bounded chart piece (using zero extension at a boundary face), then extract a finite diagonal subsequence and sum the localized limits. Hence $K:=A_D^{-1}(Q-q)$ is compact on $H_0^1(M)$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $w\in H_0^1(M)$, $(I-K)w=0$ is equivalent, after applying $A$, to $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$. The latter has only the zero solution by hypothesis, so $I-K$ is injective. By [F4], $I-K$ is boundedly invertible. This gives a unique weak zero-trace solution for every bounded functional on $H_0^1(M)$, in particular for every $F\in L^2(M)$ after subtracting any fixed boundary lift. [A1, F4, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A finite collection of flattened boundary charts, the collar neighborhood, and [F5] give a bounded extension $E:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^1(M)$ with trace $f$. Set $u=Ef+w$ and solve for $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with weak right-hand-side functional $z\mapsto\int_MF\bar z\,dV_g-a_q(Ef,z)$ by step 3.1. This proves existence for the stated data. The difference of any two solutions has zero trace and lies in the assumed trivial kernel, proving uniqueness. [A2, F1, F5, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 First take zero boundary data and $F\in L^2$. In each interior chart the operator has smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form coefficients $|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}$; in each boundary chart the collar flattens the boundary and the pulled-back coefficients remain smooth and uniformly elliptic. Applying the $m=0$ case of [F6] to localized zero-trace equations gives $u\in H^2$ and the estimate with the additional $L^2$ term. If $f$ is smooth, extend it smoothly in a boundary collar by keeping its chart representative constant in the normal variable near the boundary and multiplying by a cutoff; a finite partition patches these extensions to a smooth $Ef$. Then $w=u-Ef$ has zero trace and solves an equation with smooth datum, so the same local estimates apply to $w$. [F1, F6, step 4.1]

6.1 If $u\in H^{k+1}$ and $F\in H^k$, differentiating the localized zero-trace equation $k$ times leaves the same uniformly elliptic principal part; each commutator contains a bounded derivative of a smooth coefficient and a derivative of $u$ of order at most $k+1$, so it belongs to $L^2$. Tangential derivatives retain zero trace. Applying [F6] at order $k$ on each boundary patch and the corresponding interior estimate gives $u\in H^{k+2}$ and $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k(\|F\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2})$. The bounded inverse in step 3.1 controls $\|u\|_{H^1}$ by $\|F\|_{L^2}$ for zero trace; hence the local estimate and this inverse bound give $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$. Induction gives the claimed zero-trace estimate; for smooth nonzero $f$ apply the same induction to $u-Ef$. [F1, F6, step 3.1, step 5.1, induction] ∎

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the compact smooth Riemannian domain; a real smooth potential with trivial Dirichlet kernel; $F\in L^2(M)$; and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$.

[F1] [[def-ip-sobolev-spaces-on-compact-riemannian-domain]]: $H_0^1(M)$ is the closure of compactly supported interior smooth functions in $H^1(M)$; the boundary space $H^{1/2}$ is defined by finite chartwise Euclidean $W^{1/2,2}$ norms.

[F2] [[thm-lax-milgram]]: a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space has a unique weak solution.

[F3] [[thm-rellich-compactness-from-w-one-p-zero-to-lp]]: on a bounded Euclidean open set, $W_0^{1,2}$ is compactly embedded in $L^2$.

[F4] [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]]: for compact $K$ on a Banach space, $I-K$ is injective if and only if it is surjective, and then it is boundedly invertible.

[F5] [[thm-bounded-right-inverse-for-the-sobolev-trace]]: a smooth bounded Euclidean domain has a bounded right inverse from its $H^{1/2}$ boundary space to $H^1$.

[F6] [[thm-higher-order-boundary-regularity-for-dirichlet-problems]]: a zero-trace weak solution of a uniformly elliptic divergence-form equation on a bounded smooth Euclidean domain gains two derivatives, with the stated $H^{m+2}$ estimate.

## Proof

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 Choose a real constant $Q>1+\|q\|_{L^\infty(M)}$ and let $A=-\Delta_g+Q$ on $H_0^1(M)$, with form $a(w,z)=\int_M(g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)+Qw\bar z)\,dV_g$. The form is bounded and coercive in the chartwise $H^1$ norm, so [F2] gives a bounded inverse $A_D^{-1}:(H_0^1(M))^*\to H_0^1(M)$. [A2, given, F1, F2]

1.2 Multiplication by $Q-q$ maps $H_0^1(M)$ boundedly to $L^2(M)$, and the inclusion $H_0^1(M)\hookrightarrow L^2(M)$ is compact: localize with the finite atlas and partition, apply [F3] on each bounded chart piece (using zero extension at a boundary face), then extract a finite diagonal subsequence and sum the localized limits. Hence $K:=A_D^{-1}(Q-q)$ is compact on $H_0^1(M)$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For $w\in H_0^1(M)$, $(I-K)w=0$ is equivalent, after applying $A$, to $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$. The latter has only the zero solution by hypothesis, so $I-K$ is injective. By [F4], $I-K$ is boundedly invertible. This gives a unique weak zero-trace solution for every bounded functional on $H_0^1(M)$, in particular for every $F\in L^2(M)$ after subtracting any fixed boundary lift. [A1, F4, given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 A finite collection of flattened boundary charts, the collar neighborhood, and [F5] give a bounded extension $E:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^1(M)$ with trace $f$. Set $u=Ef+w$ and solve for $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with weak right-hand-side functional $z\mapsto\int_MF\bar z\,dV_g-a_q(Ef,z)$ by step 2.1. This proves existence for the stated data. The difference of any two solutions has zero trace and lies in the assumed trivial kernel, proving uniqueness. [A2, F1, F5, step 2.1, construct]

3.1 First take zero boundary data and $F\in L^2$. In each interior chart the operator has smooth uniformly elliptic divergence-form coefficients $|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}$; in each boundary chart the collar flattens the boundary and the pulled-back coefficients remain smooth and uniformly elliptic. Applying the $m=0$ case of [F6] to localized zero-trace equations gives $u\in H^2$ and the estimate with the additional $L^2$ term. If $f$ is smooth, extend it smoothly in a boundary collar by keeping its chart representative constant in the normal variable near the boundary and multiplying by a cutoff; a finite partition patches these extensions to a smooth $Ef$. Then $w=u-Ef$ has zero trace and solves an equation with smooth datum, so the same local estimates apply to $w$. [F1, F6, step 2.2]

3.2 If $u\in H^{k+1}$ and $F\in H^k$, differentiating the localized zero-trace equation $k$ times leaves the same uniformly elliptic principal part; each commutator contains a bounded derivative of a smooth coefficient and a derivative of $u$ of order at most $k+1$, so it belongs to $L^2$. Tangential derivatives retain zero trace. Applying [F6] at order $k$ on each boundary patch and the corresponding interior estimate gives $u\in H^{k+2}$ and $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k(\|F\|_{H^k}+\|u\|_{L^2})$. The bounded inverse in step 2.1 controls $\|u\|_{H^1}$ by $\|F\|_{L^2}$ for zero trace; hence the local estimate and this inverse bound give $\|u\|_{H^{k+2}}\leq C_k\|F\|_{H^k}$. Induction gives the claimed zero-trace estimate; for smooth nonzero $f$ apply the same induction to $u-Ef$. [F1, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, induction] ∎

## Statement

For the supplied $C^1$ objective and ambient gradient oracle, the displayed projected vector is the Frobenius metric-dual gradient of the restricted objective, and every polar trial is defined. For every input satisfying the finite-budget Stiefel gradient procedure, it returns after at most $K$ trial evaluations with an output frame $X_{\rm out}\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$. Every accepted update has nonincreasing objective value, and the returned status is `target-met` exactly when $r(X_{\rm out})\le\tau$; every other returned status has $r(X_{\rm out})>\tau$.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient|Finite-budget Stiefel gradient procedure]]

[[thm-stiefel-grassmann-tangent-projections|Stiefel tangent-space formula]]

[[def-stiefel-qr-polar-retractions|Polar retraction formula]]

[[thm-stiefel-retractions-are-first-order|Stiefel-valued polar retraction]]

[Absil, Mahony, and Sepulchre, *Optimization Algorithms on Matrix Manifolds*, Chapter 4, Example 4.1.3](https://assets.press.princeton.edu/chapters/absil/Absil_Chap4.pdf)

[Nicolas Boumal, *An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds*, §7.3](https://www.nicolasboumal.net/book/IntroOptimManifolds_Boumal_2023.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The data and inputs of [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]], including $X_0\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, a finite integer $K\ge0$, and positive step sizes $\alpha_k$ for $0\le k<K$.

[F1] [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]] supplies a $C^1$ objective on the ambient open set and an oracle with $D\Phi(X)[Z]=\langle G(X),Z\rangle_F$. At each current frame $X$, the procedure forms $g=G-X\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$ and trials $\eta=-\alpha_k g$.

[F2] [[thm-stiefel-grassmann-tangent-projections]]: $T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)=\{Z:X^{\mathsf T}Z+Z^{\mathsf T}X=0\}$.

[F3] [[thm-stiefel-retractions-are-first-order]]: the polar map on a Stiefel tangent input is defined and takes values in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$.

[F4] [[alg-ip-stiefel-constrained-regularized-gradient]]: an accepted candidate becomes the current frame, a rejected candidate returns the previous frame, the finite schedule index increases after each accepted nonterminal trial, and the residual test controls the returned status.

## Proof

1.1 For a current $X\in\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, put $M=X^{\mathsf T}G$. From [F1] and $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, the projected gradient satisfies $X^{\mathsf T}g+g^{\mathsf T}X=M+M^{\mathsf T}-2\operatorname{sym}(M)=0$. Thus $g\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by [F2], and multiplication by $-\alpha_k$ keeps $\eta$ tangent. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Put $S=\operatorname{sym}(X^{\mathsf T}G)$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$. If $Z\in T_X\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, then $A=X^{\mathsf T}Z$ is skew-symmetric by [F2]. Hence $\langle XS,Z\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(SA)=0$: transposing and cyclically reordering gives $\operatorname{tr}(SA)=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}S^{\mathsf T})=-\operatorname{tr}(AS)=-\operatorname{tr}(SA)$. The derivative of the restriction on a tangent $Z$ is therefore $D\Phi(X)[Z]=\langle G,Z\rangle_F=\langle g,Z\rangle_F$. Together with step1.1 this makes $g$ its tangent metric-dual vector. It is unique, since two such tangent vectors differ by a tangent vector whose pairing with itself is zero. This uses only the supplied first derivative, so $C^1$ suffices. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The initial frame is in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by the input condition. Whenever a current frame is in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$, step1.1 makes the trial tangent. Then $(X+\eta)^{\mathsf T}(X+\eta)=I_p+\eta^{\mathsf T}\eta$, so for $v\ne0$ its quadratic form is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\eta v\|_2^2>0$. Thus $X+\eta$ has full column rank, the polar call is in the declared domain of [F3], and [F3] puts its candidate in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)\subset U$. In particular every subsequent objective, residual and oracle evaluation has an input in its supplied domain. An accepted candidate is the next current frame; a rejected candidate returns the previous frame. Hence every current frame and every possible returned frame remains in $\operatorname{St}(n,p)$ by finite induction. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The index begins at zero, increases by one after each accepted nonterminal trial, and the loop ends when $k=K$; every other branch returns immediately. Therefore at most $K$ trial evaluations occur. The procedure accepts only candidates with objective no greater than the current value, and its residual test labels an output target-met exactly when its residual is at most $\tau$; every other return branch follows a failed target test and has residual greater than $\tau$. [given, F4, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

    - title: Barbara Kaltenbacher, Convergence rates under a range invariance

        and Theorem 3
      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704
    - title: "Jonathan M. Borwein and Jon D. Vanderwerff, Convex Functions:
        Constructions, Characterizations and Counterexamples, Exercise 4.4.1"
      url: https://carmamaths.org/jon/Preprints/Books/CUP/cup-final.pdf

        examples and is not used in this projection proof.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces, let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, and let $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be one of the full-space, Dirichlet, or Neumann TV functionals. Assume that $R$ is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively one-homogeneous, and that $u^\dagger$ is a minimum-$R$ exact solution of $Au=f$ with a dual source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Define $K:=\{p\in Y:A^*p\in\partial R(0)\}$ and $D_{\alpha,w}(p):=\langle f+w,p\rangle_Y-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p\|_Y^2$ for $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$.

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. If $u_{\alpha,w}$ is any supplied global minimizer of $u\mapsto\frac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)$, then $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(u_{\alpha,w})$, and $A^*p_{\alpha,w}\in\partial R(0)$. For every such supplied minimizer, the correctly normalized primal-dual value identity is

$$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

Let $P_0:=\{p\in K:\langle f,p\rangle_Y=R(u^\dagger)\}$ and let $p_0$ be its unique minimum-norm element. For every sequence $\alpha_n>0$ with $\alpha_n\to0$, $p_{\alpha_n,0}\to p_0$ strongly in $Y$ and $A^*p_{\alpha_n,0}\to A^*p_0$ strongly in $X$. For every $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$,

$$\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\frac{\|w\|_Y}{\alpha},\qquad \|A^*p_{\alpha,w}-A^*p_{\alpha,0}\|_X\le\frac{\|A^*\|\,\|w\|_Y}{\alpha}.$$

Moreover, for any $R_0>R(u^\dagger)$ the certificate yields a variational source condition on $\{u:R(u)\le R_0\}$ with exponent $2$, coefficient $\beta=0$, and index function $\psi(s)=(1+\|p^\dagger\|_Y)\sqrt{s}$. Consequently, if $\delta_n\downarrow0$, $\|w_n\|_Y\le\delta_n$, $\alpha_n\asymp\delta_n$, and exact global minimizers $u_n$ are supplied, then the variational-source rate theorem gives

$$D_R^{A^*p^\dagger}(u_n,u^\dagger)=O(\delta_n),\qquad \|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y=O(\delta_n).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|The classical TV source condition and certificate.]]

[[def-ip-variational-source-condition|The general variational source inequality.]]

[[thm-ip-vsc-nonlinear-regularization-rate|The Bregman and residual rates under parameter coupling.]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, Theorem 1 and Proposition 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[Kaltenbacher, *Convergence rates under a range invariance condition with application to electrical impedance tomography*, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.18704)

[Inspected historical citation: Borwein and Vanderwerff, *Convex Functions: Constructions, Characterizations and Counterexamples*, Exercise 4.4.1; it concerns convex-conjugate examples and is not used in this proof.](https://carmamaths.org/jon/Preprints/Books/CUP/cup-final.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the real Hilbert spaces and map in the Statement, a minimum-TV exact solution, a dual source certificate, and (where specified) supplied global minimizers.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the nearest-point minimizing sequences and weakly convergent subsequences used below. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $u^\dagger$ is an exact minimum-TV solution and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$; the Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$.

[F2] [[def-ip-banach-convex-subgradient-and-dual-pairing]]: $\xi\in\partial R(u)$ exactly when $R(z)\ge R(u)+\langle\xi,z-u\rangle$ for every $z\in X$.

[F3] [[def-ip-bregman-distance]]: $D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger)=R(u)-R(u^\dagger)-\langle\xi^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle_X$.

[F4] [[lem-ip-banach-fenchel-duality-for-regularization]]: $R(u)+R^*(\xi)=\langle\xi,u\rangle$ if and only if $\xi\in\partial R(u)$.

[F5] [[def-ip-variational-source-condition]]: on a named sublevel, $-\langle\xi^\dagger,u-u^\dagger\rangle\le\beta D_R^{\xi^\dagger}(u,u^\dagger)+\psi(\|Au-Au^\dagger\|_Y^2)$.

[F6] [[thm-ip-vsc-nonlinear-regularization-rate]]: when the exact global minimizer, noise bound, sublevel VSC, and conjugate parameter coupling hold, the Bregman distance and noisy residual have the displayed rates.

[F7] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\,\|v\|$ in a real Hilbert space.

[F8] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.

[F9] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: every bounded linear functional on a real Hilbert space is inner product with a vector in that space.

[F10] [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]: the real Hilbert norm satisfies $\|y\|_Y^2=\langle y,y\rangle_Y$.

## Proof

1.1 Put $q^\dagger=A^*p^\dagger$. Applying [F2] at $u^\dagger$ with $z=0$ and $z=2u^\dagger$, and using $R(0)=0$ and $R(2u^\dagger)=2R(u^\dagger)$, gives $\langle q^\dagger,u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u^\dagger)$. For arbitrary $z\in X$, [F2] then yields $R(z)\ge\langle q^\dagger,z\rangle_X$, so $q^\dagger\in\partial R(0)$ and $p^\dagger\in K$. Every $p\in K$ satisfies $\langle f,p\rangle_Y=\langle u^\dagger,A^*p\rangle_X\le R(u^\dagger)$; equality holds for $p^\dagger$. Thus $P_0$ is nonempty, closed, and convex. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 The set $K$ is nonempty because $0\in\partial R(0)$, convex by the subgradient inequality, and closed because $\partial R(0)=\{q:R(z)\ge\langle q,z\rangle_X\text{ for all }z\}$ is an intersection of closed half-spaces and $A^*$ is continuous. For any nonempty closed convex subset $C$ of a Hilbert space, let $d=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$ and use Countable Choice to select $c_n\in C$ with $\|x-c_n\|^2\le d^2+1/n$. The midpoint belongs to $C$, so the parallelogram identity gives $\|c_n-c_m\|^2\le2/n+2/m$; thus $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness and closedness yield a nearest point, and strict convexity of squared norm makes it unique. Applying this to $K$ and $P_0$ defines their projections. [A1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Completing the square gives $D_{\alpha,w}(p)=\frac{\|f+w\|_Y^2}{2\alpha}-\frac{\alpha}{2}\|p-(f+w)/\alpha\|_Y^2$. Hence its unique maximizer on $K$ is $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. [step 1.2, given, algebra]

## Statement

For each $\alpha>0$ and $w\in Y$, $D_{\alpha,w}$ has a unique maximizer $p_{\alpha,w}=\operatorname{Proj}_K((f+w)/\alpha)$. $$\min_u\{\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w)\|_Y^2+\alpha R(u)\}=\alpha D_{\alpha,w}(p_{\alpha,w}).$$

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+=\{x:u(x)>t\}$, and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-=\{x:u(x)<t\}$. Each set has finite area, almost every applicable level set has finite perimeter, and
$$TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The L² distributional-TV functional is the compactly supported test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|Finite perimeter is the TV of the level-set indicator.]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[Terra, *Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory*, §5.3](https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed for the BV coarea and test-field representation suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation]]: there are compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-coarea-formula]]: for a globally integrable BV function, the positive superlevel and negative sublevel perimeters integrate to its total variation.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: for an $L^1$ function, the extended test-field variation is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$; if finite, it equals the perimeter/TV defined by the distributional derivative.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: nonnegative level integrals may be interchanged, and absolutely integrable level/spatial functions satisfy Fubini.

[F5] [[thm-fatou-lemma]] and [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: Fatou bounds the limiting perimeter integrals, and increasing truncations of nonnegative level integrals converge to the full integral.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. For each fixed $t\ne0$, $\chi_{E_{R,t}}\to\chi_{E_t}$ in $L^1$: the symmetric difference is outside $B(0,R)$ for the cutoffs constructed in [F1] and contained in $\{|u|>|t|\}$, whose tail measure is at most $|t|^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R)}|u|^2$. Here $E_{R,t}$ and $E_t$ are the corresponding signed superlevel or sublevel sets. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For $t>0$, $|E_t^+|\le t^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$, and for $t<0$, $|E_t^-|\le |t|^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$. The indicator-valued maps are Borel on each half-line: on positive levels they are right-continuous in $L^1$ when $t_j\downarrow t>0$, by continuity from below of measure; on negative levels they are left-continuous when $t_j\uparrow t<0$. Composing with the lower semicontinuous extended variation in [F3] makes their perimeter functions measurable. Lower semicontinuity in [F3] and step 1.1 give $P(E_t^\pm;\mathbb R^2)\le\liminf_{R\to\infty}P(E_{R,t}^\pm;\mathbb R^2)$ for every applicable nonzero $t$. Fatou's lemma [F5], the BV coarea identity [F2], and the variation bound in step 1.1 imply, for every $\varepsilon>0$, $$\int_\varepsilon^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$ Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using monotone convergence [F5] proves that the full perimeter sum is at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$; its finiteness and [F3] give finite perimeter for almost every applicable level. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$. The signed layer-cake identity is $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$. On the compact support of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$, $\int |u|\,|\operatorname{div}\varphi|<\infty$, so Tonelli and Fubini [F4] permit integration of this identity against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$. At almost every level the absolute value of the resulting indicator test integral is at most its perimeter by [F3]. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the perimeter sum in step 2.1. Taking the supremum over admissible $\varphi$ gives $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$ at most that sum, which together with step 2.1 proves equality. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$. For $t>0$ set $E_t^+=\{x:u(x)>t\}$, and for $t<0$ set $E_t^-=\{x:u(x)<t\}$. Each set has finite area, almost every applicable level set has finite perimeter, and
$$TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)=\int_0^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^0P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The L² distributional-TV functional is the compactly supported test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-spatial-bv-and-distributional-tv|Finite perimeter is the TV of the level-set indicator.]]

[Iglesias, Mercier, and Scherzer, *A note on convergence of solutions of total variation regularized linear inverse problems*, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06495)

[Terra, *Introduction to Geometric Measure Theory*, §5.3](https://www.ime.usp.br/~glaucio/mat6704/textos/GMTLecureNotes.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$.

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed for the BV coarea and test-field representation suppliers. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation]]: there are compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-coarea-formula]]: for a globally integrable BV function, the positive superlevel and negative sublevel perimeters integrate to its total variation.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: for an $L^1$ function, the extended test-field variation is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$; if finite, it equals the perimeter/TV defined by the distributional derivative.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and [[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]: nonnegative level integrals may be interchanged, and absolutely integrable level/spatial functions satisfy Fubini.

[F5] [[thm-fatou-lemma]] and [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: Fatou bounds the limiting perimeter integrals, and increasing truncations of nonnegative level integrals converge to the full integral.

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], choose compactly supported $v_R\in BV(\mathbb R^2)\cap L^1$ with $v_R\to u$ in $L^2$ and $\limsup_RTV(v_R)\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$. For each fixed $t\ne0$, $\chi_{E_{R,t}}\to\chi_{E_t}$ in $L^1$: the symmetric difference is outside $B(0,R)$ for the cutoffs constructed in [F1] and contained in $\{|u|>|t|\}$, whose tail measure is at most $|t|^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus B(0,R)}|u|^2$. Here $E_{R,t}$ and $E_t$ are the corresponding signed superlevel or sublevel sets. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 For $t>0$, $|E_t^+|\le t^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$, and for $t<0$, $|E_t^-|\le |t|^{-2}\|u\|_2^2$. The indicator-valued maps are Borel on each half-line: on positive levels they are right-continuous in $L^1$ when $t_j\downarrow t>0$, by continuity from below of measure; on negative levels they are left-continuous when $t_j\uparrow t<0$. Composing with the lower semicontinuous extended variation in [F3] makes their perimeter functions measurable. Lower semicontinuity in [F3] and step 1.1 give $P(E_t^\pm;\mathbb R^2)\le\liminf_{R\to\infty}P(E_{R,t}^\pm;\mathbb R^2)$ for every applicable nonzero $t$. Fatou's lemma [F5], the BV coarea identity [F2], and the variation bound in step 1.1 imply, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\int_\varepsilon^\infty P(E_t^+;\mathbb R^2)\,dt+\int_{-\infty}^{-\varepsilon}P(E_t^-;\mathbb R^2)\,dt\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and using monotone convergence [F5] proves that the full perimeter sum is at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$; its finiteness and [F3] give finite perimeter for almost every applicable level. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)$ with $\|\varphi\|_\infty\le1$. The signed layer-cake identity is $u(x)=\int_0^\infty\chi_{E_t^+}(x)\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0\chi_{E_t^-}(x)\,dt$. On the compact support of $\operatorname{div}\varphi$, $\int |u|\,|\operatorname{div}\varphi|<\infty$, so Tonelli and Fubini [F4] permit integration of this identity against $\operatorname{div}\varphi$. At almost every level the absolute value of the resulting indicator test integral is at most its perimeter by [F3]. Therefore $\int u\operatorname{div}\varphi$ is at most the perimeter sum in step 2.1. Taking the supremum over admissible $\varphi$ gives $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$ at most that sum, which together with step 2.1 proves equality. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Every $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)<\infty$ satisfies
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|The full-space L² TV is the extended distributional test-field supremum.]]

[[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality|For globally integrable BV functions in two dimensions, $\|v\|_2\le TV(v)$.]]

[[lem-ip-tv-l2-cutoff-approximation|Compactly supported BV cutoffs approximate every finite-variation L² function.]]

**Given:** Countable Choice and $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R)$ with finite $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: every globally integrable $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfies $\|v\|_2\le TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$.

## Proof

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and it has no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A TV source certificate is an adjoint image in the convex subdifferential at a minimum-TV exact solution.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|Full-space TV on L² is the extended distributional test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions|Dirichlet TV counts zero-extension boundary variation; Neumann TV counts only interior variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement, including supplied global minimizers of $J_n$.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the countable diagonal selections in the compactness and weak-subsequence arguments. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $Au^\dagger=f$, $R(u^\dagger)$ is minimal over exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$; the Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-tv-dual-attainment-and-certificate-limit]]: every supplied global minimizer has $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, the exact-data fields $p_{\alpha,0}$ remain bounded as $\alpha\to0$, and $\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\|w\|_Y/\alpha$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-compactness-lower-semicontinuity]]: bounded-domain BV sequences with bounded $L^1$ norm and variation have an $L^1$-convergent subsequence, and TV is lower semicontinuous under $L^1$ convergence.

[F4] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: in two dimensions, $\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$ for $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.

[F5] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-sobolev-inequality]]: the same estimate holds for $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with finite extended variation: $\|u\|_2\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F6] [[lem-ip-bv-zero-gradient-constant-on-connected-domain]]: a locally integrable function with zero distributional gradient on a connected open domain is a.e. constant.

[F7] [[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions]]: Neumann TV is unchanged by adding constants; Dirichlet TV is the full-space TV of the zero extension and dominates the interior variation.

[F8] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: spatial TV is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$ and finite whenever the extended test-field variation is finite under Countable Choice.

[F9] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-finite-variation-has-radon-derivative]]: finite $TV_2$ gives a finite vector Radon derivative measure, whose restriction to bounded balls has variation at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F10] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: bounded scalar real sequences have convergent subsequences.

[F11] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.

[F12] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: bounded linear functionals on a real Hilbert space are inner products with vectors in that space.

[F13] [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]: two locally integrable functions that define the same distribution are equal almost everywhere.

[F14] [[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare]]: on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ for a fixed finite $C_\Omega$.

## Proof

1.1 If $\|A^*\|=0$, the adjoint identity implies $A=0$ and $f=0$. Since $0$ is exact, minimality gives $R(u^\dagger)=0$. The data term of $J_n$ is then constant, so every global minimizer has $R(u_n)=0$. In the full-space case [F6] makes $u_n$ constant and $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ forces it to be zero; in the Dirichlet case apply [F6] to its zero extension, which vanishes outside bounded $\Omega$, and again obtain zero; in the Neumann case [F6] makes it constant and the prescribed zero-mean choice makes it zero. Thus $u_0=0$ is an exact minimum-TV solution. Since $R\ge0$ and $R(0)=0$, $0\in\partial R(0)=\partial R(u_0)$, so $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial R(u_0)$ and the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $\|A^*\|>0$. [F1, F6, F7, given, cases, algebra]

1.2 Put $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$. By [F2], $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,w_n}$ and $p_{\alpha_n,0}$ is bounded. The noise hypothesis gives $\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta/\|A^*\|$, hence [F2] makes $(p_n)$ bounded and $\|w_n\|_Y\to0$. The identity $Au_n=f+w_n-\alpha_np_n$ therefore gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly in $Y$. Comparing the objective at $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ gives $$\tfrac12\|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u_n)\le\tfrac12\|w_n\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u^\dagger),$$ so $R(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\|w_n\|_Y^2/(2\alpha_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\eta^2\alpha_n/(2\|A^*\|^2)$. In particular the variations are bounded and $\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 In the Neumann branch on bounded connected $\Omega$, write $m_n=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$ and $v_n=u_n-m_n$. The Poincaré inequality [F14] gives $\|v_n\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(v_n;\Omega)=C_\Omega R(u_n)$, which is uniformly bounded by step 1.2. [F7, F14, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, subtracting $m_n$ leaves both $Au_n$ and Neumann TV unchanged, so we use the zero-mean minimizer specified in the Statement, which is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ by step 2.1. If $A\mathbf1_\Omega\ne0$, then [F1] and step 1.2 give bounded $\|Au_n\|_Y$ and $$|m_n|\,\|A\mathbf1_\Omega\|_Y=\|Au_n-Av_n\|_Y\le\|Au_n\|_Y+\|A\|\|v_n\|_2,$$ so the means, and therefore $\|u_n\|_2$, are bounded. In the full-space case [F5] gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. In the Dirichlet case [F4] applied to $\widetilde u_n$ gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. Thus in every branch the selected sequence is bounded in $L^2$. [F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\Omega$ is bounded, the $L^2$ bound gives an $L^1$ bound by [F11]; the interior variation is bounded by $R(u_n)$ in both boundary conventions [F7]. [F3] therefore supplies a subsequence converging strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, restrict to each ball $B(0,m)$: the $L^1$ norms are bounded by $|B(0,m)|^{1/2}\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$, and [F9] bounds the variation there. Applying [F3] on each ball and taking a countable diagonal subsequence using [A1] gives convergence in $L^1$ on every bounded ball. [A1, F3, F7, F9, F11, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere. [A1, F10, F11, F12, F13, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Weak convergence and boundedness of $A$ imply $Au_n\rightharpoonup Au_0$, while step 1.2 gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly; hence $Au_0=f$. In the full-space case, for every admissible test field $\varphi$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u_0\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_n\int u_n\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$; taking the supremum gives $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$. In the Neumann case the same lower semicontinuity follows from [F8] and strong $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence. In the Dirichlet case the zero extensions converge strongly in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, so [F8] gives the same inequality for their full-space TV. Thus $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)\le\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. Exactness and the minimum property of $u^\dagger$ force equality, so $u_0$ is a minimum-TV exact solution. [F1, F8, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Let $\xi=A^*p^\dagger$. Since $Au_0=Au^\dagger=f$, the adjoint identity in [F1] gives $\langle\xi,u_0-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,A(u_0-u^\dagger)\rangle_Y=0$. For every $v\in X$, the subgradient inequality at $u^\dagger$ therefore gives $$R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\langle\xi,v-u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u_0)+\langle\xi,v-u_0\rangle_X.$$ This is exactly $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$, as required. [F1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and let $Y=L^2(\Sigma,\mu;\mathbb R)$ be real Hilbert spaces. Let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded and real-linear, let $f=Au^\dagger$, and assume $u^\dagger$ is an exact solution minimizing a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, positively one-homogeneous TV functional $R:X\to[0,+\infty]$ with a source certificate $p^\dagger\in Y$, so $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$. Use full-space $R=TV_2(\cdot;\mathbb R^2)$ if $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$; for a bounded connected Lipschitz $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, use either Neumann $R(u)=TV(u;\Omega)$ or Dirichlet $R(u)=TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)$ for the zero extension $\widetilde u$, assigning $+\infty$ outside the respective finite-variation domain. A bounded connected Lipschitz domain here is a bounded open set with a finite Lipschitz graph cover of its boundary, with the domain on one side of each graph, and it has no separation into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets.

Let $\alpha_n>0$ tend to zero, let $w_n\in Y$, and suppose $\|A^*\|\,\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta$ for some finite $\eta$. For each $n$, suppose a supplied global minimizer $u_n\in X$ minimizes
$$J_n(u)=\tfrac12\|Au-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u).$$
In the Neumann case, if $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, take $u_n$ after subtracting its mean $|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$; this leaves $J_n$ unchanged. Then a subsequence converges weakly in $L^2(\Omega)$ and, in addition, strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$ when $\Omega$ is bounded or strongly in $L^1$ on every bounded ball when $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$. Its limit $u_0$ is an exact solution $Au_0=f$ minimizing $R$ among exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate|A TV source certificate is an adjoint image in the convex subdifferential at a minimum-TV exact solution.]]

[[def-ip-tv-functional-on-l2-distributional-variation|Full-space TV on L² is the extended distributional test-field supremum.]]

[[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions|Dirichlet TV counts zero-extension boundary variation; Neumann TV counts only interior variation.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement, including supplied global minimizers of $J_n$.

[A1] Countable Choice supplies the countable diagonal selections in the compactness and weak-subsequence arguments. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[F1] [[def-ip-tv-dual-source-certificate]]: $Au^\dagger=f$, $R(u^\dagger)$ is minimal over exact solutions, and $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u^\dagger)$; the Hilbert adjoint satisfies $\langle Au,p\rangle_Y=\langle u,A^*p\rangle_X$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-tv-dual-attainment-and-certificate-limit]]: every supplied global minimizer has $p_{\alpha,w}=(f+w-Au_{\alpha,w})/\alpha$, the exact-data fields $p_{\alpha,0}$ remain bounded as $\alpha\to0$, and $\|p_{\alpha,w}-p_{\alpha,0}\|_Y\le\|w\|_Y/\alpha$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-bv-compactness-lower-semicontinuity]]: bounded-domain BV sequences with bounded $L^1$ norm and variation have an $L^1$-convergent subsequence, and TV is lower semicontinuous under $L^1$ convergence.

[F4] [[lem-ip-bv-sobolev-inequality]]: in two dimensions, $\|v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le TV(v;\mathbb R^2)$ for $v\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$.

[F5] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-sobolev-inequality]]: the same estimate holds for $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ with finite extended variation: $\|u\|_2\le TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F6] [[lem-ip-bv-zero-gradient-constant-on-connected-domain]]: a locally integrable function with zero distributional gradient on a connected open domain is a.e. constant.

[F7] [[def-ip-boundary-tv-conventions]]: Neumann TV is unchanged by adding constants; Dirichlet TV is the full-space TV of the zero extension and dominates the interior variation.

[F8] [[lem-ip-bv-test-field-characterization-and-lsc]]: spatial TV is lower semicontinuous in $L^1$ and finite whenever the extended test-field variation is finite under Countable Choice.

[F9] [[lem-ip-tv-l2-finite-variation-has-radon-derivative]]: finite $TV_2$ gives a finite vector Radon derivative measure, whose restriction to bounded balls has variation at most $TV_2(u;\mathbb R^2)$.

[F10] [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]: bounded scalar real sequences have convergent subsequences.

[F11] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]: $|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.

[F12] [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]: bounded linear functionals on a real Hilbert space are inner products with vectors in that space.

[F13] [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]: two locally integrable functions that define the same distribution are equal almost everywhere.

[F14] [[lem-ip-neumann-bv-sobolev-poincare]]: on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain, $\|u-u_\Omega\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(u;\Omega)$ for a fixed finite $C_\Omega$.

## Proof

1.1 If $\|A^*\|=0$, the adjoint identity implies $A=0$ and $f=0$. Since $0$ is exact, minimality gives $R(u^\dagger)=0$. The data term of $J_n$ is then constant, so every global minimizer has $R(u_n)=0$. In the full-space case [F6] makes $u_n$ constant and $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ forces it to be zero; in the Dirichlet case apply [F6] to its zero extension, which vanishes outside bounded $\Omega$, and again obtain zero; in the Neumann case [F6] makes it constant and the prescribed zero-mean choice makes it zero. Thus $u_0=0$ is an exact minimum-TV solution. Since $R\ge0$ and $R(0)=0$, $0\in\partial R(0)=\partial R(u_0)$, so $A^*p^\dagger=0\in\partial R(u_0)$ and the assertion holds. For the remainder assume $\|A^*\|>0$. [F1, F6, F7, given, cases, algebra]

2.1 Put $p_n=(f+w_n-Au_n)/\alpha_n$. By [F2], $p_n=p_{\alpha_n,w_n}$ and $p_{\alpha_n,0}$ is bounded. The noise hypothesis gives $\|w_n\|_Y/\alpha_n\le\eta/\|A^*\|$, hence [F2] makes $(p_n)$ bounded and $\|w_n\|_Y\to0$. The identity $Au_n=f+w_n-\alpha_np_n$ therefore gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly in $Y$. Comparing the objective at $u_n$ and $u^\dagger$ gives
$$\tfrac12\|Au_n-(f+w_n)\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u_n)\le\tfrac12\|w_n\|_Y^2+\alpha_nR(u^\dagger),$$
so $R(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\|w_n\|_Y^2/(2\alpha_n)\le R(u^\dagger)+\eta^2\alpha_n/(2\|A^*\|^2)$. In particular the variations are bounded and $\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 In the Neumann branch on bounded connected $\Omega$, write $m_n=|\Omega|^{-1}\int_\Omega u_n$ and $v_n=u_n-m_n$. The Poincaré inequality [F14] gives $\|v_n\|_2\le C_\Omega TV(v_n;\Omega)=C_\Omega R(u_n)$, which is uniformly bounded by step 2.1. [F7, F14, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 If $A\mathbf1_\Omega=0$, subtracting $m_n$ leaves both $Au_n$ and Neumann TV unchanged, so we use the zero-mean minimizer specified in the Statement, which is uniformly bounded in $L^2$ by step 3.1. If $A\mathbf1_\Omega\ne0$, then [F1] and step 2.1 give bounded $\|Au_n\|_Y$ and
$$|m_n|\,\|A\mathbf1_\Omega\|_Y=\|Au_n-Av_n\|_Y\le\|Au_n\|_Y+\|A\|\|v_n\|_2,$$
so the means, and therefore $\|u_n\|_2$, are bounded. In the full-space case [F5] gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. In the Dirichlet case [F4] applied to $\widetilde u_n$ gives $\|u_n\|_2\le R(u_n)$. Thus in every branch the selected sequence is bounded in $L^2$. [F1, F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.1 If $\Omega$ is bounded, the $L^2$ bound gives an $L^1$ bound by [F11]; the interior variation is bounded by $R(u_n)$ in both boundary conventions [F7]. [F3] therefore supplies a subsequence converging strongly in $L^1(\Omega)$. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$, restrict to each ball $B(0,m)$: the $L^1$ norms are bounded by $|B(0,m)|^{1/2}\sup_n\|u_n\|_2$, and [F9] bounds the variation there. Applying [F3] on each ball and taking a countable diagonal subsequence using [A1] gives convergence in $L^1$ on every bounded ball. [A1, F3, F7, F9, F11, step 3.2, construct]

4.2 The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere. [A1, F10, F11, F12, F13, step 4.1, construct]

5.1 Weak convergence and boundedness of $A$ imply $Au_n\rightharpoonup Au_0$, while step 2.1 gives $Au_n\to f$ strongly; hence $Au_0=f$. In the full-space case, for every admissible test field $\varphi$, local $L^1$ convergence gives $\int u_0\operatorname{div}\varphi=\lim_n\int u_n\operatorname{div}\varphi\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$; taking the supremum gives $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)$. In the Neumann case the same lower semicontinuity follows from [F8] and strong $L^1(\Omega)$ convergence. In the Dirichlet case the zero extensions converge strongly in $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$, so [F8] gives the same inequality for their full-space TV. Thus $R(u_0)\le\liminf_nR(u_n)\le\limsup_nR(u_n)\le R(u^\dagger)$. Exactness and the minimum property of $u^\dagger$ force equality, so $u_0$ is a minimum-TV exact solution. [F1, F8, step 2.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Let $\xi=A^*p^\dagger$. Since $Au_0=Au^\dagger=f$, the adjoint identity in [F1] gives $\langle\xi,u_0-u^\dagger\rangle_X=\langle p^\dagger,A(u_0-u^\dagger)\rangle_Y=0$. For every $v\in X$, the subgradient inequality at $u^\dagger$ therefore gives
$$R(v)\ge R(u^\dagger)+\langle\xi,v-u^\dagger\rangle_X=R(u_0)+\langle\xi,v-u_0\rangle_X.$$
This is exactly $A^*p^\dagger\in\partial R(u_0)$, as required. [F1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-learned-reconstruction-estimator]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer $n\ge1$, a Borel probability $\mu$ not concentrated on an affine hyperplane, and $\sigma,\gamma>0$, with $\rho_\sigma,p_\sigma,\nu_{\sigma,z},D_\sigma,q_\sigma$ and $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ as in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: on $\mathbb R^n$, $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k$ and $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$.

[F2] [[def-probability-measure]]: $\mu$ is a measure on its Borel sigma-algebra with total mass $\mu(\mathbb R^n)=1$.

[F3] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: if an integrand is integrable for each parameter, its parameter derivative is measurable, and that derivative has one integrable majorant on an open interval, then the integral is differentiable and its derivative is the integral of the derivative.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the real exponential is smooth and $\exp'=\exp$.

[F6] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $r>0$, $\log$ is differentiable with $\log'(r)=1/r$.

[F7] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable Euclidean maps, the total derivative of a composite is the composite of the total derivatives.

[F8] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, products, scalar multiples, and quotients obey their derivative formulas wherever their denominators are nonzero.

[F9] [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]: finite componentwise sums, products, scalar multiples, and composites of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$.

[F10] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: a Euclidean map is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every finite $k$.

[F11] [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]: in positive-dimensional Euclidean space, a smooth map with invertible derivative at a point restricts to a smooth diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods; this theorem uses no choice axiom.

[F12] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a continuous scalar function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior, has an interior derivative equal to its endpoint difference divided by interval length.

[F13] [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]: a multi-index is an element $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$, and $\partial^\alpha$ is the corresponding iterated coordinate derivative.

[F14] [[def-measure-with-density]]: for nonnegative Borel $w$, $E\mapsto\int_Ew\,d\mu$ is a measure.

[F15] [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]: the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of a nonnegative simple function is its simple integral.

[F16] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous under positive finite scalars.

[F17] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions.

[F18] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: increasing pointwise limits of nonnegative measurable functions commute with the integral.

## Proof

1.1 Since $0<\rho_\sigma(z-u)\le1$, $p_\sigma(z)\le1$. For fixed $z$, the measurable sets $E_k=\{u:\rho_\sigma(z-u)\ge1/k\}$, $k\ge1$, cover $\mathbb R^n$. By [F2] and countable subadditivity, some $E_k$ has positive $\mu$-measure; hence $p_\sigma(z)\ge\mu(E_k)/k>0$. For $j=1,2$, the function $u\mapsto\|u\|_2^j\rho_\sigma(z-u)$ is bounded because a polynomial factor is dominated at infinity by the Gaussian exponential, so its $\mu$-integral is finite. Put $w_{\sigma,z}(u)=\rho_\sigma(z-u)/p_\sigma(z)$. This is a nonnegative Borel function. By [F14], $E\mapsto\int_Ew_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu$ is a measure; [F16] identifies it with $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ and gives total mass $\int w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=p_\sigma(z)^{-1}p_\sigma(z)=1$. Hence $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ is a probability measure. [given, F1, F2, F14, F16, algebra]

2.1 For a nonnegative simple Borel function $\varphi=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ on disjoint Borel sets, $\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\in L^1(\mu)$ because $\varphi$ is bounded and $w_{\sigma,z}\in L^1(\mu)$ by step 1.1. By [F15] and [F17], $$\int\varphi\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\nu_{\sigma,z}(A_j)=\int\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu.$$ For arbitrary nonnegative Borel $\varphi$, set $\varphi_k(u)=2^{-k}\lfloor2^k\min\{\varphi(u),k\}\rfloor$. These are finite-valued Borel simple functions, increase pointwise, and converge to $\varphi$. Applying [F18] under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ and $\mu$ yields $$\int\varphi\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\lim_k\int\varphi_k\,d\nu_{\sigma,z}=\lim_k\int\varphi_kw_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=\int\varphi w_{\sigma,z}\,d\mu=p_\sigma(z)^{-1}\int\varphi\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,d\mu.$$ For real Borel $\varphi$ with $\int|\varphi|\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,d\mu<\infty$, apply this identity to $\varphi^+$ and $\varphi^-$ and use [F17] to obtain the same formula for $\varphi$. Taking $\varphi(u)=\|u\|_2^2$ and using its weighted bound in step 1.1 proves the finite-second-moment claim; the finite first moment follows from $\|u\|_2\le1+\|u\|_2^2$. Thus $D_\sigma(z)$ is well-defined. [F2, F15, F16, F17, F18, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$ be a multi-index as in [F13]. At order zero, $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma=\rho_\sigma$. If $\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(w)=P(w)\rho_\sigma(w)$ for a polynomial $P$, then $\partial_j(P(w)\rho_\sigma(w))=(\partial_jP(w)-w_jP(w)/\sigma^2)\rho_\sigma(w)$, again a polynomial times $\rho_\sigma$. Induction on $|\alpha|$ proves the stated form for every finite derivative. On each compact set of $z$ values, both $|\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ and $|u_i\partial^\alpha\rho_\sigma(z-u)|$ are bounded uniformly in $u$, since every polynomial times the Gaussian tends to zero at infinity. Apply [F3] coordinate by coordinate to $p_\sigma$ and to each numerator $N_i(z)=\int u_i\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)$; the uniform bounds supply an integrable majorant and [F4] justifies passage of each derivative limit through the integral. The same bounds for derivatives of order $|\alpha|+1$ give a uniform bound $M$ for the first derivatives of each resulting derivative on any compact ball $K$. For $z,w\in K$, apply [F12] to that derivative along $z+t(w-z)$, $0\le t\le1$, to obtain a difference bound $\sqrt n M\|z-w\|_2$; thus each resulting derivative is continuous. Iterating over $\alpha$ makes $p_\sigma$ and every $N_i$ smooth. Since $p_\sigma>0$, the reciprocal $r(s)=1/s$ is smooth on $(0,\infty)$: its first derivative is $-r(s)^2$ by the difference quotient, and repeated use of [F8] shows every higher derivative is a polynomial in $r$. Thus [F9] makes $D_\sigma=(N_i/p_\sigma)_{i<n}$ smooth; [F6], [F8], and positivity of $p_\sigma$ also make $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ smooth. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F9, F10, F12, F13, step 2.1]

4.1 For $a\in\mathbb R^n$, expand $u-a=(u-D_\sigma(z))+(D_\sigma(z)-a)$ and integrate. The cross term vanishes because $\int(u-D_\sigma(z))\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)=0$, giving $$\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)=\int\|u-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)+\|a-D_\sigma(z)\|_2^2.$$ Thus $D_\sigma(z)$ is the unique posterior squared-error minimizer. 4.2 For each coordinate $j$, $\partial_j\rho_\sigma(z-u)=(u_j-z_j)\rho_\sigma(z-u)/\sigma^2$. Differentiating under the integral by [F3] and using step 2.1 gives $\nabla p_\sigma(z)=p_\sigma(z)(D_\sigma(z)-z)/\sigma^2$. Since $p_\sigma(z)>0$, [F6] gives $\nabla\log p_\sigma=\nabla p_\sigma/p_\sigma$, proving both Tweedie identities in the Statement. [F3, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $$v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z)v=\sigma^{-2}\int\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)\rangle^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$ If this were zero, then for each $k\ge1$ the set where $|\langle v,u-D_\sigma(z)\rangle|\ge1/k$ would have $\nu_{\sigma,z}$-measure zero; their union is the complement of the affine hyperplane $\{u:\langle v,u\rangle=\langle v,D_\sigma(z)\rangle\}$. 5.2 Fix $z$ and write $$\Psi_z(u)=\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2-\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-u\|_2^2+\sigma^2q_\sigma(u).$$ By the definition of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$, this equals $\frac12\|D_\sigma(u)-z\|_2^2+\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}(D_\sigma(u))$. 6.1 If $z\ne w$, put $v=w-z$ and $\psi(t)=\langle D_\sigma(z+tv),v\rangle$ on $[0,1]$. By [F7] and step 5.1, $\psi'(t)=v^{\mathsf T}J D_\sigma(z+tv)v>0$. ## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$ that is not concentrated on any affine hyperplane, and let $\sigma,\gamma>0$. Put
$$\rho_\sigma(w)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|w\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad p_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du),$$
and define the normalized posterior measure and its mean by
$$\nu_{\sigma,z}(E)=\frac{\int_E\rho_\sigma(z-u)\,\mu(du)}{p_\sigma(z)}\quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)),\qquad D_\sigma(z)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
The omitted normalizing constant of the $N(0,\sigma^2I)$ likelihood is independent of $u$ and cancels in $\nu_{\sigma,z}$. Writing $U(u)=u$ for the identity random vector under $\nu_{\sigma,z}$, its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u-D_\sigma(z))(u-D_\sigma(z))^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du).$$
Then $p_\sigma$ is positive and smooth, each $\nu_{\sigma,z}$ has finite second moment, and $D_\sigma(z)$ uniquely minimizes the posterior squared-error risk $a\mapsto\int\|u-a\|_2^2\,\nu_{\sigma,z}(du)$. Moreover, $D_\sigma$ is smooth and
$$J D_\sigma(z)=\sigma^{-2}\operatorname{Cov}_{\nu_{\sigma,z}}(U)$$
is symmetric positive definite. Hence $D_\sigma$ is injective with open image $X_\sigma=D_\sigma(\mathbb R^n)$ and smooth inverse on $X_\sigma$. Put $q_\sigma=-\log p_\sigma$ and, for $x\in X_\sigma$, define
$$h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=-\frac{\|x-D_\sigma^{-1}(x)\|_2^2}{2\gamma}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\gamma}q_\sigma(D_\sigma^{-1}(x));$$
set $h_{\sigma,\gamma}(x)=+\infty$ outside $X_\sigma$. The restriction of $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ to $X_\sigma$ is smooth. For any extended-real $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, define
$$\operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h}(z)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\frac12\|x-z\|_2^2+\gamma h(x)\right\},$$
where the argmin is the set of global minimizers and $h$ need not be convex. Then
$$D_\sigma(z)=z+\sigma^2\nabla\log p_\sigma(z)=z-\sigma^2\nabla q_\sigma(z),\qquad \operatorname{prox}^{\mathrm{glob}}_{\gamma h_{\sigma,\gamma}}(z)=\{D_\sigma(z)\}\quad(z\in\mathbb R^n).$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-learned-reconstruction-estimator]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer $n\ge1$, a Borel probability $\mu$ not concentrated on an affine hyperplane, and $\sigma,\gamma>0$, with $\rho_\sigma,p_\sigma,\nu_{\sigma,z},D_\sigma,q_\sigma$ and $h_{\sigma,\gamma}$ as in the Statement.

[F2] [[def-probability-measure]]: $\mu$ is a measure on its Borel sigma-algebra with total mass $\mu(\mathbb R^n)=1$.

[F3] [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]: if an integrand is integrable for each parameter, its parameter derivative is measurable, and that derivative has one integrable majorant on an open interval, then the integral is differentiable and its derivative is the integral of the derivative.

[F4] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: almost-everywhere convergence under one integrable majorant permits passage of the limit through the integral.

[F5] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: the real exponential is smooth and $\exp'=\exp$.

[F6] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]]: for $r>0$, $\log$ is differentiable with $\log'(r)=1/r$.

[F7] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable Euclidean maps, the total derivative of a composite is the composite of the total derivatives.

[F8] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: sums, products, scalar multiples, and quotients obey their derivative formulas wherever their denominators are nonzero.

[F9] [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]: finite componentwise sums, products, scalar multiples, and composites of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$.

[F10] [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: a Euclidean map is smooth when it is $C^k$ for every finite $k$.

[F11] [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]: in positive-dimensional Euclidean space, a smooth map with invertible derivative at a point restricts to a smooth diffeomorphism between open neighborhoods; this theorem uses no choice axiom.

[F12] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a continuous scalar function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior, has an interior derivative equal to its endpoint difference divided by interval length.

[F13] [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]: a multi-index is an element $\alpha\in\mathbb N^n$, and $\partial^\alpha$ is the corresponding iterated coordinate derivative.

[F14] [[def-measure-with-density]]: for nonnegative Borel $w$, $E\mapsto\int_Ew\,d\mu$ is a measure.

[F16] [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]: the nonnegative integral is monotone and homogeneous under positive finite scalars.

[F17] [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]: the Lebesgue integral is linear on integrable functions.

[F18] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: increasing pointwise limits of nonnegative measurable functions commute with the integral.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge0$ and $\tau>0$. In the one-dimensional Gaussian location experiment with parameter $\theta\in[-r,r]$, action space $\mathbb R$, observation density

[Iain M. Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §2.3 and §4.6](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

[given, F2, F3, F8, F9, F12, step 1.1, algebra]

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be commuting indeterminates over $\mathbb R$, and let $V_d$ be the $d\times d$ matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $t_j^{i-1}$. Then
$$\det V_d=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$
Consequently, for any distinct real numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the $d$ vectors
$$(1,s_j,s_j^2,\ldots,s_j^{d-1})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 1\le j\le d,$$
are linearly independent.

## Statement references

## Statement

Let $A$ be an indeterminate and let $D$ be a nonempty regular oriented link
diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient its
projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive
in the ambient $3$-space. At each crossing define
$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$
from the oriented projected tangents, and set
$\operatorname{wr}(D)=\sum_c\operatorname{sgn}(c)$. With
$\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$, adding a positive type-I kink multiplies the
raw bracket by $-A^3$ and increases writhe by $1$; adding a negative type-I
kink multiplies it by $-A^{-3}$ and decreases writhe by $1$. Deleting either
kink multiplies by the reciprocal factor. Consequently
$$f_D(A):=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$$
is unchanged by every oriented type-I, type-II, and type-III Reidemeister move
and by planar isotopy.

## Statement references

[Kauffman, *An Invariant of Regular Isotopy* (1990), §§III and VI](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/~kauffman/IRH.pdf)

[Kauffman, *Combinatorial Knot Theory and the Jones Polynomial* (2022), §2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.12104v2)

[Roberts, *Knots Knotes* (1999), §§4.1 and 4.3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/knotes.pdf)

[Funar, *A Crash Course in Quantum Invariants of Knots and 3-Manifolds*, Chapter 3, §1.1](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~funar/quantum.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a type-I, type-II,
or type-III move applied to it.

[F1] In the positively oriented chart with over-strand southwest–northeast,
the A-smoothing pairs left endpoints and right endpoints, while the B-smoothing
pairs top endpoints and bottom endpoints. A crossing contributes $A$ for its
A-smoothing and $A^{-1}$ for its B-smoothing; a state with $k$ circles contributes the factor
$\delta^{k-1}$, and $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$
([[def-kauffman-bracket-smoothing-and-loop-value]]).

[F2] The total writhe is the sum of the signs
$\operatorname{sgn}(c)=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$;
the positive Artin half twist has sign $+1$
([[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]]).

[F3] A type-I kink creates or deletes one crossing of either sign; type II
creates or deletes two crossings of opposite signs; type III preserves the
signs of its three crossings ([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]).

[F4] The raw bracket is unchanged under every R2 and R3 local replacement
([[lem-kauffman-bracket-r2-r3-identities]]).

## Proof

1.1 Label the crossing ports northwest $1$, northeast $2$, southeast $3$, and southwest $4$, in the chart of [F1]. The over-strand joins $4$ to $2$ and the under-strand joins $1$ to $3$. For the left exterior cap $(1,4)$ the remaining ports are $2,3$. Orient its through strand from $2$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand northeast to southwest, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors may be taken as $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,-1)$, whose determinant is $2>0$. This is a positive kink. The A-pairing $(1,4)(2,3)$ closes one additional circle against the cap; the B-pairing $(1,2)(3,4)$ gives just the through arc. Hence its bracket factor is $A\delta+A^{-1}=-A^3$. Reversing the component negates both tangent vectors and preserves the determinant. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 For the top exterior cap $(1,2)$ the remaining ports are $4,3$. Orient its through strand from $4$ to $3$: it traverses the over-strand southwest to northeast, then the cap, then the under-strand northwest to southeast. The tangent vectors $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ have determinant $-2<0$, so this is a negative kink. Here the A-pairing gives only the through arc, while the B-pairing closes one additional circle. Its factor is $A+A^{-1}\delta=-A^{-3}$. The right and bottom cap cases are the respective $180$-degree rotations; orientation-preserving chart changes and reversal of the component preserve the calculation. These are all oriented type-I variants. The calculation is inside the move disk and permits every exterior connectivity and any additional components. Deletion uses the reciprocal Laurent-unit factor. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The positive kink changes writhe from $w$ to $w+1$, and the negative kink changes it to $w-1$. Their respective normalized values are $$(-A^3)^{-(w+1)}(-A^3)\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle,$$ and $$(-A^3)^{-(w-1)}(-A^{-3})\langle D\rangle=(-A^3)^{-w}\langle D\rangle.$$ Thus both type-I additions and their inverse deletions preserve $f_D$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A type-II move creates or deletes two opposite signs, and a type-III move preserves all three signs, so writhe is unchanged. Their raw bracket is unchanged by [F4]. Planar isotopy transports the determinant crossing signs, smoothing states and state-circle counts bijectively. Therefore it preserves both factors of $f_D$, and the normalized value is invariant under every listed move. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
