## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $C$ be a finite union of distinct irreducible one-dimensional closed algebraic subsets of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$. Suppose its radical vanishing ideal in $\mathbb C[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$ is the scalar extension of a radical ideal in $\mathbb Q[M^{\pm1},L^{\pm1}]$; this is what it means here for the reduced union to be defined over $\mathbb Q$. Then its complex vanishing ideal is generated by a square-free Laurent polynomial $F$ with primitive integer coefficients. Any two such primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by multiplication by $\pm M^aL^b$, where $a,b\in\mathbb Z$.

## Statement references

[Milne, *Algebraic Geometry*, v6.10, §§1–3](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/AG.pdf)

[The Stacks Project, Section 10.9](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00CM)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the two-dimensional algebraic torus $(\mathbb C^*)^2$, and the reduced finite union $C$ of distinct irreducible one-dimensional closed subvarieties, with a rational structure on the union.

[F1] Every prime ideal of height one in a finite-variable polynomial ring over a field is principal and generated by an irreducible element ([[lem-finite-variable-polynomial-rings-over-fields-are-ufds]]).

[F2] For an affine domain of finite type over a field, its Krull dimension is the transcendence degree of its fraction field ([[thm-affine-domain-dimension-transcendence-degree]]).

[F3] Geometric dimension of an affine algebraic set over an algebraically closed field equals Krull dimension of its coordinate ring, under full AC ([[thm-affine-variety-dimension-coordinate-ring]]; [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The torus is affine: $(M,L)\mapsto(M,L,M^{-1},L^{-1})$ identifies it with $\{(M,L,U,V):MU=LV=1\}\subset\mathbb C^4$.

[F4] For a finite-type domain $A$ and prime $P$, full AC gives $\operatorname{ht}(P)+\dim(A/P)=\dim A$ ([[cor-height-plus-quotient-dimension-affine-domain]]; [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F5] Prime ideals disjoint from a localization set correspond by extension and contraction, preserving inclusions ([[thm-prime-spectrum-of-a-localisation-bijection]]).

[F6] The Laurent polynomial ring is the localization of $\mathbb C[M,L]$ obtained by inverting $M$ and $L$; its units are nonzero scalars times monomials, as follows from polynomial factorization in [F1].

[F7] The fixed field of all automorphisms of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ is $\mathbb Q$ ([[lem-fixed-field-of-automorphisms-of-c-over-q-is-q]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $R=\mathbb C[M,L]$ and $S=\{M^aL^b:a,b\ge0\}$. The coordinate ring of $(\mathbb C^*)^2$ is $A=S^{-1}R$, a finite-type domain with fraction field $\mathbb C(M,L)$ of transcendence degree two. Each irreducible curve $Y$ in $C$ has prime ideal $P_Y\subset A$, and its quotient coordinate ring has dimension one by [F3]. Thus [F2] gives $\dim A=2$ and $\dim(A/P_Y)=1$; [F4] yields $\operatorname{ht}(P_Y)=1$. [F2, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Contract $P_Y$ to $p_Y=P_Y\cap R$. It avoids $S$ because every element of $S$ is a unit in $A$. By [F5], contraction and extension identify all primes below $P_Y$ with primes below $p_Y$, so $p_Y$ has height one. By [F1], $p_Y=(f_Y)$ for an irreducible polynomial $f_Y\in R$. Since $p_Y$ avoids $M$ and $L$, neither variable divides $f_Y$. In the localization of the UFD $R$, an irreducible remains prime unless it divides an inverted element; therefore $f_Y/1$ is a nonunit prime and $P_Y=(f_Y/1)$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Distinct components have distinct prime ideals, hence their irreducible generators $f_Y$ are pairwise nonassociate in the Laurent ring. A Laurent polynomial belongs to every $(f_Y)$ exactly when each pairwise nonassociate prime factor divides it; unique factorization then makes it divisible by their product. If $C$ is empty, the vanishing ideal is the unit ideal and the empty product is $F_0=1$; otherwise the same product over the components generates the vanishing ideal. In either case the generator is square-free, and any other generator differs by a Laurent unit. [F1, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By the stated rational structure, every automorphism of $\mathbb C$ fixing $\mathbb Q$ preserves the vanishing ideal. Shift the finite support of $F_0$ so its lexicographically least exponent pair is $(0,0)$, then scale its coefficient there to $1$. This gives a unique normalized generator: by [F6] any two generators differ by a Laurent unit, and the support shift and specified coefficient remove that unit. Every such field automorphism preserves the normalization, hence fixes each coefficient. By [F7] the coefficients are rational. Clearing denominators and dividing by their integer gcd gives a primitive integer Laurent polynomial. Any two primitive integer-coefficient generators differ by a Laurent unit with rational scalar part; primitivity forces that scalar to be $\pm1$. [F6, F7, given, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 prove existence of the square-free primitive integer equation and show that its only ambiguity is $\pm M^aL^b$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses and conventions of the Levine–Tristram form definition. At every root $\omega_0\in S^1\setminus\{1\}$ of $\Delta_K$, each one-sided limit of the nonroot signature as the parameter moves along the unit circle to $\omega_0$ exists and is an integer.

## Statement

Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$,
let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, and choose one based positive meridian $m_i\in G$ for each
component. For every integer $q\geq1$, the homomorphism from the free group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ defined by $x_i\mapsto m_i$ induces a
surjection
$$F_r\longrightarrow G/\Gamma_qG.$$

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§1–3](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The link, its chosen product tubes, and based component meridians.

[F1] The positive component meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. [[lem-string-link-exterior-homology-and-meridian-maps]]

[F2] The degree-one Hurewicz map identifies $G/\Gamma_2G$ with $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] The lower-central series is $\Gamma_1G=G$ and $\Gamma_{k+1}G=[G,\Gamma_kG]$. [[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links]]

[F4] Commutators add lower-central weights, and their induced pairings on graded quotients are biadditive. [[lem-hall-malcev-lower-central-commutators-add-weights]]

## Proof

**Given:** $G$ and its selected meridians $m_1,\ldots,m_r$.

1.1 Let $H=\langle m_1,\ldots,m_r\rangle$. By [F1] and [F2], the images of these meridians generate $G/\Gamma_2G$, so $G=H\Gamma_2G$. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 For every $k\geq2$, the quotient $\Gamma_kG/\Gamma_{k+1}G$ is generated by iterated commutators of weight $k$ in the selected meridians. For $k=2$, [F4] makes the pairing $G/\Gamma_2\times G/\Gamma_2\to\Gamma_2/\Gamma_3$ biadditive, so [F1] implies this layer is generated by brackets of the $m_i$. If the claim holds at weight $k$, then [F3] writes the next layer as generated by brackets of a degree-one class with a weight-$k$ class; [F4] makes that pairing biadditive, so [F1] again reduces the degree-one entries to the $m_i$, and the induction hypothesis reduces the other entries to brackets of those meridians. Each such iterated commutator is a word in $H$ lying in $\Gamma_{k+1}G$, so its class is in the image of $H\cap\Gamma_{k+1}G$ in the graded layer. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 The conclusion of step 2.1 implies $\Gamma_kG\subseteq H\Gamma_{k+1}G$ for every $k\geq2$, because each generator of the graded layer is represented by a word in the $m_i$ that lies in $H$. Starting from $G=H\Gamma_2G$ in step 1.1 and applying these inclusions successively gives $G=H\Gamma_qG$ for every finite $q$. Therefore the image of $H$, and hence of the free group map in the statement, is all of $G/\Gamma_qG$. For $q=1$ the quotient is trivial. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link with $r$ components, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented spanning surface of genus $g$, and let $F'$ be obtained by choosing an embedded solid cylinder $[0,1]\times D^2$ that meets $F$ exactly in its two end disks and lies on the same local side at both disks, then replacing those disks by the cylinder's lateral annulus with the compatible orientation. This surgery preserves $L$. Put $m=2g+r-1$, choose an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ represented away from the two end disks, and let $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$ be its positive-push Seifert matrix. The surviving classes of that basis extend by two classes to an integral basis of $H_1(F';\mathbb Z)$, and for some column vectors $x,y\in\mathbb Z^m$ and integer $z$, the new Seifert matrix is one of
$$\begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&0\\0^T&1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}V&x&0\\y^T&z&1\\0^T&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-link-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix for a link surface]]

[[def-seifert-surface-arc-surgery|The embedded product-cylinder arc surgery]]

[[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology|The homology calculation for the handle replacement]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$, an ordered basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, and one embedded arc surgery producing $F'$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the Alexander-duality convention and compact-surface normal form. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The positive-push Seifert pairing is well-defined and bilinear on the homology of every connected link surface. [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F2] An arc surgery replaces two disks by the lateral annulus of an embedded product cylinder, leaving the oriented boundary unchanged. [[def-seifert-surface-arc-surgery]]

[F3] Mayer–Vietoris computes the homology of two surfaces glued along a common boundary circle. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F4] Linking is the signed intersection with a supplied spanning surface; linking of disjoint circles is symmetric. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]], [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

## Proof

**Given:** The data of the Statement.

1.1 The two surgery disks and a narrow strip in $F$ joining them have a disk neighbourhood $D$. Replacing the disks by the lateral annulus of the cylinder changes this neighbourhood into a once-punctured torus $P$ with the same boundary $\partial D$. Write $F_0=\overline{F\setminus D}$. Any old homology class can be represented in $F_0$: replace each of its finitely many arcs through $D$ by an arc along $\partial D$, which changes the cycle by a boundary in the disk. Take open collar neighbourhoods in $F$ and $F'$ so that $F_0$ and respectively $D$ or $P$ form open covers whose intersection retracts onto $\partial D$. In the Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F3], the map from $H_0(\partial D;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ to the direct sum of the two $H_0$ groups is $n\mapsto(n,-n)$ and is injective. For $F=F_0\cup D$, the $H_1$ map from the intersection circle has image generated by $([\partial D],0)$, since $H_1(D;\mathbb Z)=0$. For $F'=F_0\cup P$, the same image is generated by $([\partial D],0)$ because the oriented boundary of $P$ is zero in $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)$, while $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ on its longitudinal and meridional curves. Thus $H_1(F')\cong H_1(F)\oplus\mathbb Z^2$, with the old classes as a direct summand. Choose the added basis classes $b,c$ from those two curves; together with the old basis they are an integral basis. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 The surgery retains the old oriented surface outside the two attaching disks, so its positive normal there is unchanged and the old matrix block remains $V$. Use product coordinates $(t,w)$ on the cylinder, with $w\in D^2$, and take $c=\{t_0\}\times\partial D^2$. Let $b$ follow one longitudinal side of the tube and return through $F_0$; it crosses each cross-section disk once. The disks $\{t_0\}\times D^2$ and their sufficiently close parallel disks miss every old basis curve and its push-off, so [F4] gives zero for the two Seifert pairings between $c$ and every old basis curve. Along the lateral annulus, the positive normal points either out of or into the solid cylinder. If it points out, the radius-one cross-section disk misses $b^+$, giving $V(b,c)=0$, while the disk of slightly larger radius bounds $c^+$ and meets $b$ once; it gives $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=+1$ after orienting $c$, hence $V(c,b)=+1$ by the symmetry in [F4]. If it points in, the radius-one disk meets $b^+$ once, giving $V(b,c)=+1$ after orienting $c$, while the disk of slightly smaller radius bounds $c^+$ and misses $b$, giving $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=0$ and therefore $V(c,b)=0$. These intersection statements follow from the explicit single transverse point in the product coordinates and [F4]. In either case the concentric parallel meridians have $V(c,c)=0$. The remaining entries involving $b$ are integers $x$, $y$, and $z=\operatorname{lk}(b^+,b)$. Thus in the ordered basis $(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b,c)$ the matrix has exactly one of the two displayed forms. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Take open collar neighbourhoods in $F$ and $F'$ so that $F_0$ and respectively $D$ or $P$ form open covers whose intersection retracts onto $\partial D$. In the Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F3], the map from $H_0(\partial D;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ to the direct sum of the two $H_0$ groups is $n\mapsto(n,-n)$ and is injective. For $F=F_0\cup D$, the $H_1$ map from the intersection circle has image generated by $([\partial D],0)$, since $H_1(D;\mathbb Z)=0$. For $F'=F_0\cup P$, the same image is generated by $([\partial D],0)$ because the oriented boundary of $P$ is zero in $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)$, while $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ on its longitudinal and meridional curves. Thus $H_1(F')\cong H_1(F)\oplus\mathbb Z^2$, with the old classes as a direct summand. Choose the added basis classes $b,c$ from those two curves; together with the old basis they are an integral basis. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 The surgery retains the old oriented surface outside the two attaching disks, so its positive normal there is unchanged and the old matrix block remains $V$. Use product coordinates $(t,w)$ on the cylinder, with $w\in D^2$, and take $c=\{t_0\}\times\partial D^2$. Let $b$ follow one longitudinal side of the tube and return through $F_0$; it crosses each cross-section disk once. The disks $\{t_0\}\times D^2$ and their sufficiently close parallel disks miss every old basis curve and its push-off, so [F4] gives zero for the two Seifert pairings between $c$ and every old basis curve. Along the lateral annulus, the positive normal points either out of or into the solid cylinder. If it points out, the radius-one cross-section disk misses $b^+$, giving $V(b,c)=0$, while the disk of slightly larger radius bounds $c^+$ and meets $b$ once; it gives $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=+1$ after orienting $c$, hence $V(c,b)=+1$ by the symmetry in [F4]. If it points in, the radius-one disk meets $b^+$ once, giving $V(b,c)=+1$ after orienting $c$, while the disk of slightly smaller radius bounds $c^+$ and misses $b$, giving $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=0$ and therefore $V(c,b)=0$. These intersection statements follow from the explicit single transverse point in the product coordinates and [F4]. In either case the concentric parallel meridians have $V(c,c)=0$. The remaining entries involving $b$ are integers $x$, $y$, and $z=\operatorname{lk}(b^+,b)$. Thus in the ordered basis $(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b,c)$ the matrix has exactly one of the two displayed forms. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link in the oriented $3$-sphere, and let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $L$. For disjoint oriented embedded circles $C,D\subset S^3$, define $\operatorname{lk}(C,D)$ as the coefficient of the positive meridian of $D$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus D;\mathbb Z)$, and extend it bilinearly to finite integral sums of oriented circles. This linking number is symmetric on disjoint circle cycles. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. The positive push-off $x^+$ of such a representative is a sufficiently small copy in the positive normal direction determined by the ambient and surface orientations. For representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between $x^+$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off level, and is bilinear. Hence it defines the positive-push Seifert pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$.

## Statement references

[[def-link-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The link Seifert pairing and positive-push matrix convention]]

[[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection|Meridian linking, signed intersection, and the mixed-crossing formula]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, and a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the compact-surface normal form and Alexander-duality conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F1] The compact surface has a finite cellulation, and its first homology is finitely generated and represented by integral cellular cycles. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] Linking of disjoint oriented circles is the meridian coefficient; when a regular diagram and spanning surface are supplied it agrees with the signed intersection and mixed-crossing half-sum. [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F3] After moving a finite oriented link off infinity, it has a regular projection, a finite decorated immersion with finitely many mixed crossings. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F4] Every smooth oriented circle has a supplied connected compact oriented spanning surface, so the link-intersection theorem applies to it. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]

[F5] A smooth loop can be homotoped in the complement of a disjoint circle to meet a supplied spanning surface transversely. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $L$, and $F$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a finite cellulation of $F$ from [F1]. An integral cellular $1$-cycle represents each class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Replace each edge with coefficient $n$ by $|n|$ parallel oriented copies, reversing orientation when $n<0$. At each vertex the cycle condition says that incoming and outgoing copies occur in equal number. Around the boundary of a small vertex disk there is therefore an adjacent incoming/outgoing pair; join that pair by a small arc and delete its endpoints, repeating finitely until all endpoints are paired. The resulting arcs can be chosen disjoint in the disk and oriented consistently with the copies. Each smoothing changes the chain only by the boundary of a $2$-chain in that disk. The result is a finite disjoint union of oriented embedded circles representing the original homology class. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 For representatives $X,X'$ of the same class in $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, there is an integral singular $2$-chain $A$ in $F$ with $\partial A=X-X'$. Push the chain through a small positive normal level of $F$; its boundary is $X^+-X'^+$ and it is disjoint from any representative $Y\subset F$. Thus $X^+$ and $X'^+$ represent the same class in $H_1(S^3\setminus Y;\mathbb Z)$, so their meridian-coordinate linking sums with $Y$ agree. Varying the small positive level traces an annulus in the positive bicollar, also disjoint from $Y$, and gives the same class. [F2, given, algebra]

1.3 If $Y,Y'$ represent the same class, choose an integral $2$-chain $B$ in $F$ with $\partial B=Y-Y'$. For each circle component of $X^+$ and each circle component of $Y-Y'$, [F4] supplies a spanning surface and [F5] permits a homotopy of the other circle in its complement to make it transverse to that surface. By [F3] choose a regular diagram of the pair. By [F2], linking is the half-sum of mixed crossing signs; exchanging the two components leaves the same mixed crossings with the same signs, so linking is symmetric. Bilinearity then gives $\operatorname{lk}(X^+,Y-Y')=\operatorname{lk}(Y-Y',X^+)$. The cycle $Y-Y'$ bounds $B$ in $S^3\setminus X^+$, so its total meridian coefficient there is zero. Hence the two linking sums agree in the second variable as well. Additivity of meridian coefficients gives bilinearity in both variables. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 The value in the Statement is therefore independent of the chosen cycle representatives and push-off level and is bilinear on homology. In any ordered integral basis its matrix entries are $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, as required. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a fixed finite regular diagram $D$ of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, with $n$ crossings and a basepoint $p\in D$ away from the crossings, choose an admissible pointed Heegaard multi-diagram subordinate to the branched-cover surgeries and the compatible perturbation data and top-generator cycles of the link-surgery construction. Its first page and first differential are isomorphic as a cochain complex over $\mathbb F_2$ to the reduced Khovanov cochain complex of the mirror diagram $\overline D$, based at the corresponding point, in the specified normalized grading shifts. The resulting second page is therefore the based reduced Khovanov cohomology of $\overline D$. The isomorphism is for this fixed diagram and makes no claim about filtered chain complexes for different diagrams.

## Statement references

[[lem-os-first-differential-is-reduced-khovanov|Local first differential identification]]

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-based-link-over-f2|Reduced Khovanov cochain complex]]

[[lem-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-basepoint-independence|Basepoint-component independence over F2]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, Theorem 6.3 and proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

[Lipshitz, *Heegaard Floer Homologies*, §5.3](https://floer.wiki/more/courses/floer-homology/2024/lipshitz_heegaard_floer_homology.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed finite regular diagram $D$ of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, its filtered surgery complex, and a marked point $p\in D$ away from the crossings.

[F1] The filtration's first differential is the sum of the cube-edge maps ([[lem-os-first-differential-is-reduced-khovanov]]).

[F2] The exact local identification, including one common vertex basis for all incident edges, the marked quotient tables and normalized mirror shifts, is the Statement of [[lem-os-first-differential-is-reduced-khovanov]]. The reduced target complex is defined in [[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-based-link-over-f2]].

[F3] Over $\mathbb F_2$, the isomorphism class of the reduced cohomology does not depend on the marked component, for a fixed diagram ([[lem-reduced-khovanov-over-f2-basepoint-independence]]).

## Proof

1.1 The filtration quotient at each cube vertex is its resolution Floer group, and the differential on the first page is the sum of components changing one crossing. [F1, given]

2.1 Applying the asserted edge identifications [F2] to each of the finitely many edges identifies this first-page differential with the reduced Khovanov cube differential; the finite direct sum of the vertex isomorphisms is an isomorphism of cochain complexes. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Taking cohomology of the identified first-page complexes gives the based reduced Khovanov cohomology on the second page. By [F3] its graded isomorphism class is independent of the chosen link component for this fixed diagram. The local supplier [F2] includes its explicitly external actual Floer/mirror inputs and the local quotient/grading calculations, so this finite assembly proves the displayed first- and second-page identification. It asserts no map between distinct diagram presentations. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $D$ be a finite oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled closed link or string link, with a chosen smooth realization and pairwise-disjoint product tubes. Choose a crossing whose two projected branches meet transversely and for which no other branch meets a sufficiently small neighborhood, and let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is positive exactly when $(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by $(v_o,n_o)$ being positive. The source side $s$ is the side from which $n_o$ points, and the target side $t$ is the side toward which it points.

Choose an orientation-preserving local crossing chart, whose existence follows from the transversality of the projected branches, in which the over-branch is $(x,0,0)$ oriented by $+\partial_x$, the under-branch is $(0,y,-h)$ for some $h>0$, the viewing normal is $+\partial_z$, and $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ is the positive projection orientation. Use or radially shrink the chosen product tube near the under-branch to a radius $r$ with $0<r<h$. Choose $d,H>0$ small enough that the chart contains the points below. The source and target points on the upper boundary of the under-tube are $(0,-d,-h+r)$ and $(0,d,-h+r)$; join them by $\beta(y)=(0,y,-h+r)$ for $-d\le y\le d$. Choose a common basepoint in the chosen exterior above the chart and a path $\delta$ in the chosen exterior from it to $(0,0,H)$. ## Statement

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

## Statement references

[[def-bounding-chain-torsion-linking-pairing|The signed bounding-chain formula]]

[Charles Livingston and Swatee Naik, *Introduction to Knot Concordance*, §7.6, pp. 140–141](https://chuck-livingston.github.io/math/Concordance_Book.pdf)

[Patrick Gilmer, *Slice Knots in S3*, §1, pp. 306–307](https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/gilmer3.pdf)

[[def-axiom-of-choice|Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold $Y$ with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed wherever the cover and orientation conventions use the choice axiom. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Poincaré duality for closed oriented manifolds gives $H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(Y;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]]

[F2] The cohomology universal coefficient sequence over $\mathbb Z$ identifies $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q)$ and $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$, since $H_0(Y;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ is free. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

[F3] The coefficient sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ gives the long exact cohomology sequence and its natural Bockstein map $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-in-cohomology]]

[F4] **External triangulation input.** A compact topological $3$-manifold admits a finite manifold triangulation (Moise's theorem, as stated in Aschenbrenner–Friedl–Wilton, Theorem 3.1, p. 211, under their compact-manifold convention, p. 203). We use its barycentric dual cells as a chain model, not as an additional smoothness hypothesis on $Y$. Orient a dual cell so that its oriented transverse intersection with the corresponding primal cell is positive. The dual-cell description of Poincaré duality is recalled in Hatcher, §3.3, pp. 232–233; the specific bounding-chain/Bockstein identity is proved below, rather than assumed.

[F5] Cellular homology computes singular homology for every CW complex and every abelian coefficient group. Under [A1], cellular cochains compute singular cohomology for CW pairs with local coefficients, naturally for coefficient morphisms. Apply these comparisons to the finite triangulation and its dual CW complex, the pair $(Y,\varnothing)$, and the trivial coefficient systems $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$. Thus cellular cycles and bounding chains represent precisely the singular homology classes, and the cellular coefficient-sequence Bockstein and evaluation agree with their singular counterparts. [[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]] [[thm-cellular-cochains-compute-cohomology-with-local-coefficients]]

## Proof

1.1 Since $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$ is finite, $H^1(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F2], and $H^2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$ by [F1]. Exactness of [F3] therefore makes $\beta:H^1(Y;\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ an isomorphism. Write $\operatorname{PD}:H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to H^2(Y;\mathbb Z)$ for inverse cap duality. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra, A1]

1.2 We first fix the intersection sign and verify independence directly. For transverse oriented $2$-chains $C,T$ in an oriented $3$-manifold, orient their intersection so that $$\partial(C\cap T)=(\partial C)\cap T-C\cap(\partial T).$$ This sign follows by the outward-normal-first boundary convention in an oriented coordinate ball: taking a boundary in the second sheet passes its outward normal past the one normal direction of the first sheet. Consequently, the total signed endpoint count gives $$C\cdot\partial T=(\partial C)\cdot T.$$ These identities extend linearly to chains; the terms on paired interior faces cancel. For a closed $2$-chain $E$ and torsion cycle $y$, choose $m>0$ and $\partial T=my$. Then $m(E\cdot y)=E\cdot\partial T=0$, so $E\cdot y=0$. Thus if $\partial C=nx$ and $\partial C'=n'x$, the closed chain $n'C-nC'$ has zero intersection with $y$, giving $(C\cdot y)/n=(C'\cdot y)/n'$. Replacing $x$ by $x+\partial S$ permits replacing $C$ by $C+nS$ and changes the quotient by the integer $S\cdot y$. Replacing $y$ by $y+\partial T$ changes it by $(C\cdot\partial T)/n=x\cdot T$, also an integer. ## Statement

Assume AC. If $Y$ is a closed connected oriented $3$-manifold with finite $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)$, then the bounding-chain torsion linking pairing $\lambda_Y$ is symmetric and nonsingular: its adjoint $H_1(Y;\mathbb Z)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(Y;\mathbb Z),\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

## Statement references

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properness, local-flatness charts, and product collars]]

[[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere|Alexander duality for compact locally contractible subsets]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the locally flat disk and surface of the Statement and their matching boundary collars. The first part additionally assumes that the disk is smooth; the final part proves the TOP branch using the explicitly cited external normal-bundle and transversality inputs.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypotheses of the smooth approximation, ODE and transversality suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A locally flat surface has the pair charts and prescribed boundary collars in the Definition. For a smooth surface these are smooth charts. The Definition alone does not assert a global TOP normal disk bundle. [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]

[F2] Local smooth ODEs, the inverse-function theorem and Euclidean smooth approximation apply with compact parameters. Parametric transversality applies to finite smooth perturbation families. [[thm-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-local-smooth-evolution-operators]], [[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]], [[thm-whitney-approximation-for-euclidean-valued-maps]], [[thm-parametric-transversality]]

[F3] Boundary linking equals the intersection of collared bounding chains in the four-ball. Smooth compact manifolds have finite CW homotopy models under countable choice. [[lem-linking-number-equals-four-dimensional-intersection-number]], [[lem-compact-smooth-manifolds-have-finite-cw-models-under-countable-choice]]

[F4] Mayer–Vietoris computes the actual collared decomposition homology; the oriented meridian is dual to a Seifert surface. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F5] Alexander duality gives the meridional complement class for the capped locally flat surface, but it supplies no regular fiber or collar at that surface. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]

[F6] **External input — actual relative normal-bundle criterion.** Freedman–Quinn, original §9.3, Theorem 9.3A, printed p.137 (scan PDF143), states: if $N$ is a closed subspace of an ANR homology four-manifold $Y$, $Y\setminus N$ is a manifold, $N\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold, the specified local complement fundamental-group conditions hold (infinite cyclic when $\dim N=2$), and an actual normal vector bundle is given near a closed set $C\subset N$ containing $\partial N$, then there is a normal vector bundle which agrees with that given bundle on a neighborhood of $C$. The relative agreement is part of the existence conclusion, not an inference from uniqueness. In the 2013 reformatted edition this is §9.5, Theorem 9.7, printed pp.144–145/PDF158–159, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/2/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-Reformatted2013.pdf. Its p.145 footnote warns that local $\pi_2$ vanishing may also be necessary; step 3.2 satisfies that stronger condition as well. Apply the criterion to the CLOSED doubled sphere in boundaryless $S^4$, with the actual seam-annulus bundle germ constructed there, not directly to $B^4$. This supplies only a normal vector bundle, not a circle-map fiber or a Seifert hypersurface. Full AC is retained.

[F7] **External input — strongly relative TOP transversality.** Quinn1988, Theorem printed145: for proper submanifolds $M,X\subset Y$, a specified normal microbundle $\xi$ of $X$, and closed $C\subset D\subset Y$, if $M$ is transverse to $\xi$ near $C$, an isotopy of $M$, supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $(D\setminus C)\cap M\cap X$, makes it transverse near $D$. Boundary properness is part of the theorem. Transversality means that the intersection is a manifold whose normal microbundle in $M$ is the restriction of the specified $\xi$. The theorem includes the dimensions used below, namely $4$-submanifolds of a $5$-manifold with intersection dimension $3$. This theorem is imported, not reconstructed locally.

[F8] **External input — circle representatives on TOP manifolds.** Metrizable TOP manifolds have CW homotopy type by the ANR/CW-type criterion of Milnor1959. On that homotopy type, Hatcher Proposition1B.9 for $S^1=K(\mathbb Z,1)$ represents every integral first-cohomology class by a continuous map to $S^1$; two such maps with the same induced integer homomorphism are homotopic. These classification inputs are used only to construct a continuous meridian map. They are not transversality assertions.


[F9] An actual compact TOP manifold with boundary has a TOP product collar of its entire boundary. Apply this only after the exterior has been constructed as such a manifold. [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]]

## Proof

**Given:** First take a smooth proper disk $D$, retaining the full AC of the Statement.

1.1 Use the given boundary product collar to extend $D$ a little beyond $S^3$. Its normal quotient planes are represented by smooth orthogonal projection matrices $Q$ in the ambient Euclidean space. Parametrize the original disk radially from one interior point. Along each radial segment solve $\dot U=[\dot Q,Q]U$ from one fixed oriented orthonormal frame. The skew-symmetric coefficient preserves norms, and compactness gives a bounded coefficient on the finite parameter disk and time interval, so the local solutions of [F2] extend over the entire interval and depend smoothly on the endpoint. This gives a smooth frame of the disk's normal quotient bundle. Choose an ambient metric product-shaped on the end collar, by a one-variable cutoff interpolation with its product metric. Its orthogonal normal bundle is isomorphic to the quotient and inherits the frame. Its geodesic map is the local flow of the smooth coordinate equation $\ddot x^k=-\tfrac12g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_jg_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij})\dot x^i\dot x^j$, whose transformation rule follows by the chain rule. At the zero section its derivative adds tangent and normal vectors, hence is invertible. Extend across the end collar and apply [F2] there. Compactness of the original disk gives a uniform injective tube radius: otherwise equal images of distinct normal vectors tending to zero have convergent basepoints, their limits are equal, and the local inverse at that zero vector is contradicted. Shrink also inside all local flow domains. This constructs an actual smooth disk tube $D^2\times D^2$, product-shaped at its boundary. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 A small nonzero constant frame vector gives a disjoint proper parallel disk $D'$. By [F3], the linking of its boundary with $K$ equals $D\mathbin\cdot D'=0$. Hence the tube's induced boundary framing is precisely the preferred zero framing. Remove its interior and round the product corners to obtain the actual compact smooth disk exterior $X$. In the decomposition $B^4=X\cup(D^2\times D^2)$ the overlap retracts to $D^2\times S^1$. Since the ball and tube are contractible, integral Mayer–Vietoris gives $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$. Its marked boundary is the zero surgery $M(K)=E_K\cup_{T^2}(D^2\times S^1)$, with the disk meridian the zero longitude and the circle the positive meridian. The boundary meridian therefore induces an $H_1$ isomorphism to $X$. [F3, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 We construct a boundary circle map with the actual prescribed fiber, rather than presuming that $K$ is fibered. Truncate $F$ at the knot tube to a proper surface in $E_K$, and cap its boundary with $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. Call the resulting closed connected surface $\Sigma_0\subset M(K)$. Give a small normal product of $F$ the signed coordinate $u$ whose positive direction is the positive Seifert push, and put $f_0=\exp(2\pi i u)$ there. On the inner $D^2\times S^1$ put $f_0(x,z)=z$, matching these choices in the peripheral collar. Cut the rest of the knot exterior along that product of $F$. Its two faces have real phase values $\epsilon$ and $1-\epsilon$, and its remaining torus annulus has the ordinary lifted angular coordinate between them. These prescriptions agree in their product corner collars. Extend the real phase to the remaining compact cut manifold by finite smooth collar cutoffs and a partition of unity, with all values in $(0,1)$ and constant $1/2$ away from its prescribed boundary collars. Convexity keeps the extended values away from $0$ modulo $1$. Exponentiating gives a smooth map $f_0:M(K)\to S^1$ with $1$ as a regular value, fiber exactly $\Sigma_0$, and positive coorientation on the $F$ part. Its induced homomorphism on $H_1$ is the positive meridian map: crossing $F$ once positively increases the lifted phase by one, exactly the intersection convention in [F4]. [F2, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 Now let $D$ be the arbitrary locally flat disk of the Statement. First construct the actual boundary germ. The smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ has an oriented normal two-plane tube $\tau:K\times D^2_\delta\to S^3$: take the positive normal of the given smooth Seifert surface along $K$, complete it by the orientations of $K,S^3$, and use a uniformly small smooth tube over the compact circle, by the smooth inverse-chart/ODE construction [F2]. The matched disk and ambient product collars in the Given identify $D$ there with $K\times[0,\epsilon)\subset S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$. Thus $(q,t,v)\mapsto(\tau(q,v),t)$ is an ACTUAL rank-two normal-bundle germ over the entire boundary collar. No global TOP bundle is inferred from the Definition alone. Double the standard ball and the collared disk to $(Y,N)=(S^4,D_+\cup_KD_-)$, where $N\cong S^2$. The tube doubles to the explicit product germ $K\times(-2a,2a)\times D^2_\delta$ for small $a>0$. Choose the CLOSED seam annulus $C=K\times[-a,a]\subset N$. This is the prescribed bundle on a neighborhood of $C$; restrict its fiber radius inside a slightly larger tube for the extendable-neighborhood convention. The doubled pair is locally flat: away from the seam use the given charts; at the seam its actual product chart is $(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\{0\})$. Every hypothesis of [F6] is now literal. The ambient $S^4$ is a boundaryless smooth manifold and hence an ANR homology four-manifold; $Y\setminus N$ is an open four-manifold. The surface $N$ is closed, $N\times\mathbb R\cong S^2\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold and $\partial N=\varnothing$. Nested flat charts have complement homotopy type $S^1$; the local meridian maps give the infinite cyclic local fundamental group, and local $\pi_2=0$. Thus even the stronger condition in the reformatted erratum holds. The actual prescribed bundle near $C$ is the displayed product. Apply [F6] to obtain a normal vector bundle on $N$ whose embedding AGREES with that product on a smaller neighborhood of $C$. Restrict to $D_+$. Near its boundary, agreement with the germ keeps the collar coordinate $t$ unchanged, so sufficiently short fibers stay in the original hemisphere. ## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. After matching product collars and pushing the interior of $F$ slightly into $B^4$, the closed locally flat surface $\Sigma=F\cup_KD$ bounds a compact connected oriented locally flat three-manifold $R\subset B^4$. The conclusion includes an oriented ambient product neighborhood of $R$ on both sides, with the positive normal push-off along the $F$ portion of $\partial R=\Sigma$ lying on the complementary side of $R$.

## Statement references

[[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars|Properness, local-flatness charts, and product collars]]

[[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere|Alexander duality for compact locally contractible subsets]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the locally flat disk and surface of the Statement and their matching boundary collars. The first part additionally assumes that the disk is smooth; the final part proves the TOP branch using the explicitly cited external normal-bundle and transversality inputs.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypotheses of the smooth approximation, ODE and transversality suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] A locally flat surface has the pair charts and prescribed boundary collars in the Definition. For a smooth surface these are smooth charts. The Definition alone does not assert a global TOP normal disk bundle. [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]]

[F2] Local smooth ODEs, the inverse-function theorem and Euclidean smooth approximation apply with compact parameters. Parametric transversality applies to finite smooth perturbation families. [[thm-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-local-smooth-evolution-operators]], [[thm-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-on-manifolds]], [[thm-whitney-approximation-for-euclidean-valued-maps]], [[thm-parametric-transversality]]

[F3] Boundary linking equals the intersection of collared bounding chains in the four-ball. Smooth compact manifolds have finite CW homotopy models under countable choice. [F4] Mayer–Vietoris computes the actual collared decomposition homology; the oriented meridian is dual to a Seifert surface. [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F5] Alexander duality gives the meridional complement class for the capped locally flat surface, but it supplies no regular fiber or collar at that surface. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]

[F6] **External input — actual relative normal-bundle criterion.** Freedman–Quinn, original §9.3, Theorem 9.3A, printed p.137 (scan PDF143), states: if $N$ is a closed subspace of an ANR homology four-manifold $Y$, $Y\setminus N$ is a manifold, $N\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold, the specified local complement fundamental-group conditions hold (infinite cyclic when $\dim N=2$), and an actual normal vector bundle is given near a closed set $C\subset N$ containing $\partial N$, then there is a normal vector bundle which agrees with that given bundle on a neighborhood of $C$. The relative agreement is part of the existence conclusion, not an inference from uniqueness. In the 2013 reformatted edition this is §9.5, Theorem 9.7, printed pp.144–145/PDF158–159, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/2/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-Reformatted2013.pdf. Apply the criterion to the CLOSED doubled sphere in boundaryless $S^4$, with the actual seam-annulus bundle germ constructed there, not directly to $B^4$. This supplies only a normal vector bundle, not a circle-map fiber or a Seifert hypersurface. Full AC is retained.

[F7] **External input — strongly relative TOP transversality.** Quinn1988, Theorem printed145: for proper submanifolds $M,X\subset Y$, a specified normal microbundle $\xi$ of $X$, and closed $C\subset D\subset Y$, if $M$ is transverse to $\xi$ near $C$, an isotopy of $M$, supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $(D\setminus C)\cap M\cap X$, makes it transverse near $D$. Boundary properness is part of the theorem. Transversality means that the intersection is a manifold whose normal microbundle in $M$ is the restriction of the specified $\xi$. The theorem includes the dimensions used below, namely $4$-submanifolds of a $5$-manifold with intersection dimension $3$. This theorem is imported, not reconstructed locally.

[F8] **External input — circle representatives on TOP manifolds.** Metrizable TOP manifolds have CW homotopy type by the ANR/CW-type criterion of Milnor1959. On that homotopy type, Hatcher Proposition1B.9 for $S^1=K(\mathbb Z,1)$ represents every integral first-cohomology class by a continuous map to $S^1$; two such maps with the same induced integer homomorphism are homotopic. These classification inputs are used only to construct a continuous meridian map. They are not transversality assertions.

      locator: "§3, PDF pp. 7–12"

## Statement

Let $F_r$ be the free group and $E$ the Magnus expansion from the preceding
definition, with augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$. If
$u\in\Gamma_pF_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$ for $p,q\ge1$, then
$$
E([u,v])\in 1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}.
$$
Consequently $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, reduction of $E$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$ factors through
$F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$ and its coefficients through degree $d$ are independent
of the representative word.

## Statement references

[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links|Lower-central series and Magnus expansion]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The free group, lower-central series, Magnus map, and augmentation
ideal from the preceding definition.

[F1] The series map $E$ is a group homomorphism, $E(F_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m$,
and $\mathfrak m^a\mathfrak m^b\subseteq\mathfrak m^{a+b}$.
[[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links]]

## Proof

1.1 In any filtered associative ring, write $U=1+a$ and $V=1+b$ with $a\in\mathfrak m^p$ and $b\in\mathfrak m^q$. Since $U,V$ are units, $$ [U,V]-1=(UV-VU)U^{-1}V^{-1}=(ab-ba)U^{-1}V^{-1}. $$ By [F1], $ab-ba\in\mathfrak m^{p+q}$, and multiplication by units preserves this two-sided ideal. Therefore $[U,V]\in1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}$. Applying this to $U=E(u)$ and $V=E(v)$ proves the first claim. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Every free generator and its inverse map to a series with constant term $1$, so [F1] gives $E(\Gamma_1F_r)=E(F_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m$. Assume $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$. Each generator $[u,v]$ of $\Gamma_{q+1}F_r=[F_r,\Gamma_qF_r]$ has $u\in F_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$, so step 1.1 puts its image in $1+\mathfrak m^{q+1}$. Products and inverses of elements in $1+\mathfrak m^{q+1}$ remain in that subgroup; hence the inclusion holds for all of $\Gamma_{q+1}F_r$. Induction proves it for every $q$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

3.1 If two words represent the same element of $F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$, their quotient lies in $\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$. By step 2.1 its expansion is $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$. Multiplicativity of $E$ then makes the two truncated expansions equal, proving representative-independence of every coefficient of degree at most $d$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F_r$ be the free group with Magnus expansion $E$, let $u,\lambda\in F_r$,
and let $w$ be a nonempty word of length $m$. The coefficient of $X_w$ in
$E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda)$ is an integer linear combination of
coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords of $w$. Thus, when
$w$ is the prefix of a Milnor index $I=(w,j)$, conjugating the longitude can
change its degree-$m$ coefficient only by an integer combination of
coefficients indexed by proper subsequences of $I$.

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§3–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The noncommutative formal-series ring, augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$, and Magnus expansion in the preceding definition.

[F1] Every Magnus expansion has constant term $1$, its positive-degree part lies in $\mathfrak m$, and multiplication concatenates words. [[def-lower-central-series-and-magnus-expansion-for-links]]

## Proof

1.1 Write $E(u)=1+U$ and $E(\lambda)=1+V$ with $U,V\in\mathfrak m$. Then $$E(u^{-1}\lambda u)-E(\lambda) =(1+U)^{-1}V(1+U)-V.$$ Expand $(1+U)^{-1}=\sum_{a\geq0}(-U)^a$. The term with no $U$ on either side is $V$ and cancels the subtracted $V$. Every remaining term is a product $(-U)^a VU^b$ with $a+b\geq1$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 A coefficient of degree $m$ in such a product uses a degree-$p$ monomial of $U^a$, a degree-$s$ monomial of $V$, and a degree-$q$ monomial of $U^b$ with $p+s+q=m$ and $p+q\geq1$. The $V$ monomial therefore has degree $s<m$ and occupies a contiguous middle block of the target word $w$, while the nonempty left or right block comes from $U$. Summing the finitely many decompositions of $w$ expresses its coefficient as an integer linear combination of coefficients of $E(\lambda)$ on proper contiguous subwords. Appending the longitude index $j$ makes each such index a proper subsequence of $(w,j)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L$ be a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$, compact exterior $E_L$, and maximal abelian cover $E_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to E_L$ with deck group $H\cong\mathbb Z^r$ and group ring $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H]$. For any finite CW structure on $E_L$, the inverse-image cells and one chosen lift of each open cell form a finite-rank free $\Lambda_r$ cellular chain complex. Its first homology is the absolute multivariable Alexander module $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$, with the deck action specified by the positive meridians.

## Statement references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

[[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a nonempty oriented smooth $r$-component link with $r\ge1$; its chosen compact exterior $E_L$; its regular maximal abelian cover $E_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to E_L$ with deck group $H\cong\mathbb Z^r$; and a finite CW structure on $E_L$.

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis under which the maximal-abelian-cover definition is being used; selecting the finitely many cell lifts below itself needs no choice principle ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The absolute multivariable Alexander module is $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$, with Laurent variables acting by the positive-meridian deck transformations ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The compact exterior cover is the restriction of the open-complement cover; lifted deformation retraction gives a deck-equivariant isomorphism $H_1(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)\cong A_L$ ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F3] Cellular homology is naturally isomorphic to singular homology for every CW complex, and the isomorphism commutes with cellular maps ([[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]).

## Proof

1.1 A finite CW structure has finitely many open cells. Each open cell is contractible, so its inverse image under a covering is a disjoint union of copies of that cell. The regular deck group $H$ acts freely and transitively on those copies. Choose one lifted copy for each cell; finitely many choices suffice. Every other lift is uniquely a deck translate of the chosen lift, so the lifted cellular chain group in degree $n$ is a free $\mathbb Z[H]=\Lambda_r$-module with one basis element per $n$-cell of $E_L$. [F1, given, choose]

2.1 Translating a lifted characteristic map by $h\in H$ translates all of its oriented boundary cells by the same $h$. Thus every cellular boundary map is $\Lambda_r$-linear. The cellular identity $\partial^2=0$ then makes these finite-rank free modules a chain complex over $\Lambda_r$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Each deck transformation is cellular on the lifted CW structure. By the naturality in [F3], the cellular-to-singular homology isomorphism commutes with every deck transformation and hence is $\Lambda_r$-linear. In degree one it identifies the homology of the lifted cellular complex with $H_1(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Under the Axiom-of-Choice convention [A1], [F2] says inclusion of the restricted maximal abelian cover into $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$ induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism on first homology. Therefore the lifted cellular complex has first homology $A_L$ with the stated deck action. [A1, F2, step 3.1] ∎

[[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]

[[thm-cellular-homology-computes-singular-homology]]

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]

Every other lift is uniquely a deck translate of the chosen lift, so the lifted cellular chain group in degree $n$ is a free $\mathbb Z[H]=\Lambda_r$-module with one basis element per $n$-cell of $E_L$. [F1, given, choose]

1.2 Translating a lifted characteristic map by $h\in H$ translates all of its oriented boundary cells by the same $h$. Thus every cellular boundary map is $\Lambda_r$-linear. The cellular identity $\partial^2=0$ then makes these finite-rank free modules a chain complex over $\Lambda_r$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Each deck transformation is cellular on the lifted CW structure. By the naturality in [F3], the cellular-to-singular homology isomorphism commutes with every deck transformation and hence is $\Lambda_r$-linear. In degree one it identifies the homology of the lifted cellular complex with $H_1(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, step 1.2]

2.2 Under the Axiom-of-Choice convention [A1], [F2] says inclusion of the restricted maximal abelian cover into $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$ induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism on first homology. Therefore the lifted cellular complex has first homology $A_L$ with the stated deck action. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$

## Statement references

[[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the link, its chosen pairwise-disjoint closed normal disk tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$, the compact exterior $E_L$, the open complement $X_L$, a basepoint $b\in E_L$, and the maximal abelian cover $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$.

[A1] AC is assumed in the maximal-abelian-cover definition and its link-complement supplier ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The cover $p$ is the connected regular cover classified by the kernel of abelianization, and its deck group is $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^r$ ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] A homotopy of maps into a base of a covering, together with an initial lift, has a unique homotopy lift ([[thm-homotopy-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F3] Paths lift uniquely from a prescribed point of a covering fibre ([[thm-path-lifting-for-covering-maps]]).

[F4] Connected covers of a path-connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected space are classified by their induced fundamental-group subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F5] A map defined continuously on the members of a finite closed cover, with agreeing restrictions on overlaps, is continuous ([[lem-continuity-is-local-and-pastes]]).

[F6] The link complement is a connected smooth three-manifold under AC ([[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]]).

[F7] In a connected regular covering, the deck group acts transitively on each fibre ([[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]]).

[F8] A deformation retract is fixed pointwise by a homotopy from the identity to the retraction-inclusion composite ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]).

[F9] Inclusion of a deformation retract induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups at every basepoint in the retract ([[prop-retracts-inject-fundamental-groups]]).

[F10] Homotopic maps induce the same homomorphism on singular homology ([[cor-homotopic-maps-induce-the-same-map-on-singular-homology]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $x=\Phi_i(v)\in N(K_i)\setminus K_i$, write $\rho=\lVert v\rVert>0$ and define $$ F_s(x)=\Phi_i\!\left(\left((1-s)\rho+s\epsilon_i\right)\frac{v}{\rho}\right),\qquad 0\le s\le1. $$ On $E_L$ set $F_s(x)=x$. The formula is continuous on each punctured tube and agrees with the identity on its boundary $\rho=\epsilon_i$. The products with $I$ of the finitely many punctured closed tubes and $E_L$ form a finite closed cover of $X_L\times I$; [F5] therefore makes $F:X_L\times I\to X_L$ continuous. It starts at the identity, fixes $E_L$ pointwise, and at $s=1$ maps every punctured tube to its boundary, so it is a strong deformation retraction onto $E_L$. [given, F5, construct]

2.1 The link complement is path-connected by [F6], so its deformation retract $E_L$ is path-connected. The tube construction makes $E_L$ a smooth manifold with boundary, hence locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected. By [F8] and [F9], inclusion induces an isomorphism $i_*:\pi_1(E_L,b)\to\pi_1(X_L,b)$. By [F8] and [F10], it also induces an isomorphism $i_*:H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. The positive meridians lie in $E_L$ and map to the same classes, so the meridian basis is preserved. An $E_L$-loop closes in the restricted cover exactly when its image under $i_*$ lies in $\ker\phi$, so the component containing $\widetilde b$ induces the subgroup $$ i_*^{-1}(\ker\phi)=\ker(\phi\circ i_*). $$ This subgroup is exactly the kernel of the abelianization of $\pi_1(E_L,b)$ because $i_*$ is an isomorphism. To check connectedness, take $y\in E_L$, a path $\delta$ in $E_L$ from $b$ to $y$, and a lift $\widetilde\delta$ from a chosen point $\widetilde b$ over $b$. Any other point over $y$ is $h\widetilde\delta(1)$ for some deck transformation $h$, by [F7]. Surjectivity of $i_*$ gives a loop $\alpha$ in $E_L$ whose lift from $\widetilde b$ ends at $h\widetilde b$. The reverse of $\widetilde\delta$, this lifted loop, and $h\widetilde\delta$ concatenate to a path in $p^{-1}(E_L)$ from $\widetilde\delta(1)$ to $h\widetilde\delta(1)$. Thus the restriction is connected. By [F4] it is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, with the same deck group $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\cong H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$. [F1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Apply [F2] to $F$ with initial lift the identity of $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$. For a point over $E_L$, its constant path is a lift of its path under $F$; uniqueness makes the lifted homotopy fix every point of $p^{-1}(E_L)$. At time $1$ the image lies in $p^{-1}(E_L)$, so the lifted homotopy is a strong deformation retraction of $X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}$ onto that restricted cover. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For every deck transformation $h$, the maps $(x,s)\mapsto h\widetilde F_s(x)$ and $(x,s)\mapsto\widetilde F_s(hx)$ lift the same homotopy $F(p(x),s)$ and agree at $s=0$. Uniqueness in [F2] makes them equal. The retraction is therefore deck-equivariant, and its induced isomorphism on first homology is $\Lambda_r$-linear. By [F1] the target homology of the full cover is $A_L$, proving the asserted module isomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; a nonempty oriented $r$-component link $L$ with $r\ge1$; its maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$; $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$; a basepoint $b\in E_L$, and the first Hurewicz map $\phi_E:\pi_1(E_L,b)\to H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$.

[A1] AC, as assumed by the link-complement and one-variable-cover suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F1] The maximal-abelian-cover module is $A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)$ with its $\Lambda_r$ deck action ([[def-maximal-abelian-cover-alexander-module]]).

[F2] The ring $\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian and a UFD, with units exactly signed Laurent monomials ([[lem-multivariable-laurent-ring-noetherian-ufd]]).

[F3] For a finitely presented module, the $j$th elementary ideal is the ideal generated by all minors of the prescribed size in a finite presentation matrix ([[def-elementary-ideals-of-a-finitely-presented-module]]).

[F4] For every commutative ring and finitely presented module, each elementary ideal is independent of the finite presentation and invariant under module isomorphism ([[lem-elementary-ideals-are-independent-of-the-presentation]]).

[F5] A finite CW structure on $E_L$ lifts to a finite-rank free $\Lambda_r$ cellular chain complex whose first homology is $A_L$ ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-cellular-chain-model]]).

[F6] The one-variable Alexander module is first homology of the cover classified by total linking, whose defining map sums the Alexander-dual meridian coordinates ([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]).

[F7] Connected covers are classified by their induced fundamental-group subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F8] The maximal abelian cover deformation retracts equivariantly onto the restricted compact-exterior cover ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

[F9] A connected regular cover has deck group the quotient of its fundamental group by the induced subgroup ([[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]]).

## Proof

1.1 Write the lifted finite free complex from [F5] as $C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0$. Since $\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian by [F2], every submodule of a finite free module is finitely generated: induct on the rank $n$ of $\Lambda_r^n$; project a submodule $N$ to the first coordinate, choose lifts of finitely many generators of its image ideal, and apply the induction hypothesis to the kernel in $\Lambda_r^{n-1}$. Thus $Z_1=\ker d_1$ is finitely generated, and $B_1=\operatorname{im}d_2$ is generated by the finitely many columns of $d_2$. The quotient $A_L=Z_1/B_1$ is finitely generated. Choose a surjection $\Lambda_r^m\to A_L$ with finite $m$; its kernel is a submodule of $\Lambda_r^m$ and hence finitely generated by the same argument. This is a finite presentation of $A_L$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, given, construct]

1.2 Let $\bar\eta:H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ be the total-linking map. By [F1] the positive meridians are the coordinate basis, so the coordinate-sum definition [F6] sends each one to $1$. Define $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1$ to be its induced ring map $t_i\mapsto t$. By [F7], quotienting the maximal abelian cover of $E_L$ by $\ker\bar\eta$ gives the connected cover classified by $\ker(\bar\eta\circ\phi_E)$; this quotient cover is regular with deck group $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)/\ker\bar\eta\cong\mathbb Z$ by [F9]. The equivariant deformation retraction [F8] descends to a deformation retraction of this quotient cover onto the corresponding quotient of the open-complement cover; by [F6] the latter is the one-variable total-linking cover. For every lifted cell orbit, tensoring its free rank-one $\Lambda_r$ summand with $\Lambda_1$ along $\eta$ identifies the quotient-orbit generator with a free rank-one $\Lambda_1$ generator, and sends each boundary coefficient to its image under $\eta$. Therefore $C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ is the cellular chain complex of the total-linking cover of $E_L$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, construct]

2.1 Use the resulting finite presentation to define each $E_j(A_L)$ as in [F3]. Any other triangulation of the same marked exterior lifts to another CW structure on the same topological cover; [F5] identifies the homology of either lifted cellular complex with the same singular module $A_L$, and the deck action in both identifications is the same. A different lift of a cell multiplies its basis element by a deck monomial, also leaving the resulting singular module unchanged. Hence the modules computed from the two choices are isomorphic. By [F4] all their elementary ideals agree. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)$ and $q=\dim_K(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}K)$. For a finite presentation matrix with $n$ target generators, tensoring with $K$ shows its rank is $n-q$. Therefore at least one $(n-q)\times(n-q)$ minor is nonzero (with the empty minor equal to $1$ when $n=q$), so $E_q(A_L)\ne0$. This ideal has finitely many generators by its finite presentation, and in the UFD [F2] their gcd exists and is unique up to a unit. Since [F4] makes the ideal presentation-independent, the gcd is well-defined up to a unit of $\Lambda_r$, which by [F2] is $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Homology does not in general commute with this coefficient extension. ## Statement

Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F6] The one-variable Alexander module is first homology of the cover classified by total linking, whose defining map sums the Alexander-dual meridian coordinates ([[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]).

[F7] Connected covers are classified by their induced fundamental-group subgroups ([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]).

[F8] The maximal abelian cover deformation retracts equivariantly onto the restricted compact-exterior cover ([[lem-maximal-abelian-cover-link-exterior-retraction]]).

1.1 Write the lifted finite free complex from [F5] as $C_2\xrightarrow{d_2}C_1\xrightarrow{d_1}C_0$. Choose a surjection $\Lambda_r^m\to A_L$ with finite $m$; its kernel is a submodule of $\Lambda_r^m$ and hence finitely generated by the same argument. This is a finite presentation of $A_L$. 1.2 Use the resulting finite presentation to define each $E_j(A_L)$ as in [F3]. Any other triangulation of the same marked exterior lifts to another CW structure on the same topological cover; [F5] identifies the homology of either lifted cellular complex with the same singular module $A_L$, and the deck action in both identifications is the same. 3.1 Let $\bar\eta:H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ be the total-linking map. By [F1] the positive meridians are the coordinate basis, so the coordinate-sum definition [F6] sends each one to $1$. Therefore $C_*^{\mathrm{cell}}(E_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ is the cellular chain complex of the total-linking cover of $E_L$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, construct]

Thus for $r\ge2$ the chain specialization does not in general identify the specialized chain-complex homology with the tensor product of $A_L$, and no equality of specialized homology orders follows without additional hypotheses. [F2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integer $r\ge1$ and commuting indeterminates $t_1,\ldots,t_r$.

[F1] The one-variable Laurent ring $\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1}]$ is Noetherian and a UFD, and its units are $\pm t_1^k$ ([[lem-the-laurent-polynomial-ring-is-noetherian-and-a-unique-factorisation-domain]]).

[F2] A polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a Noetherian commutative ring is Noetherian ([[cor-finite-variable-polynomial-ring-noetherian]]).

[F3] Every localization of a Noetherian commutative ring is Noetherian ([[thm-noetherian-ring-quotients-and-localisations]]).

[F4] Products of primitive polynomials over a UFD are primitive, and a primitive positive-degree polynomial is irreducible over the UFD exactly when it is irreducible over its fraction field ([[lem-gauss-lemma-over-a-ufd]]).

[F5] For every field $K$, $K[x]$ is a UFD ([[thm-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-ufd]]).

## Proof

1.1 For $r=1$ the statement is [F1]. Suppose $r>1$, put $P_r=\Lambda_1[t_2,\ldots,t_r]$, and let $S_r$ be the multiplicative set generated by $t_2,\ldots,t_r$. Clearing negative powers identifies $\Lambda_r$ with $S_r^{-1}P_r$. [given, F1, construct, base]

1.2 We prove by induction on the number of added variables that $\Lambda_1[t_2,\ldots,t_r]$ is a UFD. The base is [F1]. For the induction step let $R$ be the preceding UFD and $K$ its fraction field. Every nonzero $f\in R[x]$ is its content $c\in R$ times a primitive polynomial $f_0$: since $f$ has finitely many coefficients, take the product over irreducibles of their minimum exponents in those coefficients. Factor $c$ in $R$ and factor $f_0$ in $K[x]$ using [F5]. Clear denominators in each positive-degree irreducible factor and divide by its content to obtain primitive polynomials $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in R[x]$. By [F4], their product $q$ is primitive and is associated to $f_0$ in $K[x]$. Write this scalar as $a/b$ with coprime $a,b\in R$, so $bf_0=aq$. Any irreducible divisor of $a$ then divides every coefficient of $f_0$, and any irreducible divisor of $b$ divides every coefficient of $q$; primitiveness forces $a$ and $b$ to be units. Thus $f_0$ is associated in $R[x]$ to the product of the $q_i$. Each $q_i$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ by [F4], and the content factors in $R$, so every nonzero nonunit of $R[x]$ factors into irreducibles. [given, F1, F4, F5, induction, construct, IH]

2.1 By [F2], $P_r$ is Noetherian because $\Lambda_1$ is Noetherian by [F1]. Its localization $S_r^{-1}P_r=\Lambda_r$ is Noetherian by [F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

2.2 For uniqueness in the same induction step, contents have unique factorization in $R$. Two factorizations of the primitive part become factorizations in the UFD $K[x]$, so their primitive positive-degree factors pair up up to scalar associates. If primitive $f,g\in R[x]$ satisfy $f=(a/b)g$ for coprime $a,b\in R$, then $bf=ag$; any irreducible factor of $a$ must divide every coefficient of $f$, and any irreducible factor of $b$ must divide every coefficient of $g$. Primitiveness forces $a,b$ to be units, so the scalar is a unit of $R$. This proves uniqueness in $R[x]$ and completes the induction. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, induction, algebra]

3.1 Localizing the UFD $P_r$ at $S_r$ preserves unique factorization: factor a numerator in $P_r$ and discard the irreducible factors that divide an element of $S_r$, since precisely those factors become units. Every remaining irreducible stays prime: if it divides a product of localized fractions, clearing denominators gives divisibility of the product of their numerators in $P_r$, so primality in $P_r$ makes it divide one numerator; it cannot divide a cleared denominator because it was not inverted. Uniqueness follows by clearing denominators and using uniqueness in $P_r$. Thus $\Lambda_r$ is a UFD. [given, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 If $u=f/s\in S_r^{-1}P_r$ is a unit, then $fg=sq$ for some $q\in S_r$. Every irreducible factor of $f$ therefore divides a product of powers of $t_2,\ldots,t_r$, so it is associated in $P_r$ to one of these variables. The only units already in $P_r$ are the units of $\Lambda_1$, namely $\pm t_1^k$, by degree in $t_2,\ldots,t_r$ and [F1]. Consequently the units of $\Lambda_r$ are exactly $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. [given, F1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 prove Noetherianity, unique factorization, and the stated unit description for every $r\ge1$. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC when the form is obtained from a knot. For every integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, the class represented by $(H,-V)$ is the additive inverse of the class represented by $(H,V)$ in $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

## Statement references

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The group presentation of algebraic concordance and the definition of a metabolic lattice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$ and the defining relations of $G_{\mathbb Z}$.

[A1] Full AC is inherited only when the abstract lattice is instantiated as a knot's Seifert pairing; the diagonal calculation below is choice-free. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] In $G_{\mathbb Z}$, direct sum is addition and every metabolic lattice represents zero. [[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]]

## Proof
