## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot such that its double branched cover $M=\Sigma_2(K)$ is a rational homology sphere. Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth proper embedded disk with boundary $K$, and let $B_D$ be the connected double cover of $B^4$ branched over $D$. Let $W$ be a compact connected smooth simply connected oriented four-manifold with boundary identified orientation-compatibly with $M$, and assume its boundary intersection form is positive definite. Assume also that the image of $\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(B_D)$ normally generates $\pi_1(B_D)$, meaning its normal closure is the whole group. Then the oriented gluing $X=W\cup_M(-B_D)$ is a closed smooth simply connected positive-definite four-manifold, and inclusion induces an isometric full-rank embedding $Q_W\hookrightarrow Q_X$ of integral intersection lattices with $b_2(X)=b_2(W)$.

## Statement references

[[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot|The oriented double branched cover of a knot]]

[[lem-double-cover-branched-over-a-slice-disk-is-a-rational-homology-ball|A smooth slice disk has a rational-homology-ball double branched cover]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; the knot, slice disk, rational-homology-sphere boundary, positive-definite simply connected filling, boundary identification, and normal-generation hypothesis in the statement.

[F1] For a smooth proper disk, the double cover branched over the disk is a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold with rational homology of a point, and its boundary is the double branched cover of the boundary knot. The result does not assert a fundamental-group conclusion. [[lem-double-cover-branched-over-a-slice-disk-is-a-rational-homology-ball]]

[F2] The double branched cover is defined by the connected cover of the knot exterior classified by the positive-meridian map to $\mathbb Z/2$, filled along the closed lift of the squared meridian. [[def-cyclic-branched-cover-of-a-knot]]

[F3] Smooth four-ball genus is the minimum genus of a smooth proper oriented surface in $B^4$; a smooth slice disk is the genus-zero case. [[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus]]

[F4] The boundary form is the signed intersection pairing on the torsion-free quotient, and is rationally nondegenerate when the boundary is a rational homology sphere. [[def-intersection-lattice-of-a-four-manifold-with-boundary]] [[lem-boundary-intersection-pairing-well-defined-and-nondegenerate]]

[F5] Seifert–van Kampen computes the fundamental group of a union along a path-connected collar as the pushout of the two inclusion homomorphisms. [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F6] Mayer–Vietoris gives the singular-homology exact sequence for the collar-thickened decomposition along $M$. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F7] Smooth collars on the two boundaries allow the orientation-compatible gluing and its collar-thickened open cover. [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]

[F8] For any abelian group $A$, $A\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ is its positive-integer localization, and $a\otimes1=0$ exactly when some positive integer kills $a$. The natural coefficient map identifies $H_j(Y;\mathbb Z)\otimes\mathbb Q$ with $H_j(Y;\mathbb Q)$. [[lem-rationalization-is-exact-and-commutes-with-singular-homology]]

[A1] For this particular branched cover $B_D$, the boundary inclusion normally generates $\pi_1(B_D)$. This is an explicit additional hypothesis; it is not a consequence of the rational-homology-ball supplier [F1].

[A2] Full AC is assumed by the branched-cover and homology suppliers in [F1]–[F3].

## Proof

**Given:** The data and assumptions above.

1.1 By [F3], $D$ is a smooth proper slice disk; [F1] and [F2] then give a compact rational homology four-ball $B_D$ with boundary $M=\Sigma_2(K)$. ## Statement

Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary knot
$K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$. Choose a product tubular neighborhood
$\nu(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ whose intersection with $S^3$ is the chosen tube
$N(K)$, and let $X=\overline{B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu(D)}$. Then the
inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
carrying the positive meridian of $K$ to the positive normal-circle generator.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Lemma 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hatcher, §2.2](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch2.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth proper disk $D$ in the standard $B^4$, its product tubular neighborhood, and the induced knot exterior on the boundary.

[F1] [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K]$.

[F2] [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] and [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]: relative homology excision and the natural pair sequence apply to the compact manifold pairs below.

[F3] [[cor-homology-of-spheres]]: $B^4$ is contractible, so its positive-degree homology vanishes.

[F4] [[def-knot-exterior]] and [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] fix the boundary exterior and positive-meridian orientation.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The portion of $\partial X$ added by deleting $\nu(D)$ is the normal-circle bundle $D^2\times S^1$, and it meets $E_K$ in $S^1\times S^1$. By excision [F2], the relative pair $(B^4,X)$ has the homology of $(D^2\times D^2,D^2\times S^1)$. The latter solid-torus subspace has $H_1\cong\mathbb Z$ generated by a normal circle and $H_2=0$, while $D^2\times D^2$ is contractible by [F3]. Its pair sequence [F2] therefore identifies $H_2(B^4,X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z$, generated by a normal disk whose boundary is that normal circle. [F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 In the pair sequence of $(B^4,X)$, the segment $$H_2(B^4)\longrightarrow H_2(B^4,X)\xrightarrow{\partial}H_1(X)\longrightarrow H_1(B^4)$$ has zero end groups by [F3]. Hence $\partial$ is an isomorphism. The generator from step 1.1 maps to the normal circle on $D^2\times S^1$. A path in the base disk $D^2$ from an interior point to a boundary point gives a homotopy of these normal circles to the boundary meridian of $K$, with orientation fixed by [F4]. Thus $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_X]$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 The inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ carries the boundary meridian $\mu_K$ to the same normal circle $\mu_X$. It is therefore an isomorphism between the infinite cyclic groups in [F1] and step 2.1. [F1, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard $3$-sphere, let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented Seifert surface of genus $g$, and let $D\subset B^4$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk with oriented boundary $K$. Then the positive-push Seifert lattice $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is metabolic: it has a rank-$g$ primitive direct summand on which $V$ vanishes identically.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert pairing on integral first homology]]

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The rank-half primitive direct-summand definition of a metabolizer]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a Seifert surface $F$ of genus $g$, and a locally flat slice disk $D$ with the same oriented boundary knot.

[A1] Full AC is the family-of-nonempty-sets choice axiom used by the Seifert-pairing convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] For an ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, the matrix entries are $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, and $V$ is bilinear on homology. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[lem-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F2] Poincaré–Lefschetz duality for a compact oriented $3$-manifold $R$ with boundary $\Sigma$ identifies $H_i(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ with $H^{3-i}(R;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F3] The linking number of disjoint rational boundary cycles in $S^3=\partial B^4$ is the signed intersection number of collared rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ that bound them. [[lem-linking-number-equals-four-dimensional-intersection-number]]

[F4] A $g$-dimensional rational subspace on which $V$ vanishes saturates to a rank-$g$ direct summand of the integral lattice, still with vanishing restriction. [[lem-rational-isotropic-subspace-saturates-to-integral-metabolizer]]

[F5] For the given locally flat slice disk the hypersurface supplier constructs the compact oriented locally flat Seifert three-manifold with an actual two-sided product and positive-push alignment. Its pre-collar-push model meets the outer sphere in $F$, with the stated product corners at $K$. Its smooth branch remains the previously supplied smooth construction; its TOP branch explicitly imports separate relative normal-bundle and microbundle-transversality theorems. [[lem-locally-flat-slice-surface-bounds-seifert-hypersurface]]

[F6] Smooth chains compute continuous real homology, including for a smooth manifold with boundary. This is invoked below only in smooth ambient neighborhoods, not by treating a locally flat $R$ as an already smooth submanifold. [[thm-smooth-singular-chains-compute-singular-homology]]

[F7] Under full AC a compact TOP three-manifold has a finite compatible PL triangulation, with boundary a subcomplex. In particular its Betti numbers and Euler characteristic are finite. This is intrinsic to the three-manifold and does not smooth its embedding in the four-ball. [[thm-compact-topological-three-manifolds-admit-finite-pl-triangulations]]

[F8] The positive-push pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has skew part equal to the algebraic intersection form on $F$, which is unimodular. Hence $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is an integral Seifert lattice in the sense of the metabolic-form definition. [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F9] A connected compact oriented surface of genus $g$ with one boundary component has $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ free of rank $2g$, and capping that boundary gives a closed genus-$g$ surface of Euler characteristic $2-2g$. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F10] The homology sequence of a pair is exact, including $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$. [[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-a-pair-in-singular-homology]]

[F11] The compact TOP manifold $R$ has a collar of $\Sigma$; open thickenings of the two copies in its double retract to the copies of $R$, and their overlap retracts to $\Sigma$. Mayer–Vietoris with constant rational coefficients therefore gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$; the Betti ranks are finite by [F7]. [[thm-topological-collaring-for-manifold-boundaries]], [[thm-excision-and-mayer-vietoris-with-local-coefficients]]

[F13] For the finite CW models supplied by [F7], the alternating rank-nullity identity on the rational cellular chain complex gives $\chi(X)=\sum_i(-1)^i\dim_{\mathbb Q}H_i(X;\mathbb Q)$. This is the Euler–Poincaré calculation for a finite complex. [[thm-euler-poincare-formula-for-finite-cw-complexes]]

[F12] The closed oriented double $\widehat R$ is a compact TOP three-manifold with finite Betti ranks by [F7]. Poincaré duality over $\mathbb Q$ pairs its Betti numbers in complementary degrees, so [F13] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=0$. [[thm-poincare-duality-for-oriented-topological-manifolds]]

[F14] Over $\mathbb Q$, the universal coefficient theorem identifies $H^i(R;\mathbb Q)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q}(H_i(R;\mathbb Q),\mathbb Q)$ because the $\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Q}$ term vanishes. By [F7], these homology groups are finite-dimensional, so $\dim H^i(R;\mathbb Q)=b_i(R)$. [[thm-universal-coefficient-theorem-for-cohomology-over-a-pid]]

## Proof

1.1 First assume the given disk is smooth. Construct $R$ by [F5], and write $\Sigma=\partial R=F\cup D$ after matching collars. The Axiom of Choice [A1] is the hypothesis under which the supplied Seifert-pairing and duality interfaces are invoked. Capping the sole boundary circle of $F$ by a disk does not change $H_1$ because that circle is already the boundary of the oriented fundamental $2$-chain of $F$; by [F9] and exactness [F10], $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. ## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot smoothly concordant to the unknot. Then there are finite-rank free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ bifiltered chain complexes $A$ and $B$, each having zero total homology, such that
$$ \mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A\simeq \Lambda\oplus B, $$
where $\Lambda=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ is the normalized unknot complex with zero differential and generator in Maslov grading and both filtration coordinates zero, and $\simeq$ is a Maslov-graded filtered chain homotopy equivalence whose maps and homotopies do not increase either filtration. The acyclic summands are acyclic only after the filtrations are forgotten; no acyclicity of their associated-graded complexes is asserted.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth concordance from a knot to the unknot]]

[Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, Theorem 1 and §3.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383)

[Hom, *The knot Floer complex and the smooth concordance group*, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.6635)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth concordance from $K$ to the unknot, the accepted normalized knot complex over $\Lambda=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$, and ACω.

[F1] Smooth concordance is represented by the actual annulus in the Statement. [[def-smooth-knot-concordance]]

[F2] The accepted normalized knot/grid and analytic comparisons identify the finite homogeneous bifiltered complex, total generator and both grading origins. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]], [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]]

[F3] **External Floer input under CLAUDE.md §12:** a smoothly slice knot has $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\simeq\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(U)\oplus D$ as a graded bifiltered Laurent chain complex, with $D$ finite-rank free and totally acyclic. The finite homogeneous filtered-basis splitting and the concordance-to-slice application are [Hom, *A survey on Heegaard Floer homology and concordance*, Theorem1, Proposition3.11 and its proof, and proof of Theorem1, printed1–2,12–14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00383v3). Coefficients are $\mathbb F_2$; acyclicity concerns total homology and not associated gradeds. The unknot factor has the usual Maslov-zero and $(0,0)$ origin. This is an external established input, not a completed local decorated-annulus/movie construction. The cited statements and finite splitting proof on printed1–2,12–14 were read; no complete reading of the survey or its upstream surgery references is claimed.

[F4] **Choice scope of the external input:** use it for the fixed knot diagram and finite smooth concordance/surface under consideration, not for a simultaneous choice of data for every knot. Integer domains and Spin-c labels form countable sets; all coefficient matrices and final graded basis changes are finite. Compact source charts give separable Sobolev and almost-complex parameter spaces with countable bases. Their fixed Fredholm problems admit a countable family of finite-cokernel perturbation charts, selected using ACω; the usual finite-dimensional Sard reduction and least-basis nested-ball Baire construction select one datum regular for the countable list. Compactness/gluing is used pointwise for these data, with finite covers of the compact low-index moduli and least-integer shrinking thresholds, not an arbitrary family of choices. Thus the imported fixed-data construction has a finite/countable specialization; full AC is not substituted for the declared ACω branch. The cited papers are not claimed to contain an explicit foundational choice audit.

## Proof

1.1 The given annulus makes $K$ smoothly slice in exactly the sense of [F3]. Use [F2] to identify the input with its normalized finite homogeneous model. Apply [F3] at these fixed data, with the finite/countable specialization [F4], to obtain $C(K)\simeq\Lambda\oplus D$ with all maps and homotopies preserving both filtrations and Maslov grading. Its displayed unknot factor has the same origins as the Statement; no Alexander translation or positive $U$-power is inserted. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 Set $A=0$ and $B=D$. The zero complex is finite-rank free and totally acyclic, as is $D$ by [F3]. The equivalence in step1.1 is therefore the exact stable equivalence requested. No associated-graded acyclicity or filtration-preserving contraction of $D$ is claimed. This closes the original Statement by the explicit external slice-splitting input; the earlier locally attempted movie admission is not represented as a proof. [F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot smoothly concordant to the unknot. Then there are finite-rank free $\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ bifiltered chain complexes $A$ and $B$, each having zero total homology, such that
$$ \mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\oplus A\simeq \Lambda\oplus B, $$
where $\Lambda=\mathbb F_2[U,U^{-1}]$ is the normalized unknot complex with zero differential and generator in Maslov grading and both filtration coordinates zero, and $\simeq$ is a Maslov-graded filtered chain homotopy equivalence whose maps and homotopies do not increase either filtration. The acyclic summands are acyclic only after the filtrations are forgotten; no acyclicity of their associated-graded complexes is asserted.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth concordance from a knot to the unknot]]

[F1] Smooth concordance is represented by the actual annulus in the Statement. [[def-smooth-knot-concordance]]

[F2] The accepted normalized knot/grid and analytic comparisons identify the finite homogeneous bifiltered complex, total generator and both grading origins. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]], [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]]

[F3] **External Floer input under CLAUDE.md §12:** a smoothly slice knot has $\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)\simeq\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(U)\oplus D$ as a graded bifiltered Laurent chain complex, with $D$ finite-rank free and totally acyclic. This is an external established input, not a completed local decorated-annulus/movie construction. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $F$ be a fixed minimum-genus oriented Seifert surface, and let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H_1$ be admissible doubly pointed Heegaard diagrams for the same pair $(K,F)$ whose hat complexes have total homology $\mathbb F_2$ and the same absolute Alexander normalization. Their diagramwise thresholds agree. Moreover, every grid presentation of $(K,F)$ gives this same value after the full filtered grid complex is converted to the normalized singly pointed model, with all basepoint-variable and stabilization factors accounted for. The common value is $\tau(K)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice, a knot $K$, a fixed minimum-genus Seifert surface $F$, and two admissible doubly pointed diagrams with the stated one-dimensional total homology and common absolute normalization.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] states the axiom that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function; it is inherited by the current diagram/move suppliers that require selected finite data.

[F1] [[lem-tau-preserved-by-filtered-chain-homotopy-equivalence]] proves that a filtration-preserving chain homotopy equivalence between finite models with one-dimensional total homology preserves their tau thresholds.

Specializing the actual finite identities at U=0 gives the filtered hat comparisons; this does not supply the separate grid-to-analytic identification.

[L2] [[thm-grid-commutation-stabilization-invariance-proof]] gives the local filtered equivalences for commutations and stabilizations, using the stated polygon maps and the stabilization cone comparison. [L3] [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]] constructs the normalized comparison from the grid full filtered minus complex to the singly pointed analytic model. This proves the analytic-diagram comparison in the first sentence. [F1, L1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Fix a grid $G$ with $n$ marking pairs and choose one marking variable $U_i$. Use the actual normalized grid-to-analytic comparison in [L3], together with the pointed-move comparison in [L1], to convert its full filtered minus complex to the finite singly pointed model for $(K,F)$. ## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link, let $F$ be a compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $L$, and put $X=S^3\setminus L$. For each component $K_i$, let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian, oriented as the boundary of a small normal disk so that a positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by the disk's positive basis gives the ambient orientation. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the free abelian group on $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_r]$. Define the total-linking homomorphism $\varphi:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ by $\varphi(\sum_i m_i[\mu_i])=\sum_i m_i$. If a smooth oriented loop $J\subset X$ is transverse to the interior of $F$, define its signed intersection number $J\cdot F$ by counting $+1$ when $J$ crosses from the negative to the positive side of the oriented normal of $F$ and $-1$ for the reverse crossing. Then $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$.

## Statement references

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|Alexander-duality coordinates and the total-linking homomorphism]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty smooth oriented link $L$, a compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$, and a smooth loop $J$ in $X=S^3\setminus L$ transverse to the interior of $F$.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient choice hypothesis for the Alexander-duality convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The link complement $X$ is connected, and Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ on the positive meridian basis; total linking is the sum of the component coordinates. [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F2] Smooth loops and homotopies in $X$ can be perturbed to be transverse to the interior of $F$, while a prescribed closed region on which the map is already suitable is kept fixed. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

[F3] The degree-one Hurewicz map sends $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ onto $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ and factors through abelianization. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $L$, $F$, $X$, $J$, and the conventions of the Statement.

1.1 Choose a basepoint $x_0\in X\setminus F$, which exists on a local side of any interior point of $F$. Represent any class of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ by a smooth loop transverse to $\operatorname{Int}F$, using [F2]. Define $I_F$ on that class to be its signed intersection count. If two such loops are homotopic in $X$, perturb the homotopy relative to its boundary by [F2]. The inverse image of $\operatorname{Int}F$ is then a compact oriented one-manifold in the homotopy annulus; it is compact because the annulus image is disjoint from $L=\partial F$. Orient it using the orientations of the annulus and the normal of $F$. Its oriented boundary signs at the two ends are the intersection signs of the endpoint loops with opposite signs on the two boundary circles. The total signed boundary count is zero, so the endpoint intersection counts agree. Concatenation adds counts, hence $I_F:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 Near a point of $K_i$, choose oriented local coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in which $K_i$ is the $x$-axis and $F$ is the half-plane $y\ge0$, $z=0$. The boundary orientation and the stated positive-meridian convention make $(x,y,z)$ ambient-positive. The small positive meridian crosses this half-plane exactly once, at $(0,\rho,0)$ for some $\rho>0$, in the $+z$ direction. Thus $\overline I_F([\mu_i])=1$ for every $i$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F3], this homomorphism factors through a homomorphism $\overline I_F:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$. The signed intersection convention in the Statement agrees with this induced map on the class represented by $J$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], the classes $[\mu_i]$ form a basis of $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$. The homomorphisms $\overline I_F$ and $\varphi$ agree on every basis element by step 1.2 and [F1], so they are equal. Evaluating this equality on $[J]$ gives $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$. [F1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty smooth oriented link, let $F$ be a compact smooth oriented embedded surface with oriented boundary $L$, and put $X=S^3\setminus L$. For each component $K_i$, let $\mu_i$ be the positive meridian, oriented as the boundary of a small normal disk so that a positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by the disk's positive basis gives the ambient orientation. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with the free abelian group on $[\mu_1],\ldots,[\mu_r]$. Define the total-linking homomorphism $\varphi:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$ by $\varphi(\sum_i m_i[\mu_i])=\sum_i m_i$. If a smooth oriented loop $J\subset X$ is transverse to the interior of $F$, define its signed intersection number $J\cdot F$ by counting $+1$ when $J$ crosses from the negative to the positive side of the oriented normal of $F$ and $-1$ for the reverse crossing. Then $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$.

## Statement references

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|Alexander-duality coordinates and the total-linking homomorphism]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty smooth oriented link $L$, a compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$, and a smooth loop $J$ in $X=S^3\setminus L$ transverse to the interior of $F$.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient choice hypothesis for the Alexander-duality convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The link complement $X$ is connected, and Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ on the positive meridian basis; total linking is the sum of the component coordinates. [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F2] Smooth loops and homotopies in $X$ can be perturbed to be transverse to the interior of $F$, while a prescribed closed region on which the map is already suitable is kept fixed. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

[F3] The degree-one Hurewicz map sends $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ onto $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ and factors through abelianization. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

**Given:** Full AC, $L$, $F$, $X$, $J$, and the conventions of the Statement.

1.1 Choose a basepoint $x_0\in X\setminus F$, which exists on a local side of any interior point of $F$. Represent any class of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ by a smooth loop transverse to $\operatorname{Int}F$, using [F2]. Define $I_F$ on that class to be its signed intersection count. If two such loops are homotopic in $X$, perturb the homotopy relative to its boundary by [F2]. The inverse image of $\operatorname{Int}F$ is then a compact oriented one-manifold in the homotopy annulus; it is compact because the annulus image is disjoint from $L=\partial F$. Orient it using the orientations of the annulus and the normal of $F$. Its oriented boundary signs at the two ends are the intersection signs of the endpoint loops with opposite signs on the two boundary circles. The total signed boundary count is zero, so the endpoint intersection counts agree. Concatenation adds counts, hence $I_F:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 By [F3], this homomorphism factors through a homomorphism $\overline I_F:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$. The signed intersection convention in the Statement agrees with this induced map on the class represented by $J$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Near a point of $K_i$, choose oriented local coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in which $K_i$ is the $x$-axis and $F$ is the half-plane $y\ge0$, $z=0$. The boundary orientation and the stated positive-meridian convention make $(x,y,z)$ ambient-positive. The small positive meridian crosses this half-plane exactly once, at $(0,\rho,0)$ for some $\rho>0$, in the $+z$ direction. Thus $\overline I_F([\mu_i])=1$ for every $i$. [F1, given, construct]

2.2 By [F1], the classes $[\mu_i]$ form a basis of $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$. The homomorphisms $\overline I_F$ and $\varphi$ agree on every basis element by step 2.1 and [F1], so they are equal. Evaluating this equality on $[J]$ gives $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $C(K)=\mathrm{CFK}^{\infty}(K)$ have a finite homogeneous basis $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ with Maslov grading $M(x_r)$ and Alexander filtration $A(x_r)$. Let $C^-(K)$ be the subcomplex spanned over $\mathbb F_2[U]$ by $U^n x_r$ for $n\ge0$, with $M(U^n x_r)=M(x_r)-2n$ and $A(U^n x_r)=A(x_r)-n$, and assume $H_*(C^-(K))\cong\mathbb F_2[U]$ with generator in Maslov degree zero. For each integer $s$, let $\mathcal A(K,s)$ be the subcomplex spanned over $\mathbb F_2$ by those terms $U^n x_r$ with $n\ge0$ and $A(x_r)-n\le s$. For any Maslov-graded $\mathbb F_2[U]$ complex $D$, let $\delta(D)$ be the maximal Maslov grading of a homogeneous non-torsion class in $H_*(D)$, with $\delta(D)=-\infty$ if no such class exists. Define $\nu^-(K)$ to be the least integer $s$ for which $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))=0$. Then
$$ 0\le \nu^-(K)\le g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K), $$
where $g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ is the minimum genus of a smooth compact connected oriented properly embedded surface in the four-ball bounded by $K$.

## Statement references

[[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex|The finite bifiltered complex and filtration-coordinate convention]]

[[def-smooth-and-topological-slice-genus|The smooth four-ball genus branch]]

[[lem-knot-floer-large-surgery-and-filtered-cobordism-input|The separate tau cobordism inequality, which does not replace the nu-minus estimate]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz, and Szabo, *Concordance homomorphisms from knot Floer homology*, §2.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795)

[Hom and Wu, *Four-ball genus bounds and a refinement of the Ozsvath-Szabo tau-invariant*, Proposition 2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1565)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot, its normalized minus complex, and the smooth four-ball genus.

[F1] [[def-upsilon-function-from-filtered-complex]]: the finite bifiltered complex has a finite homogeneous basis, multiplication by $U$ lowers both filtration coordinates by one and Maslov grading by two, and its total localized homology has a normalized Maslov-zero generator.

[F2] The accepted normalized grid-to-analytic comparison identifies the knot complexes, with all marked-variable and stabilization factors accounted for. It is reused at that exact knot scope. [[thm-grid-homology-independent-of-grid-and-equals-knot-floer]]

[A6] [[lem-heegaard-floer-holomorphic-disk-regularity-compactness-gluing]] supplies actual full-filtered chosen disk counts and compactification for knots in $S^3$, without the grid/Heegaard identification or the absolute large-surgery normalization.

[A7] [[def-countable-choice]]: the declared analytic cobordism branch uses countable choice; no full choice is inferred.

[F3] The accepted normalized analytic coordinate-swap equivalence is Maslov-zero and Laurent-linear, exchanges both filtrations, and preserves the normalized total generator, with its filtered inverse and homotopies. [[lem-knot-floer-duality-and-filtration-swap]]

[F4] **External genus input under CLAUDE.md §12:** for the normalized $\mathbb F_2[U]$ knot complex, the least $s$ with $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))=0$ is at most the smooth four-ball genus. Its module, Maslov and Alexander conventions are exactly Definitions2.11–2.12 and Theorem2.14 of [Ozsváth–Stipsicz–Szabó, printed10–11](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.1795v3). Proposition2.13 identifies this threshold with Hom–Wu's $\nu^+$; [Hom–Wu, Proposition2.4, printed5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.1565v1) supplies the smooth genus inequality. This imports the established large-surgery/cobordism bound, not just a formal triangle identity or a localized nonzero map. The exact OSS §2.3 statement and plus/minus proof on printed10–11 and Hom–Wu definition/propositions on printed3–5 were read; Rasmussen’s upstream proof is not represented as read or locally reconstructed.

[F5] **Choice scope of the external input:** use it for the fixed knot diagram and finite smooth concordance/surface under consideration, not for a simultaneous choice of data for every knot. Integer domains and Spin-c labels form countable sets; all coefficient matrices and final graded basis changes are finite. Compact source charts give separable Sobolev and almost-complex parameter spaces with countable bases. Their fixed Fredholm problems admit a countable family of finite-cokernel perturbation charts, selected using ACω; the usual finite-dimensional Sard reduction and least-basis nested-ball Baire construction select one datum regular for the countable list. Compactness/gluing is used pointwise for these data, with finite covers of the compact low-index moduli and least-integer shrinking thresholds, not an arbitrary family of choices. Thus the imported fixed-data construction has a finite/countable specialization; full AC is not substituted for the declared ACω branch. The cited papers are not claimed to contain an explicit foundational choice audit.

## Proof

1.1 Write $M_r=M(x_r)$ and $A_r=A(x_r)$. The terms of $\mathcal A(K,s)$ on the $r$th $U$-tower are $U^n x_r$ with $n\ge\max(0,A_r-s)$, so their Maslov gradings are at most $M_r-2\max(0,A_r-s)$. By [F1], this bound tends to $-\infty$ as $s$ tends to $-\infty$; since the basis is finite, choose $s_0$ so that it is strictly negative for every $r$ when $s\le s_0$. Then $H_*(\mathcal A(K,s))$ has no class of degree zero and $\delta(\mathcal A(K,s))\ne0$. For all $s\ge\max_r A_r$, $\mathcal A(K,s)=C^-(K)$ and its normalized tower gives $\delta=0$. Thus the set defining $\nu^-$ is nonempty and bounded below, and its least element exists. This argument does not prove that the least element is nonnegative. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Put $R=\mathbb F_2[U]$, $B=C^-(K)$ and $A_s=\mathcal A(K,s)$. The latter has finite free basis $U^{\max(0,A_r-s)}x_r$. Its actual inclusion $v_s:A_s\to B$ becomes the identity of $C(K)$ after localization. Therefore the kernel of its homology map is $U$-torsion and its image is a nonzero homogeneous ideal $U^{V_s}R$, with $V_s\ge0$. A homogeneous polynomial-torsion class is $U$-torsion: the different powers of $U$ have distinct Maslov degrees, so a polynomial annihilator implies a monomial annihilator for that class. Consequently homogeneous non-torsion classes are exactly the homogeneous classes having nonzero image in the localized tower. Their maximal grading is the top grading of the image ideal, and hence $\delta(A_s)=-2V_s$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Reuse the supplied Maslov-zero Laurent-linear analytic coordinate-swap equivalence $\Phi:C(K)\to C(K)$, preserving the normalized total generator and swapping the two filtrations, with its swap-filtered inverse and homotopies. For $s\in\mathbb Z$, $h_s=\Phi U^s:A_s\to B$ is an actual polynomial-target map: a point with $i\le0,j\le s$ goes to $(j-s,i-s)$, whose first coordinate is at most zero. Its Maslov degree is $-2s$. It localizes to an isomorphism, so its homology image is $U^{H_s}R$, $H_s\ge0$. The same non-torsion-domain calculation gives $-2H_s=\delta(A_s)-2s$, and thus $H_s=V_s+s$. This argument permits negative $s$ in the Laurent intermediate complex and proves that the final target lies in the polynomial subcomplex; it does not treat $U^s$ alone as an endomorphism of $B$ for negative $s$. [F3, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 If $s<0$, $V_s=H_s-s\ge -s>0$. Therefore $\delta(A_s)\ne0$ for every negative $s$. Together with step1.1 this proves existence of the threshold and $\nu^-(K)\ge0$. A direct local alternative for the upper inequality would require an actual surface input. Sufficient would be an $R$-linear Maslov-zero map from the unknot tower to $B$, with image in $A_g$, sending the homology generator to the normalized generator1. Its image cycle would force $V_g=0$ and $\nu^-(K)\le g$. A map with value a positive $U$-power, a localized nonzero map, or a tau inequality does not suffice. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The finite free basis of $A_s$ in step2.1 is exactly the basis in the external Definition2.12, since its exponent condition is $n\ge\max(0,A_r-s)$, and the normalized top minus grading is zero in both conventions. Thus [F4] applies to the SAME threshold, not to a shifted plus invariant. It gives $\nu^-(K)\le g_4^{\mathrm{sm}}(K)$ at the fixed data with [F5]. Combine this with step2.3 to obtain both original inequalities. The upper bound is explicitly external; the local exponent/nonnegativity argument is retained. [given, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, the Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In all cases the punctured normal tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The knot, its finite diagram code, and a sufficiently small normal tube.

[F1] A finite regular code has $c$ underpassing points and, for $c>0$, $c$ maximal under-arcs. Its finite drawing separates every pair of disjoint closed arc pieces by a positive distance. [[def-knot-planar-code]]

[F2] The compact-tube construction supplies the normal coordinates and radial retraction. [[lem-compact-knot-has-choice-free-tube]]

[F3] A CW subcomplex whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence is a strong deformation retract; homotopic attaching maps of a CW pair give homotopy equivalent adjunction spaces. [[lem-cw-homotopy-equivalence-inclusions-are-strong-deformation-retracts]]

[F4] Collapsing a supplied contractible CW subcomplex gives a homotopy equivalence. [[lem-cw-quotients-and-collapse-of-a-contractible-subcomplex]]

[F6] A simple polygon has its bounded polygonal region and the crossing-parity side structure. [[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]]

[F5] Wedges of circles have the free group on their circle loops, and the sphere is simply connected. [[thm-fundamental-group-of-finite-wedge-of-circles]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]], [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

## Proof

1.1 Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. The remaining projected arcs are embedded and pairwise disjoint: an interior double point would have an underpassing preimage, which has been removed. Put these arcs at height $1$, their ends in the plane $z=0$, and join each pair of ends of a removed underpass below that plane. This normalization preserves the complement pair. Indeed, inside a crossing box the two branches retain a strict height inequality while their heights interpolate; away from these boxes projection is injective and vertical interpolation cannot introduce intersections. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar. [given, F1, construct]

1.2 For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. In this strip the ambient map $(\Psi(s,r),z)\mapsto(\Psi(s,r),z-t\chi(r)g(s))$, with $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi$ zero near the strip boundary, is a homeomorphism for each $t$ (it is a translation on every vertical fibre), and is the identity outside the strip. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Here is a precise convenient tunnel model for the normalized knot. In each crossing box choose a small convex polygonal footprint $F_i$ and a convex lower cap $C_i=\{(q,z):q\in F_i,\ h_i(q)\le z\le0\},$ where $h_i$ is piecewise linear, negative inside $F_i$ and zero on its boundary. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$; its coordinates are a disk bundle around $K$, not an assumption about an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. Such bounds exist because the closed ear has no other polygon points, nonadjacent edges have positive separation, and the two remaining incident edges have a positive angle away from the ear; finite determinant and distance comparisons select the bounds. Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement. [F1, F6, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The model can be compared with the given sufficiently small normal tube without invoking a uniqueness theorem or choice. Make its disk-bundle chart smooth near the core and normalize its differential there to the given normal chart; the required linear change is fibrewise, with the tangential component removed by a change of core parameter. In finitely many charts the two resulting embeddings differ by $O(|v|^2)$, with derivative difference $O(|v|)$. Replace the model chart near $v=0$ by the given one using a radial cutoff supported where $|v|<2\delta$ and equal to one for $|v|\le\delta$. The derivative of the correction is $O(\delta)$; compactness and a finite minimum of the chart injectivity bounds therefore preserve a bundle embedding for small $\delta$. Injectivity between nonadjacent core charts follows from their positive separation. The modified chart equals the given normal chart for $|v|\le\delta$ and retains $N_*$ as its outer boundary. Choose the normal-tube radius $\rho<\delta$. In these product coordinates, replace every fibre radius $r\in[\rho,1]$ by $(1-s)r+s$ and fix the exterior of $N_*$. This is a strong deformation retraction from $E_K$ to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N_*$, fixed on its target. It agrees on the outer boundary and never enters the removed radius-$\rho$ tube. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. The top plates of the caps belong to $A$ as tube-boundary faces, except for the two exits occupied by upper tubes. Thus $X=A\cup B$ and $A\cap B$ is the equatorial disk with the interiors of the $F_i$ removed. On $B$ use $(q,z)\mapsto(q,(1-s)z+s h(q))$ and on $A$ the identity. These maps agree on the overlap, remain in the indicated vertical intervals, and paste continuously because the two sets are closed in $X$. They fix their target $Y_*=A\cup\bigcup_i D_i,\qquad D_i=\{(q,h_i(q)):q\in F_i\},$ pointwise. This proves the global strong deformation retraction, including the lower region and infinity. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The upper region $A$ is a ball with the neighborhoods of $c$ disjoint boundary-parallel arcs removed. The parallelism disks are the vertical curtains beneath their disjoint projected arcs. Their strip neighborhoods are disjoint. Cutting these strips off the upper half-ball leaves a ball with finitely many boundary indentations: flatten each indentation in its rectangular strip coordinate, fixing the other faces. The strip containing an arc is a ball with a straight diameter tube removed. In cylindrical coordinates this last space is $S^1\times\{(r,z):r\ge\epsilon,\ r^2+z^2\le1\},$ whose second factor is a convex disk. Hence $A$ is a boundary connected sum of $c$ solid tori, glued through specified disks to the remaining ball. For an actual bouquet spine, cut each solid torus across a meridian disk and absorb its remaining ball into the central ball. The result is a central ball with $c$ product one-handles. Join the centers of the $2c$ attaching disks to an interior point by disjoint star arms in that ball; after flattening the finitely many boundary disks, these are radial arms from their centers to the central point. Add the one-handle core intervals. The resulting embedded graph is a bouquet of $c$ circles, since every vertex other than the central one has degree two. To specify the CW structure for the relative contraction, use a finite polyhedral ball model for the central ball. Triangulate its boundary so that each attaching disk is a subcomplex and its center is a vertex, then cone that boundary triangulation to one interior vertex. Each radial star arm is an edge of this cone triangulation. The union $C$ of the attaching disks and these star edges is a finite CW subcomplex. It is contractible by contracting each disk to its center and then the star to the interior vertex. The central ball $B_0$ and $C$ are both nonempty and contractible, so the inclusion $C\hookrightarrow B_0$ is a homotopy equivalence. By [F3], $B_0$ strongly deformation retracts onto $C$, fixing $C$ pointwise; HEP alone is not being used to assert a contraction. Next contract every attaching disk linearly to its center, and contract the transverse disk factor of each product one-handle by the same linear factor. These formulas agree on the end disks and fix the star edges and handle cores, so they paste to a strong deformation retraction onto the stated bouquet. For each drilled arc, orient its graph loop to represent the based positive meridian. In an oriented normal-disk chart along the oriented knot tangent, choose the disk orientation so that tangent followed by disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation, and traverse the disk boundary in its induced positive direction. In the complement product $S^1\times D^2$ of the drilled tube, this boundary is the $S^1$ factor; contracting the disk factor and using the retained collar access path carries it to the corresponding bouquet loop. Thus the chosen generator is the positive meridian, not its inverse. Each such loop crosses precisely its own curtain once. Consequently [F5] identifies these positively oriented meridians as the free basis, rather than merely normal generators. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Fix disk coordinates $\phi_i:\overline D^2\to D_i$ and constants $0<r_0<r_1<1$. In $Y_*$ set $V_i=\phi_i(\{|v|<r_1\})$ and let $U$ be the complement of the union of the closed disks $\phi_i(\{|v|\le r_0\})$. These sets are relative-open: the cap interiors have their ordinary disk topology, their closures away from their boundary are disjoint from $A$, and the omitted closed disks are closed in $Y_*$. They cover because $r_0<r_1$. Each $V_i$ is an open disk, different $V_i$ are disjoint, and their overlaps with $U$ are exactly the annuli $r_0<|v|<r_1$. On each outer collar, increasing its radius by $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ retracts $U$ to $A$, fixing $A$. Step 5.1 supplies its meridian basis. Transfer these sets and the composed homotopies back through the finite normalizations in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. They give the stated subspace and cover in the original exterior. [step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 For the resulting round circle use $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, $K=\{z_1=0\}$, and infinity $p=(1,0)$. Choose the angular coordinate so that increasing $t$ gives the positively oriented meridian (replace $t$ by $-t$ if the carried knot orientation requires it). The map $(w,e^{it})\longmapsto(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}e^{it},w)$ identifies $S^3\setminus K$ with $D^\circ\times S^1$, and $p$ with $(0,1)$. Choose a center-preserving homeomorphism from $D^\circ$ to $(-1,1)^2$. For $q\in(-1,1)^2$, put $r=\|q\|_\infty$ and define $$c(q)=\begin{cases}q,&r\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt]q/(2r),&r>\tfrac12.\end{cases}$$ The homotopy $C_s(q)=(1-s)q+sc(q)$ stays in the open square, fixes $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^2$, and preserves $q=0$. Therefore $(q,z)\mapsto(C_s(q),z)$ is a strong deformation retraction of $(D^\circ\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ onto $([-1/2,1/2]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$: when $z=1$, every point in the punctured fiber has $q\ne0$, and $C_s(q)$ is a positive scalar multiple of $q$, so the homotopy never reaches the puncture. Rescaling the square gives $([-1,1]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$. Write $S^1=[-1,1]/(-1\sim1)$ with the puncture at circle coordinate $0$. For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy $$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$ retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Its image $X_0$ is a finite CW complex: the lateral faces form the torus $T=\partial[-1,1]^2\times S^1$, and the two square end faces become one disk $D^2$ attached along $\ell=\partial[-1,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Give $T$ its product CW structure with $\ell$ as a subcomplex; then $D^2$ is a contractible CW subcomplex of $X_0$. By [F4], collapsing it is a homotopy equivalence, and the quotient is $T$ with $\ell$ collapsed. Cutting $T$ along $\ell$ gives a cylinder; after the two boundary copies of $\ell$ are collapsed to their common point, the quotient is a sphere with its two poles identified. To identify its homotopy type explicitly, let $Z$ be $S^2$ with an interval attached at its two distinct poles. Give $Z$ the finite CW structure in which the interval is a 1-cell and its endpoints are 0-cells, so the interval is a contractible subcomplex. Collapsing it identifies the poles, so [F4] makes $Z$ homotopy equivalent to the sphere-with-poles-identified quotient. The two endpoint maps of the interval into $S^2$ are homotopic along a fixed path; choose this path to be the $e^{it}$ meridian cut at $t=0$. By the attaching-map clause of [F3], $Z$ is homotopy equivalent to the adjunction space with both endpoints attached at one pole, namely $S^2\vee S^1$, and the new circle is the retained positive meridian. For this wedge with wedge point $w$, choose $q\in S^2\setminus\{w\}$ and $r\in S^1\setminus\{w\}$, and set $$A=S^1\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\}),\qquad B'=(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup S^2.$$ These are open in the wedge topology and cover $S^1\vee S^2$. The first deformation retracts to $S^1$, the second to $S^2$, so both are path-connected; their overlap $(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\})$ is nonempty and contracts to $w$ by contracting each punctured summand to $w$. Thus the sets and overlap satisfy the path-connected open-cover hypotheses of van Kampen [F5], which gives $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^2,w)\cong\pi_1(S^1,w)*\pi_1(S^2,w)\cong\mathbb Z*1\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the positive meridian circle. Finally the normal radial homotopy [F2] proves the asserted retraction onto $E_K$ in every case. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct] ∎

Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement. [F1, F6, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The model can be compared with the given sufficiently small normal tube without invoking a uniqueness theorem or choice. Make its disk-bundle chart smooth near the core and normalize its differential there to the given normal chart; the required linear change is fibrewise, with the tangential component removed by a change of core parameter. In finitely many charts the two resulting embeddings differ by $O(|v|^2)$, with derivative difference $O(|v|)$. Replace the model chart near $v=0$ by the given one using a radial cutoff supported where $|v|<2\delta$ and equal to one for $|v|\le\delta$. The derivative of the correction is $O(\delta)$; compactness and a finite minimum of the chart injectivity bounds therefore preserve a bundle embedding for small $\delta$. Injectivity between nonadjacent core charts follows from their positive separation. The modified chart equals the given normal chart for $|v|\le\delta$ and retains $N_*$ as its outer boundary. Choose the normal-tube radius $\rho<\delta$. In these product coordinates, replace every fibre radius $r\in[\rho,1]$ by $(1-s)r+s$ and fix the exterior of $N_*$. This is a strong deformation retraction from $E_K$ to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N_*$, fixed on its target. It agrees on the outer boundary and never enters the removed radius-$\rho$ tube. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. The top plates of the caps belong to $A$ as tube-boundary faces, except for the two exits occupied by upper tubes. Thus $X=A\cup B$ and $A\cap B$ is the equatorial disk with the interiors of the $F_i$ removed. On $B$ use $(q,z)\mapsto(q,(1-s)z+s h(q))$ and on $A$ the identity. These maps agree on the overlap, remain in the indicated vertical intervals, and paste continuously because the two sets are closed in $X$. They fix their target $Y_*=A\cup\bigcup_i D_i,\qquad D_i=\{(q,h_i(q)):q\in F_i\},$ pointwise. This proves the global strong deformation retraction, including the lower region and infinity. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The upper region $A$ is a ball with the neighborhoods of $c$ disjoint boundary-parallel arcs removed. The parallelism disks are the vertical curtains beneath their disjoint projected arcs. Their strip neighborhoods are disjoint. Cutting these strips off the upper half-ball leaves a ball with finitely many boundary indentations: flatten each indentation in its rectangular strip coordinate, fixing the other faces. The strip containing an arc is a ball with a straight diameter tube removed. In cylindrical coordinates this last space is $S^1\times\{(r,z):r\ge\epsilon,\ r^2+z^2\le1\},$ whose second factor is a convex disk. Hence $A$ is a boundary connected sum of $c$ solid tori, glued through specified disks to the remaining ball. For an actual bouquet spine, cut each solid torus across a meridian disk and absorb its remaining ball into the central ball. The result is a central ball with $c$ product one-handles. Join the centers of the $2c$ attaching disks to an interior point by disjoint star arms in that ball; after flattening the finitely many boundary disks, these are radial arms from their centers to the central point. Add the one-handle core intervals. The resulting embedded graph is a bouquet of $c$ circles, since every vertex other than the central one has degree two.
To specify the CW structure for the relative contraction, use a finite polyhedral ball model for the central ball. Triangulate its boundary so that each attaching disk is a subcomplex and its center is a vertex, then cone that boundary triangulation to one interior vertex. Each radial star arm is an edge of this cone triangulation. The union $C$ of the attaching disks and these star edges is a finite CW subcomplex. It is contractible by contracting each disk to its center and then the star to the interior vertex. The central ball $B_0$ and $C$ are both nonempty and contractible, so the inclusion $C\hookrightarrow B_0$ is a homotopy equivalence. By [F3], $B_0$ strongly deformation retracts onto $C$, fixing $C$ pointwise; HEP alone is not being used to assert a contraction. Next contract every attaching disk linearly to its center, and contract the transverse disk factor of each product one-handle by the same linear factor. These formulas agree on the end disks and fix the star edges and handle cores, so they paste to a strong deformation retraction onto the stated bouquet.
For each drilled arc, orient its graph loop to represent the based positive meridian. In an oriented normal-disk chart along the oriented knot tangent, choose the disk orientation so that tangent followed by disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation, and traverse the disk boundary in its induced positive direction. In the complement product $S^1\times D^2$ of the drilled tube, this boundary is the $S^1$ factor; contracting the disk factor and using the retained collar access path carries it to the corresponding bouquet loop. Thus the chosen generator is the positive meridian, not its inverse. Each such loop crosses precisely its own curtain once. Consequently [F5] identifies these positively oriented meridians as the free basis, rather than merely normal generators. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Fix disk coordinates $\phi_i:\overline D^2\to D_i$ and constants $0<r_0<r_1<1$. In $Y_*$ set $V_i=\phi_i(\{|v|<r_1\})$ and let $U$ be the complement of the union of the closed disks $\phi_i(\{|v|\le r_0\})$. These sets are relative-open: the cap interiors have their ordinary disk topology, their closures away from their boundary are disjoint from $A$, and the omitted closed disks are closed in $Y_*$. They cover because $r_0<r_1$. Each $V_i$ is an open disk, different $V_i$ are disjoint, and their overlaps with $U$ are exactly the annuli $r_0<|v|<r_1$. On each outer collar, increasing its radius by $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ retracts $U$ to $A$, fixing $A$. Step 5.1 supplies its meridian basis. Transfer these sets and the composed homotopies back through the finite normalizations in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. They give the stated subspace and cover in the original exterior. [step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 For the resulting round circle use $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, $K=\{z_1=0\}$, and infinity $p=(1,0)$. Choose the angular coordinate so that increasing $t$ gives the positively oriented meridian (replace $t$ by $-t$ if the carried knot orientation requires it). The map $(w,e^{it})\longmapsto(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}e^{it},w)$ identifies $S^3\setminus K$ with $D^\circ\times S^1$, and $p$ with $(0,1)$. Choose a center-preserving homeomorphism from $D^\circ$ to $(-1,1)^2$. For $q\in(-1,1)^2$, put $r=\|q\|_\infty$ and define
$$c(q)=\begin{cases}q,&r\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt]q/(2r),&r>\tfrac12.\end{cases}$$
The homotopy $C_s(q)=(1-s)q+sc(q)$ stays in the open square, fixes $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^2$, and preserves $q=0$. Therefore $(q,z)\mapsto(C_s(q),z)$ is a strong deformation retraction of $(D^\circ\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ onto $([-1/2,1/2]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$: when $z=1$, every point in the punctured fiber has $q\ne0$, and $C_s(q)$ is a positive scalar multiple of $q$, so the homotopy never reaches the puncture. Rescaling the square gives $([-1,1]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$. Write $S^1=[-1,1]/(-1\sim1)$ with the puncture at circle coordinate $0$. For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy
$$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$
retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Its image $X_0$ is a finite CW complex: the lateral faces form the torus $T=\partial[-1,1]^2\times S^1$, and the two square end faces become one disk $D^2$ attached along $\ell=\partial[-1,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Give $T$ its product CW structure with $\ell$ as a subcomplex; then $D^2$ is a contractible CW subcomplex of $X_0$. By [F4], collapsing it is a homotopy equivalence, and the quotient is $T$ with $\ell$ collapsed. Cutting $T$ along $\ell$ gives a cylinder; after the two boundary copies of $\ell$ are collapsed to their common point, the quotient is a sphere with its two poles identified.
To identify its homotopy type explicitly, let $Z$ be $S^2$ with an interval attached at its two distinct poles. Give $Z$ the finite CW structure in which the interval is a 1-cell and its endpoints are 0-cells, so the interval is a contractible subcomplex. Collapsing it identifies the poles, so [F4] makes $Z$ homotopy equivalent to the sphere-with-poles-identified quotient. The two endpoint maps of the interval into $S^2$ are homotopic along a fixed path; choose this path to be the $e^{it}$ meridian cut at $t=0$. By the attaching-map clause of [F3], $Z$ is homotopy equivalent to the adjunction space with both endpoints attached at one pole, namely $S^2\vee S^1$, and the new circle is the retained positive meridian.
For this wedge with wedge point $w$, choose $q\in S^2\setminus\{w\}$ and $r\in S^1\setminus\{w\}$, and set
$$A=S^1\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\}),\qquad B'=(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup S^2.$$
These are open in the wedge topology and cover $S^1\vee S^2$. The first deformation retracts to $S^1$, the second to $S^2$, so both are path-connected; their overlap $(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\})$ is nonempty and contracts to $w$ by contracting each punctured summand to $w$. Finally the normal radial homotopy [F2] proves the asserted retraction onto $E_K$ in every case. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget|The six adjacent posterior, solver, discretization, kernel, burn-in, and Monte Carlo error terms.]]

[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws|Total variation is the event supremum and has no factor $1/2$ in that convention.]]

[[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations|With this convention, a measurable function bounded by $M$ has expectation difference at most $2M$ times total variation.]]

[[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel|An invariant law satisfies $\pi K=\pi$.]]

[[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel|The one-step conditional law is given by the transition kernel.]]

[[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift|Strict stationarity means all finite-dimensional laws are unchanged by time shifts.]]

[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance|Variance and covariance are expectations of centered products.]]

[[thm-pathwise-error-ledger-decomposition|A finite scalar reference chain telescopes into its adjacent signed errors.]]

[Gibbs and Su, §2, total-variation dual form](https://math.hmc.edu/su/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2019/06/ON-CHOOSING-AND-BOUNDING-PROBABILITY.pdf)

[Levin, Peres, and Wilmer, §4.1, Proposition 4.5](https://pages.uoregon.edu/dlevin/MARKOV/markovmixing.pdf)

[Geyer, §1.1, stationary sample-mean variance](https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/f05/8931/n1998.pdf)

## Remarks

An ESS is functional-specific and is not a substitute for a Monte Carlo standard
error. The variance bound in this Proposition is a population statement under
its chain assumptions; it does not validate a finite-chain empirical ESS
estimate.

## Remarks references

[Vehtari et al., §3.2, functional-specific ESS and MCSE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.08008v5)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, the complete error budget when its pathwise bound is used, and a stationary Markov chain in the separate sample-error branch.

[F1] Total variation is the event supremum $\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$; it has no half-factor. [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]

[F2] If $\mu,\nu$ are probability measures and $|f|\le M$, then $|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}$. [[thm-total-variation-bounds-for-expectations]]

[F3] The error budget consists of the six absolute adjacent differences from $\mu_\star(f)$ through $\bar f_{b,N}$, and its Monte Carlo component is pathwise. [[def-ip-posterior-computation-error-budget]]

[F4] A stationary chain has marginal law $\pi_K$ at every time, and the covariance of $f(X_i),f(X_j)$ depends only on the lag $|j-i|$. [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]] [[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]

[F5] For square-integrable real random variables, variance is the expected squared centered value and covariance is the expected product of centered values. [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]

[F6] For a finite scalar reference chain, the total signed error telescopes and its absolute value is bounded by the sum of absolute adjacent errors. [[thm-pathwise-error-ledger-decomposition]]

[A1] AC is assumed only for the library time-homogeneous Markov-chain interface; this proposition assumes stationarity and makes no chain-existence claim. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-time-homogeneous-markov-chain-with-transition-kernel]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 Since $|f|\le M$, [F2] applies to $\mu$ and $\nu$; [F1] fixes the event-supremum convention, so it yields the stated total-variation expectation bound. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 The successive scalar references in [F3] have signed adjacent differences whose sum is $\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}$. Apply [F6] to this finite reference chain to obtain $|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f$. [given, F3, F6, algebra]

1.3 For the stationary branch, set $Y_j=f(X_{b+j})-\pi_K(f)$. By [F4], each $Y_j$ has mean zero and $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=\gamma_{|i-j|}$. Expanding the finite square gives $\mathbb E[(N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N Y_j)^2]=N^{-2}(N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k)$: there are $N$ diagonal terms, and for each lag $k$ there are $N-k$ off-diagonal pairs, each counted twice. [A1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $0\le N-k\le N$ and $\gamma_0=\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))\ge0$, the expression in step 1.3 is at most $N^{-1}(\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}|\gamma_k|)$, which is bounded by the claimed infinite-series expression. Absolute summability makes the bound finite. [step 1.3, F5, given, algebra] ∎
