## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary and good fundamental group $G=\pi_1(X)$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_n:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$ be proper generic immersed disks with pairwise disjoint embedded boundary circles. Suppose they admit framed immersed algebraically dual spheres $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ with $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$, and suppose $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for all $i$, in the equivariant intersection conventions of the disk-embedding data definition. Then the disks are homotopic rel boundary, preserving the boundary framings, to pairwise disjoint locally flat properly embedded disks in $X$.

## Statement references

[[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data|The relative disk data and equivariant intersection hypotheses]]

[[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding|The good-group condition]]

[[thm-freedman-disk-embedding-theorem-proof-modules|The standardized-tower core construction]]

[[def-countable-choice|Axiom of Countable Choice used by the tower construction]]

Michael H. Freedman and Frank Quinn, *Topology of 4-Manifolds*, §5.1, Theorems 5.1A–5.1B, https://archive.mpim-bonn.mpg.de/4789/1/FreedmanQuinn-TopologyOf4Manifolds-PMS39.pdf

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, good $G$, and the stated finite algebraically unobstructed disk datum. The disk data specify actual boundary normal-microbundle framings, not merely stable classes; the relative extension obstruction is separate, and each dual sphere has a full normal-microbundle trivialization.

[F1] [[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data]] gives locally flat TOP sheet charts, prescribed disk-boundary normal framings, framed spheres and the signed group-labelled intersection conventions. A disk's relative framing-extension obstruction is tracked separately and is not assumed to vanish from the algebraic Wall conditions.

[F2] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]] is the good-group property, invariant under a based group isomorphism.

[F3] [[lem-freedman-casson-handle-skyscraper-and-surgery-modules]] supplies the proved smooth-input good-group construction: in a supplied smooth neighborhood it gives disjoint locally flat disks in the original relative homotopy classes, with the supplied extending frames and retained geometric duals. Its Sections13–14 give relative approximation, finite affine-jet genericity and the relative Euler/intersection comparison; these operations are used below, rather than assuming TOP transversality. Its standard handle charts supply [[thm-freedman-disk-embedding-theorem-proof-modules]].

[F4] [[lem-finite-framed-locally-flat-links-in-smooth-three-manifolds-have-smooth-image-models]] gives, under CC, a supported boundary ambient TOP isotopy smoothing a finite locally flat link, positive source-circle reparametrizations, and smooth representatives of its full transported rank-two normal-microbundle framing classes.

[F5] [[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]] and [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]] supply actual smooth collars and smooth tubes under CC.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is available. All subsequent choices beyond [F3]–[F5] are finite.

## Proof

1.1 The normal microbundle in [F1] is a neighborhood germ with its zero section and retraction, not merely an abstract stable vector bundle. On the embedded boundary of a proper locally flat sheet, its relative half-space chart is $(\mathbb R^2_+\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^2_+\times0)$. Restricting the given normal trivialization to its boundary gives a TOP tube germ of that boundary circle in $\partial X$; its normal fiber is the second $\mathbb R^2$. Compactness permits a sufficiently small representative around each of the finitely many circles, and disjointness permits these representatives to be disjoint. This uses the GIVEN normal germ, not a theorem constructing normal neighborhoods for arbitrary TOP surfaces. Apply [F4] to this boundary link in the given compact smooth three-manifold $\partial X$. Denote its isotopy by $h_s$ and its smooth framing representatives by $\eta_i$. [given, F1, F4, A1]

2.1 Extend the actual isotopy over a smooth collar $c:\partial X\times[0,a)\to X$ from [F5]. Choose a cutoff $\beta$ equal to one near zero and zero before $a$. Set $H_s(c(x,r))=c(h_{s\beta(r)}(x),r)$, and use the identity outside the collar. The inverse uses $h_{s\beta(r)}^{-1}$, so $H_s$ is an orientation-preserving ambient TOP isotopy with joint inverse. Transport all maps, whiskers and normal classes by $H_1$. Every old signed intersection and group label is transported by the same based group isomorphism; goodness is unchanged. For the positive circle homeomorphism $\theta_i$ of [F4], let $\Theta_i:D^2\to D^2$ be its radial cone, and replace the disk temporarily by $H_1f_i\Theta_i$. Its boundary MAP is now a smooth regular parametrization. At the end we undo both $H_1$ and $\Theta_i$, so no change of the original boundary parameter is concealed. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Construct a NEW smooth source collar. In the product of a smooth boundary-circle tube and the ambient collar, write the transported map on a small source collar as $(b_i(\theta,t),v_i(\theta,t),r_i(\theta,t))$, with boundary values $(\theta,0,0)$ and $r_i>0$ for $t>0$. Uniform continuity gives a unique small real lift of $b_i-\theta$ after restricting the collar. For $\kappa(t)$ equal to one on a smaller collar and zero outside the chosen one, interpolate these coordinates to $(\theta,0,\rho t)$ by $((1-s\kappa)b_i+s\kappa\theta,(1-s\kappa)v_i,(1-s\kappa)r_i+s\kappa\rho t)$. Choose the finite positive $\rho$ and collar small enough to stay in the coordinate tube. The last coordinate is positive for every interior point throughout this homotopy, and the boundary is fixed. At its end the smaller collar is smooth. The homotopy may pass through nongeneric maps: the conclusion requires a homotopy, not a regular homotopy of the old TOP ribbons. It can be arbitrarily small, and its support misses all old double points. [F1, F5, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Use [F3]'s relative smooth approximation and finite affine-jet perturbations simultaneously on the disks and spheres, fixed on these smaller smooth collars. In a target with boundary perform approximation in its smooth double, with error less than half the positive target-boundary distance on the remaining compact source interiors; the output therefore stays in $X$. The same retraction interpolation gives a homotopy fixed on the collars. Independent value and first-jet bumps avoid the rank-deficient jet strata, make the two-point evaluation transverse to the diagonal and avoid triple points; compactness then gives only finitely many double points. This is exactly the finite genericity operation already proved in [F3]. Denote the resulting smooth generic maps by $f'_i,g'_j$. [F3, A1, step 3.1]

5.1 Here is the full group-ring comparison. At each old transverse crossing choose its supplied oriented TOP sheet chart and two small parameter disks. On their four-dimensional product the chart difference of the old sheet maps has one zero, of local degree the old sign, and no zero on the product boundary. For a sufficiently close approximation its chart difference is joined to the old one by a straight homotopy nonzero on that compact boundary. The signed sum of its transverse zeros is therefore the same local degree. All their group labels are the old label, since their connectors lie in that contractible chart. This uses a degree of continuous maps in a TOP chart, not differentiation of that chart. Outside these finitely many products and a neighborhood of each source diagonal, the compact source-pair set has positive image separation. Thus there are no other intersections between DIFFERENT source surfaces. Near a source diagonal both preimages lie in one of finitely many embedded-sheet charts, so a new self-double loop is null in $X$. It follows that every off-diagonal $\lambda$, including every disk–sphere pairing, retains its full original value, and $\mu(f'_i)=n_i1$, $\mu(g'_j)=m_j1$ for integers $n_i,m_j$. These equalities are in the actual sheet-involution quotient, not just after augmentation. [F1, F3, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The self-pairing $\lambda(g'_j,g'_j)$ is still zero. To compute it without assuming TOP parametric transversality, take a small parallel using the original framed normal germ, with the same whisker. Apply the preceding degree comparison to that pair; it computes the original self-pairing. Approximate the two homotopic representatives smoothly and interpolate their maps in the smooth double, relative any protected collar. The ordinary finite smooth two-value transversality argument computes homotopy invariance of the pairing: the one-dimensional intersection tracks have cancelling signed interior endpoints, with unchanged group labels along each track. Thus the new self-pairing is the old zero. The same argument for a disk and its boundary parallel computes the relative intersection integer determined by a specified boundary framing. [F1, F3, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Track the actual relative Euler obstruction rather than declaring it zero. For a smooth oriented disk $u$ and a boundary frame $\eta$, a generic normal section extending its first boundary vector has isolated zeros; their signed sum is $e(u,\eta)$. A parallel sheet meets $u$ at those zeros, and at both ordered branches of every self-point. Hence its relative intersection integer is $e(u,\eta)+2\sum_p\epsilon(p)$. The analogous equivariant sphere identity is $\lambda(u,u)=e(u)1+\mu(u)+\overline{\mu(u)}$. These follow by the stated local zero count; the two self-point labels are inverses. Twisting a boundary frame changes its relative Euler integer by the corresponding signed winding, so every desired integer value is realized by a smooth frame, and the difference from $\eta$ is recorded. Vanishing relative Euler is precisely the obstruction to extending that frame over a disk: extend on a finite cell subdivision and move the integer zero indices into one interior two-cell, where index zero extends across the cell. [F1, F3, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 A signed interior cusp changes $(\mu,e)$ by $(\pm1,\mp2)$ and changes no relative map homotopy class or off-diagonal pairing. For concreteness the birth chart is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y^2,y^3-ty,xy)$: for $t<0$ it is immersed without a double point, and for $t>0$ its sole double pair is $(0,\sqrt t),(0,-\sqrt t)$, with independent tangent planes. Reflecting a normal coordinate changes its sign. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a compact connected oriented smooth $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary and good fundamental group $G=\pi_1(X)$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_n:(D^2,S^1)\looparrowright(X,\partial X)$ be proper generic immersed disks with pairwise disjoint embedded boundary circles. Suppose they admit framed immersed algebraically dual spheres $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ with $\lambda(f_i,g_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $\lambda(g_i,g_j)=0$, and $\mu(g_i)=0$, and suppose $\lambda(f_i,f_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\mu(f_i)=0$ for all $i$, in the equivariant intersection conventions of the disk-embedding data definition. Then the disks are homotopic rel boundary, preserving the boundary framings, to pairwise disjoint locally flat properly embedded disks in $X$.

[F2] [[def-good-fundamental-group-for-disk-embedding]] is the good-group property, invariant under a based group isomorphism.

## Statement

Let $X$ be a compact oriented topological $4$-manifold with nonempty boundary. A **kinky handle** is a standard $2$-handle whose core disk has finitely many transverse self-plumbings; a **framed Casson-handle tower** is a nested sequence of such stages in which each self-plumbing point of one stage is replaced by a framed kinky handle at the next stage, with the attaching regions matching the preceding stage. Suppose a finite family of these tower $4$-neighborhoods is embedded pairwise disjointly in $X$, with attaching circles in $\partial X$, and carries the algebraic dual data of a disk-embedding datum. If each embedded tower has a homeomorphism of pairs to the standard open $2$-handle $D^2\times\mathbb R^2$ that takes its specified framed attaching region, including its core circle and normal-framing class, to the standard attaching region $S^1\times\mathbb R^2$ with its standard framing, then the inverse images of the cores $D^2\times\{0\}$ form a pairwise disjoint family of locally flat properly embedded disks in $X$, with the prescribed framed boundary circles.

## Statement references

[[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data|The relative disk and dual-sphere interface]]

Stefan Behrens et al., *The Disc Embedding Theorem*, Chapters 17–18 and 24–28, https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780198841319.001.0001

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated family of towers and their relative standardization homeomorphisms.

[F1] [[def-freedman-good-group-and-disk-embedding-data]]: A disk-embedding datum specifies proper disk boundary circles and their boundary normal-framing classes.

## Proof

1.1 A standard open $2$-handle is $D^2\times\mathbb R^2$, and its core $D^2\times\{0\}$ is a locally flat properly embedded disk whose boundary is the core attaching circle with the standard normal-framing class. [given, construct]

2.1 Pull back each core by the corresponding framing-preserving homeomorphism of pairs. A homeomorphism preserves local flatness, properness and pairwise disjointness, and the stated framing condition transports the standard boundary frame to the prescribed boundary normal-framing class. The pulled-back cores are therefore the required disks. [F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. There exists a closed connected simply connected oriented topological four-manifold $Y_{E_8}$ whose integral intersection form is isometric to the positive-definite even unimodular lattice $L_{E_8}$. ## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For a nonempty oriented link $L$, the diagram quandle presentations from any two regular oriented diagrams of $L$ are isomorphic by the local quandle Tietze transformations for R1, R2 and R3. If $L=K$ has one component and $D$ is its diagram, let
$$W(D)=\langle g_a\ (a\in A(D))\mid g_v=g_o^{-1}g_ug_o\text{ at every crossing with source }u,\text{ target }v,\text{ and overarc }o\rangle.$$
Then the positive-meridian Wirtinger constructor uses these same under-arcs and crossing relations, and
$$\operatorname{Adj}(Q(D))\cong W(D)\cong\pi_1(S^3\setminus K).$$
No completeness or knot-classification assertion is made.

## Statement references

[[def-rack-fundamental-quandle-and-adjoint-group]].

[[def-group-presentation]].

[[def-knot-planar-code]].

[[alg-knot-wirtinger-presentation-from-code]].

[[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]].

[Manturov, *Knot Theory*, Chapter 5, §5.2](https://varf.ru/rudn/manturov/book.pdf).

[Carter, *A Survey of Quandle Ideas*](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1002.4429).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty oriented link $L$, its diagrams, and, for the group comparison, a one-component link $L=K$; also the diagram quandle, $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and the common positive-normal crossing convention.

[F1] [[def-rack-fundamental-quandle-and-adjoint-group]]: $Q(D)$ is generated by the under-arcs with crossing relations, and $\operatorname{Adj}(Q)$ has relations $e_{q*r}=e_r^{-1}e_qe_r$.

[F2] [[def-group-presentation]]: $\langle X\mid S\rangle$ is the quotient of the free group on $X$ by the normal closure of the relator words $S$.

[F3] [[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]]: assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, equivalent oriented diagrams are related by finitely many planar isotopies and oriented R1, R2, and R3 moves.

[F4] [[def-knot-planar-code]]: a valid code is a finite rational polygonal drawing with declared incidences, cyclic orders, edge orientations, and over/under data, whose only intersections are the declared bends and transverse crossings and whose branch tracing is one oriented circle; its under-arcs are maximal between consecutive underpasses, and it stores no algebraic crossing sign.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is the axiom that every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function.

[F5] The constructor names source and target by the positive over-normal and emits $g_o^{-1}g_ug_og_v^{-1}$; its correctness theorem identifies this presented group with the knot complement group. [[alg-knot-wirtinger-presentation-from-code]], [[thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctness]]

[F6] [[def-knot-planar-code]]: rational polygonal edge paths may be smoothed at bends in disjoint disks without changing their crossing data.

## Proof

1.1 Under R1, the new underarc generator $y$ satisfies either $y=x*x$ or $x=y*x$ for the unchanged arc color $x$. In the first case idempotency gives $y=x$; in the second, $x=x*x$ and right invertibility give the unique solution $y=x$. Thus the new generator is eliminated. Under R2, each added underarc generator is uniquely solved from its neighboring arc and the overarc by $*$ or $\bar *$; the reverse move gives the inverse substitution. Thus these moves are quandle Tietze transformations. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Under R3, assigning boundary colors $x,y,z$ gives the two possible iterated labels $(x*y)*z$ and $(x*z)*(y*z)$; these agree by right self-distributivity. With the over-colors fixed, each under-color substitution is invertible by right invertibility, so the reverse replacements give inverse substitutions. The same calculation for reversed crossings follows by applying the inverse right translations, which preserve both operations by self-distributivity. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 For the knot-group comparison assume $L=K$. Let $\Gamma$ be the finite planar graph obtained by taking the crossings as vertices and the strand pieces between consecutive crossings as edges. Choose disjoint small disks about the crossing vertices, each meeting $D$ only in its two transverse branches, and disjoint tubular strips around the compact edge pieces outside those disks. At a crossing, oriented local coordinates straighten the branches to two transverse axes. Choose a nearby rational point and two rational direction vectors, still transverse and in the same cyclic order as the original branches; the four rational half-segments give the coded crossing and its over/under choice. Extend each edge strip a short distance into its endpoint disks through the corresponding disjoint branch sectors, and choose rational bend ports there. In each strip choose a simple rational polygonal path that is a graph in strip coordinates and joins its ports; choose it fine enough that rounding its bends gives a small normal graph over the original edge. If there are no crossings, choose a simple rational polygon in a tubular annulus of the projected circle. Since there are finitely many compact edge pieces, nonincident pieces have positive separation, and each crossing is transverse; density of $\mathbb Q^2$ and a sufficiently fine finite subdivision therefore let all vertices and bends be rational while preserving the one-circle tracing, crossing cyclic orders, orientations, and over/under data, with no other intersections. The resulting record is a valid code by [F4]; smoothing its bends in disjoint disks gives a smooth regular diagram with the same crossing data by [F6]. To compare it with $D$, move each crossing point to its nearby rational point by an isotopy supported in its disk and the short branch sectors, fixed at the outer ends of the strips, and interpolate its four half-branches, within their disjoint sectors, through transverse direction pairs to the rational branches. This is an isotopy preserving the cyclic order and over/under choice. After these local adjustments, each rounded edge replacement is a sufficiently small normal graph $r=f(s)$ over the original edge in its strip, with $f=0$ at the ports. Choose the approximation so $|f|\,\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$ for a cutoff $\chi$ that is $1$ near the edge and $0$ near the strip boundary. Then $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+t\chi(r)f(s))$, $0\le t\le1$, is a diffeomorphism in each strip, fixed at its boundary, and gives an ambient isotopy of that edge. These finitely many disk and strip isotopies paste to a compactly supported ambient isotopy of the plane. Its product with the identity in height carries a lift of $D$ to a realization of the code diagram, so the code represents the same knot $K$. The induced bijection on under-arcs preserves source, target, and overarc at each crossing because the positive over-normal and branch orientations are preserved. This finite construction uses no choice axiom. [F4, F6, construct]

1.4 The conjugation operation on $W(D)$ is idempotent because $g*g=g^{-1}gg=g$. Its right translation by $h$ is conjugation by $h^{-1}$, with inverse conjugation by $h$. It is right self-distributive because both $(g*h)*k$ and $(g*k)*(h*k)$ reduce to $k^{-1}h^{-1}ghk$. Thus $\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$ is a quandle. Its generators $g_a$ satisfy the crossing equations by the relators of $W(D)$, so recursive evaluation of terms gives a quandle homomorphism $f:Q(D)\to\operatorname{Conj}(W(D))$. Define $\psi$ on adjoint generators by $\psi(e_q)=f(q)$. Since $f(q*r)=f(r)^{-1}f(q)f(r)$, every adjoint relator maps to the identity; [F2] therefore makes $\psi$ a group homomorphism. [F1, F2, F5, construct]

2.1 For the knot-group comparison define $\phi:W(D)\to\operatorname{Adj}(Q(D))$ on generators by $\phi(g_a)=e_{x_a}$. The code from step 1.3 has the same under-arcs and crossing relations as $D$, so the constructor's relators in [F5] are exactly those of $W(D)$. At each crossing, $x_v=x_u*x_o$ in $Q(D)$, and the adjoint relation gives $e_{x_v}=e_{x_o}^{-1}e_{x_u}e_{x_o}$. Thus every relator of $W(D)$ maps to the identity; [F2] makes the homomorphism from the free group on its arc generators descend to $W(D)$. [F1, F2, F5, construct]

2.2 By [F3], diagrams of $L$ are related by a finite sequence of these moves, and step 1.1 and step 1.2 identify the corresponding quandle presentations at each move. Their composites give an isomorphism between the two diagram quandles. Countable choice is used only for [F3]; these local presentation transformations use no choice. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 The composites $\psi\phi$ fix each $g_a$. The other composite fixes each generator $e_q$: every $q\in Q(D)$ is represented by a term in the arc generators using $*$ and $\bar *$, and the adjoint relations give $e_{u*v}=e_v^{-1}e_ue_v$ and $e_{u\bar *v}=e_ve_ue_v^{-1}$, so induction on the term gives $\phi\psi(e_q)=e_q$. Hence $\phi$ and $\psi$ are inverse isomorphisms. By [F5] and step 1.3, $W(D)$ is the group of the Wirtinger constructor for a code of $K$, and is isomorphic to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. [F1, F5, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

[[def-countable-choice]].

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, and let $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive. If their full physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree on all boundary data, then every inward boundary-normal derivative agrees:
$$\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_1|_{\partial\Omega} =\partial_{x_n}^k\gamma_2|_{\partial\Omega} \qquad(k=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
where $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ in a boundary normal collar.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full physical conductivity DN map]]

[[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity|Conductivity Alessandrini identity]]

[[lem-ip-boundary-quasimode-jets-and-borel-correction|Boundary concentrating quasimodes and exact correction]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and exact correction suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and exact correction suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the smooth bounded domain, two strictly positive smooth conductivities with equal full-data DN maps, and the fixed-atlas trace convention.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: $\Lambda_\gamma$ is the weak full-boundary map of $\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$ with physical flux $\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity]]: for conductivity solutions $u_j$ with boundary values $f_j$, $\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_1\cdot\overline{\nabla u_2}\,dx$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-boundary-quasimode-jets-and-borel-correction]]: for every boundary point, unit tangential covector, cutoff $\chi=1$ near that point, integer $k\geq0$, and residual order $N>k$, the approximate solutions have residual and exact-correction $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$; their weighted gradient product satisfies $\lambda^k\int \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^kF\nabla v_1\cdot\overline{\nabla v_2}\,dx\to c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS$ with $c_k>0$.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Fix $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ and a sufficiently small patch. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported in the patch and equal to one near $x_0$, and use [F3] to construct approximate beams for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ with the same boundary trace. Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give $$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$ Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$, $$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$ If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$. [F3, step 1.1, contradiction]

3.1 Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives $$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$ for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then $$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$ Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 2.1 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there. [A1, A2, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Step 2.1 is the base case for the induction. Step 3.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion. [step 2.1, step 3.1, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, hence Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded connected domain with smooth boundary, and let $\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega;\operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbb R))$ be uniformly positive definite. Let $F:\overline\Omega\to\overline\Omega$ be a diffeomorphism smooth through the boundary, with smooth inverse and $F|_{\partial\Omega}=\operatorname{id}$. For $x=F(y)$, put $J_F(y)=|\det DF(y)|$ and define

$$ (F_*\gamma)(x)=\frac{DF(y)\,\gamma(y)\,DF(y)^T}{J_F(y)},\qquad y=F^{-1}(x). $$

Then $F_*\gamma$ is a smooth uniformly positive-definite matrix conductivity and its weak anisotropic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map equals that of $\gamma$. Explicitly, for every pair of boundary trace-data classes $f,h\in\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$,

$$\langle\Lambda_{F_*\gamma}f,h\rangle=\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle,$$

where each map is the weak energy form $\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx$, $u_{\gamma,f}$ is the unique weak solution with boundary class $f$, and $V_h$ is any $H^1$ representative of $h$.

The same gauge invariance has a Riemannian form. Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary, $g$ a smooth Riemannian metric, $\Gamma\subseteq\partial M$ relatively open, and $\Phi:M\to M$ a smooth diffeomorphism with $\Phi|_\Gamma=\operatorname{id}$. Define $(\Phi^*g)_p(v,w):=g_{\Phi(p)}(D\Phi_pv,D\Phi_pw)$. The cotangent inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_g$ is induced by $g^{-1}$, and in coordinates $dV_g=\sqrt{\det(g_{ij})}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. A smooth function $u$ is $g$-harmonic when $\int_M\langle du,d\psi\rangle_g\,dV_g=0$ for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$. Then $u\circ\Phi$ is $\Phi^*g$-harmonic; for any two smooth $g$-harmonic functions $u,v$,

$$\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g.$$

If the boundary traces of $u,v$ are supported in $\Gamma$, then composition by $\Phi$ leaves both traces fixed, so the local energy measurement of every such smooth harmonic pair is unchanged. In particular, if for each $f\in C_c^\infty(\Gamma)$ the Dirichlet solutions for $g$ and $\Phi^*g$ with trace $f$ are unique and smooth, then the corresponding local energy DN maps agree.

Step 2.2 gives equality of the local measurements for every such pair. When the stated Dirichlet solutions are unique, these harmonicity and trace facts identify the solution for $\Phi^*g$ with the pullback of the solution for $g$, so their local energy maps agree. [F3, step 2.2, algebra, given] ∎

Given $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, choose ambient smooth restrictions $u_k\to u$ in $H^1$ by [F5]. For each $k$, the classical chain rule gives
$$\nabla(u_k\circ F^{-1})(F(y))=DF(y)^{-T}\nabla u_k(y),\qquad \nabla(u_k\circ F)(y)=DF(y)^T\nabla u_k(F(y)).$$
The composition estimates just established give convergence of the left sides in $L^2$; the uniform bounds on $DF^{\pm1}$ and the Jacobian, together with [F4], give convergence of the right sides in $L^2$. Passing to the limits identifies the weak gradients of $u\circ F^{-1}$ and $u\circ F$ by the same formulas. Applying these identities to $u,v\in H^1(\Omega)$ and using [F4] on the positive and negative parts of the integrable energy density yields
$$\int_\Omega(F_*\gamma)(x)\nabla(u\circ F^{-1})(x)\cdot\nabla(v\circ F^{-1})(x)\,dx=\int_\Omega\gamma(y)\nabla u(y)\cdot\nabla v(y)\,dy.$$
Integrability follows from boundedness of the coefficients and Cauchy--Schwarz. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F11, step 1.1, construct]

1.3 Let $f\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and let $u=u_{\gamma,f}$. Set $v=u\circ F^{-1}$. By step 1.2 its boundary class is $f$. For any $\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, $\varphi\circ F\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ by step 1.2. The energy identity of step 1.2, with second input $\varphi\circ F$, gives
$\int_\Omega(F_*\gamma)(x)\nabla v(x)\cdot\nabla\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_\Omega\gamma(y)\nabla u(y)\cdot\nabla(\varphi\circ F)(y)\,dy=0$.
The matrix factors cancel because $DF^TDF^{-T}=I$, and the Jacobian $J_F$ in $dx$ cancels the denominator in $F_*\gamma$. Thus $v$ is the weak solution with coefficient $F_*\gamma$ and boundary class $f$; uniqueness [F2] identifies $v=u_{F_*\gamma,f}$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F11, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Fix any $h\in\mathcal B_\Omega$ and a representative $V_h\in H^1(\Omega)$. Since $F$ fixes the boundary, step 1.2 gives $V_h\circ F$ the same boundary class $h$. The energy identity of step 1.2, with second input $V_h\circ F$, and the solution identification in step 1.3 give

3.1 In the Riemannian setting of the statement, the chain rule [F3] gives $d(u\circ\Phi)=D\Phi^T(du\circ\Phi)$ in a coordinate chart, while [F8] gives $(\Phi^*g)=D\Phi^T(g\circ\Phi)D\Phi$. The boundary has zero Riemannian volume: in each boundary chart it is contained in a coordinate hyperplane, which has Lebesgue measure zero by Fubini, and the smooth volume density is locally bounded. Cover $M$ by finitely many source neighborhoods each lying in a chart and mapped by $\Phi$ into another chart; such neighborhoods exist by continuity and compactness. Partition their interiors into finitely many disjoint measurable pieces subordinate to this cover. On each piece apply the Euclidean change-of-variables formula [F4], whose choice hypothesis follows from [A1] by [F11], to the positive and negative parts of the smooth integrand, extended by zero within the corresponding chart. Summing the finitely many equalities and ignoring the null boundary gives $\int_M\langle d(u\circ\Phi),d(v\circ\Phi)\rangle_{\Phi^*g}\,dV_{\Phi^*g}=\int_M\langle du,dv\rangle_g\,dV_g$. [A1, F4, F8, F9, F11, step 3.1, construct]

Step 3.2 gives equality of the local measurements for every such pair. When the stated Dirichlet solutions are unique, these harmonicity and trace facts identify the solution for $\Phi^*g$ with the pullback of the solution for $g$, so their local energy maps agree. [F3, step 3.2, algebra, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\psi\in C^\infty$ be real on a neighborhood of the transversal projection of $M$, with $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$. Suppose $a\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb C)$ satisfies
$$2\partial_{x_1}a+2i\,g_0(\nabla_{g_0}\psi,\nabla_{g_0}a)+i(\Delta_{g_0}\psi)a=0.$$
Then, for all sufficiently large $\tau$, there is an exact solution
$$u_\tau=e^{-\tau(x_1+i\psi)}a+e^{-\tau x_1}r_\tau,\qquad (-\Delta_g+q)u_\tau=0\ \text{in }M^\circ,$$
with $r_\tau\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_\tau\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_{L^2(M)}$. No boundary value is prescribed for $r_\tau$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product metric and dimension]]

[[lem-ip-limiting-carleman-estimate-on-product|Product Carleman estimate and L2 right solvability]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is used for the Hahn--Banach extension in the product Carleman right solver [F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is used for its Hilbert-space Riesz representation [F2].

**Given:** the product domain, smooth real $q$, real eikonal function $\psi$ with unit transversal gradient, and smooth transport amplitude $a$.

[F1] [[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain]]: $g=dx_1^2\oplus g_0$ and $\Delta_g=\partial_{x_1}^2+\Delta_{g_0}$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-limiting-carleman-estimate-on-product]]: for $\varphi=x_1$, the conjugated operator $P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}$ has a distributional right inverse on $L^2$ with norm at most $C h^{-1}$.

[F3] [[def-riemannian-gradient]] and [[def-laplace-beltrami-operator-as-trace-of-the-hessian]]: the product metric extends the gradient bilinearly to complex phases, and $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$.

[F4] **External input:** Dos Santos Ferreira--Kurylev--Lassas--Salo, Proposition 2.1 (PDF p. 10), for a compact oriented CTA manifold, bounded potential, either sign of sufficiently large real $\tau$, and arbitrary $f\in L^2$, gives $r\in H^1$ solving $e^{\tau x_1}(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\tau x_1}r=f$, with $\|r\|_{H^\alpha}\le C|\tau|^{\alpha-1}\|f\|_2$ for $0\le\alpha\le1$, with no prescribed boundary value. We import this statement, not a reconstructed shifted Carleman proof. Its statement and the application in Propositions 2.1--2.2, PDF pp. 10--11, were inspected; the older Proposition 4.4 citation issue is not treated as a local proof.

[F5] The orientation restriction in [F4] is removed for scalar equations by the orientation double cover of $M_0$. Lift $M,q,f$ to its product cover, solve there, and average the solution with its deck transform. The invariant solution descends to $H^1(M)$ and solves the original equation. The degree-two factors in the squared $L^2$ norms cancel in the estimate; the same applies to the local Sobolev norms. A disconnected cover is handled componentwise, using only finitely many choices.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$, $$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$ Direct conjugation gives $$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$ The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is $$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$ The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with $$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$ Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally. [A1, A2, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 2.1. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The additional boundary regularity is the external input [F4], rather than a consequence asserted for the $L^2$ solver [F2]. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $0<\epsilon$, let $(s_j)_{j\ge1}$ be the positive singular values in the Gaussian sequence inverse model, and let a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger=(\theta^\dagger_j)_{j\ge1}$ belong to $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$. In particular, if $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$ for a constant $C$ and a positive $r_\epsilon\to0$, then $r_\epsilon$ is a posterior contraction rate in the sense of the preceding definition.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model|The compact-SVD coordinates have a square-summable parameter space, product-Borel data, and normalized observations.]]

[[def-ip-posterior-contraction-rate|A contraction rate is defined by expected posterior mass outside every diverging multiple of the rate tending to zero under the fixed-truth data laws.]]

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|Finite Gaussian conditioning gives the scalar posterior mean and variance used coordinatewise.]]

[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel|Under AC, a consistent countable family of finite Gaussian laws has a probability law on the coordinate cylinder sigma-algebra.]]

[Knapik, van der Vaart, and van Zanten, *Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors*, §§3–4 and §7.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2692)

[Johnstone, *Gaussian estimation: Sequence and wavelet models*, §§1.2 and 2.3](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jbradic/math281a/Johnstone.pdf)

[Ding and Mathé, *Minimax rates for statistical inverse problems under general source conditions*, §1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01706)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; the positive-noise Gaussian sequence inverse experiment; a fixed truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$; an independent-coordinate Gaussian prior with $\tau_j>0$ and $\sum_j\tau_j^2<\infty$; and prior/noise independence.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice states that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] Countable Choice supplies a choice function for every countable family of nonempty sets; this is the branch assumed by the compact-SVD coordinate model. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The Gaussian sequence inverse model has parameter $\theta\in\ell^2$, product-Borel data $Z\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, and coordinates $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j$ with independent standard normal $\xi_j$. Multiplying by $s_j>0$ gives $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$. [[def-ip-gaussian-sequence-inverse-model]]

[F2] In a finite linear Gaussian model with Gaussian prior $N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and positive-definite observation-noise covariance $\Gamma$, the posterior law is multivariate normal with mean $m_0+C_0A^T(AC_0A^T+\Gamma)^{-1}(y-Am_0)$ and covariance $C_0-C_0A^T(AC_0A^T+\Gamma)^{-1}AC_0$. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F3] Under AC, a consistent family of finite Gaussian laws on countably many real coordinates has a unique probability law on the product cylinder sigma-algebra. [[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\tau_j>0$ satisfy $\sum_{j\ge1}\tau_j^2<\infty$, and let the prior be a Borel probability on $\ell^2$ whose coordinates are independent $N(0,\tau_j^2)$ variables, independent of the observation noise. Under the prior-predictive law the observations are $Y_j=s_j\theta_j+\epsilon\xi_j$; under the fixed truth they are $Y_j=s_j\theta^\dagger_j+\epsilon\xi_j$, where the $\xi_j$ are independent $N(0,1)$ variables. Define $v_j=(\tau_j^{-2}+s_j^2/\epsilon^2)^{-1}$ and $\lambda_j=\tau_j^2s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)$. For fixed-truth-almost every data sequence, a posterior version on $\ell^2$ is the restriction of $\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jY_j/s_j,v_j)$. Its expected posterior squared distance from the truth is
$$S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger):=\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}\!\left[\int_{\ell^2}\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid Y)\right]=\sum_{j\ge1}\left[(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta^\dagger_j)^2+\frac{v_j^2s_j^2}{\epsilon^2}+v_j\right].$$
The identity holds in $[0,+\infty]$; under the stated trace condition its right side is finite. For every $R>0$, the expected posterior mass outside the radius-$R$ ball is at most $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)/R^2$.       locator: "Theorem 4.8 and its complete proof, §4.4, printed pp. 23–25."

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and $C^\infty$, let $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$, and fix the ellipticity, collar and regularity parameters defining $X_d(R)$. Let $M=\partial\Omega$, let $K\subset L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)$ be compact, and for $\delta\ge0$ put $K_\delta=\{\eta\in K:\|\eta\|_{L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)}\le\delta\}$. Let $\kappa_\gamma$ be the zero-mean-in-each-variable kernel of the dimension-dependently smoothed mean-zero NtD observation for $\gamma\in X_d(R)$. Regard $L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)$ as a real Hilbert space and let $\mathfrak R f=(\operatorname{Re}f,\operatorname{Im}f)$ be its isometric realification into $L^2(M\times M;\mathbb R^2)$. Let $\widetilde\Psi^\star:L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ extend the exact-data inverse map and satisfy
$$\|\widetilde\Psi^\star(f)-\widetilde\Psi^\star(g)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)}\le C_\star\omega_\star(\|f-g\|_{L^2(M\times M;\mathbb C)}),$$
where $\omega_\star$ is continuous, nondecreasing and concave with $\omega_\star(0)=0$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a generalized Fourier neural operator $\Phi:L^2(M\times M;\mathbb R^2)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with two real input channels such that, on complex inputs, $\Psi(f):=\Phi(\mathfrak R f)$ satisfies
$$\sup_{\gamma\in X_d(R),\,\eta\in K_\delta}\|\gamma-\Psi(\kappa_\gamma+\eta)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)}\le\varepsilon+C_\star\omega_\star(\delta).$$
This is an existence statement for continuum NtD kernels and compact noise sets; it makes no training, finite-sample, network-size, finite-element, electrode-matrix or calibration guarantee.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-mean-zero-ntd-and-smoothed-kernel-observation|The dimension-dependent smoothed mean-zero NtD kernel convention.]]

[[lem-ip-ntd-smoothing-and-hilbert-schmidt-kernel-bound|The Hilbert–Schmidt kernel representation and kernel stability interface.]]

[[lem-ip-eit-forward-continuity-and-class-compactness|Compactness of the exact kernel image.]]

[[thm-ip-hilbert-map-extension-with-concave-modulus|The stable Hilbert-space extension of the exact inverse map.]]

[[thm-ip-generalized-fno-uniform-approximation-on-compact-sets|Generalized FNO approximation on compact input sets.]]

[de Hoop et al., Theorem 4.8 and proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** the EIT domain and class, compact complex-valued perturbation set $K$, noise threshold $\delta$, kernel map and Hilbert extension in the Statement.

[F1] The exact kernel image $\mathcal K_X=\{\kappa_\gamma:\gamma\in X_d(R)\}$ is compact in $L^2(M\times M)$. ([[lem-ip-eit-forward-continuity-and-class-compactness]])

[F2] The extension agrees with the exact-data inverse, $\widetilde\Psi^\star(\kappa_\gamma)=\gamma$, and satisfies the displayed $C_\star\omega_\star$ bound. ([[lem-ip-stable-extension-of-the-eit-inverse-map]], [[thm-ip-hilbert-map-extension-with-concave-modulus]])

[F3] $K_\delta$ is a closed subset of compact $K$, and addition is continuous on the complex $L^2$ space viewed as a real Hilbert space.

[F4] A continuous map from $L^2(M\times M;\mathbb R^2)$ to $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ can be uniformly approximated on every compact input set by a generalized FNO of the stated multichannel architecture. ([[thm-ip-generalized-fno-uniform-approximation-on-compact-sets]])

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are used at the conductivity, boundary spectral, and Hilbert extension interfaces. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\geq3$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded, nonempty, connected smooth domain, and let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Suppose zero is not a Dirichlet eigenvalue of either $-\Delta+q_j$, and the full Schrödinger Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps satisfy $\Lambda_{q_1}=\Lambda_{q_2}$ on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. Then $q_1=q_2$ on $\Omega$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full Schrödinger Dirichlet-to-Neumann map]]

[[lem-ip-euclidean-cgo-solvability|Euclidean exact CGO solutions]]

[[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity|Schrödinger Alessandrini identity]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and Countable Choice; a bounded smooth Euclidean domain in dimension $n\geq3$; real smooth nonresonant potentials $q_1,q_2$; and equality of their full boundary maps.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is assumed by the finite-measure Fourier uniqueness supplier [F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed by the Euclidean CGO Fourier-basis construction [F2].

[F1] [[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity]] and [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the Alessandrini Statement gives the Schrödinger identity for smooth boundary values, while the DN definition gives weak boundary forms on $H^{1/2}$. The exact $H^1$ solutions used below have only $H^{1/2}$ traces, so step 1.1 derives the needed extension directly from those forms.

[F2] [[lem-ip-euclidean-cgo-solvability]]: for each large null $\zeta$, the equation $(-\Delta+q)u=0$ has an exact solution $u=e^{i\zeta\cdot x}(1+r)$ with $\|r\|_{L^2}=O(|\zeta|^{-1}\|q\|_2)$.

[F3] [[cor-uniqueness-of-finite-borel-measures-from-their-fourier-transforms]]: finite complex Borel measures on $\mathbb R^n$ with the same Fourier transform are equal.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the Statement.

1.1 Set $Q=q_1-q_2$. For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ and define the Hermitian weak forms $a_j(v,w)=\int_\Omega(\nabla v\cdot\nabla\overline w+q_jv\overline w)\,dx$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(\Omega)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the two weak pairings gives $\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle=\int_\Omega Q u_1\overline{u_2}\,dx$. The maps agree on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, so this integral vanishes. This establishes the weak-trace extension of [F1] used here. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. Since $n\geq3$, choose orthonormal $\omega_1,\omega_2\in\mathbb R^n$ perpendicular to $\xi$; when $\xi=0$, choose any orthonormal pair. For $\tau\geq1$, set $\sigma_\tau=(\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4)^{1/2}$ and $$\zeta_1=\tau\omega_1+i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2,\qquad \zeta_2=-\tau\omega_1-i\sigma_\tau\omega_2+\xi/2.$$ The orthogonality gives $\zeta_j\cdot\zeta_j=\tau^2-\sigma_\tau^2+|\xi|^2/4=0$, $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=\xi$, and $|\zeta_j|\to\infty$. Apply [F2] to $q_1$ with phase $\zeta_1$ and to $q_2$ with phase $-\overline{\zeta_2}$; the latter is null, and reality of $q_2$ lets us conjugate the resulting solution. Thus $$u_1=e^{i\zeta_1\cdot x}(1+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{-i\overline{\zeta_2}\cdot x}(1+r_2),\qquad \|r_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}=O(\tau^{-1}).$$ Substitute in step 1.1. Since $Q\in L^2(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$, $$\left|\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\big(r_1+\overline{r_2}+r_1\overline{r_2}\big)\,dx\right| \leq \|Q\|_2(\|r_1\|_2+\|r_2\|_2)+\|Q\|_\infty\|r_1\|_2\|r_2\|_2=O(\tau^{-1}).$$ Taking $\tau\to\infty$ proves $\int_\Omega Qe^{i\xi\cdot x}\,dx=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$. [A2, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

3.1 Define the finite complex Borel measure $\mu(E)=\int_{E\cap\Omega}Q(x)\,dx$ on $\mathbb R^n$. It has finite total variation because $\Omega$ is bounded and $Q$ is bounded. The identity in step 2.1 gives $\widehat\mu(\eta)=0$ for every $\eta\in\mathbb R^n$ (take $\xi=-2\pi\eta$). By [F3], $\mu=0$. Hence $\int_E\operatorname{Re}Q\,dx=\int_E\operatorname{Im}Q\,dx=0$ for every Borel $E$; applying this to the sets $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\geq1/m\}$, $\{\operatorname{Re}Q\leq-1/m\}$, and their imaginary-part analogues shows $Q=0$ almost everywhere. Continuity of $Q$ gives $Q=0$ throughout $\Omega$. [A1, F3, given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention.

Assume the finite-candidate algorithm's hypotheses. A candidate is admissible when it is dimension-valid and its symmetric noise covariance is positive definite; let $\mathcal V$ be the ordered list of admissible candidates and let $\mathcal F=(d\in\mathcal V:c_d\le B)$ in the inherited order. For each $d\in\mathcal F$, let $U_d=\operatorname{EIG}(d)-c_d$ be its exact utility. In exact-real mode, if $\mathcal F$ is nonempty, the algorithm returns the first index in $\mathcal F$ attaining $\max_{d\in\mathcal F}U_d$; if $\mathcal V$ is empty it returns `all-inadmissible`, and if $\mathcal V$ is nonempty but $\mathcal F$ is empty it returns `budget-exhausted`.

For the floating-point mode, suppose each $d\in\mathcal F$ has a computed score $\widehat U_d$, a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $\widehat Z_d$, a successful factor $\widehat R_d$, and certified radii $\delta_d\ge0$, $0\le\rho_d<1$, and $\lambda_d\ge0$ such that
$$\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d,\qquad \|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d,$$
where $Z_d$ is the exact Cholesky-whitened matrix in the algorithm's Definition, and
$$\left|\widehat U_d-\left(\frac12\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-c_d\right)\right|\le\lambda_d.$$
For example, the matrix-radius component can use the information-matrix perturbation result in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I$ specialization: if $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$, $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$, and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ is sufficient, with any separate formation residual added. A rounded triangular-solve backward-error bound must be converted to the needed forward matrix error using a verified conditioning bound. ## Statement

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

## Statement references

[Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/lecturenotes/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Frank Natterer, “X-ray Tomography,” §2.1](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/profile/Frank-Natterer/publication/226521751_X-ray_Tomography/links/02e7e525392792a0a3000000/X-ray-Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$.

[F1] [[def-ip-2d-radon-transform]]: $Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt$, and the compact-support Fourier transform uses the phase $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$.

[F2] [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact Jordan set is Riemann integrable; apply this to real and imaginary parts on a bounding rectangle.

[F3] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: for a Riemann-integrable function on a product of closed rectangles, the iterated Riemann integrals equal the product-rectangle integral when the sections are integrable.

[F4] [[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]]: an injective $C^1$ change of variables with nonvanishing Jacobian carries a compactly supported Riemann integral to the integral multiplied by the absolute Jacobian.

[F5] [[thm-ftc-second-part]]: if a real function $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, including one-sided endpoint derivatives, and $G'$ is Riemann integrable there, then $\int_a^bG'=G(b)-G(a)$.

[F6] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for totally differentiable maps between finite-dimensional real spaces, $D(g\circ T)=Dg(T)\circ DT$. Apply this separately to real and imaginary parts; when $T$ is linear, $DT=T$ is constant, so repeated application gives the corresponding directional derivatives of a smooth composition.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $\theta$ and define $T(s,t)=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$ and $F(s,t)=f(T(s,t))$. The columns of $T$ are an orthonormal positively oriented basis, so $T$ is a linear diffeomorphism and $K:=T^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}f)$ is compact. Choose $M>0$ with $K\subset[-M,M]^2$. Then $F(s,t)=0$ for $|t|>M$, and $Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{-M}^{M}F(s,t)\,dt$; it vanishes unless $s$ belongs to the compact projection of $K$ onto the first coordinate. [given, F1, choose]

2.1 Write $f=f_{\mathrm R}+if_{\mathrm I}$ and $F_\nu=f_\nu\circ T$ for $\nu\in\{\mathrm R,\mathrm I\}$. Each $f_\nu$ is real smooth; since $DT$ is constant, repeated applications of [F6] give $\partial_s^kF_\nu(s,t)=(\theta\cdot\nabla)^k f_\nu(T(s,t))$. Thus, for each integer $k\ge0$, $\partial_s^kF$ is continuous. On every compact $s$-interval, $\partial_s^{k+1}F$ is uniformly continuous on the product with $[-M,M]$. ## Statement

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

## Statement references

[Mikko Salo, RICAM lecture notes v1, §2.1](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/lecturenotes/RICAM_notes_v1.pdf)

[Frank Natterer, “X-ray Tomography,” §2.1](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/profile/Frank-Natterer/publication/226521751_X-ray_Tomography/links/02e7e525392792a0a3000000/X-ray-Tomography.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, $\theta\in S^1$, and $\sigma\in\mathbb R$.

[F2] [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact Jordan set is Riemann integrable; apply this to real and imaginary parts on a bounding rectangle.

[F3] [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]: for a Riemann-integrable function on a product of closed rectangles, the iterated Riemann integrals equal the product-rectangle integral when the sections are integrable.

[F4] [[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]]: an injective $C^1$ change of variables with nonvanishing Jacobian carries a compactly supported Riemann integral to the integral multiplied by the absolute Jacobian.

$$\frac{\partial_s^kF(s+h,t)-\partial_s^kF(s,t)}{h}=\int_0^1\partial_s^{k+1}F(s+uh,t)\,du.$$

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, the Hahn–Banach theorem, and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space, and let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in $B$ with law $\mu$. Define its covariance by $C\ell=\mathbb E[\ell(W)W]$ for $\ell\in B^*$, let $N=\{\ell:\mathbb E[\ell(W)^2]=0\}$, and let $E$ be the completion of $B^*/N$ with inner product $\langle[\ell],[m]\rangle_E=\mathbb E[\ell(W)m(W)]$. Write $i:E\to B$ for the canonical injection extending $[\ell]\mapsto C\ell$. Under AC, the image of the closed $E$-unit ball is compact in the $B$ norm. Let $\Phi:B\to\mathbb R$ be Borel measurable, locally bounded above, and locally Lipschitz. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $M_\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$ \Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2\qquad(u\in B). $$
Define the evidence $Z=\int_B e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du)$ and, when $0<Z<\infty$, the posterior $\Pi(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u)}\mu(du)$. Then $0<Z<\infty$. For $h\in E$, define
$$ I(ih)=\Phi(ih)+\frac12\|h\|_E^2, \qquad I(u)=+\infty\quad(u\notin iE). $$
The functional $I$ attains a finite minimum on $iE$, and for every fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$,
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow \exp\!\bigl(I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)\bigr) \qquad(r\downarrow0). $$
Its minimizers are exactly the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. This pairwise result makes no claim of a global strong small-ball MAP.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain|a Borel probability prior is concentrated on its declared forward domain]]

[[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law|the fixed-data posterior is the normalized potential-weighted prior]]

[[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator|strong small-ball MAP and Cameron–Martin ratio-mode conventions]]

[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs|the Cameron–Martin norm and canonical injection]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, HB, countable choice, a real separable Banach space $B$, a centered Borel Gaussian random element $W$ with law $\mu$ and Cameron–Martin space $E$, and a Borel locally bounded-above locally Lipschitz potential $\Phi$ satisfying the displayed lower bound.

[A1] AC is required by the Gaussian, Cameron–Martin support, compactness, and Fernique interfaces used here. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] HB and countable choice are assumed by the finite-projection Gaussian ratio result. [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A prior is a Borel probability with full mass on its declared domain; the fixed-data posterior is the normalized measure with density proportional to $e^{-\Phi}$ on that domain. We specialize to $D=B$. [[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain]], [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F2] If a finite continuous potential on a Borel-prior domain has a common integrable lower envelope, then its evidence is finite and positive and the normalized update is a probability. [[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety]]

[F3] For some $a>0$, $\int_B e^{a\|u\|_B^2}\,\mu(du)<\infty$. [[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]

[F4] Since $B$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability, it is tight; the support theorem then gives $\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline{iE}$, so $0$ is a support point. [[def-polish-space]], [[thm-every-borel-probability-on-a-polish-space-is-tight]], [[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]]

[F5] The Cameron–Martin space is a Hilbert completion with continuous canonical injection and $\ell(ih)=\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E$ for $\ell\in B^*$. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F6] The closed unit ball of $E$ has compact image in $B$. [[lem-banach-gaussian-rkhs-unit-ball-is-compact]]

[F7] The Gaussian prior's fixed-center ball ratios converge to $\exp((\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2)$. [[lem-ip-gaussian-shift-small-ball-ratio]]

[F8] A Cameron–Martin ratio mode compares every fixed pair of Cameron–Martin ball probabilities by a limit at least $1$. [[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator]]

[F9] Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence. [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** establish posterior propriety using Fernique's exponential-square moment, transfer the Gaussian ball-ratio limit through the locally Lipschitz likelihood, and apply the direct method using the compact Cameron–Martin unit ball.

1.1 Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and $$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$ The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$, $$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$ Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$. [F5, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore $$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$ For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives $$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$ The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there. [A2, F1, F4, F7, given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives $$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$ The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. Local Lipschitz continuity gives $\Phi(ih_n)\to\Phi(ih)$, and therefore $$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$ Thus $I$ attains its finite minimum. [F5, F6, F9, step 1.2, given, choose, algebra]

3.1 By [F7], the posterior ball ratio for fixed $ih,ik\in iE$ is $e^{I(ik)-I(ih)}$. This limit is at least $1$ for every $k\in E$ exactly when $I(ih)\le I(ik)$ for every $k\in E$. By [F8], those points are precisely the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. The comparison is only over fixed centers in $iE$; no supremum over all $B$ centers has been controlled, so it does not establish a global strong small-ball MAP. [F7, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, HB, countable choice, a real separable Banach space $B$, a centered Borel Gaussian random element $W$ with law $\mu$ and Cameron–Martin space $E$, and a Borel locally bounded-above locally Lipschitz potential $\Phi$ satisfying the displayed lower bound.

[A1] AC is required by the Gaussian, Cameron–Martin support, compactness, and Fernique interfaces used here. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] HB and countable choice are assumed by the finite-projection Gaussian ratio result. [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] A prior is a Borel probability with full mass on its declared domain; the fixed-data posterior is the normalized measure with density proportional to $e^{-\Phi}$ on that domain. We specialize to $D=B$. [[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain]], [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F2] If a finite continuous potential on a Borel-prior domain has a common integrable lower envelope, then its evidence is finite and positive and the normalized update is a probability. [[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety]]

[F3] For some $a>0$, $\int_B e^{a\|u\|_B^2}\,\mu(du)<\infty$. [[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]

[F4] Since $B$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability, it is tight; the support theorem then gives $\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline{iE}$, so $0$ is a support point. [[def-polish-space]], [[thm-every-borel-probability-on-a-polish-space-is-tight]], [[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]]

[F5] The Cameron–Martin space is a Hilbert completion with continuous canonical injection and $\ell(ih)=\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E$ for $\ell\in B^*$. [[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], [[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]]

[F6] The closed unit ball of $E$ has compact image in $B$. [[lem-banach-gaussian-rkhs-unit-ball-is-compact]]

[F7] The Gaussian prior's fixed-center ball ratios converge to $\exp((\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2)$. [[lem-ip-gaussian-shift-small-ball-ratio]]

[F8] A Cameron–Martin ratio mode compares every fixed pair of Cameron–Martin ball probabilities by a limit at least $1$. [[def-ip-small-ball-map-estimator]]

[F9] Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence. [[thm-bolzano-weierstrass]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** establish posterior propriety using Fernique's exponential-square moment, transfer the Gaussian ball-ratio limit through the locally Lipschitz likelihood, and apply the direct method using the compact Cameron–Martin unit ball.

1.1 Choose $0<\varepsilon<a$ with $a$ from [F3]. The lower bound gives $\Phi(u)\ge M_\varepsilon-\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2$. Define the nonnegative Borel function $M_1(t)=\max\{0,\varepsilon t^2-M_\varepsilon\}$. Then $\Phi(u)\ge-M_1(\|u\|_B)$ and
$$ e^{M_1(\|u\|_B)} \le 1+e^{-M_\varepsilon}e^{\varepsilon\|u\|_B^2}. $$
The right side is $\mu$-integrable by [F3]. Since $\Phi$ is locally Lipschitz it is finite and continuous on $B$. Apply [F2] with the single datum and $D=B$; the prior definition in [F1] makes $\mu$ a prior on $B$. Thus $0<Z<\infty$ and $\Pi$ is a probability. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $h\in E$. Local Lipschitz continuity at $ih$ supplies constants $L_h<\infty$ and $\rho_h>0$ such that $|\Phi(u)-\Phi(ih)|\le L_h r$ whenever $\|u-ih\|_B\le r<\rho_h$. Therefore
$$ e^{-\Phi(ih)-L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)) \le \int_{\overline B_B(ih,r)}e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu(du) \le e^{-\Phi(ih)+L_hr}\mu(\overline B_B(ih,r)). $$
For fixed $h_1,h_2\in E$, divide the two integral bounds and cancel the common normalizer $Z$ in [F1]. The factors from the Lipschitz errors tend to $1$, and [F7] gives
$$ \frac{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_1,r))}{\Pi(\overline B_B(ih_2,r))} \longrightarrow e^{\Phi(ih_2)-\Phi(ih_1)} e^{(\|h_2\|_E^2-\|h_1\|_E^2)/2} =e^{I(ih_2)-I(ih_1)}. $$
The denominator is positive for small $r$: [F4] gives positive prior mass to every open ball about $ih_2$ (since $ih_2\in iE$), and the likelihood is strictly positive and continuous there. [A2, F1, F4, F7, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $C_i=\|i:E\to B\|$. If $E=\{0\}$, $I$ has the sole candidate $0$ and is minimized there. Otherwise $C_i>0$. Choose $\varepsilon<1/(4C_i^2)$ and use the potential lower bound to obtain, for every $h\in E$,
$$ I(ih)\ge M_\varepsilon+\frac12\|h\|_E^2-\varepsilon\|ih\|_B^2 \ge M_\varepsilon+\frac14\|h\|_E^2. $$
Since $I(0)=\Phi(0)$ is finite, $\inf_E I$ is finite and any minimizing sequence is bounded in $E$. [F5, given, choose, algebra]

3.2 Choose a minimizing sequence $(h_n)$ in $E$ and, by [F9], pass to a subsequence for which $\|h_n\|_E\to L$. Its images lie in a fixed multiple of the closed $E$-unit ball, whose image is compact in $B$ by [F6]. Pass to a further subsequence with $ih_n\to v$ in $B$; compactness means $v=ih$ for some $h\in E$. For each $\ell\in B^*$, [F5] gives
$$ |\ell(ih)|=\lim_n|\ell(ih_n)| =\lim_n|\langle h_n,[\ell]\rangle_E| \le L\|[\ell]\|_E. $$
The classes $[\ell]$ are dense in $E$ by [F5]. For every unit $g\in E$, choose nonzero classes $[\ell_n]\to g$ and normalize them; then $[\ell_n]/\|[\ell_n]\|_E\to g$. Thus the normalized covariance classes are dense in the unit sphere, and the supremum of $|\langle h,[\ell]\rangle_E|$ over them is $\|h\|_E$. The displayed bound gives $\|h\|_E\le L$. Local Lipschitz continuity gives $\Phi(ih_n)\to\Phi(ih)$, and therefore
$$ I(ih)\le\lim_n\left(\Phi(ih_n)+\frac12\|h_n\|_E^2\right)=\inf_E I. $$
Thus $I$ attains its finite minimum. [F5, F6, F9, step 3.1, given, choose, algebra]

4.1 By [F7], the posterior ball ratio for fixed $ih,ik\in iE$ is $e^{I(ik)-I(ih)}$. This limit is at least $1$ for every $k\in E$ exactly when $I(ih)\le I(ik)$ for every $k\in E$. By [F8], those points are precisely the Cameron–Martin ratio modes. The comparison is only over fixed centers in $iE$; no supremum over all $B$ centers has been controlled, so it does not establish a global strong small-ball MAP. [F7, F8, step 2.1, step 3.2, given, algebra] ∎

    - title: "Nikola Kovachki et al., On Universal Approximation and Error Bounds for Fourier Neural Operators"
      url: "https://jmlr.org/papers/volume22/21-0806/21-0806.pdf"
      locator: "Theorem 5 and complete proof in Appendix D.1–D.4."
---

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M=\partial\Omega\times\partial\Omega$ for a nonempty bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$, $d\ge2$, and let $a,b\in\mathbb N$ be positive finite channel dimensions. If $T:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ is continuous, then for every compact set $C\subset L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a generalized Fourier neural operator $\Psi:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)$ using a fixed smooth globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation and the boundary charts of the statement such that
$$\sup_{h\in C}\|T(h)-\Psi(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon.$$

## Statement references

[[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator|The generalized FNO architecture, chart lifting and dimension-reduction layer.]]

[de Hoop et al., §4.4, Theorem 4.8 and proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.20361)

[Kovachki et al., Theorem 5 and Appendix D: compact-uniform FNO approximation](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume22/21-0806/21-0806.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\Omega$, $M$, $T$, compact $C$, and $\varepsilon$ as in the statement.

[F1] There are bounded chart maps $G_a:L^2(M;\mathbb R^a)\to\bigoplus_{j,k}L^2(\mathbb T^{2d-2};\mathbb R^a)$ and $L_a$ in the reverse direction, obtained by applying the scalar chart maps componentwise, with $L_aG_a=I$. ([[lem-ip-boundary-chart-lifting-and-fourier-projection]])

[F2] On a torus, a Fourier neural operator with the specified activation uniformly approximates every continuous map on every compact input set in the $L^2$ norm. ([[lem-ip-fno-torus-compact-universality]])

[F3] Zero extension from $L^2(\Omega)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T^d)$ is isometric because $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$; the product extension constant in the last $d-2$ coordinates is also isometric under normalized Haar measure.

[F4] The generalized-FNO architecture contains the zero operator by setting its finite-layer coefficients to zero. ([[def-ip-generalized-fourier-neural-operator]])

[A1] Countable Choice is assumed at the finite boundary-chart partition interface. ([[def-countable-choice]])

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and the data in the statement.

1.1 If $C=\varnothing$, choose the zero generalized FNO from [F4]; the uniform error condition is vacuous. Otherwise let $n=2d-2$ and let $J_0:L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^b)$ be zero extension. Let $I_{d,n}:L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^b)\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ send $g(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ to the function constant in the last $n-d=d-2$ coordinates. The chart-pair components identify $\bigoplus_{j,k}L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^a)$ with $L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{J^2a})$. Define $S:=I_{d,n}J_0TL_a$ on this direct-sum space. This is continuous by [F1] and [F3], and $G_a(C)$ is compact because $G_a$ is continuous and $C$ is compact. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to the continuous map $S:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^{J^2a})\to L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)$ on compact $G_a(C)$ with tolerance $\varepsilon$. There is a torus FNO $\Phi$ such that $\sup_{u\in G_a(C)}\|S(u)-\Phi(u)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon$. [F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 Set $\mathbb T^0=\{()\}$ with unit mass, so the following integral is the identity when $d=2$. For any finite channel dimension $c$, define $A_c:L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^c)\to L^2(\mathbb T^d;\mathbb R^c)$ by $(A_cv)(x)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-2}}v(x,z)\,dz$, componentwise. Cauchy–Schwarz on the unit-measure torus and Fubini give $\|A_c\|\le1$. Let $R$ be restriction from $\mathbb T^d$ to $\Omega$, also of norm at most one. Since $A_bI_{d,n}=I$, $RJ_0=I$, and $L_aG_a=I$, the generalized FNO $\Psi:=R\circ A_b\circ\Phi\circ G_a$ satisfies $$\|T(h)-\Psi(h)\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}=\|RA_b(S(G_ah)-\Phi(G_ah))\|_{L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^b)}\le\|S(G_ah)-\Phi(G_ah)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb R^b)}<\varepsilon$$ for every $h\in C$. Write the torus FNO as $\Phi=Q_\Phi\circ\Phi_0$, where $\Phi_0$ ends before its final constant affine channel map $Q_\Phi(v)=Wv+c$ and has $r$ output channels. Its initial affine channel lift is composed into the first affine part of $\Phi_0$ after $G_a$. Normalized averaging commutes with the final map, $A_bQ_\Phi=Q_\Phi A_r$, and restriction commutes with the same pointwise map. Hence $R A_b\Phi G_a=Q_\Phi R A_r\Phi_0G_a$. This has the generalized architecture: identity pointwise lift, chart lift $G_a$, torus layers $\Phi_0$, the constant-kernel dimension reduction $A_r$, restriction $R$, and final pointwise affine map $Q_\Phi$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎
