id: thm-ip-linear-gaussian-information-gain-logdet
kind: theorem
title: Linear Gaussian information gain has a log-determinant formula
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: inverse-problems-knot-theory-all-109-2026-10-19
dependency_level: 5
deps:
  - thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy
  - thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior
  - def-multivariate-normal-law
  - lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal
  - thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density
  - thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique
  - def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix
  - def-natural-logarithm
  - thm-determinant-multiplicative
  - def-axiom-of-choice
justified_by: []
forward_refs: []
proof_strategy: direct
axiom_use: >-
  AC is inherited from the library KL convention, finite Gaussian and
  conditional-law interfaces. The expectation and finite matrix algebra in the
  local proof use no stronger choice principle and never require an inverse of
  the possibly singular state covariance.
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304"
      url: "https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps"
      locator: "§2.2, normal-linear Bayesian D-optimality and its determinant criterion."
    - title: "David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604"
      url: "https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf"
      locator: "§3.1, equations (3.4)–(3.6), Gaussian information gain from a determinant ratio."
    - title: "Carl Edward Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press (2006)"
      url: "https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf"
      locator: "Chapter 2 §§2.1–2.2, finite Gaussian conditioning and predictive laws."
---

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy|Expected information gain is the joint KL divergence of parameter and observation from the product of their marginals.]]

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|For singular prior covariance and positive-definite observation noise, the finite linear Gaussian posterior exists and only the observation covariance is inverted.]]

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|A finite multivariate Gaussian law may have singular covariance.]]

[[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density|Positive-definite Gaussian covariance gives the stated Lebesgue density.]]

[[def-natural-logarithm|Logarithms use the natural logarithm.]]

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, Chapter 2](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, with the expected information gain defined for the dominated conditional Gaussian likelihood and its proper Gaussian prior.

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the finite Gaussian posterior interface and the library KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The joint-KL identity gives $\operatorname{EIG}=D(P_{\theta,Y}\|P_\theta\otimes P_Y)$ under the dominated model. [[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy]]

[F2] For $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and independent $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ with $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$ is positive definite and the posterior formula uses only $S^{-1}$; singular $C$ is permitted. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F3] A finite independent stack of possibly singular Gaussian vectors is jointly Gaussian, and linear projections of a multivariate normal have the corresponding projected mean and covariance. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A positive-definite multivariate normal with covariance $V$ has density $(2\pi)^{-m/2}\det(V)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(y-a)^TV^{-1}(y-a))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F5] A positive-definite symmetric matrix has a unique positive-definite square root; determinants are multiplicative. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^m$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$ because $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$. Thus $S\succ0$ and both observation covariances have positive determinants. The same conclusion is recorded in [F2]. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $(\theta,\eta)$ is jointly Gaussian, so its linear image $Y=A\theta+\eta$ is Gaussian with mean $Am_0$ and covariance $S$. Conditional on $\theta$, $Y$ is a translate of $\eta$ and has covariance $\Gamma$. Since both $S$ and $\Gamma$ are positive definite, [F4] gives the positive conditional and predictive densities needed in [F1]. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $z=Y-Am_0$ and $e=Y-A\theta=\eta$. By [F4], the log likelihood ratio in [F1] is $\log\frac{p(Y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(Y)}=\frac12\log\frac{\det S}{\det\Gamma}-\frac12e^T\Gamma^{-1}e+\frac12z^TS^{-1}z$. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

## Statement references

[[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy|Expected information gain is the joint KL divergence of parameter and observation from the product of their marginals.]]

[[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior|For singular prior covariance and positive-definite observation noise, the finite linear Gaussian posterior exists and only the observation covariance is inverted.]]

[[def-multivariate-normal-law|A finite multivariate Gaussian law may have singular covariance.]]

[[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density|Positive-definite Gaussian covariance gives the stated Lebesgue density.]]

[[def-natural-logarithm|Logarithms use the natural logarithm.]]

[Chaloner and Verdinelli, §2.2](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/tr/tr599/tr599.ps)

[MacKay, §3.1](https://gwern.net/doc/reinforcement-learning/exploration/active-learning/1992-mackay.pdf)

[Rasmussen and Williams, Chapter 2](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/chapters/RW.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement, with the expected information gain defined for the dominated conditional Gaussian likelihood and its proper Gaussian prior.

[A1] AC is the explicit hypothesis of the finite Gaussian posterior interface and the library KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The joint-KL identity gives $\operatorname{EIG}=D(P_{\theta,Y}\|P_\theta\otimes P_Y)$ under the dominated model. [[thm-ip-eig-is-joint-relative-entropy]]

[F2] For $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and independent $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ with $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$, $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$ is positive definite and the posterior formula uses only $S^{-1}$; singular $C$ is permitted. [[thm-ip-finite-linear-gaussian-posterior]]

[F3] A finite independent stack of possibly singular Gaussian vectors is jointly Gaussian, and linear projections of a multivariate normal have the corresponding projected mean and covariance. [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]

[F4] A positive-definite multivariate normal with covariance $V$ has density $(2\pi)^{-m/2}\det(V)^{-1/2}\exp(-\tfrac12(y-a)^TV^{-1}(y-a))$. [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F5] A positive-definite symmetric matrix has a unique positive-definite square root; determinants are multiplicative. [[thm-non-negative-square-root-exists-and-is-unique]] [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^m$, $v^TSv=(A^Tv)^TC(A^Tv)+v^T\Gamma v>0$ because $C\succeq0$ and $\Gamma\succ0$. Thus $S\succ0$ and both observation covariances have positive determinants. The same conclusion is recorded in [F2]. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 By [F3], $(\theta,\eta)$ is jointly Gaussian, so its linear image $Y=A\theta+\eta$ is Gaussian with mean $Am_0$ and covariance $S$. Conditional on $\theta$, $Y$ is a translate of $\eta$ and has covariance $\Gamma$. Since both $S$ and $\Gamma$ are positive definite, [F4] gives the positive conditional and predictive densities needed in [F1]. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Write $z=Y-Am_0$ and $e=Y-A\theta=\eta$. By [F4], the log likelihood ratio in [F1] is $\log\frac{p(Y\mid\theta)}{p_Y(Y)}=\frac12\log\frac{\det S}{\det\Gamma}-\frac12e^T\Gamma^{-1}e+\frac12z^TS^{-1}z$. Their expectations cancel, so [F1] yields $\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log(\det S/\det\Gamma)$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $W=\Gamma^{-1/2}$. Since $\Gamma^{1/2}W=I_m$, matrix multiplication gives $S=\Gamma^{1/2}(I_m+WACA^TW)\Gamma^{1/2}$. The middle matrix is positive definite because $ACA^T\succeq0$. By [F5], $\det S=\det(\Gamma^{1/2})^2\det(I_m+WACA^TW)=\det\Gamma\,\det(I_m+WACA^TW)$. Substitution in step 2.1 proves the formula. No inverse or determinant of $C$ was used, so singular $C$ is included; centering by $m_0$ in $z$ proves the mean cancellation. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the inputs of the prior-preserving
Crank–Nicolson algorithm: a separable real Hilbert space $H$, centered Borel
Gaussian reference probability $\mu_0$, full-mass Borel domain $D$, Borel
potential $\Phi_D:D\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, positive finite evidence $Z$, and
scale $\beta\in[0,1]$. Let $\mu$ be the normalized target on $H$ obtained by
extending $\Phi_D$ by $+\infty$ off $D$, and let $P_\beta$ be the algorithm's
accept-reject transition. Then $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$:
its joint flow
$$\Lambda_\beta(C):=\int_H P_\beta(u,C_u)\,\mu(du),\qquad C_u:=\{v\in H:(u,v)\in C\},$$
is unchanged by $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ for every Borel
$C\subseteq H\times H$. Consequently, $\mu$ is invariant:
$$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal B(H)).$$
This conclusion gives invariance only; it does not assert uniqueness,
convergence, mixing, an effective-sample-size bound, mesh-independent cost,
or correctness of an approximate forward solver.

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson|The pCN target, total potential extension, proposal, and accept-reject transition.]]

[[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure|Reversibility means symmetry of the joint flow measure under coordinate swap.]]

[[thm-general-state-reversibility-implies-invariance|A symmetric joint flow implies invariance of its probability target.]]

[[lem-ip-pcn-reference-pair-law-is-symmetric|The Gaussian pCN proposal pair law under the reference probability is symmetric.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The algorithm inputs in the Statement.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice and the algorithm's full-mass domain, potential extension, evidence, target density, proposal, and acceptance convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]]

[F1] The proposal rule $Q_\beta$ and accept-reject rule $P_\beta$ are Borel probability kernels; for each $u$,
$$Q_\beta(u,B)=\int_H\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz),\qquad P_\beta(u,A)=\int_A\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)+\mathbf1_A(u)(1-a(u)),$$
where $a(u)=\int_H\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)$. [[lem-ip-pcn-transition-kernel-is-measurable]]

[F2] If $w(u)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}$, then $\mu(du)=Z^{-1}w(u)\mu_0(du)$, $w(u)=0$ when $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$, and $\alpha(u,v)=0$ if either potential is infinite. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]] [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F3] For $U_0,\xi$ independent with law $\mu_0$ and $V_0=\rho U_0+\beta\xi$, the joint Borel law of $(U_0,V_0)$ is symmetric under coordinate swap; on the separable Hilbert product, the Borel sigma-algebra equals the product sigma-algebra. [[lem-ip-pcn-reference-pair-law-is-symmetric]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F4] A prior and probability kernel define a joint flow probability measure with the rectangle formula and nonnegative iterated-integral identity. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[def-probability-measure]]

[F5] Equality of probability laws is preserved under measurable changes of variables, and integration against a law equals expectation of the corresponding random-element function. [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]

[F6] The product of two probability measures exists and has the rectangle formula; the rectangle criterion then makes its coordinate projections independent random elements. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] [[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]] [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]

[F7] A probability kernel is reversible with respect to a probability measure when its joint flow equals its coordinate transpose; this definition requires no density. [[def-general-state-reversibility-by-symmetric-flow-measure]]

[F8] Reversibility with respect to a probability measure implies its invariance. [[thm-general-state-reversibility-implies-invariance]]

[F9] Since $H$ is separable, norm balls centered at a countable dense subset
with positive rational radii form a countable base of its induced metric
topology: given $x\in U$ with $U$
open, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then a dense point $d$ with
$\|d-x\|<r/3$ and a positive rational $s$ with
$\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$; the triangle inequality gives
$x\in B(d,s)\subseteq U$. Hence $H$ is second-countable, and the Borel
sigma-algebra of $H\times H$ equals $\mathcal B(H)\otimes\mathcal B(H)$.
[[def-separable-space]] [[def-second-countable-space]]
[[thm-product-of-countable]] [[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]
[[lem-subset-of-countable]] [[def-hilbert-space]]
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] [[def-metric-ball]] [[def-metric-topology]]
[[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]
[[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F10] Continuous maps have Borel preimages of Borel sets.
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

1.1 AC is assumed as recorded in [A1]. By [F9], $H$ is second-countable and the Borel sigma-algebra of $H\times H$ is the product sigma-algebra. Put $\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and let $\Lambda_0(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$ be the joint flow of the reference probability and proposal kernel. It exists by [F4]. Take the product probability space $(H\times H,\mu_0\otimes\mu_0)$ and its coordinate random elements $U_0,\xi$; [F6] gives their independence and common law $\mu_0$. For every nonnegative product-Borel $h$, the iterated-integral identity in [F4] and [F1] give $$\int h\,d\Lambda_0=\int_H\int_H h(u,\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)\,\mu_0(du)=\mathbb E[h(U_0,\rho U_0+\beta\xi)],$$ where the proposal-row pushforward and the change-of-variables identity [F5] identify the flow integral with expectation under $U_0\sim\mu_0$, and the product joint law [F6] together with the measurable proposal map identifies that expectation with the displayed one. Thus $\Lambda_0$ is the law in [F3], so $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, construct]

1.2 Define $w(u)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}$ and $m(u,v)=\min\{w(u),w(v)\}$. For every $(u,v)$, if both potential values are finite, then $$w(u)\alpha(u,v)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\min\{1,e^{\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=\min\{e^{-\bar\Phi(u)},e^{-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=m(u,v).$$ If either value is $+\infty$, the algorithm sets $\alpha(u,v)=0$ and $m(u,v)=0$, so the identity still holds. In particular, $m$ is a symmetric nonnegative Borel function. [A1, F2, given, algebra]

1.3 Set $r(u)=1-a(u)\in[0,1]$. The diagonal map $d(u)=(u,u)$ is continuous from $H$ into the product topology on $H\times H$, so by [F10] it is Borel. Thus $u\mapsto\mathbf1_C(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(d(u))$ is measurable for every Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$. By the diagonal term in [F1] and the joint-flow formula [F4], the rejection part of the target joint flow has mass on $C$ $$\Lambda_{\rm rej}(C)=\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,u)r(u)\,\mu(du).$$ It is symmetric because $\tau(d(u))=d(u)$ for every $u$: for every Borel $C$, $\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(u,u)$. [F1, F4, F10, given, algebra]

2.1 For Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$, the accepted part of the target joint flow is $$\Lambda_{\rm acc}(C):=\int_H\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,v)\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)\,\mu(du)=Z^{-1}\int_{H\times H}\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,\Lambda_0(du,dv).$$ The equality follows from the target density in [F2], identity 1.2, and the iterated-integral formula [F4]. Since $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric by step 1.1 and $m(u,v)=m(v,u)$, this accepted measure is symmetric. Indeed, for $\tau(u,v)=(v,u)$, the change-of-variables identity [F5] gives $$\int\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_C(v,u)m(v,u)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0.$$ Equality for every Borel $C$ is symmetry under $\tau$. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By the decomposition of $P_\beta$ in [F1] and the joint-flow identity [F4], $\Lambda_\beta=\Lambda_{\rm acc}+\Lambda_{\rm rej}$. The accepted and rejection pieces are symmetric by steps 2.1 and 1.3, hence $\Lambda_\beta$ is symmetric. By [F7], $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$. [F1, F4, F7, step 2.1, step 1.3, given]

4.1 The hypotheses of [F8] hold: [F1] gives a probability kernel and the algorithm gives the probability measure $\mu$. Therefore [F8] yields $\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel $A$. The proof uses only the symmetric-flow identity; it establishes no uniqueness or convergence claim. [F1, F8, step 3.1, given] ∎

[F1] The proposal rule $Q_\beta$ and accept-reject rule $P_\beta$ are Borel probability kernels; for each $u$,
$$Q_\beta(u,B)=\int_H\mathbf1_B(\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz),\qquad P_\beta(u,A)=\int_A\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)+\mathbf1_A(u)(1-a(u)),$$
where $a(u)=\int_H\alpha(u,v)Q_\beta(u,dv)$. [[lem-ip-pcn-transition-kernel-is-measurable]]

[F2] If $w(u)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}$, then $\mu(du)=Z^{-1}w(u)\mu_0(du)$, $w(u)=0$ when $\bar\Phi(u)=+\infty$, and $\alpha(u,v)=0$ if either potential is infinite. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]] [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]]

[F3] For $U_0,\xi$ independent with law $\mu_0$ and $V_0=\rho U_0+\beta\xi$, the joint Borel law of $(U_0,V_0)$ is symmetric under coordinate swap; on the separable Hilbert product, the Borel sigma-algebra equals the product sigma-algebra. [[lem-ip-pcn-reference-pair-law-is-symmetric]] [[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]

[F4] A prior and probability kernel define a joint flow probability measure with the rectangle formula and nonnegative iterated-integral identity. [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[def-probability-measure]]

with positive rational radii form a countable base of its induced metric

open, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then a dense point $d$ with
$\|d-x\|<r/3$ and a positive rational $s$ with
$\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$; the triangle inequality gives

[[def-separable-space]] [[def-second-countable-space]]
[[thm-product-of-countable]] [[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]

[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] [[def-metric-ball]] [[def-metric-topology]]
[[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]

**Given:** The hypotheses and notation in the Statement.

the Borel sigma-algebra of $H\times H$ is the product sigma-algebra. Put
$\rho=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and let
$\Lambda_0(du,dv)=\mu_0(du)Q_\beta(u,dv)$ be the joint flow of the reference
probability and proposal kernel. It exists by [F4]. Take the product
probability space $(H\times H,\mu_0\otimes\mu_0)$ and its coordinate random
elements $U_0,\xi$; [F6] gives their independence and common law $\mu_0$.
For every nonnegative
product-Borel $h$, the iterated-integral identity in [F4] and [F1] give
$$\int h\,d\Lambda_0=\int_H\int_H h(u,\rho u+\beta z)\,\mu_0(dz)\,\mu_0(du)=\mathbb E[h(U_0,\rho U_0+\beta\xi)],$$
where the proposal-row pushforward and the change-of-variables identity [F5]
identify the flow integral with expectation under $U_0\sim\mu_0$, and the
product joint law [F6] together with the measurable proposal map identifies
that expectation with the displayed one. Thus
$\Lambda_0$ is the law in [F3], so $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric.
[A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, given, construct]

$m(u,v)=\min\{w(u),w(v)\}$. For every $(u,v)$, if both potential values are
finite, then
$$w(u)\alpha(u,v)=e^{-\bar\Phi(u)}\min\{1,e^{\bar\Phi(u)-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=\min\{e^{-\bar\Phi(u)},e^{-\bar\Phi(v)}\}=m(u,v).$$

nonnegative Borel function. [A1, F2, given, algebra]

flow is

The equality follows from the target density in [F2], identity 1.2, and the
iterated-integral formula [F4]. Since $\Lambda_0$ is symmetric by step 1.1
and $m(u,v)=m(v,u)$, this accepted measure is symmetric. Indeed, for
$\tau(u,v)=(v,u)$, the change-of-variables identity [F5] gives
$$\int\mathbf1_C(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_C(v,u)m(v,u)\,d\Lambda_0=\int\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,v)m(u,v)\,d\Lambda_0.$$
Equality for every Borel $C$ is symmetry under $\tau$.
[F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Set $r(u)=1-a(u)\in[0,1]$. The diagonal map $d(u)=(u,u)$ is continuous
from $H$ into the product topology on $H\times H$, so by [F10] it is Borel.
Thus $u\mapsto\mathbf1_C(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(d(u))$ is measurable for every
Borel $C\subseteq H\times H$. By the diagonal term in [F1] and the joint-flow
formula [F4], the rejection part of the target joint flow has mass on $C$
$$\Lambda_{\rm rej}(C)=\int_H\mathbf1_C(u,u)r(u)\,\mu(du).$$
It is symmetric because $\tau(d(u))=d(u)$ for every $u$: for every Borel
$C$, $\mathbf1_{\tau^{-1}C}(u,u)=\mathbf1_C(u,u)$. [F1, F4, F10, given, algebra]

3.1 By the decomposition of $P_\beta$ in [F1] and the joint-flow identity
[F4], $\Lambda_\beta=\Lambda_{\rm acc}+\Lambda_{\rm rej}$. The accepted
and rejection pieces are symmetric by steps 2.1 and 2.2, hence $\Lambda_\beta$
is symmetric.
By [F7], $P_\beta$ is reversible with respect to $\mu$. [F1, F4, F7, step 2.1, step 2.2, given]

3.2 The hypotheses of [F8] hold: [F1] gives a probability kernel and the
algorithm gives the probability measure $\mu$. Therefore [F8] yields
$\int_H P_\beta(u,A)\,\mu(du)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel $A$. The proof uses
only the symmetric-flow identity; it establishes no uniqueness or convergence
claim. [F1, F8, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let
$\mu_0$ be a centered Borel Gaussian probability measure on $H$. Let
$\Phi:H\to[0,\infty)$ be finite-valued and Borel measurable. Suppose that
there are constants $p,K>0$ such that
$$0\le\Phi(u)\le K(1+\|u\|^p)\qquad(u\in H),$$
and for every $R>0$ there is a finite $L_R$ such that
$$|\Phi(u)-\Phi(v)|\le L_R\|u-v\|\quad\text{whenever }\max\{\|u\|,\|v\|\}<R.$$
Set $Z=\int_H e^{-\Phi(u)}\,\mu_0(du)$ and
$\mu(du)=Z^{-1}e^{-\Phi(u)}\mu_0(du)$. For $\beta\in[0,1]$, let
$U\sim\mu$ and $\xi\sim\mu_0$ be independent, put
$V_\beta=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}U+\beta\xi$, and define
$$\alpha_\beta=\min\{1,\exp(\Phi(U)-\Phi(V_\beta))\}.$$
Then $0<Z<\infty$, $\mu$ is a probability measure, and the stationary mean
acceptance satisfies
$$\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\mathbb E[\alpha_\beta]=1.$$

## Statement references

[[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson|The pCN proposal combines the current state with an independent Gaussian reference draw and accepts by the potential ratio.]]

[[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety|A continuous potential with a common integrable lower envelope gives positive finite evidence and a proper posterior.]]

[[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law|A centered Gaussian law on a separable Banach space has an exponential-square moment.]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

[A1] AC is assumed, as required by the centered Borel Gaussian interface and the pCN algorithm. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]]

[F1] The pCN proposal is $V_\beta=\sqrt{1-\beta^2}U+\beta\xi$, and its acceptance for finite potential values is $\min\{1,\exp(\Phi(U)-\Phi(V_\beta))\}$. [[alg-ip-prior-preserving-crank-nicolson]]

[F2] A prior on a full-mass Borel forward domain and a finite continuous potential with a common integrable lower envelope have positive finite evidence and a normalized posterior. [[def-ip-prior-on-a-forward-domain]] [[def-ip-misfit-evidence-and-posterior-law]] [[thm-ip-function-space-posterior-propriety]]

[F3] A centered Borel Gaussian random element in a separable Banach space has $\mathbb E e^{a\|X\|^2}<\infty$ for some $a>0$; a centered Borel Gaussian probability on $H$ is realized by the identity random element on $(H,\mathcal B(H),\mu_0)$. [[def-borel-gaussian-random-element-on-a-separable-banach-space]] [[thm-fernique-integrability-for-separable-banach-gaussian-law]]

[F4] If a nonnegative measurable function has integral zero, it vanishes almost everywhere; integrating on a measurable set is integrating its indicator times the function. [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]] [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]

[F5] If measurable functions converge pointwise and are dominated in absolute value by one integrable function, their integrals converge to the integral of the pointwise limit. [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F6] Since $H$ is separable, countable dense $D\subseteq H$ and positive
rational radii give a countable base of open norm balls in its induced metric
topology: for $x\in U$ with $U$ open,
choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$, then $d\in D$ with $\|d-x\|<r/3$ and
a rational $s$ with $\|d-x\|<s<r-\|d-x\|$; then
$x\in B(d,s)\subseteq B(x,r)$. Thus $H$ is second-countable and
$\mathcal B(H\times H)=\mathcal B(H)\otimes\mathcal B(H)$. The law notation in
the Statement makes $U$ and $\xi$ Borel random elements; the pair $(U,\xi)$ is
measurable into the product sigma-algebra because inverse images of measurable
rectangles are intersections of measurable coordinate events.
For each $\beta$, $(u,z)\mapsto\sqrt{1-\beta^2}u+\beta z$ is continuous, so
$V_\beta$ is Borel; composing with the Borel $\Phi$ and the continuous scalar
operations shows $\Delta_\beta=\Phi(V_\beta)-\Phi(U)$ and
$\alpha_\beta=\min\{1,e^{-\Delta_\beta}\}$ are measurable.
[[def-separable-space]] [[def-second-countable-space]]
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]
[[def-independent-random-elements]] [[thm-product-of-countable]]
[[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] [[def-metric-ball]] [[def-metric-topology]]
[[thm-metric-open-set-algebra]]
[[lem-subset-of-countable]]
[[lem-borel-product-of-second-countable-spaces]]
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]
[[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]]
[[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses and definitions in the Statement.

1.1 Apply [F2] with parameter space $H$, domain $D=H$, one-point data space $\{*\}$, potential $\widetilde\Phi(u,*)=\Phi(u)$, and envelope $M_1=0$. The domain has full $\mu_0$-mass. For any $u\in H$, choose $R>\|u\|$; all sufficiently close $v$ satisfy $\max\{\|u\|,\|v\|\}<R$, so the stated Lipschitz bound proves continuity at $u$. Also $\int_H e^{M_1(\|u\|)}\,\mu_0(du)=1$. Hence $0<Z<\infty$ and $\mu$ is a probability. The density $e^{-\Phi}$ is strictly positive everywhere. If $\mu(A)=0$, then $\int_H e^{-\Phi}\mathbf1_A\,d\mu_0=0$, so [F4] gives $e^{-\Phi}\mathbf1_A=0$ $\mu_0$-almost everywhere; strict positivity yields $\mu_0(A)=0$. Conversely, $\mu_0(A)=0$ implies $\mu(A)=0$ directly from the integral formula. Thus $\mu$ and $\mu_0$ are equivalent. [F2, F4, given, construct]

1.2 Fix any sequence $\beta_n\in[0,1]$ with $\beta_n\to0$. For every realization with $U,\xi\in H$, $\rho_n:=\sqrt{1-\beta_n^2}\to1$ and $$\|V_{\beta_n}-U\|\le |1-\rho_n|\|U\|+\beta_n\|\xi\|\longrightarrow0.$$ Choose $R>\|U\|+1$ for that realization. Eventually $\max\{\|U\|,\|V_{\beta_n}\|\}<R$, and the assumed ball-wise Lipschitz bound gives $$|\Phi(V_{\beta_n})-\Phi(U)|\le L_R\|V_{\beta_n}-U\|\longrightarrow0.$$ Therefore $\Delta_n:=\Phi(V_{\beta_n})-\Phi(U)\to0$ almost surely. Its measurability, and that of $\alpha_{\beta_n}$, was established in [F6]. [F1, F6, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 View the identity map $x\mapsto x$ on $(H,\mathcal B(H),\mu_0)$ as a centered Borel Gaussian random element. By [F3], there is $a>0$ such that $\int_H e^{a\|x\|^2}\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty$. For every $q>0$, the function $r\mapsto r^q e^{-ar^2}$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$, so $\int_H\|x\|^q\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty$. Since $e^{-\Phi}\le1$ and $Z>0$, $$\mathbb E\|U\|^q=Z^{-1}\int_H\|x\|^q e^{-\Phi(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)\le Z^{-1}\int_H\|x\|^q\,\mu_0(dx)<\infty.$$ The same Gaussian moment bound gives $\mathbb E\|\xi\|^q<\infty$ for every $q>0$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The growth bound and $\|V_{\beta_n}\|\le\|U\|+\|\xi\|$ imply $$|\Delta_n|\le 2K+K\|U\|^p+K(\|U\|+\|\xi\|)^p\le C_{p,K}(1+\|U\|^p+\|\xi\|^p),$$ where the last inequality follows from $(a+b)^p\le2^p(a^p+b^p)$ for $a,b\ge0$ (use $a+b\le2\max(a,b)$ and $\max(a,b)^p\le a^p+b^p$), with $C_{p,K}:=\max\{2K,K(1+2^p),K2^p\}$. By step 2.1 the right side is integrable and does not depend on $n$. Applying [F5] to the measurable sequence $|\Delta_n|$ from [F6] and step 1.2 gives $\mathbb E|\Delta_n|\to0$. [F5, F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

4.1 The scalar function $g(t)=\min\{1,e^{-t}\}$ is continuous and $g(0)=1$. Step 1.2 therefore implies $\alpha_{\beta_n}=g(\Delta_n)\to1$ almost surely. Since $0\le\alpha_{\beta_n}\le1$, [F5] with the integrable dominating constant $1$ yields $\mathbb E\alpha_{\beta_n}\to1$. The sequence $\beta_n\to0$ was arbitrary, so the sequential criterion for real limits proves $\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\mathbb E[\alpha_\beta]=1$. This is the stationary mean acceptance limit; it asserts no convergence or mixing rate for the resulting chain. [F5, F6, step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with $[0]=\varnothing$, and let $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$. Use the standard dot product $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{k<d}u_kv_k$, identify $x,z\in\mathbb R^d$ when $z=x$ or $z=-x$, and write $[x]$ for the resulting class. Define $\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=(\langle a_i,x\rangle^2)_{i\in[m]}$, a formula independent of the representative because replacing $x$ by $-x$ leaves every square unchanged. For $S\subseteq[m]$, let $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)$ be the set of finite real linear combinations of its vectors, with the empty span equal to $\{0\}$. Then $\mathcal I_\Phi$ is injective on the global-sign classes if and only if for every $S\subseteq[m]$ at least one of $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)$ and $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})$ equals $\mathbb R^d$.

## Statement references

[Radu Balan, Pete Casazza, and Dan Edidin, complement-property equivalence, Theorem 2.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0412411)

[Philipp Grohs, Sarah Koppensteiner, and Martin Rathmair, complement-property equivalence and proof, Theorem 2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1901.07911v2)

[Radu Balan, complement-property criterion, Theorem 3.2](https://www.norbertwiener.umd.edu/Education/IMA2015/t4/lecture.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite real family $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ in $\mathbb R^d$, where $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-ip-real-frame-phase-retrieval]]: phase retrieval means injectivity of the intensity map on classes modulo one global sign; the real measurement at label $i$ is $\langle a_i,x\rangle$.

[F2] [[lem-ip-real-phase-retrieval-quotient-metric]]: the induced intensity map is well defined on those classes, and $[x]=[z]$ exactly when $x=z$ or $x=-z$.

[F3] [[def-ip-frame-complement-property]]: the complement property requires that for each $S\subseteq[m]$, the span indexed by $S$ or the span indexed by its complement is all of $\mathbb R^d$.

[F4] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]], [[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]: the real coordinate pairing is bilinear, symmetric, and positive definite, so it is a real inner product; $v\in U^\perp$ means its pairing with every vector of $U$ is zero.

[F5] [[def-linear-combination-and-span]], [[def-linear-subspace]], [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]: the library span is the smallest real linear subspace containing its generators and equals the set of their finite real linear combinations. Bilinearity therefore extends orthogonality from the generators to their span.

[F6] [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], [[def-dimension]], [[def-linear-basis]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]: every subspace of $\mathbb R^n$ is finite-dimensional with dimension at most $n$, equality holds only for the whole space, and $\dim\mathbb R^n=n$, including $n=0$; finite dimension supplies a finite basis.

[F7] [[def-linear-map]], [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]], [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]], [[def-rank-and-nullity]], [[thm-rank-nullity]]: for a linear map with finite-dimensional domain, its kernel and image are subspaces, its rank is the image dimension, and domain dimension is nullity plus rank.

[F8] [[thm-reals-field]], [[thm-reals-ordered-field]]: $2=1+1>0$ in $\mathbb R$, so $2\ne0$ and cannot annihilate a nonzero real vector.

[A1] No form of the axiom of Choice is assumed; the dimension results are finite-dimensional and the selections in the proof are finite.

## Proof


1.1 Assume $\mathcal I_\Phi([x])=\mathcal I_\Phi([z])$. At every label $i$, equality of the intensity coordinates gives $\langle a_i,x\rangle^2=\langle a_i,z\rangle^2$. [given, F1]

2.1 Factoring the difference of squares over $\mathbb R$ yields $(\langle a_i,x-z\rangle)(\langle a_i,x+z\rangle)=0$ for every $i\in[m]$. This factorization also holds when $x=0$, $z=0$, or $a_i=0$; no nonzero-signal or nonzero-measurement hypothesis is used. [step 1.1, F4, F8, algebra]

3.1 Put $S=\{i\in[m]:\langle a_i,x-z\rangle=0\}$. For $i\in S$, $a_i\perp(x-z)$; for $i\notin S$, the first factor in step 2.1 is nonzero, so $a_i\perp(x+z)$. By [F5], each vector in either span is a finite linear combination of its generators, and bilinearity extends each orthogonality statement to the whole span. [step 2.1, F4, F5, construct]

4.1 By the complement property [F3], either $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_S)=\mathbb R^d$ or $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})=\mathbb R^d$. In the first case step 3.1 makes $x-z$ orthogonal to every vector of $\mathbb R^d$, hence to itself; positive definiteness [F4] gives $x-z=0$. In the second case it gives $x+z=0$. Thus $[x]=[z]$ by [F2], proving injectivity. [step 3.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

5.1 The forward implication is proved in step 4.1. For the converse, suppose the complement property fails; then some $S\subseteq[m]$ has the proper subspaces $U=\operatorname{span}(\Phi_S)$ and $V=\operatorname{span}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})$. We prove that every proper subspace $W\le\mathbb R^d$ has a nonzero orthogonal vector. Let $r=\dim W<d$ by [F6], choose a basis $w_0,\ldots,w_{r-1}$ of $W$, and define $L_W:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^r$ by $L_W(x)=(\langle x,w_j\rangle)_{j<r}$. Bilinearity makes $L_W$ linear. Its kernel is $W^\perp$: vanishing against the basis implies vanishing against every vector of $W$ because the basis spans $W$ and [F5] expresses each span vector as a finite linear combination; the converse is immediate. By [F7], the image is a subspace of $\mathbb R^r$, so [F6] gives $\operatorname{rank}L_W=\dim(\operatorname{im}L_W)\le r$. Rank-nullity [F7] and $\dim\mathbb R^d=d$ then give $\dim W^\perp=\dim\ker L_W=d-\operatorname{rank}L_W\ge d-r>0$. By [F6] a zero subspace has dimension zero, so $W^\perp$ contains a nonzero vector. Apply this argument to $U$ and $V$ and choose nonzero $u\in U^\perp$ and $v\in V^\perp$. [given, F5, F6, F7, A1, construct, choose]

6.1 Set $x=u+v$ and $z=u-v$. Since $v\ne0$, $x=z$ would imply $2v=0$, impossible by [F8]; since $u\ne0$, $x=-z$ would imply $2u=0$, also impossible. Hence $[x]\ne[z]$ by [F2]. [step 5.1, F2, F8, algebra]

6.2 If $i\in S$, then $a_i\in U$ and $u\perp a_i$, so $\langle a_i,x\rangle=\langle a_i,v\rangle$ and $\langle a_i,z\rangle=-\langle a_i,v\rangle$. If $i\notin S$, then $a_i\in V$ and $v\perp a_i$, so both measurements equal $\langle a_i,u\rangle$. If $a_i=0$, it lies in $U$ and both measurements are zero. Squaring shows equality of the intensity coordinates at every label, including when either component of the partition is empty. [step 5.1, F4, F5, algebra]

7.1 When $m=0$, the only partition has both sides empty, and both spans equal $\{0\}\ne\mathbb R^d$ by [F5] and $d\ge1$. The complement property fails, while steps 5.1–6.2 give distinct global-sign classes with the same unique empty data. Thus the zero-measurement case is included. [F2, F5, F6, F7, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2]

8.1 Steps 6.1 and 6.2 give distinct quotient classes with the same intensity data, so $\mathcal I_\Phi$ is not injective. Together with step 4.1 and the definition of phase retrieval [F1], this proves the stated equivalence. [step 4.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. Let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$. Suppose that for every finite family of smooth boundary directions, the corresponding small-data nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps for
$$-\Delta_g u+q_j u^3=0$$
agree for all sufficiently small real parameter values. Then $q_1=q_2$ on $\overline M$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product geometry]]

[[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability|Small-data nonlinear DN maps]]

[[lem-ip-cubic-dn-third-linearization-identity|Third derivative identity]]

[[lem-ip-intersecting-gaussian-beam-four-factor-limit|Four-factor concentration]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the small-data, third-linearization, and four-factor suppliers [F1]--[F3].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the small-data, third-linearization, and four-factor suppliers [F1]--[F3].

**Given:** the CTA product with simple surface transversal, real smooth cubic coefficients, and equality of the finite-parameter nonlinear DN maps for every finite list of smooth boundary directions.

[F1] [[lem-ip-cubic-dn-small-data-differentiability]]: each finite-parameter solution and its nonlinear DN data are $C^3$ in the real parameters near zero.

[F2] [[lem-ip-cubic-dn-third-linearization-identity]]: the third DN derivative determines $6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g$ for any four harmonic boundary solutions.

[F3] [[lem-ip-intersecting-gaussian-beam-four-factor-limit]]: the claimed four-factor limit at any transversal intersection is a nonzero constant times the longitudinal Fourier transform of the coefficient difference.

[F4] [[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]: an $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function with identically zero Fourier transform vanishes almost everywhere.

[F5] The four-factor supplier imports the smooth harmonic-product density theorem of Lassas--Liimatainen--Lin--Salo, Proposition 5.1, PDF p. 14; its hypotheses are a compact oriented CTA manifold of dimension at least three, a $C^1$ coefficient, and four or more smooth harmonic factors. See *Geometric inverse problems, with emphasis on two dimensions*, Section 3.8 ([author-hosted full text](https://users.jyu.fi/~salomi/pub/GIP2D_driver.pdf)). The complete proof of LL--LS Proposition 5.1 in Section 5, PDF pp. 14--23, including Lemma 5.2, was inspected for this repair; only its density conclusion is imported, not locally reconstructed. The four-factor witnesses are smooth on $\overline M$, depend on the coefficient being tested, and are constant in $\tau$, so the smooth-boundary identity [F2] applies directly; no extension of that identity to arbitrary $H^1$ boundary traces is required. ## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 Fix four smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Equality of the finite-parameter DN maps for $q_1$ and $q_2$ implies equality of their mixed third derivatives at the origin. Applying [F2] to each coefficient and subtracting gives $$\int_M(q_1-q_2)v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g=0$$ for every four harmonic functions $v_j$ arising from smooth boundary data. [A1, A2, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The identity in step 1.1 holds also for complex smooth harmonic functions: write their boundary values as real and imaginary parts and expand the separately linear or conjugate-linear expression. Since the Laplacian has real coefficients, conjugation preserves harmonicity; replacing the fourth function by its conjugate therefore gives $\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV=0$ for every four smooth complex harmonic functions, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $p\in M_0^\circ$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R$. Choose the transverse boundary-to-boundary geodesic segments through $p$ supplied by [F3] (their existence is established in that supplier's proof). ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the minimax detection-risk definition with $0<q<2$, $a_j=j^\alpha$, $\sigma_j=j^\beta$, and $\alpha,\beta>0$. Let $r_\varepsilon\to0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and put
$$\lambda=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}-\frac{\beta}{q}.$$
For $\lambda>0$, put $A=2\alpha+1/q-1/2$, $B=2(\alpha+\beta)+1/q$, and $D=\alpha+\beta(1-2/q)>0$. Choose any $\delta_\varepsilon>0$ with $\delta_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\delta_\varepsilon\log\varepsilon^{-1}\to\infty$, set $\widetilde r_\varepsilon=r_\varepsilon(1-\delta_\varepsilon)$, and define
$$u_\varepsilon^2=2\inf\left\{\sum_{j\ge1}h_j^2\sinh^2(z_j^2/2):\ 0\le h_j\le1,\ z_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j\ge1}j^{2\beta}h_jz_j^2\ge\frac{\widetilde r_\varepsilon^2}{\varepsilon^2},\ \sum_{j\ge1}j^{q(\alpha+\beta)}h_jz_j^q\le\frac1{\varepsilon^q}\right\}.$$
For each fixed significance level $\ell\in(0,1)$, the sharp errors have Gaussian form
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\ell)=\Phi(H_\ell-u_\varepsilon)+o(1),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))=2\Phi(-u_\varepsilon/2)+o(1),$$
where $\Phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^t e^{-x^2/2}\,dx$ and $H_\ell$ is its $(1-\ell)$-quantile. Moreover, if $r_\varepsilon=o(\varepsilon^{a_c})$ with $a_c=(q\alpha+1-q/2)/(q(\alpha+\beta)+1)$, then
$$u_\varepsilon\sim c_{\alpha,\beta,q}\,\varepsilon^{-A/D}r_\varepsilon^{B/D}$$
for a constant $c_{\alpha,\beta,q}>0$. Without this additional restriction on $r_\varepsilon$, the sharp error formulas above remain valid for every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, and a minimax separation rate is
$$r_\varepsilon^*=\varepsilon^{A/B}.$$
If $\lambda\le0$, for the same fixed significance level $\ell\in(0,1)$ put $n_\varepsilon=r_\varepsilon^{-1/\alpha}$ and $D_\varepsilon=n_\varepsilon^{-\beta}r_\varepsilon/\varepsilon-\sqrt{2\log n_\varepsilon}$. Then the sharp errors have degenerate form
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\ell)=(1-\ell)\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))=\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1),$$
and a sharp separation-rate normalization is
$$r_\varepsilon^*=\Lambda\,\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{\alpha/[2(\alpha+\beta)]},\qquad \Lambda=\left(\frac{2}{\alpha+\beta}\right)^{\alpha/[2(\alpha+\beta)]}.$$
Thus the sparse boundary $\lambda=0$ belongs to the degenerate regime, and the two regimes have different separation rates.

The deterministic globalized score-and-maximum family and the finite maximum tests constructed in the proof are asymptotically minimax in the Gaussian and degenerate regimes, respectively; the significance tests include deterministic randomization to satisfy the exact level constraint.

## Statement references

[Ingster, Sapatinas and Suslina, *Minimax signal detection in ill-posed inverse problems*, §4.7, Theorem 4.7, PDF pp. 18–19](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.1853)

[Ingster and Suslina, *Nonparametric Goodness-of-Fit Testing Under Gaussian Models*, cited by the 2012 article for Theorem 4.7, Chapters 4 and 6](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-0-387-21580-8)

[[lem-ip-sparse-gaussian-extremal-profile|The local scalar certificate and relaxed extremal profile]]

[[lem-ip-finite-independent-array-fourth-moment-normal-limit|A finite normal-replacement approximation under Countable Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the sequence experiment and alternatives in the Statement. Write $s=\alpha+\beta$, use $\ell\in(0,1)$ for the fixed significance level, and put $X_i=Y_i/\varepsilon=\mu_i+G_i$, where $\mu_i=\eta_i/\varepsilon$. The supplied normal probability law has density $\phi$ and distribution function $\Phi$.

[F1] [[def-ip-minimax-detection-risk-and-separation]]: the actual alternatives satisfy $\sum i^{2\beta}\mu_i^2\ge r^2/\varepsilon^2$ and $\sum i^{qs}|\mu_i|^q\le\varepsilon^{-q}$; finite-support alternatives are allowed, and tests are randomized product-Borel maps.

[F2] [[lem-ip-sparse-gaussian-extremal-profile]] supplies the positive scalar certificate $a,b$, inverse profile $z(x)$, coefficient $d(x)=x^{2\beta}/(2a(z(x)))$, constants $c_0,c_1,c_2,M_1,M_2$, their endpoint bounds and Riemann sums, and the relaxed extremal equivalent when $n\to\infty,h_0\to0$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-finite-independent-array-fourth-moment-normal-limit]]: given normalized Gaussian probability laws, finite centered independent arrays whose summed variances tend to $v>0$ and whose summed fourth moments tend to zero have distribution functions converging uniformly to $\Phi(\,\cdot\,/\sqrt v)$, under Countable Choice.

[F4] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]] supplies independent standard-normal coordinates, including their normalized scalar probability density. Normalization is a hypothesis of that supplied process; no stronger-choice normalization theorem is used.

[F5] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] supplies scalar affine changes of variables under Countable Choice.

[F6] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]] gives Markov's inequality, including Chebyshev's inequality by applying it to a squared centered variable.

[F7] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]] and [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]] identify finite independent coordinate laws and factor their integrable products. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] supplies the finite probability products used for finite priors.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] and [[thm-dominated-convergence]] justify the specified nonnegative series and dominated scalar integrals.

[F9] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]] identifies probability laws agreeing on finite cylinders of the product sigma-algebra.

[F10] [[lem-taylor-lagrange-remainder-from-mean-value]] bounds a third-order Taylor remainder by the supremum of the third derivative times the cube of the increment, divided by six.

[F11] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]] defines $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_E|P(E)-Q(E)|$ over measurable events for probability laws on the same measurable space.

[F12] [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]: for decreasing measurable events under a probability law, their probabilities decrease to the probability of their intersection.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed; all other limits and finite products below use the supplied coordinate laws. No full-Choice central-limit theorem is invoked.

## Proof

The two regimes below are separate cases. A paragraph in the Gaussian branch uses its profile notation from step 1.3; a paragraph in the degenerate branch uses the notation from step 2.4. Repeated local letters in these two cases have separate scopes.

1.1 The finite coordinate density of $X_i$ with mean $\mu_i$ divided by its null density is $\exp(\mu_iX_i-\mu_i^2/2)$. Thus a finite uniform mixture of the two signs at a coordinate of absolute mean $z$ has likelihood $e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zX_i)$, and the prior with probabilities $1-g,g/2,g/2$ at $0,z,-z$ has likelihood $1+g\xi_z(X_i)$, where $\xi_z(t)=e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zt)-1$. Multiplication over finitely many coordinates is justified by [F7]. Off these coordinates the law is unchanged; equality first on finite cylinders and then [F9] proves the likelihood identity on the whole sequence sample space. Every prior below has finite coordinate support; no new countable product probability law is constructed. [given, F4, F7, F9, A1, algebra]

1.2 Completing the square and applying [F5] to the given unit density gives $\mathbb E e^{tG}=e^{t^2/2}$. Consequently, by expanding the hyperbolic functions, $$\mathbb E\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z\mu)-1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z^2)-1+(e^{z^2}-1)\sinh^2(z\mu).$$ For fixed $B$, $\mathbb E\xi_z(G)^4\le C_B(\cosh(z^2)-1)^2$ when $0<z\le B$: the bound $|\xi_z(G)|\le C_Bz^2(1+G^2)e^{B|G|}$ follows from the Taylor bound for $\cosh$ and $e^{-z^2/2}$, its fourth-power integral is finite by completing the square, and $\cosh(z^2)-1\ge z^4/2$. We will also use $\mathbb P(|G|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}$, obtained from [F6] and the same exponential moment, and the elementary Mills bounds $\overline\Phi(t)\le\phi(t)/t$ and $\overline\Phi(t)\ge\phi(t+1/t)/t$ for $t\ge1$. The first follows by integrating $x\phi(x)/t$ over $[t,\infty)$, and the second by integrating $\phi$ over $[t,t+1/t]$. [given, F4, F5, F6, F10, algebra]

1.3 First suppose $\lambda>0$ and set $L=qs-2\beta>0$, $\kappa=L/(2-q)$. Use [F2] to define the unique positive $n,h_0$ by $$c_1h_0n^{2\beta+1}=r^2\varepsilon^{-2},\qquad c_2h_0n^{qs+1}=\varepsilon^{-q},\qquad U^2=c_0h_0^2n,$$ and put $z_i=z(i/n)$, $h_i=h_0d(i/n)$. Then $n^L=(c_1/c_2)\varepsilon^{2-q}/r^2$. The scalar certificate in [F2] gives $$\sum_{i\le m}h_i(\cosh(z_iv_i)-1)\ge\frac{h_0}2\left(n^{-2\beta}\sum_{i\le m}i^{2\beta}v_i^2-n^{-qs}\sum_{i\le m}i^{qs}|v_i|^q\right).$$ Also $\sum h_i<\infty$ and $V:=\sum h_i^2(\cosh(z_i^2)-1)\sim U^2$ as $n\to\infty$. These are score coefficients, which need not be at most one. On compact subsets of $0<r/r_\varepsilon^*<\infty$, $U$ stays bounded and bounded away from zero, $n$ grows as a positive power of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, the extremal value in the Statement is exactly $J_\varepsilon(\widetilde r)$ in [F2], because $\cosh(z^2)-1=2\sinh^2(z^2/2)$. That lemma proves its power equivalent whenever $\widetilde r=o(\varepsilon^{a_c})$, equivalently when its associated $n\to\infty,h_0\to0$. Since $\widetilde r/r\to1$, this is the asserted restriction and the equivalent may be written with $r$. In particular on each compact transition range, $$u_\varepsilon\sim U=c_{\alpha,\beta,q}\varepsilon^{-A/D}r^{B/D}.$$ No equivalent outside the stated sufficient zone is used. [given, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the Gaussian lower bound, fix a compact transition range. The feasible construction in [F2] can be made with expected energy $(1+\tau)r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$ and expected budget $(1-\tau)\varepsilon^{-q}$, on a finite window $a\le i/n'\le b$, with probabilities $g_i=h'_0d(i/n')\le1$ and amplitudes $z(i/n')$. Let the margins tend slowly to zero and windows tend slowly to $(0,\infty)$. This can be specified without a rate assumption: use windows $[1/k,k]$, margin $1/k$, and pass to each next integer $k$ only after its finite Riemann errors, feasibility bounds and the concentration errors below are smaller than the prescribed margins; the preceding compact-window estimates hold uniformly on the chosen compact transition range. The profile moments $M_1,M_2$ give relative variances $O((nh_0)^{-1})=O(n^{-1/2})$ for both random constraint sums before the slowly varying window constants. Choose the numerical diagonal slowly enough that those relative variances divided by $\tau^2$ tend to zero. Chebyshev then puts prior probability $1-o(1)$ on the actual alternative. Each draw has finite coordinate support and hence is in $\ell^2$. The prior cost tends to $U^2$, its largest coordinate cost tends to zero, and its cost on $z_i>B$ tends uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$, by the bounded small-end and exponential large-end envelopes in [F2]. Let $\Pi$ denote this finite-support prior on parameter sequences, let $\mathcal A$ be the event that a draw satisfies both alternative constraints, and put $p=\Pi(\mathcal A)=1-o(1)$. If $p=1$, conditioning changes no mixture law. Otherwise, eventually $0<p<1$ and the unconditioned observation law decomposes as $P_\Pi=pP_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}+(1-p)P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}$. For every measurable event $E$, this gives $|P_\Pi(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|=(1-p)|P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|\le1-p$, so [F11] yields $\|P_\Pi-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}\|_{\rm TV}\le1-p$. For every randomized test $\psi$ with values in $[0,1]$, the functions $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\psi\ge k/N\}}$ approximate $\psi$ uniformly within $1/N$; applying the event bound to each summand and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $|\mathbb E_{P_\Pi}\psi-\mathbb E_{P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}}\psi|\le1-p=o(1)$ uniformly over tests. [given, F1, F2, F6, F7, F11, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

2.3 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the matching upper bounds define the product-Borel score $$F(X)=\sum_{i\ge1}h_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iX_i)-\sum_{i\ge1}h_i.$$ The first series is nonnegative and may be infinite; then the test rejects. Under the null its expectation is $\sum h_i<\infty$, so it is finite almost surely by [F6], and its centered partial sums converge in mean square with variance $V$. The bounded-amplitude fourth-moment calculation in step 1.2 and [F3], followed by the null variance tail bound in [F2], give $F\Rightarrow N(0,U_0^2)$. For $n$ large put $$Q_i^2=2\log(i+1)+4\log\log(i+3)+4\log\log n,\qquad \mathcal Y=\{\exists i:|X_i|>Q_i\}.$$ Step 1.2 and a countable union bound give $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal Y)\le2(\log n)^{-2}\sum_{i\ge1}[(i+1)(\log(i+3))^2]^{-1}=o(1)$. For every fixed $K$, $\max_{i\le n(\log n)^K}Q_i=\sqrt{2\log n}+o(\sqrt{\log n})$. Reject on $\{F>H_\ell\sqrt V\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for the significance problem, and on $\{F>V/2\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for total error. These are unions with a centered-cosh score, rather than an intersection or a positive-exponential uncentered score. [given, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

2.4 Now suppose $\lambda\le0$, put $e=2\beta-qs\ge0$, $n=r^{-1/\alpha}$, $m=r^{s/\alpha}$, $A_\varepsilon=m/\varepsilon$ and $D_\varepsilon=A_\varepsilon-\sqrt{2\log n}$. Every alternative has an index $i\le\lfloor n\rfloor$ with $|\eta_i|\ge m$. Indeed with $w_i=i^{qs}|\eta_i|^q$, its energy summand is $w_i i^e|\eta_i|^{2-q}$. If $i\le n$ and $|\eta_i|<m$, this multiplier is strictly below $n^em^{2-q}=r^2$. If $i>n$, the termwise budget gives $|\eta_i|\le i^{-s}$, so the multiplier is at most $i^{-2\alpha}<r^2$. If all the indicated coordinates were smaller than $m$, summing with $\sum w_i\le1$ would give energy strictly below $r^2$, a contradiction. Let $N=\lfloor n\rfloor$ and $t_N=\sqrt{2\log N}$. The finite maximum test $R=\mathbf1\{\max_{i\le N}|X_i|>t_N\}$ has size $p_0\le2N\overline\Phi(t_N)=O(1/t_N)=o(1)$ by step 1.2. Its maximal type-II error is at most $\Phi(t_N-A_\varepsilon)=\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$, uniformly in $A_\varepsilon$, since $t_N-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$ and $\Phi'$ is bounded. For significance $\ell$, the randomized test $\rho+(1-\rho)R$ with $\rho=(\ell-p_0)/(1-p_0)$ is eventually valid and has size exactly $\ell$; its type-II error is at most $(1-\ell)\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$. The unrandomized maximum gives the total-error upper bound. [given, F1, F4, F6, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, under the null put $A_i=g_i\xi_{z_i}(G_i)$ for the finite prior in step 2.2. They are centered and independent, and $\sum\mathbb E A_i^2\to U_0^2$ along any subsequence with $U\to U_0\in(0,\infty)$. On $z_i\le B$, step 1.2 and the vanishing maximum coordinate variance give $\sum\mathbb E A_i^4\to0$. The omitted linear sum has variance tending uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$; the omitted quadratic sum has expectation tending to zero. Apply [F3] to the finite bounded-amplitude arrays and then let $B\to\infty$, using Chebyshev for the linear tail. The same fourth-moment bound gives concentration of their quadratic sums. Thus $$\sum A_i\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,U_0^2),\qquad \sum A_i^2\to U_0^2,\qquad \max_i|A_i|\to0$$ in probability for the last two limits. Each factor $1+A_i=1-g_i+g_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iG_i)$ is positive. On $\max|A_i|\le\delta<1/2$, [F10] gives $|\sum\log(1+A_i)-\sum A_i+\tfrac12\sum A_i^2|\le C\delta\sum A_i^2$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$. The likelihood from step 1.1 therefore has $\log L\Rightarrow N(-U_0^2/2,U_0^2)$. The addition of terms converging in probability and the successive tail limits preserve the displayed distribution limit by squeezing distribution functions between thresholds differing by an arbitrary positive tolerance. [given, F3, F6, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, fix $d\in(0,1)$. Alternatives with $\mathbb P_\mu(\mathcal Y^c)<d$ already have type-II error below $d$. For every other alternative, writing $p_i=\mathbb P_\mu(|X_i|>Q_i)$, finite independence gives $\prod_{i\le m}(1-p_i)\ge d$ for each $m$. Hence $\sum_i p_i\le-\log d$ and $|\mu_i|\le Q_i+C_d$, the latter because the probability of the inside interval is at most $\Phi(Q_i-|\mu_i|)$. Choose $K>(2-q)/(2L)$ and $N=\lceil n(\log n)^K\rceil$. The energy of indices $i>N$ is at most $$\varepsilon^{-q}\sup_{i>N}i^{-L}(Q_i+C_d)^{2-q}\le C_d\varepsilon^{-q}N^{-L}(\log N)^{(2-q)/2}=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2}).$$ The envelope is eventually decreasing and $\varepsilon^{-q}n^{-L}$ is a fixed multiple of $r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Among $i\le N$ delete those with $|\mu_i|>c\sqrt{\log n}$, where $c=0.45\in(\sqrt2-1,1/2)$. The lower Mills bound in step 1.2 implies $p_i\ge n^{-a+o(1)}$ there, with $a=(\sqrt2-c)^2/2<1/2$, uniformly over these indices. Thus at most $n^{a+o(1)}$ are deleted. Their energy is at most $n^{2\beta+a+o(1)}=o(n^{2\beta+1/2})=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2})$, including the polynomial logarithmic factors from $N$ and the means. Define $\mu_i^*=\mu_i$ for $i\le N$ not deleted and $\mu_i^*=0$ for every deleted index and every $i>N$. This vector has finite support, satisfies $|\mu_i^*|\le c\sqrt{\log n}$, and has no increased $q$-budget. Its energy loss is at most the sum of the already bounded tail energy and deleted-coordinate energy, so its retained energy is $(1-o(1))r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Its score mean $M=\mathbb E_{\mu^*}F$ is therefore at least $U^2-o(1)$ by the certificate in step 1.3 and $c_0=(c_1-c_2)/2$. Coordinatewise $|\mu_i^*|\le|\mu_i|$, and $|G+\mu|$ is stochastically increasing in $|\mu|$, since $\Phi(t-|\mu|)-\Phi(-t-|\mu|)$ decreases with $|\mu|$. Independence and the positive coefficients imply the score comparison for every finite partial sum. The full score event is the decreasing intersection of these partial-sum events after adding the fixed $\sum h_i$; [F12] passes the comparison to the full nonnegative series, giving $\mathbb P_\mu(F\le t)\le\mathbb P_{\mu^*}(F\le t)$. [given, F1, F2, F7, F12, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

3.3 In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, for the matching degenerate lower bound first take $D_\varepsilon\to d\in\mathbb R$. Put $M=\lfloor n/(\log n)^2\rfloor$, $I=\{\lfloor n\rfloor-M+1,\ldots,\lfloor n\rfloor\}$, and mix uniformly over indices $i\in I$ and signs with $\eta_i=\pm r i^{-\beta}$, all other coordinates zero. Every point has energy $r^2$ and budget $(ri^\alpha)^q\le1$. Write $T=\sqrt{2\log M}$ and $\mu_i=r/(\varepsilon i^\beta)$; uniformly on $I$, $\mu_i=T+d+o(1)$ since $M/n=O((\log n)^{-2})$ and $T-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$. The null likelihood from step 1.1 is $L=M^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}e^{-\mu_i^2/2}\cosh(\mu_iG_i)$. Truncate each summand to $|G_i|\le T$, obtaining $\widetilde L$. Completing the square gives its summand mean $\Phi(T-\mu_i)-\Phi(-T-\mu_i)\to c=\Phi(-d)$ and its second moment at most $\tfrac12e^{\mu_i^2}\Phi(T-2\mu_i)+\tfrac12e^{-\mu_i^2}$. The upper Mills bound and $$\mu_i^2-\tfrac12(2\mu_i-T)^2-\log M=-(\mu_i-T)^2$$ bound this second moment divided by $M$ by $O(1/T)$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}\widetilde L=O(1/T)\to0$, and $\mathbb P_0(L\ne\widetilde L)\le2M\overline\Phi(T)=O(1/T)\to0$. Thus $\mathbb E_0|\widetilde L-c|\to0$ and $L\to c$ in null probability. Since $L\ge\widetilde L$, every size-$\ell$ test has mixture type-II error at least $c(1-\ell)-\mathbb E|\widetilde L-c|$; every total error is at least $\mathbb E\min(1,L)\to c$. Bounded convergence in probability here follows directly by splitting at any fixed positive deviation; no likelihood uniform integrability is asserted. This proves both lower bounds for finite $d$. [given, F1, F5, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.4, construct, algebra]

4.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for any likelihood $L$, randomized test $\chi$ and $c>0$, scalar algebra gives $L(1-\chi)\ge\min(L,c)-c\chi$. The limit law in step 3.1 has no positive atoms, so $$\mathbb E_0\min(L,c)=\int_0^c\mathbb P_0(L>t)\,dt$$ converges by [F8]; the identity itself follows first for step functions and then by increasing finite subdivisions. Choose $c=\exp(-U_0^2/2+U_0H_\ell)$. Its limiting upper-tail probability is $\ell$, and completing the square gives the limiting lower bound $\Phi(H_\ell-U_0)$ for every test of size at most $\ell$. Likewise every total error is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(1,L)\to2\Phi(-U_0/2)$. Conditioning in step 2.2 costs only $o(1)$ uniformly over tests. This proves both minimax lower bounds on compact transitions without an additional Neyman--Pearson or unrestricted-choice supplier. [given, F5, F8, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the residual vector set $m_i=h_i(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)-1)$, so $M=\sum m_i\ge0$. The exact variance formula in step 1.2 shows that the excess above $V$ is $$\sum h_i^2(e^{z_i^2}-1)\sinh^2(z_i\mu_i^*)\le\sum K_i m_i,\qquad K_i=h_i(e^{z_i^2}-1)(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)+1).$$ For $z_i\le\sqrt{\log n}$, the global bound $\psi(z)(e^{z^2}-1)\le C$ in [F2], its relation $x\le C(1+z^{1/\kappa})$ at large $z$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$ give $K_i\le n^{-1/2+c+o(1)}=o(1)$. For $z_i>\sqrt{\log n}$ the other global bound in [F2] gives an absolute excess bound $$C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}\exp(-z_i^2+2cz_i\sqrt{\log n})\le C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}e^{-(1-2c)z_i^2}=o(1).$$ The final estimate follows from the exponential profile tail and $h_0^2n=O(1)$; its discrete tail is bounded by the integral of an eventually decreasing polynomial-times-exponential envelope plus a mesh term, as in [F2]. Thus uniformly over residual alternatives, $\operatorname{Var}_{\mu^*}F\le V+o(1)M+o(1)$. Unbounded $z_i$ have been controlled by an absolute variance bound, not a uniform bounded-amplitude assumption. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

4.3 In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, if $D_\varepsilon\to+\infty$, step 2.4 settles both errors by nonnegativity. If $D_\varepsilon\to-\infty$, fix $K>0$. The continuous strictly increasing function $r\mapsto\varepsilon^{-1}r^{s/\alpha}-\sqrt{(2/\alpha)\log(1/r)}$ ranges from $-\infty$ to a positive value on $(0,1)$, so it has a unique radius $r_{\varepsilon,K}$ at value $-K$, and this radius tends to zero. Eventually $r<r_{\varepsilon,K}$; inclusion of alternative sets and step 3.3 give lower limits at least $\Phi(K)$ for total error and $(1-\ell)\Phi(K)$ for type-II error. Let $K\to\infty$. Subsequences in the extended real line now establish the two degenerate formulas for arbitrary $D_\varepsilon$. Finally put $p=s/\alpha$ and $\Lambda=(2/s)^{\alpha/(2s)}$, so $\Lambda^p=\sqrt{2/s}$. For each fixed $c>0$, direct substitution into the displayed $r_\varepsilon^*$ gives $$D_\varepsilon(cr_\varepsilon^*)=(c^p-1)\sqrt{2\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/s}+o(1).$$ The logarithmic correction is $O(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/\sqrt{\log(\varepsilon^{-1})})$, which tends to zero. Thus the stated sharp constant, zero/infinite-ratio separation limits and the assignment of $\lambda=0$ all follow, with no strict inequality imposed on $e$. [given, F1, step 2.4, step 3.3, algebra]

5.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, if $M$ stays bounded, fix $B>0$. For $z_i\le B$, $h_iz_i^2\le C_Bh_0(i/n)^{2\beta}$ by [F2]. Writing the hyperbolic addition formula and using $|\sinh(z\mu)|\le z|\mu|e^{B|\mu|}$ gives $$\mathbb E\left|h_i\bigl(\xi_{z_i}(G_i+\mu_i^*)-\mathbb E\xi_{z_i}(G_i+\mu_i^*)\bigr)\right|^4\le C_B(h_iz_i^2)^4(1+|\mu_i^*|^4)e^{4B|\mu_i^*|}.$$ Here the fourth moments of $\cosh(zG)-\mathbb E\cosh(zG)$ and $\sinh(zG)$ are bounded respectively by $C_Bz^8$ and $C_Bz^4$, by the same Gaussian exponential integration as in step 1.2. Since $z_i\le B$ implies $i\le C_B n$, the summed fourth moments are $O_B(nh_0^4)n^{o(1)}=n^{-1+o(1)}\to0$. The variance of the omitted $z_i>B$ centered sum is at most its null variance tail plus $o(1)$, by step 4.2 and bounded $M$. Apply [F3] to the retained finite arrays and then let $B\to\infty$ to obtain $F-M\Rightarrow N(0,U_0^2)$. The assertion is uniform in the sense that every sequence of residual alternatives with bounded $M$ obeys this limit. If $M\to\infty$, step 4.2 and Chebyshev instead show $\mathbb P_{\mu^*}(F\le t)\to0$ for every bounded threshold. These conclusions and $M\ge U^2-o(1)$ prove the upper type-II limits $\Phi(H_\ell-U_0)$ and $\Phi(-U_0/2)$. To justify passage to the supremum, any contrary sequence has either a bounded-mean subsequence (then a convergent-mean subsequence) or a subsequence with $M\to\infty$; both cases give the asserted bound. Let $d\downarrow0$ for the alternatives excluded in step 3.2. Under the null step 2.3 gives the corresponding errors $\ell+o(1)$ and $\Phi(-U_0/2)+o(1)$. If the first test has size $p_\varepsilon>\ell$, multiply its indicator by $\ell/p_\varepsilon$; otherwise leave it unchanged. Its size is then at most $\ell$ and every power changes by $o(1)$. This proves the exact-level Gaussian upper bound and the total-error upper bound. [given, F2, F3, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 4.1, step 2.3, step 3.2, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 In the Gaussian branch, write $\rho=r/r_\varepsilon^*$, $p=B/D>0$ and $c=c_{\alpha,\beta,q}$. For a comparison radius $R=t r_\varepsilon^*$, let $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,t}$ be the score-and-maximum significance test in steps 2.3 and 5.1, with its exact-level scaling, and let $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,t}$ be their unscaled total-error test. The proved estimates are uniform over each fixed $t\in[1/k,k]$: otherwise a countersequence has a convergent subsequence of $t$ in that compact interval, and all the compact-transition estimates already proved apply with a positive finite limiting $U=ct^p$, contradicting the countersequence. Consequently, for every integer $k\ge2$ there is a sufficiently small noise threshold such that for all smaller $\varepsilon$ and every $t\in[1/k,k]$, the profile dimension is $n>e$, $|u_\varepsilon(t r_\varepsilon^*)-ct^p|\le1/k$, the maximal type-II error of $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,t}$ at radius $t r_\varepsilon^*$ is at most $\Phi(H_\ell-ct^p)+1/k$, and the total error of $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,t}$ there is at most $2\Phi(-ct^p/2)+1/k$. Both tests are therefore defined on this whole compact range, and the significance test has size at most $\ell$ for every such noise level. Fix $j_1=1$ and recursively let $j_k$ be the least integer $j>j_{k-1}$, $j\ge k$, for which all these uniform properties hold for every $0<\varepsilon\le2^{-j}$. These integers exist by the uniform convergence just proved. For $0<\varepsilon\le2^{-j_2}$ define $k_\varepsilon=\max\{k\ge2:\varepsilon\le2^{-j_k}\}$. This is a nonempty finite set because $j_k\ge k$; $k_\varepsilon\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The least-integer rule and this finite maximum specify one deterministic diagonal, depending only on the fixed model, significance level and the given $\delta_\varepsilon$ family, not on the unknown truth or the observations. [given, A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.3, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 For this single diagonal, define the Gaussian-regime test family for every known radius $r>0$ as follows. When $\rho<1/k_\varepsilon$, use the constant randomized significance test $\chi^\ell_{\varepsilon,r}\equiv\ell$ and the never-reject total-error test $\chi^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,r}\equiv0$. When $1/k_\varepsilon\le\rho\le k_\varepsilon$, use $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,\rho}$ and $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,\rho}$. When $\rho>k_\varepsilon$, use $T^\ell_{\varepsilon,k_\varepsilon}$ and $T^{\rm tot}_{\varepsilon,k_\varepsilon}$, constructed at the smaller comparison radius $k_\varepsilon r_\varepsilon^*$, never at the possibly invalid profile dimension associated with $r$. For $\varepsilon>2^{-j_2}$ set the family to the same two trivial tests; this finite-noise convention does not affect an asymptotic statement. Every test is product-Borel, each significance test has size at most $\ell$, and every formula $\log\log n$ actually evaluated has $n>e$. Write $k=k_\varepsilon$. In the middle case the upper risk bounds in step 6.1 hold with error $1/k$, and $|u_\varepsilon(r)-c\rho^p|\le1/k$, so the attained errors are bounded by the stated Gaussian profiles plus a quantity tending to zero. In the small-radius case, monotonicity of the relaxed extremal problem gives $0\le u_\varepsilon(r)\le ck^{-p}+1/k\to0$; the two trivial tests have respective errors $1-\ell$ and $1$ whenever the alternative is nonempty, and no larger errors if it is empty, matching the profile upper bounds up to a vanishing quantity. In the large-radius case, the actual alternative is a subset of the comparison-radius alternative, so both achieved errors are no larger than their comparison-radius errors, bounded by $\Phi(H_\ell-ck^p)+1/k$ and $2\Phi(-ck^p/2)+1/k$, respectively, and these tend to zero. Also $u_\varepsilon(r)\ge ck^p-1/k\to\infty$, as required for the displayed profiles. These bounds apply to all three cases with the same deterministic $k_\varepsilon$; hence they also apply to ratios oscillating between them, without selecting a test by a subsequence. [given, F1, F2, step 6.1, construct, algebra]

8.1 The compact-transition lower bounds in step 4.1 extend globally by monotonicity of the minimax errors and of $J_\varepsilon(r(1-\delta_\varepsilon))$. Comparing $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$ with each fixed small positive transition constant gives $u_\varepsilon\to0$, $\liminf\gamma_\varepsilon\ge1$ and $\liminf\beta_\varepsilon(\ell)\ge1-\ell$; the corresponding upper bounds are the trivial tests. Comparing $r/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ with each fixed large transition constant gives $u_\varepsilon\to\infty$ and vanishing minimax errors. For any other sequence of positive ratios, every subsequence has a further subsequence tending to zero, a finite positive constant or infinity, so the same lower-profile conclusion applies. Together with the globally defined upper family in step 7.1 this proves both sharp Gaussian formulas and asymptotic minimax attainment for every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, including oscillating ratios. In particular the displayed $r_\varepsilon^*$ is a separation rate with both impossibility and consistency halves. In the degenerate regime, the finite maximum and exact-level randomized tests in step 2.4 already apply along every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, because $N\to\infty$ and $p_0\to0$ irrespective of the noise/radius ratio; to define them also before $N\ge2$ and $p_0<\ell$, use the constant significance test and never-reject total-error test until those inequalities hold. Their global sharp attainment follows from step 4.3 and its matching upper bounds. No unrestricted power equivalent or undefined transition threshold is used in either family. [given, F1, F2, step 2.4, step 4.1, step 4.3, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 The separation-rate definition in [F1] allows every positive radius sequence, not only vanishing ones. In either regime the displayed positive rate $r_\varepsilon^*$ tends to zero. If $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to0$, then $r_\varepsilon\to0$, so the impossibility half already proved applies. For the consistency half, let $r_\varepsilon>0$ satisfy $r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*\to\infty$ and set $\bar r_\varepsilon=\min\{r_\varepsilon,\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}$. Then $0<\bar r_\varepsilon\le r_\varepsilon$, $\bar r_\varepsilon\to0$, and $\bar r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*=\min\{r_\varepsilon/r_\varepsilon^*,1/\sqrt{r_\varepsilon^*}\}\to\infty$. The Gaussian tests of step 7.1 and the degenerate tests of steps 2.4 and 8.1, evaluated at $\bar r_\varepsilon$, therefore have vanishing total error and vanishing maximal type-II error at each fixed significance level on $\Theta_q(\bar r_\varepsilon)$. The defining energy inequality gives $\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon)\subseteq\Theta_q(\bar r_\varepsilon)$, so using these same tests at the requested radius leaves their null size unchanged and cannot increase their maximal type-II error. Thus both minimax errors at $r_\varepsilon$ are bounded above by their counterparts at $\bar r_\varepsilon$ and tend to zero. If $\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon)$ is empty, both minimax errors are zero by the explicit convention in [F1]; the never-reject test also realizes zero total error in that case. This proves the rate implications for all positive radius sequences, including nonvanishing or oscillating radii, in both regimes. All cutoffs and profile parameters used in this reduction are evaluated at the vanishing comparison radius. [given, F1, step 2.4, step 4.3, step 7.1, step 8.1, construct, algebra]

10.1 The Gaussian and degenerate bounds agree with their respective lower bounds, and the globally specified tests in steps 7.1 and 8.1 attain them asymptotically, including exact significance adjustment. Step 2.1 proves the qualified extremal power equivalent, step 8.1 proves the full Gaussian separation claim, and step 4.3 proves the degenerate sharp normalization. Step 9.1 supplies the separation-rate implications for all positive radius sequences. Each test is product-Borel, using a specified nonnegative countable series or finitely many coordinates and deterministic randomization. All Gaussian laws were given by [F4], all auxiliary probability products were finite, and the finite-array approximation used [F3] under Countable Choice. This proves every stated clause without a stronger choice assumption or a citation in place of a local proof. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, F7, step 2.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 4.3] ∎

## Remarks

The unrestricted all-radius extremal power equivalent in the cited 2012 display is not used: for some radii tending to zero the relaxed value grows faster than every power of the noise level. The sufficient moderate-zone restriction above preserves the full sharp error profiles, whose endpoint cases follow by monotonicity. The explicit upper test uses a centered factor $e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zt)-1$ and a union with the maximum event. These corrections are verified directly in the proof rather than inferred from the sign and set-operation displays in the source. The 2003 book remains bibliographic context; no unread book or supplemental argument is a premise.
