## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the minimax detection-risk definition with $0<q<2$, $a_j=j^\alpha$, $\sigma_j=j^\beta$, and $\alpha,\beta>0$. Let $r_\varepsilon\to0$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and put
$$\lambda=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}-\frac{\beta}{q}.$$
For $\lambda>0$, put $A=2\alpha+1/q-1/2$, $B=2(\alpha+\beta)+1/q$, and $D=\alpha+\beta(1-2/q)>0$. Choose any $\delta_\varepsilon>0$ with $\delta_\varepsilon\to0$ and $\delta_\varepsilon\log\varepsilon^{-1}\to\infty$, set $\widetilde r_\varepsilon=r_\varepsilon(1-\delta_\varepsilon)$, and define
$$u_\varepsilon^2=2\inf\left\{\sum_{j\ge1}h_j^2\sinh^2(z_j^2/2):\ 0\le h_j\le1,\ z_j\ge0,\ \sum_{j\ge1}j^{2\beta}h_jz_j^2\ge\frac{\widetilde r_\varepsilon^2}{\varepsilon^2},\ \sum_{j\ge1}j^{q(\alpha+\beta)}h_jz_j^q\le\frac1{\varepsilon^q}\right\}.$$
For each fixed significance level $\ell\in(0,1)$, the sharp errors have Gaussian form
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\ell)=\Phi(H_\ell-u_\varepsilon)+o(1),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))=2\Phi(-u_\varepsilon/2)+o(1),$$
where $\Phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{-\infty}^t e^{-x^2/2}\,dx$ and $H_\ell$ is its $(1-\ell)$-quantile. Moreover, if $r_\varepsilon=o(\varepsilon^{a_c})$ with $a_c=(q\alpha+1-q/2)/(q(\alpha+\beta)+1)$, then
$$u_\varepsilon\sim c_{\alpha,\beta,q}\,\varepsilon^{-A/D}r_\varepsilon^{B/D}$$
for a constant $c_{\alpha,\beta,q}>0$. Without this additional restriction on $r_\varepsilon$, the sharp error formulas above remain valid for every $r_\varepsilon\to0$, and a minimax separation rate is
$$r_\varepsilon^*=\varepsilon^{A/B}.$$
If $\lambda\le0$, for the same fixed significance level $\ell\in(0,1)$ put $n_\varepsilon=r_\varepsilon^{-1/\alpha}$ and $D_\varepsilon=n_\varepsilon^{-\beta}r_\varepsilon/\varepsilon-\sqrt{2\log n_\varepsilon}$. Then the sharp errors have degenerate form
$$\beta_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon),\ell)=(1-\ell)\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1),\qquad \gamma_\varepsilon(\Theta_q(r_\varepsilon))=\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1),$$
and a sharp separation-rate normalization is
$$r_\varepsilon^*=\Lambda\,\varepsilon^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{\alpha/[2(\alpha+\beta)]},\qquad \Lambda=\left(\frac{2}{\alpha+\beta}\right)^{\alpha/[2(\alpha+\beta)]}.$$
Thus the sparse boundary $\lambda=0$ belongs to the degenerate regime, and the two regimes have different separation rates.

The deterministic globalized score-and-maximum family and the finite maximum tests constructed in the proof are asymptotically minimax in the Gaussian and degenerate regimes, respectively; the significance tests include deterministic randomization to satisfy the exact level constraint.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, the sequence experiment and alternatives in the Statement. Write $s=\alpha+\beta$, use $\ell\in(0,1)$ for the fixed significance level, and put $X_i=Y_i/\varepsilon=\mu_i+G_i$, where $\mu_i=\eta_i/\varepsilon$. The supplied normal probability law has density $\phi$ and distribution function $\Phi$.

[F1] [[def-ip-minimax-detection-risk-and-separation]]: the actual alternatives satisfy $\sum i^{2\beta}\mu_i^2\ge r^2/\varepsilon^2$ and $\sum i^{qs}|\mu_i|^q\le\varepsilon^{-q}$; finite-support alternatives are allowed, and tests are randomized product-Borel maps.

[F2] [[lem-ip-sparse-gaussian-extremal-profile]] supplies the positive scalar certificate $a,b$, inverse profile $z(x)$, coefficient $d(x)=x^{2\beta}/(2a(z(x)))$, constants $c_0,c_1,c_2,M_1,M_2$, their endpoint bounds and Riemann sums, and the relaxed extremal equivalent when $n\to\infty,h_0\to0$.

[F3] [[lem-ip-finite-independent-array-fourth-moment-normal-limit]]: given normalized Gaussian probability laws, finite centered independent arrays whose summed variances tend to $v>0$ and whose summed fourth moments tend to zero have distribution functions converging uniformly to $\Phi(\,\cdot\,/\sqrt v)$, under Countable Choice.

[F4] [[def-ip-isonormal-white-noise-experiment]] supplies independent standard-normal coordinates, including their normalized scalar probability density. Normalization is a hypothesis of that supplied process; no stronger-choice normalization theorem is used.

[F5] [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]] supplies scalar affine changes of variables under Countable Choice.

[F6] [[thm-chebyshev-markov-inequality-for-the-integral]] gives Markov's inequality, including Chebyshev's inequality by applying it to a squared centered variable.

[F7] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]] and [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]] identify finite independent coordinate laws and factor their integrable products. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] supplies the finite probability products used for finite priors.

[F8] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] and [[thm-dominated-convergence]] justify the specified nonnegative series and dominated scalar integrals.

[F9] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]] identifies probability laws agreeing on finite cylinders of the product sigma-algebra.

[F10] [[lem-taylor-lagrange-remainder-from-mean-value]] bounds a third-order Taylor remainder by the supremum of the third derivative times the cube of the increment, divided by six.

[F11] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]] defines $\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}=\sup_E|P(E)-Q(E)|$ over measurable events for probability laws on the same measurable space.

[F12] [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]: for decreasing measurable events under a probability law, their probabilities decrease to the probability of their intersection.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable Choice is assumed; all other limits and finite products below use the supplied coordinate laws. No full-Choice central-limit theorem is invoked.

## Proof

The two regimes below are separate cases. A paragraph in the Gaussian branch uses its profile notation from step 1.3; a paragraph in the degenerate branch uses the notation from step 2.4. Repeated local letters in these two cases have separate scopes.

1.1 The finite coordinate density of $X_i$ with mean $\mu_i$ divided by its null density is $\exp(\mu_iX_i-\mu_i^2/2)$. Thus a finite uniform mixture of the two signs at a coordinate of absolute mean $z$ has likelihood $e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zX_i)$, and the prior with probabilities $1-g,g/2,g/2$ at $0,z,-z$ has likelihood $1+g\xi_z(X_i)$, where $\xi_z(t)=e^{-z^2/2}\cosh(zt)-1$. Multiplication over finitely many coordinates is justified by [F7]. Off these coordinates the law is unchanged; equality first on finite cylinders and then [F9] proves the likelihood identity on the whole sequence sample space. Every prior below has finite coordinate support; no new countable product probability law is constructed. [given, F4, F7, F9, A1, algebra]

1.2 Completing the square and applying [F5] to the given unit density gives $\mathbb E e^{tG}=e^{t^2/2}$. Consequently, by expanding the hyperbolic functions, $$\mathbb E\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z\mu)-1,\qquad \operatorname{Var}\xi_z(G+\mu)=\cosh(z^2)-1+(e^{z^2}-1)\sinh^2(z\mu).$$ For fixed $B$, $\mathbb E\xi_z(G)^4\le C_B(\cosh(z^2)-1)^2$ when $0<z\le B$: the bound $|\xi_z(G)|\le C_Bz^2(1+G^2)e^{B|G|}$ follows from the Taylor bound for $\cosh$ and $e^{-z^2/2}$, its fourth-power integral is finite by completing the square, and $\cosh(z^2)-1\ge z^4/2$. We will also use $\mathbb P(|G|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}$, obtained from [F6] and the same exponential moment, and the elementary Mills bounds $\overline\Phi(t)\le\phi(t)/t$ and $\overline\Phi(t)\ge\phi(t+1/t)/t$ for $t\ge1$. The first follows by integrating $x\phi(x)/t$ over $[t,\infty)$, and the second by integrating $\phi$ over $[t,t+1/t]$. [given, F4, F5, F6, F10, algebra]

1.3 First suppose $\lambda>0$ and set $L=qs-2\beta>0$, $\kappa=L/(2-q)$. Use [F2] to define the unique positive $n,h_0$ by $$c_1h_0n^{2\beta+1}=r^2\varepsilon^{-2},\qquad c_2h_0n^{qs+1}=\varepsilon^{-q},\qquad U^2=c_0h_0^2n,$$ and put $z_i=z(i/n)$, $h_i=h_0d(i/n)$. Then $n^L=(c_1/c_2)\varepsilon^{2-q}/r^2$. The scalar certificate in [F2] gives $$\sum_{i\le m}h_i(\cosh(z_iv_i)-1)\ge\frac{h_0}2\left(n^{-2\beta}\sum_{i\le m}i^{2\beta}v_i^2-n^{-qs}\sum_{i\le m}i^{qs}|v_i|^q\right).$$ Also $\sum h_i<\infty$ and $V:=\sum h_i^2(\cosh(z_i^2)-1)\sim U^2$ as $n\to\infty$. These are score coefficients, which need not be at most one. On compact subsets of $0<r/r_\varepsilon^*<\infty$, $U$ stays bounded and bounded away from zero, $n$ grows as a positive power of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, the extremal value in the Statement is exactly $J_\varepsilon(\widetilde r)$ in [F2], because $\cosh(z^2)-1=2\sinh^2(z^2/2)$. That lemma proves its power equivalent whenever $\widetilde r=o(\varepsilon^{a_c})$, equivalently when its associated $n\to\infty,h_0\to0$. Since $\widetilde r/r\to1$, this is the asserted restriction and the equivalent may be written with $r$. In particular on each compact transition range, $$u_\varepsilon\sim U=c_{\alpha,\beta,q}\varepsilon^{-A/D}r^{B/D}.$$ No equivalent outside the stated sufficient zone is used. [given, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the Gaussian lower bound, fix a compact transition range. The feasible construction in [F2] can be made with expected energy $(1+\tau)r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$ and expected budget $(1-\tau)\varepsilon^{-q}$, on a finite window $a\le i/n'\le b$, with probabilities $g_i=h'_0d(i/n')\le1$ and amplitudes $z(i/n')$. Let the margins tend slowly to zero and windows tend slowly to $(0,\infty)$. This can be specified without a rate assumption: use windows $[1/k,k]$, margin $1/k$, and pass to each next integer $k$ only after its finite Riemann errors, feasibility bounds and the concentration errors below are smaller than the prescribed margins; the preceding compact-window estimates hold uniformly on the chosen compact transition range. The profile moments $M_1,M_2$ give relative variances $O((nh_0)^{-1})=O(n^{-1/2})$ for both random constraint sums before the slowly varying window constants. Choose the numerical diagonal slowly enough that those relative variances divided by $\tau^2$ tend to zero. Chebyshev then puts prior probability $1-o(1)$ on the actual alternative. Each draw has finite coordinate support and hence is in $\ell^2$. The prior cost tends to $U^2$, its largest coordinate cost tends to zero, and its cost on $z_i>B$ tends uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$, by the bounded small-end and exponential large-end envelopes in [F2]. Let $\Pi$ denote this finite-support prior on parameter sequences, let $\mathcal A$ be the event that a draw satisfies both alternative constraints, and put $p=\Pi(\mathcal A)=1-o(1)$. If $p=1$, conditioning changes no mixture law. Otherwise, eventually $0<p<1$ and the unconditioned observation law decomposes as $P_\Pi=pP_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}+(1-p)P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}$. For every measurable event $E$, this gives $|P_\Pi(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|=(1-p)|P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A^c}(E)-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}(E)|\le1-p$, so [F11] yields $\|P_\Pi-P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}\|_{\rm TV}\le1-p$. For every randomized test $\psi$ with values in $[0,1]$, the functions $N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\psi\ge k/N\}}$ approximate $\psi$ uniformly within $1/N$; applying the event bound to each summand and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $|\mathbb E_{P_\Pi}\psi-\mathbb E_{P_{\Pi\mid\mathcal A}}\psi|\le1-p=o(1)$ uniformly over tests. [given, F1, F2, F6, F7, F11, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

2.3 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the matching upper bounds define the product-Borel score $$F(X)=\sum_{i\ge1}h_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iX_i)-\sum_{i\ge1}h_i.$$ The first series is nonnegative and may be infinite; then the test rejects. Under the null its expectation is $\sum h_i<\infty$, so it is finite almost surely by [F6], and its centered partial sums converge in mean square with variance $V$. The bounded-amplitude fourth-moment calculation in step 1.2 and [F3], followed by the null variance tail bound in [F2], give $F\Rightarrow N(0,U_0^2)$. For $n$ large put $$Q_i^2=2\log(i+1)+4\log\log(i+3)+4\log\log n,\qquad \mathcal Y=\{\exists i:|X_i|>Q_i\}.$$ Step 1.2 and a countable union bound give $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal Y)\le2(\log n)^{-2}\sum_{i\ge1}[(i+1)(\log(i+3))^2]^{-1}=o(1)$. For every fixed $K$, $\max_{i\le n(\log n)^K}Q_i=\sqrt{2\log n}+o(\sqrt{\log n})$. Reject on $\{F>H_\ell\sqrt V\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for the significance problem, and on $\{F>V/2\}\cup\mathcal Y$ for total error. These are unions with a centered-cosh score, rather than an intersection or a positive-exponential uncentered score. [given, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

2.4 Now suppose $\lambda\le0$, put $e=2\beta-qs\ge0$, $n=r^{-1/\alpha}$, $m=r^{s/\alpha}$, $A_\varepsilon=m/\varepsilon$ and $D_\varepsilon=A_\varepsilon-\sqrt{2\log n}$. Every alternative has an index $i\le\lfloor n\rfloor$ with $|\eta_i|\ge m$. Indeed with $w_i=i^{qs}|\eta_i|^q$, its energy summand is $w_i i^e|\eta_i|^{2-q}$. If $i\le n$ and $|\eta_i|<m$, this multiplier is strictly below $n^em^{2-q}=r^2$. If $i>n$, the termwise budget gives $|\eta_i|\le i^{-s}$, so the multiplier is at most $i^{-2\alpha}<r^2$. If all the indicated coordinates were smaller than $m$, summing with $\sum w_i\le1$ would give energy strictly below $r^2$, a contradiction. Let $N=\lfloor n\rfloor$ and $t_N=\sqrt{2\log N}$. The finite maximum test $R=\mathbf1\{\max_{i\le N}|X_i|>t_N\}$ has size $p_0\le2N\overline\Phi(t_N)=O(1/t_N)=o(1)$ by step 1.2. Its maximal type-II error is at most $\Phi(t_N-A_\varepsilon)=\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$, uniformly in $A_\varepsilon$, since $t_N-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$ and $\Phi'$ is bounded. For significance $\ell$, the randomized test $\rho+(1-\rho)R$ with $\rho=(\ell-p_0)/(1-p_0)$ is eventually valid and has size exactly $\ell$; its type-II error is at most $(1-\ell)\Phi(-D_\varepsilon)+o(1)$. The unrandomized maximum gives the total-error upper bound. [given, F1, F4, F6, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, under the null put $A_i=g_i\xi_{z_i}(G_i)$ for the finite prior in step 2.2. They are centered and independent, and $\sum\mathbb E A_i^2\to U_0^2$ along any subsequence with $U\to U_0\in(0,\infty)$. On $z_i\le B$, step 1.2 and the vanishing maximum coordinate variance give $\sum\mathbb E A_i^4\to0$. The omitted linear sum has variance tending uniformly to zero as $B\to\infty$; the omitted quadratic sum has expectation tending to zero. Apply [F3] to the finite bounded-amplitude arrays and then let $B\to\infty$, using Chebyshev for the linear tail. The same fourth-moment bound gives concentration of their quadratic sums. Thus $$\sum A_i\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,U_0^2),\qquad \sum A_i^2\to U_0^2,\qquad \max_i|A_i|\to0$$ in probability for the last two limits. Each factor $1+A_i=1-g_i+g_ie^{-z_i^2/2}\cosh(z_iG_i)$ is positive. On $\max|A_i|\le\delta<1/2$, [F10] gives $|\sum\log(1+A_i)-\sum A_i+\tfrac12\sum A_i^2|\le C\delta\sum A_i^2$. Let $\delta\downarrow0$. The likelihood from step 1.1 therefore has $\log L\Rightarrow N(-U_0^2/2,U_0^2)$. The addition of terms converging in probability and the successive tail limits preserve the displayed distribution limit by squeezing distribution functions between thresholds differing by an arbitrary positive tolerance. [given, F3, F6, F10, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, fix $d\in(0,1)$. Alternatives with $\mathbb P_\mu(\mathcal Y^c)<d$ already have type-II error below $d$. For every other alternative, writing $p_i=\mathbb P_\mu(|X_i|>Q_i)$, finite independence gives $\prod_{i\le m}(1-p_i)\ge d$ for each $m$. Hence $\sum_i p_i\le-\log d$ and $|\mu_i|\le Q_i+C_d$, the latter because the probability of the inside interval is at most $\Phi(Q_i-|\mu_i|)$. Choose $K>(2-q)/(2L)$ and $N=\lceil n(\log n)^K\rceil$. The energy of indices $i>N$ is at most $$\varepsilon^{-q}\sup_{i>N}i^{-L}(Q_i+C_d)^{2-q}\le C_d\varepsilon^{-q}N^{-L}(\log N)^{(2-q)/2}=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2}).$$ The envelope is eventually decreasing and $\varepsilon^{-q}n^{-L}$ is a fixed multiple of $r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Among $i\le N$ delete those with $|\mu_i|>c\sqrt{\log n}$, where $c=0.45\in(\sqrt2-1,1/2)$. The lower Mills bound in step 1.2 implies $p_i\ge n^{-a+o(1)}$ there, with $a=(\sqrt2-c)^2/2<1/2$, uniformly over these indices. Thus at most $n^{a+o(1)}$ are deleted. Their energy is at most $n^{2\beta+a+o(1)}=o(n^{2\beta+1/2})=o(r^2\varepsilon^{-2})$, including the polynomial logarithmic factors from $N$ and the means. Define $\mu_i^*=\mu_i$ for $i\le N$ not deleted and $\mu_i^*=0$ for every deleted index and every $i>N$. This vector has finite support, satisfies $|\mu_i^*|\le c\sqrt{\log n}$, and has no increased $q$-budget. Its energy loss is at most the sum of the already bounded tail energy and deleted-coordinate energy, so its retained energy is $(1-o(1))r^2\varepsilon^{-2}$. Its score mean $M=\mathbb E_{\mu^*}F$ is therefore at least $U^2-o(1)$ by the certificate in step 1.3 and $c_0=(c_1-c_2)/2$. Coordinatewise $|\mu_i^*|\le|\mu_i|$, and $|G+\mu|$ is stochastically increasing in $|\mu|$, since $\Phi(t-|\mu|)-\Phi(-t-|\mu|)$ decreases with $|\mu|$. Independence and the positive coefficients imply the score comparison for every finite partial sum. The full score event is the decreasing intersection of these partial-sum events after adding the fixed $\sum h_i$; [F12] passes the comparison to the full nonnegative series, giving $\mathbb P_\mu(F\le t)\le\mathbb P_{\mu^*}(F\le t)$. [given, F1, F2, F7, F12, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

3.3 In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, for the matching degenerate lower bound first take $D_\varepsilon\to d\in\mathbb R$. Put $M=\lfloor n/(\log n)^2\rfloor$, $I=\{\lfloor n\rfloor-M+1,\ldots,\lfloor n\rfloor\}$, and mix uniformly over indices $i\in I$ and signs with $\eta_i=\pm r i^{-\beta}$, all other coordinates zero. Every point has energy $r^2$ and budget $(ri^\alpha)^q\le1$. Write $T=\sqrt{2\log M}$ and $\mu_i=r/(\varepsilon i^\beta)$; uniformly on $I$, $\mu_i=T+d+o(1)$ since $M/n=O((\log n)^{-2})$ and $T-\sqrt{2\log n}\to0$. The null likelihood from step 1.1 is $L=M^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}e^{-\mu_i^2/2}\cosh(\mu_iG_i)$. Truncate each summand to $|G_i|\le T$, obtaining $\widetilde L$. Completing the square gives its summand mean $\Phi(T-\mu_i)-\Phi(-T-\mu_i)\to c=\Phi(-d)$ and its second moment at most $\tfrac12e^{\mu_i^2}\Phi(T-2\mu_i)+\tfrac12e^{-\mu_i^2}$. The upper Mills bound and $$\mu_i^2-\tfrac12(2\mu_i-T)^2-\log M=-(\mu_i-T)^2$$ bound this second moment divided by $M$ by $O(1/T)$. Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}\widetilde L=O(1/T)\to0$, and $\mathbb P_0(L\ne\widetilde L)\le2M\overline\Phi(T)=O(1/T)\to0$. Thus $\mathbb E_0|\widetilde L-c|\to0$ and $L\to c$ in null probability. Since $L\ge\widetilde L$, every size-$\ell$ test has mixture type-II error at least $c(1-\ell)-\mathbb E|\widetilde L-c|$; every total error is at least $\mathbb E\min(1,L)\to c$. Bounded convergence in probability here follows directly by splitting at any fixed positive deviation; no likelihood uniform integrability is asserted. This proves both lower bounds for finite $d$. [given, F1, F5, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.4, construct, algebra]

4.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for any likelihood $L$, randomized test $\chi$ and $c>0$, scalar algebra gives $L(1-\chi)\ge\min(L,c)-c\chi$. The limit law in step 3.1 has no positive atoms, so $$\mathbb E_0\min(L,c)=\int_0^c\mathbb P_0(L>t)\,dt$$ converges by [F8]; the identity itself follows first for step functions and then by increasing finite subdivisions. Choose $c=\exp(-U_0^2/2+U_0H_\ell)$. Its limiting upper-tail probability is $\ell$, and completing the square gives the limiting lower bound $\Phi(H_\ell-U_0)$ for every test of size at most $\ell$. Likewise every total error is at least $\mathbb E_0\min(1,L)\to2\Phi(-U_0/2)$. Conditioning in step 2.2 costs only $o(1)$ uniformly over tests. This proves both minimax lower bounds on compact transitions without an additional Neyman--Pearson or unrestricted-choice supplier. [given, F5, F8, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, for the residual vector set $m_i=h_i(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)-1)$, so $M=\sum m_i\ge0$. The exact variance formula in step 1.2 shows that the excess above $V$ is $$\sum h_i^2(e^{z_i^2}-1)\sinh^2(z_i\mu_i^*)\le\sum K_i m_i,\qquad K_i=h_i(e^{z_i^2}-1)(\cosh(z_i\mu_i^*)+1).$$ For $z_i\le\sqrt{\log n}$, the global bound $\psi(z)(e^{z^2}-1)\le C$ in [F2], its relation $x\le C(1+z^{1/\kappa})$ at large $z$, and $h_0\asymp n^{-1/2}$ give $K_i\le n^{-1/2+c+o(1)}=o(1)$. For $z_i>\sqrt{\log n}$ the other global bound in [F2] gives an absolute excess bound $$C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}\exp(-z_i^2+2cz_i\sqrt{\log n})\le C h_0^2\sum_{z_i>\sqrt{\log n}}(i/n)^{4\beta}e^{-(1-2c)z_i^2}=o(1).$$ The final estimate follows from the exponential profile tail and $h_0^2n=O(1)$; its discrete tail is bounded by the integral of an eventually decreasing polynomial-times-exponential envelope plus a mesh term, as in [F2]. Thus uniformly over residual alternatives, $\operatorname{Var}_{\mu^*}F\le V+o(1)M+o(1)$. Unbounded $z_i$ have been controlled by an absolute variance bound, not a uniform bounded-amplitude assumption. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

4.3 In the degenerate branch, with the notation of step 2.4, if $D_\varepsilon\to+\infty$, step 2.4 settles both errors by nonnegativity. If $D_\varepsilon\to-\infty$, fix $K>0$. The continuous strictly increasing function $r\mapsto\varepsilon^{-1}r^{s/\alpha}-\sqrt{(2/\alpha)\log(1/r)}$ ranges from $-\infty$ to a positive value on $(0,1)$, so it has a unique radius $r_{\varepsilon,K}$ at value $-K$, and this radius tends to zero. Eventually $r<r_{\varepsilon,K}$; inclusion of alternative sets and step 3.3 give lower limits at least $\Phi(K)$ for total error and $(1-\ell)\Phi(K)$ for type-II error. Let $K\to\infty$. Subsequences in the extended real line now establish the two degenerate formulas for arbitrary $D_\varepsilon$. Finally put $p=s/\alpha$ and $\Lambda=(2/s)^{\alpha/(2s)}$, so $\Lambda^p=\sqrt{2/s}$. For each fixed $c>0$, direct substitution into the displayed $r_\varepsilon^*$ gives $$D_\varepsilon(cr_\varepsilon^*)=(c^p-1)\sqrt{2\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/s}+o(1).$$ The logarithmic correction is $O(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})/\sqrt{\log(\varepsilon^{-1})})$, which tends to zero. Thus the stated sharp constant, zero/infinite-ratio separation limits and the assignment of $\lambda=0$ all follow, with no strict inequality imposed on $e$. [given, F1, step 2.4, step 3.3, algebra]

5.1 In the Gaussian branch, with the profile notation of step 1.3, if $M$ stays bounded, fix $B>0$. For $z_i\le B$, $h_iz_i^2\le C_Bh_0(i/n)^{2\beta}$ by [F2]. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$, with compact transversal $(M_0,g_0)$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ,\mathbb R)$. Assume zero is not a Dirichlet eigenvalue of either $-\Delta_g+q_j$, assume the unweighted scalar geodesic ray transform on $M_0$ is injective on compactly supported smooth functions, and suppose the full Schrödinger Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps agree:
$$\Lambda_{q_1}=\Lambda_{q_2}:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M).$$
Then $q_1=q_2$ on $M$.

## Statement references

[[def-ip-transversally-anisotropic-product-domain|Product domain and distinguished coordinate]]

[[def-ip-injective-geodesic-ray-transform|Unweighted transversal ray transform]]

[[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map|Full Schrödinger DN map]]

## Facts & Assumptions
[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and CGO solver suppliers [F1]--[F2].

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]] is inherited from the DN identity and CGO solver suppliers [F1]--[F2].

**Given:** the compact CTA product, real smooth interior-supported potentials, nonresonance of both operators, injectivity of the real scalar ray transform, and equality of full DN maps.

[F1] [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: under nonresonance, each Schrödinger DN map is a full boundary map on $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with normal derivative convention.

[F2] [[lem-ip-alessandrini-identity]] and [[def-ip-conductivity-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]: the Alessandrini Statement gives the Schrödinger identity for smooth boundary values, while the DN definition gives weak boundary forms on $H^{1/2}$. The exact $H^1$ solutions used below have only $H^{1/2}$ traces, so step 1.1 derives the needed extension directly from those forms.

[F3] [[def-ip-injective-geodesic-ray-transform]]: if a real compactly supported smooth function has zero unweighted integrals over all nontangential transversal geodesics, then it is zero; the same implication for complex functions follows by applying the real statement to real and imaginary parts.

[F4] [[cor-uniqueness-of-the-l-one-fourier-transform]]: two $L^1(\mathbb R)$ functions with equal Fourier transforms are equal almost everywhere.

[F5] [[thm-ip-cgo-solvability-and-remainder-bound]] now imports the $H^1$ real-weight right solver with $O(|\tau|^{-1})$ $L^2$ norm from Dos Santos Ferreira--Kurylev--Lassas--Salo, Proposition 2.1, PDF p. 10, with finite orientation-cover descent. The external result accepts arbitrary $L^2$ forcing and both signs of the real weight, rather than only the particular transport amplitude in that supplier's Statement.

[F6] [[lem-ip-cta-gaussian-beam-ray-limit]] supplies the normalized beam, arbitrarily small residual, and self-intersection ray limit, including nonorientable transversals by orientation-cover descent. The external source is Proposition 3.1, PDF p. 14, with the cross-term estimate on pp. 21--22. Proposition 2.2, PDF p. 11, gives the associated exact-solution correction. These external statements and the cross-term pages were inspected for the bounded repair; no complete new Carleman or beam proof is claimed.

## Proof

**Given:** the data in the statement.

1.1 For exact $H^1$ solutions $u_j$ let $f_j=\operatorname{tr}u_j\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ and define $a_j(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla_gv,\nabla_g\overline w)+q_jv\overline w)\,dV_g$. By the weak DN definition, $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_1(u_1,u_2)$. Let $\widetilde u_1\in H^1(M)$ be the $q_2$ solution with trace $f_1$, which exists by nonresonant weak solvability. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_2(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, $a_2(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_2(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$, where the conjugation uses real-valuedness of $q_2$. Subtracting the weak pairings and using equality of the DN maps on all $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ gives $\int_M Q(x_1,x')u_1(x_1,x')\overline{u_2(x_1,x')}\,dV_g=0$, where $Q=q_1-q_2$. This derives the needed weak-trace extension of [F2]. Because $q_j\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ and $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$, extension of $Q$ by zero gives a smooth compactly supported function on $\mathbb R\times M_0$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, put $s=\tau+i\lambda$, and choose the beam $v_s$ of [F6] with residual $O(\tau^{-K})$. Use the signed real-weight solver [F5] to obtain exact solutions $$u_1=e^{-s x_1}(v_s+r_1),\qquad u_2=e^{s x_1}(v_s+r_2)$$ for the respective potentials, with $r_j\in H^1(M)$ and $\|r_j\|_2=O(\tau^{-1})$. Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Applying [F6] proves the attenuated ray identity for every $\lambda$ and every nontangential $\gamma$. This argument works on the base manifold; it does not assume injectivity of a ray transform on its orientation cover. [A1, A2, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Step 2.1 supplies $$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$ where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$. At $\lambda=0$, [F3] gives $\widehat Q_0=0$. Assume inductively that $\partial_\lambda^j\widehat Q_0=0$ for every $j<k$. Differentiate the ray identity $k$ times at $\lambda=0$. Differentiation under the finite geodesic integral is valid because $Q$ is smooth with compact $x_1$ support. Leibniz' rule leaves the unweighted ray integral of $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0$; all other terms contain lower derivatives and vanish by the induction hypothesis. Thus [F3], applied to real and imaginary parts, gives $\partial_\lambda^k\widehat Q_0=0$. Induction proves that every Taylor coefficient of $\lambda\mapsto\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ vanishes for each fixed $x'$. [F3, given, step 2.1, induction, algebra]

4.1 For each fixed $x'$, compact $x_1$ support makes $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')$ entire in $\lambda$, so its zero Taylor series implies it vanishes for all real $\lambda$. This is the Fourier transform of the $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function $Q(\cdot,x')$ at every frequency $2\lambda$; [F4] gives $Q(\cdot,x')=0$ almost everywhere. Smoothness of $Q$ then yields $Q=0$ on $M$. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot cobordism in $S^3\times[0,1]$, the ordinary even integral Khovanov assignment has source and target the bigraded groups $Kh^{i,j}$ and is defined up to an overall sign; after quotienting morphisms by sign, it is invariant under ambient isotopy fixed on the boundary and respects composition. If the surface is equipped with a dividing set and one $w$- and one $z$-basepoint on each boundary knot, the decorated knot Floer assignment has source and target the filtered complexes $CFL^-_{UV}(S^3,K)$ over $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$, and is invariant up to filtered equivariant chain homotopy. For a general gluing of decorated four-dimensional cobordisms, the link Floer composition law sums over Spin-c structures on the composite that restrict to the chosen structures on the pieces; for the product $S^3\times[0,1]$ this sum has one term. The two assignments therefore have separately specified targets, coefficient rings, decorations, and equivalence relations.

## Statement references

[[thm-barnatan-khovanov-cobordism-functoriality-up-to-sign|Even integral Khovanov cobordism functoriality]]

[[def-decorated-link-cobordism-and-floer-target|The decorated Floer target and dividing-set data]]

[[def-knot-floer-cobordism-map|The Spin-c-indexed decorated Floer map]]

[[lem-knot-floer-cobordism-naturality-and-movie-invariance|Floer naturality and composition law]]

[Bar-Natan, *Khovanov's homology for tangles and cobordisms*, Theorems 4–5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0410495v2)

[Zemke, *Link cobordisms and functoriality in link Floer homology*, Theorems A and B](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05207v3)

[Jacobsson, *An invariant of link cobordisms from Khovanov homology*, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0206303)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and the smooth oriented knot cobordism in the Statement; for the Floer assignment also its dividing set, marked points and specified Spin-c structures.

[F1] The retained even integral Khovanov functor gives the indicated bigraded groups and cobordism maps up to one overall sign, with boundary-fixed isotopy invariance and composition after quotienting by sign. This locally resolved result is reused unchanged. ([[thm-barnatan-khovanov-cobordism-functoriality-up-to-sign]])

[F2] The decorated Floer map construction and naturality lemma give the two-color filtered $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$-equivariant maps, with one Spin-c label and the extension-sum composition law. Their explicitly external inputs are Zemke's Theorems A and B, arXiv:1610.05207v3, pp.3 and 85–98, at the full divided-surface, parametrized-boundary and colored-chain-complex scope; their explicit finite/countable-choice specialization is retained, and no full-Choice theorem is silently substituted for the stated hypothesis. Neither the hat-only Juhasz construction nor the graph reduction is being asserted to construct this two-variable functor. ([[def-knot-floer-cobordism-map]], [[lem-knot-floer-cobordism-naturality-and-movie-invariance]], [source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05207v3))

## Proof

1.1 Apply [F1] to the smooth oriented surface. Its target is ordinary even integral $Kh^{i,j}$, and identifying a map with its negative removes exactly the one sign ambiguity. Its isotopy and composition conclusions are the first assertion of the Statement. [F1, given]

1.2 For the separately decorated surface apply [F2], coloring all w-regions by $U$ and z-regions by $V$. The intermediate multiply based link modules and their endpoint naturality identifications are part of that construction. Zero curvature makes the endpoint objects the specified complexes, and external Theorem A gives filtered equivariant chain-homotopy invariance. This assertion has coefficient field $\mathbb F_2$ and its own decoration and Spin-c data; no integral Khovanov sign ambiguity or comparison between the two theories is transferred to it. [F2, given]

2.1 The general composition law is the extension sum in [F2]. On $S^3\times[0,1]$ the Spin-c set has one element, so composition has one term. Combining the two independently established assignments proves the entire Statement with its distinct targets, coefficients and equivalence relations. It asserts neither equality of the functors nor a canonical chain-level top generator, and requires no new local reconstruction of the imported Cerf checks. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The set of smooth oriented knot concordance classes in the standard three-sphere is an abelian group under connected sum, with identity the standard unknot and inverse of $[K]$ represented by the reverse mirror $K^\dagger$. Separately, the set of locally flat topological oriented knot concordance classes is an abelian group under connected sum, with the same identity and inverse convention.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth oriented knot concordance]]

[[def-locally-flat-topological-knot-concordance|Locally flat topological oriented knot concordance]]

[[def-reverse-mirror-of-oriented-knot|The reverse-mirror inverse convention]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum operation and standard unknot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the smooth and topological concordance relations, and their oriented connected-sum operation.

[F1] Smooth and locally flat topological concordance are equivalence relations on oriented ambient-isotopy classes. ([[lem-smooth-and-topological-knot-concordance-is-an-equivalence-relation]])

[F2] Concordance respects connected sum in both categories under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The smooth implication is the retained local annulus construction. The TOP implication uses the explicitly imported classical operation and the compact real-code/$L[r]$ specialization in the compatibility supplier; it is not inferred from bare-core straightening. ([[lem-knot-concordance-compatible-with-connected-sum]])

[F3] On oriented ambient-isotopy classes, connected sum is associative and commutative and has the standard unknot as two-sided identity under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. ([[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]])

[F4] For every smooth oriented knot $K$, $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk in $B^4$; the disk is locally flat as a topological proper surface. ([[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]], [[def-locally-flat-proper-surface-and-concordance-collars]])

[F5] A knot bounds a smooth proper disk in $B^4$ if and only if it is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot. ([[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]])

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice is used by the actual connected-sum and isotopy-extension supplier branches cited in this theorem; the TOP external input is specialized to the required compact data under that same hypothesis in [F2], rather than assuming ambient full Choice. ([[def-countable-choice]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]])

## Proof

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the two concordance relations.

1.1 In the smooth category, [F1] makes the smooth concordance classes a quotient set. [F2] ensures that replacing either connected-sum input by a concordant knot leaves the resulting class unchanged, so connected sum defines a binary operation on that quotient. [F3] supplies associativity, commutativity, and the two-sided identity on oriented knot types; these equalities pass to the quotient because the operation is well-defined. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]

2.1 For every $K$, [F4] gives a smooth disk bounded by $K\#K^\dagger$. By [F5], this connected sum is smoothly concordant to the standard unknot, so $[K]+[K^\dagger]=[U]$ in the smooth quotient. Together with the commutative monoid structure from step 1.1, every element has an inverse; thus the smooth quotient is an abelian group with the stated inverse. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, given]

3.1 In the locally flat topological category, [F1] again gives a quotient set, and the TOP implication of [F2] makes connected sum independent of both concordance representatives. Associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity descend from [F3] exactly as in step 1.1. For each smooth knot representative $K$, the smooth disk from [F4] and its smooth concordance to $U$ from [F5] are also locally flat by the surface/collar convention. Therefore $[K]+[K^\dagger]=[U]$ in the TOP quotient. Every element has the stated inverse, so this quotient too is an abelian group. The Countable Choice strength here is that of the bounded compatibility specialization [F2], not an unstated full-AC hypothesis. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

[[lem-knot-concordance-compatible-with-connected-sum]]

[[lem-general-knot-reverse-mirror-sum-is-ribbon]]

[[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]]

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $\nu_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $\nu_K\cong S^1\times\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1\times D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$ uses the product Euclidean norm induced by the chosen trivialization. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1\times D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K\to S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

## Statement references

[Hatcher, Theorem 3.44 and Corollary 3.45](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATch3.pdf)

[Cattabriga and Francaviglia, §§4.1 and 4.4](https://poisson.phc.dm.unipi.it/~camponovo/libri/knot.pdf)

[Calegari, §3.3](https://math.uchicago.edu/~dannyc/notes/knot_theory.pdf)

[F1] [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]] defines $K$ as a smooth embedding of an oriented circle in the standard oriented $S^3$.

[F2] [[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]] defines the quotient normal bundle $\nu_K$.

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.2 Write $D_r^2=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:|z|\le r\}$ in the product coordinates and set $U=\Phi(S^1\times\{|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$ and $V=S^3\setminus\Phi(S^1\times D^2_{\epsilon/2})$. The removed disk image is compact, hence closed in Hausdorff $S^3$, so $V$ is open. They cover $S^3$, and $U\cap V=\Phi(S^1\times\{\epsilon/2<|z|<3\epsilon/2\})$. [F1, F5, construct]

2.1 Radial homotopies retract $U$ onto $N(K)$ by replacing each fibre radius $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\min(r,\epsilon)$, fixing the zero vector; retract $V$ onto $E_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\max(r,\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon/2<r<2\epsilon$ and fixing points outside the product tube; and retract $U\cap V$ onto $T_K$ by replacing $r$ with $(1-t)r+t\epsilon$. Each formula remains within its domain, agrees with the identity at the relevant boundary, and fixes its target. Thus these are deformation retractions. [F3, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 On the overlap, composing its inclusion into $U$ with the first retraction gives radius $\min(r,\epsilon)$, while retracting first to $T_K$ and including into $N(K)$ gives radius $\epsilon$; linear interpolation stays in $N(K)$. For the inclusion into $V$, the corresponding radii are $\max(r,\epsilon)$ and $\epsilon$, and their interpolation stays in $E_K$. Every subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$ is free of rank at most two: projection to one coordinate has cyclic image; if nonzero, choose a preimage of its positive generator to split it off, and the kernel is a subgroup of $\mathbb Z$; if zero, the subgroup already lies in $\mathbb Z$. In the new basis, $i_*(a[\mu]+b[\lambda])=a[\mu]$, so the kernel is exactly $\mathbb Z[\lambda]$, a primitive rank-one direct summand. Every degree-one class is $[\sigma]+a[\mu]$ and maps to zero exactly when $a=-k$, proving uniqueness. The curve $t\mapsto(e^{2\pi it},e^{-2\pi ikt})$ is embedded in $S^1\times S^1$ because its first coordinate is injective on $S^1$; it represents $[\lambda]$ and is a preferred longitude. [F4, F8, step 6.1, algebra, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, and let $g(K)$ be the least genus of a compact connected oriented embedded surface in $S^3$ with boundary $K$. With the integral Alexander normalization, the maximum Alexander grading in which the hat knot Floer homology of $K$ is nonzero is $g(K)$:

$$g(K)=\max\{i\in\mathbb Z:\widehat{\mathrm{HFK}}(S^3,K,i;\mathbb Z)\ne0\}.$$

## Statement references

[[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus|The minimum genus among embedded Seifert surfaces]]

[[def-top-alexander-grading-of-knot-floer-homology|The integral absolute Alexander grading]]

[Ozsvath and Szabo, *Holomorphic disks and genus bounds*, Theorem 1.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0311496)

[Juhasz, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Corollary 8.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609779v3)

[Manolescu, *An Introduction to Knot Floer Homology*, Theorem 2.3](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/hfk.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]] gives the two ball sides of a smooth embedded sphere in the actual three-sphere.

[F2] [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-taut-hierarchy-nonvanishing]] gives a split copy of Z in the integral homology of a taut balanced sutured manifold, with its specified coherent orientation class induced through the finite hierarchy.

[F3] [[lem-ni-holomorphic-disk-and-jsj-analytic-inputs]] constructs the actual marked adapted diagram and identifies the entire integral degree-g differential with the cut differential, with the specified orientation character retained.

[F4] [[lem-fiber-outer-grading-and-integral-cut-euler-matrix]] computes the absolute Alexander degree of every adapted generator as g minus its number of interior polygon coordinates.

[F5] [[def-oriented-seifert-surface-and-knot-genus]] defines the minimum among compact connected oriented embedded Seifert surfaces. Such surfaces exist. Their nonnegative integer genera have a least realized value; this finite integer minimization uses no additional choice principle beyond the assumptions of the statement.

[F6] **Classical analytic input and exact axiom boundary.** Under the Axiom of Choice in the Statement, use the general integral sutured analytic framework explicitly imported in F5 of [[lem-integral-sutured-floer-compactness-and-orientations]], at the actual balanced/adapted diagrams, admissibility, boundary-region/divisor and coherent-orientation conditions of F2–F4. This supplies the pointwise Fredholm, regularity, compactification and strip/polygon gluing prerequisite; the preserved local area, grading, signed cut and hierarchy constructions then use it at their stated targets. The published framework is Juhász, *Holomorphic discs and sutured manifolds*, §§3,6–7, especially Definition7.1 and Theorems7.2/7.5, together with the referenced Ozsváth–Szabó analytic framework, and Juhász, *Floer homology and surface decompositions*, Proposition7.6 and Theorems1.4–1.5. These are explicit external inputs in the classical setting, not a newly reconstructed weak-choice theorem. [[lem-countable-analytic-choice-for-fixed-sutured-floer-data]] retains its conditional Countable Choice conclusion: GIVEN the actual pointwise constructions, its fixed finite diagram/cut and at-most-two-parameter choices are finite or countable. It does not itself prove that those pointwise constructions follow under Countable Choice. The Countable-Choice-only genus strengthening is not certified here; neither its falsity nor an independent new geometric open problem is asserted. [Juhász2006](https://msp.org/agt/2006/6-3/agt-v6-n3-p16-s.pdf), [Juhász2008](https://msp.org/gt/2008/12-1/gt-v12-n1-p07-s.pdf)

## Statement

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude. Call $K$ smoothly slice when it bounds a smooth
properly embedded disk in the standard $B^4$, with a product collar at its
boundary. Then $K$ is smoothly slice if and only if the compact smooth
$4$-manifold $X_0(K)$, formed using that preferred-longitude framing, admits a
smooth codimension-zero embedding into the standard $S^4$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Lemma 1.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$ with its fixed tubular
neighborhood and preferred longitude; the standard decomposition
$S^4=B_1\cup_{S^3}B_2$ into two $4$-balls; and the zero-trace convention.
The tube and peripheral curve are fixed data throughout; no choice principle
is used to select a family of them.

[F1] [[def-smooth-zero-trace]]: $X_0(K)$ is $B^4$ with a $2$-handle attached
using the framing whose pushoff represents the preferred zero-linking
longitude.

[F2] [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]]: the preferred longitude is
the degree-one peripheral class whose image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero.

[F3] [[lem-slice-disk-complement-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]: for a proper
slice disk $D$, the boundary exterior $E_K$ includes into the disk exterior $X$
with $H_1(E_K)\to H_1(X)$ an isomorphism carrying meridian to meridian.

[F4] [[def-smooth-immersion-and-embedding-for-manifolds-with-boundary]]: a
smooth embedding is a smooth immersion and homeomorphism onto its image; here
both source and target have dimension four.

[F5] [[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]: a $C^1$ map between open
subsets of $\mathbb R^4$ with invertible derivative at a point is a local
diffeomorphism there.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $D\subset B_1$ is a smooth proper slice disk for $K$. Its oriented normal $2$-plane bundle is trivial because $D$ is a disk. Choose a nowhere-zero normal section and push $D$ slightly along it to a parallel disk $D'$ in the exterior $X$ of a tubular neighborhood of $D$. The boundary $K'$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ in $E_K$, and it bounds $D'$ in $X$. By [F3], its class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude. [F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$ from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk $D^2\times\{0\}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth away from the cone point $p$. [F1, given, construct]

1.3 In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$. [F4, F5, given, construct]

2.1 A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently $B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed $2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$, followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link $\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where $\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite $P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of $\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$. It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$. [F2, F5, step 1.3, algebra, construct]

3.1 Choose the coordinate ball bounded by that small sphere. Its complement $W=S^4\setminus\operatorname{int}(B_\epsilon)$ is a standard $4$-ball. The image sphere is smooth away from the cone point; transversality makes its remainder after deleting the cone cap a smooth properly embedded disk in $W$ with product boundary collar and boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. Append the trace annulus of the isotopy in step 2.2 inside a boundary collar of $W$, with the isotopy stationary near its ends. The result is a smooth slice disk with boundary exactly $K$. [step 1.2, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 Steps 1.1, 2.1 construct an embedding from a slice disk, and steps 1.2, 1.3, 2.2, 3.1 construct a slice disk from an embedding. These are the two implications in the statement. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 3.1, given] ∎

\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9]
  \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (1.15);
  \node at (0,1.42) {$K\subset\partial B^4$};
  \draw[thick] (-0.72,0.05) .. controls (-0.55,0.62) and (0.55,0.62) .. (0.72,0.05);
  \draw[thick] (-0.72,0.05) .. controls (-0.55,-0.52) and (0.55,-0.52) .. (0.72,0.05);
  \fill (0,0.04) circle (1.5pt);
  \node[below] at (0,-0.05) {$p$};
  \node at (2.15,0.38) {$\text{cone disk}$};
  \draw[->] (1.8,0.32) -- (0.66,0.22);
  \node at (2.15,-0.15) {$\text{2-handle core}$};
  \draw[->] (1.8,-0.15) -- (0.65,-0.18);
  \draw[dashed] (0,0.04) circle (0.34);
  \node at (0,-1.55) {remove a small cap at $p$: the remainder is a slice disk};
\end{tikzpicture}
~~~

The sketch records the cone-on-$K$ disk and the $2$-handle core that form the
piecewise-smooth sphere. The dashed circle marks the cap removed near the cone
point. The proof uses the local coordinate-ball argument above, not the sketch.

class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude. [F2, F3,
given, construct]

1.2 A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other
hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently
$B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed
$2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union
is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth
codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$
from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk
$D^2\times\{0\}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After
smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth
away from the cone point $p$. [F1, given, construct]

2.2 In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is
invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions
are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local
orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing
reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the
embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in
$\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$. [F4, F5, given, construct]

2.3 Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along
each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target
distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative
uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for
all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$,
followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where
$\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to
the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite
$P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the
connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The
chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of
$\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection
restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$.
It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has
degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a
diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that
section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$. [F2, F5, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

2.4 Choose the coordinate ball bounded by that small sphere. Its complement
$W=S^4\setminus\operatorname{int}(B_\epsilon)$ is a standard $4$-ball. The
image sphere is smooth away from the cone point; transversality makes its
remainder after deleting the cone cap a smooth properly embedded disk in $W$
with product boundary collar and boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. Append the trace
annulus of the isotopy in step 2.3 inside a boundary collar of $W$, with the
isotopy stationary near its ends. The result is a smooth slice disk with
boundary exactly $K$. [step 2.1, step 2.3, construct]

3.1 Steps 1.1–1.2 construct an embedding from a slice disk, and steps
2.1–2.4 construct a slice disk from an embedding. These are the two
implications in the statement. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 2.4, given] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot. The total normalized integral reduced Khovanov cohomology is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$ concentrated in bidegree $(0,0)$ if and only if $K$ is the unknot.

## Statement references

[[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot|Normalized integral reduced cohomology]]

[[thm-reduced-khovanov-basepoint-and-reidemeister-invariance|Based reduced invariance]]

[[thm-khovanov-to-instanton-spectral-sequence|Reduced instanton spectral sequence]]

[[thm-sutured-instanton-khi-rank-detects-unknot|Sutured instanton rank detector]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Khovanov homology is an unknot-detector* (2011), Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.3, and Theorem 8.12](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/khovanov-unknot.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Knots, three-manifolds and instantons* (2018), Corollary 5.4](https://math.pku.edu.cn/puremath/docs/2018-10/20181010175415114589.pdf)

[Yang, *An Overview of Floer Homologies* (2025), §5.7](https://web.stanford.edu/~cm5/286.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, and the normalized reduced integral Khovanov cohomology of $K$.

[F1] The fixed reflection satisfies $\overline{\overline K}=K$ and carries the standard unknot to itself ([[def-mirror-of-a-classical-knot]], Definition).

[F2] For the crossingless based unknot diagram, the reduced quotient removes the based-circle $X$ label and places the surviving $1$ generator in bidegree $(0,0)$ ([[def-reduced-khovanov-cohomology-of-a-knot]], Definition).

[A1] For every knot $J$, there is a finite spectral sequence from $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline J;\mathbb Z)$ to $I^\natural(J;\mathbb Z)$ ([[thm-khovanov-to-instanton-spectral-sequence]], Statement). The integral resolution/cube construction is the retained original-facing completed supplier; it does not include the KHI rank implication.

[A2] For every knot $J$, $I^\natural(J;\mathbb Q)\cong KHI(J;\mathbb Q)$ and $\dim_{\mathbb Q}KHI(J;\mathbb Q)\ge1$, with equality exactly for the unknot ([[thm-sutured-instanton-khi-rank-detects-unknot]], Statement). The supplier now records the needed ordinary surface, closure/excision and genus/nonvanishing results as explicitly published external inputs under the run-specific permission, retaining its local singular and unknot calculations. This does not pretend that the analytic complex or integral cube alone proves rank detection.

[A3] The reduced groups are independent of the based diagram and basepoint under AC$_\omega$ ([[thm-reduced-khovanov-basepoint-and-reidemeister-invariance]], Statement). This is consumed at its declared mathematical interface; workflow readiness or historical owner hashes are not mathematical premises of this proof.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $\widetilde{Kh}(K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ as a total graded group. Set $J=\overline K$. By [F1], $\overline J=K$. The $E_2$ group in [A1] for $J$ is therefore $\mathbb Z$, so its rationalization has dimension one. [A1, F1, A3, given, construct]

2.1 Put $S=\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Localization $S^{-1}(-)=(-)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ preserves exact sequences: if $f:A\to B$ is injective and $f(a)/s=0$, some $t\in S$ has $f(ta)=0$, hence $ta=0$ and $a/s=0$; if $g:B\to C$ follows $f$ and $g(b)/s=0$, choose $t\in S$ with $tb\in\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, say $f(a)=tb$, so $b/s=f(a)/(ts)$; if $g$ is surjective, each $c/s$ is the image of a lift divided by $s$. Thus localization commutes with kernels, images, and homology. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The spectral sequence in [A1] is obtained by taking successive homology pages of a finite filtered complex. Exact localization therefore identifies its rationalized pages with the pages of the rationalized filtered complex, and identifies the localized abutment with $I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)$. The $E_2$ page has rational dimension one by step 1.1. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On each finite-dimensional rational page, the next page is homology. For any differential $d$ on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, rank-nullity gives $\dim H(V,d)=\dim V-2\dim\operatorname{im}d\le\dim V$. Iterating this inequality over the finite spectral sequence bounds the total dimension of $E_\infty$ by its one-dimensional $E_2$ page; since the finite abutment filtration has associated graded $E_\infty$, its total dimension equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q} I^\natural(\overline K;\mathbb Q)\le1$. [A1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [A2], this target has dimension at least one, so it has dimension one. The rank-detection clause of [A2] implies that $\overline K$ is the unknot; applying the same reflection gives that $K$ is the unknot. [A2, F1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Conversely, for the crossingless one-circle unknot diagram the reduced complex has the single generator from [F2] and no differential. Its total cohomology is therefore $\mathbb Z$ in bidegree $(0,0)$. This proves the converse and hence the stated equivalence. [F2, given, algebra] ∎

## Proof status

The rank argument is complete relative to the explicitly labelled supplier interfaces [A1]–[A3]. The accepted integral resolution construction supplies [A1]; its proof is reused without rereading or revalidating it. The rank detector [A2] now supplies its precise published ordinary-surface, closure/excision and genus/nonvanishing inputs under the expanded run-specific permission; this is a source-qualified use, not a claim of local reconstruction of those inputs. With [A1]–[A3], the finite localization/rank argument proves the unchanged Statement. It uses no distinguished instanton vector and gives no workflow-readiness conclusion.

## Statement

Assume full AC. Let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$ and $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{top}}$ denote, respectively, the smooth and locally flat topological concordance groups of smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented $3$-sphere, with connected sum as operation. Let $G_{\mathbb Z}$ be the integral algebraic concordance group generated by integral Seifert lattices modulo direct-sum and metabolic relations. In either category $\mathcal C$, the rule $[K]\mapsto[(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V_F)]$, where $F$ is any connected oriented Seifert surface of $K$ and $V_F$ is its positive-push Seifert pairing, defines a surjective group homomorphism $\Phi_{\mathcal C}:\mathcal C\to G_{\mathbb Z}$.

## Statement references

[[def-smooth-knot-concordance|Smooth concordance is represented by an oriented proper annulus]]

[[def-locally-flat-topological-knot-concordance|Locally flat topological concordance is represented by an oriented proper annulus]]

[[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance|The integral algebraic concordance group]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the smooth and locally flat categories in the Statement, and the positive-push Seifert-pairing convention.

[A1] Full AC is assumed and implies the countable-choice hypotheses of the smooth concordance-group suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] Each smooth oriented knot has a connected oriented Seifert surface, and the pairing on its first integral homology is an integral Seifert lattice. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]], [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[lem-seifert-matrix-skew-part-is-surface-intersection]]

[F2] Integral Seifert lattices generate $G_{\mathbb Z}$ with direct-sum and metabolic relations; the negative form represents the group inverse. [[def-metabolic-seifert-form-and-algebraic-knot-concordance]], [[lem-negative-seifert-form-represents-algebraic-inverse]]

[F3] Every integral matrix with unimodular skew part is realized by a smooth oriented knot and a connected oriented Seifert surface. [[lem-integral-seifert-form-is-realized-by-a-knot]]

[F4] Any two Seifert matrices of the same smooth oriented knot are related by a finite sequence of integral congruences, elementary Seifert enlargements and their inverses; these moves preserve the class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$. Transporting an oriented surface under an oriented ambient isotopy preserves its matrix in the transported basis. [[lem-seifert-matrices-of-a-knot-are-s-equivalent]], [[lem-seifert-matrix-s-enlargement-preserves-algebraic-concordance-class]], [[lem-seifert-matrix-s-equivalence-under-isotopy]]

[F5] Oriented connected sum is formed by a band joining separated knot representatives. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F6] Smooth concordance classes form an abelian group with inverse represented by the reverse mirror, and a knot is smoothly concordant to the unknot exactly when it bounds a smooth proper disk. [[thm-knot-concordance-is-an-abelian-group]], [[lem-smooth-slice-iff-concordant-to-unknot]]

[F7] Linking of disjoint oriented curves is the signed intersection with a spanning two-chain. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F8] When the given disk is smooth, every chosen Seifert surface has a metabolic Seifert lattice. This is the proved smooth branch of the actual slice-metabolizer source, using its constructed two-sided smooth hypersurface and integral saturation. [[lem-slice-disk-induces-seifert-metabolizer]]

[F9] Under the full AC assumed here, for any locally flat proper slice disk of $K$ and any chosen smooth Seifert surface, the Seifert lattice has a primitive half-rank direct summand on which the pairing vanishes. This is the exact repaired TOP slice-metabolizer interface, using its explicitly external TOP geometry and its retained chain/duality/saturation argument. [[lem-slice-disk-induces-seifert-metabolizer]]

[F10] **External TOP input:** locally flat topological concordance classes of smooth oriented knots form a group under the well-defined connected-sum operation, with unknot identity and reverse-mirror inverse. This is the classical operation in Ray, §3, Definitions 3.1/3.5 and Proposition 3.6, printed II–11–II–12. It is imported under the full AC assumed in this theorem; no Countable Choice specialization or locally reconstructed proper-pair tube is asserted by this input. The separate compatibility/group carriers retain their stronger explicitly stated choice accounting.


## Proof

1.1 For a smooth oriented knot $K$, choose a surface and basis from [F1] and define $a(K)=[V_F]\in G_{\mathbb Z}$. The class is independent of this choice: [F4] relates any two such matrices by finitely many congruences and elementary enlargements or their inverses. A congruence is an isomorphism of the integral lattice, and each enlargement preserves the class. This also handles every integral basis choice. Applied to a transported surface under an oriented ambient isotopy, the same surface-independence statement and the pairing convention give a function on oriented knot types. This part is proved without a slice-disk premise. [A1, F1, F2, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put representatives of $K,J$ and their chosen surfaces in separated balls, and join the surfaces by the connected-sum band away from the old basis curves. ## Statement

Assume AC. Every integer Milnor coefficient of a based string link is invariant
under smooth isotopy through string links fixing the endpoint collars. For
closed labeled oriented links, the residue candidate $\bar\mu_L(I)$ is invariant
under ambient isotopy. A link-homotopy is a finite sequence of ambient isotopies
and local crossing changes in which the two branches at every crossing change
belong to the same component. Under link-homotopy, $\bar\mu_L(I)$ is invariant
when the entries of $I$ are pairwise distinct. No invariance for repeated-index
sequences under link-homotopy is asserted.

## Statement references

[Milnor, *Link Groups*, §§4–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/milnorlink.pdf)

[Stees, §2.5](https://scholarworks.iu.edu/iuswrrest/api/core/bitstreams/54c7d68f-d982-4e1f-9550-e54140ada5ea/content)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the based peripheral data, and the definitions of the integer and residue coefficients.

[A1] Full AC, written AC, is [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] Based string-link coefficients are extracted from unique longitude classes in finite nilpotent quotients using the Magnus expansion. [[def-milnor-integer-and-residue-invariants]], [[thm-string-link-nilpotent-peripheral-identifications]]

[F2] Closed-link basing and self-crossing changes preserve the stated residues for pairwise-distinct indices. [[lem-milnor-basing-indeterminacy-and-self-crossing-scope]]

[F3] Ambient isotopy of oriented links carries exteriors, positive meridians, and peripheral tori to the corresponding data. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-based-string-link-and-labeled-link-peripheral-system]]

[L1] Full AC implies countable choice. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F4] Under countable choice, a smooth vector field along a closed embedded submanifold extends to a global smooth vector field. [[lem-a-vector-field-along-an-embedded-submanifold-extends-to-a-neighbourhood-and-globally-when-closed]]

[F5] A compact set in an open set of a smooth manifold admits a smooth cutoff equal to one near the compact set and supported in the open set. [[thm-smooth-urysohn-lemma-for-a-closed-set-in-an-open-set]]

[F6] A smooth time-dependent vector field with uniformly compact support has a global evolution on a compact time interval. [[thm-compactly-supported-time-dependent-vector-fields-have-global-evolution-on-a-compact-time-interval]]

## Proof

**Given:** The isotopy or link-homotopy described in the statement.

1.1 Let $\tau_t$ be the given smooth isotopy through string links, fixed on common endpoint collars. Reparametrize it to be stationary near $t=0,1$. Choose fixed disjoint smooth closure arcs outside $C=D^2\times[0,1]$, using the closure construction in the based-string-link definition, and adjoin them to the moving intervals. The result is a smooth family of closed links in $S^3$, constant on the closure arcs and endpoint collars; extend it constantly in time outside $[0,1]$. The map $\Theta:\mathbb R\times\bigsqcup_i S^1\to\mathbb R\times S^3$, $\Theta(t,s)=(t,\overline\tau_t(s))$, is an injective immersion and is proper: injectivity and immersion follow from the time coordinate and the embedding of each link slice, while the preimage of a compact set lies in a compact time interval times the finite union of circles. Thus its image is a closed embedded submanifold. The vector field $Y(t,\overline\tau_t(s))=(0,\partial_t\overline\tau_t(s))$ along this graph is smooth and vanishes on the fixed closure arcs and endpoint collars. Since the motion is confined to a compact subinterval of each string component away from its endpoint collars, choose a compact set $K\subset\operatorname{int}C$ containing every point where this velocity can be nonzero. By [A1] and [L1], [F4] extends $Y$ to a global smooth vector field on $\mathbb R\times S^3$. Let $X_t$ be its $S^3$ component. By [F5] choose $\chi:S^3\to[0,1]$ equal to one near $K$ and supported in $\operatorname{int}C$, and replace $X_t$ by $\chi X_t$. This field still equals the prescribed velocity along the entire closed link: it is unchanged wherever the velocity is nonzero and is zero on the stationary arcs. Its supports lie in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset\operatorname{int}C$. Integrate it by [F6]. Uniqueness of the flow gives an ambient isotopy $H_t$ with $H_t\overline\tau_0=\overline\tau_t$; its support in $\operatorname{int}C$ makes $H_t$ the identity near $\partial C$, so it preserves $C$ and fixes the endpoint collars, bottom basepoint, and side connector. This is the relative based isotopy-extension argument for string links. [A1, L1, F4, F5, F6, given, construct]

2.1 Restricting $H_1$ gives a based homeomorphism of string-link exteriors that transports the selected tubes, positive meridians, parallels, and access paths. It fixes the endpoint basepoints and side connector, so the two end inclusions commute with the induced based group isomorphisms. By [F1], the longitude has a unique preimage in each finite bottom-end quotient; naturality carries that preimage to the corresponding class for the isotopic string link. The Magnus expansion is the same homomorphism on the transported meridian symbols, so every integer coefficient agrees. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Under [A1], an ambient isotopy of closed links induces the peripheral correspondence in [F3]. Applying that correspondence to the based word-lift data gives the transported based residue candidate. The first assertion of [F2] proves independence of every meridian basing and finite longitude-word lift, with exactly equal lower-coefficient ideals. Applying it to the transported word data proves that the two closed-link residues agree in the same residue group. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Under [A1], a link-homotopy is generated by ambient isotopies and self-crossing changes. For pairwise-distinct indices, ambient isotopy is handled by step 3.1 and each self-crossing change is the second assertion of [F2]. Each move identifies the lower-coefficient ideals by [F2]; composing these finitely many equalities proves the asserted residue equality. No repeated-index conclusion is drawn. [A1, F2, step 3.1] ∎

By [F5] choose $\chi:S^3\to[0,1]$ equal to one near $K$ and supported in $\operatorname{int}C$, and replace $X_t$ by $\chi X_t$. This field still equals the prescribed velocity along the entire closed link: it is unchanged wherever the velocity is nonzero and is zero on the stationary arcs. Its supports lie in the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\chi\subset\operatorname{int}C$. Integrate it by [F6]. Uniqueness of the flow gives an ambient isotopy $H_t$ with $H_t\overline\tau_0=\overline\tau_t$; its support in $\operatorname{int}C$ makes $H_t$ the identity near $\partial C$, so it preserves $C$ and fixes the endpoint collars, bottom basepoint, and side connector. This is the relative based isotopy-extension argument for string links. [A1, L1, F4, F5, F6, given, construct]

1.2 Restricting $H_1$ gives a based homeomorphism of string-link exteriors that transports the selected tubes, positive meridians, parallels, and access paths. It fixes the endpoint basepoints and side connector, so the two end inclusions commute with the induced based group isomorphisms. By [F1], the longitude has a unique preimage in each finite bottom-end quotient; naturality carries that preimage to the corresponding class for the isotopic string link. The Magnus expansion is the same homomorphism on the transported meridian symbols, so every integer coefficient agrees. [A1, F1, step 1.1, construct]

2.1 Under [A1], an ambient isotopy of closed links induces the peripheral correspondence in [F3]. Applying that correspondence to the based word-lift data gives the transported based residue candidate. The first assertion of [F2] proves independence of every meridian basing and finite longitude-word lift, with exactly equal lower-coefficient ideals. Applying it to the transported word data proves that the two closed-link residues agree in the same residue group. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 Under [A1], a link-homotopy is generated by ambient isotopies and self-crossing changes. For pairwise-distinct indices, ambient isotopy is handled by step 2.1 and each self-crossing change is the second assertion of [F2]. Each move identifies the lower-coefficient ideals by [F2]; composing these finitely many equalities proves the asserted residue equality. No repeated-index conclusion is drawn. [A1, F2, step 2.1] ∎
