## Statement

Assume AC and the ACω Heegaard Floer analytic package. Let $D$ be any finite regular diagram of a nonempty oriented link $L\subset S^3$, with a marked point away from crossings. There is a spectral sequence over $\mathbb F_2$ associated to the link-surgery filtered complex for this fixed diagram whose $E_2$ page is isomorphic, with the normalized grading shifts of the chosen smoothing convention, to $\widetilde{Kh}(\overline L,p;\mathbb F_2)$ computed from the mirror diagram, and whose abutment is $\widehat{HF}(\Sigma(L);\mathbb F_2)$ with its image filtration. This is a fixed-diagram construction; it does not assert a diagram-independent filtered quasi-isomorphism type.

## Statement references

[[def-double-branched-cover-of-an-oriented-link|Branched cover convention]]

[[def-link-surgery-filtered-complex-for-double-branched-cover|Filtered link-surgery module]]

[[lem-link-surgery-e-one-differential-is-reduced-khovanov|E1 differential identification]]

[[lem-os-filtered-convergence-and-invariance-scope|Finite filtration convergence]]

[Ozsváth and Szabó, *On the Heegaard Floer homology of branched double-covers*, Theorem 6.3 and proof](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309170v1)

[Lipshitz, *Heegaard Floer Homologies*, §5.3](https://floer.wiki/more/courses/floer-homology/2024/lipshitz_heegaard_floer_homology.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, a nonempty oriented link diagram $D$ with a basepoint, and the stated ACω Floer disk and polygon theory.

[F1] The diagram determines the surgery cube of branched covers and its filtration ([[def-link-surgery-filtered-complex-for-double-branched-cover]]).

[F2] The surgery cube is a filtered chain complex with total homology identified with the hat Floer homology of the branched cover ([[lem-os-link-surgery-filtered-complex-and-triangle]], [[thm-hat-heegaard-floer-is-a-closed-three-manifold-invariant]]).

[F3] The first page and its differential identify with the reduced Khovanov cube of the mirror diagram ([[lem-link-surgery-e-one-differential-is-reduced-khovanov]]).

[F4] A finite filtration yields a convergent spectral sequence to the associated graded of the filtered homology ([[lem-os-filtered-convergence-and-invariance-scope]]).

## Proof

1.1 The crossing resolutions of $D$ give the vertices of the cube, and the surgery maps give the differential components. By [F2] these components square to zero and preserve the increasing cube filtration, so the associated spectral sequence is defined. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 The filtration has only the $n+1$ levels $0,\ldots,n$, where $n$ is the number of crossings. By [F4] the spectral sequence stabilizes and abuts to the image filtration on the total homology, which [F2] identifies with $\widehat{HF}(\Sigma(L);\mathbb F_2)$. [F2, F4, step 1.1]

2.2 The associated graded vertex groups form the $E_1$ page, and their first differential is the sum of the single-crossing edge maps. By [F3], this complex is isomorphic to the reduced Khovanov complex of the mirror diagram; taking its cohomology gives the stated $E_2$ page. [F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The proof used one fixed $D$ and the finite filtration only. It supplies no filtered map between the constructions for two diagrams, so it establishes the stated fixed-diagram spectral sequence but no diagram-independent filtered quasi-isomorphism. Here [F2] uses the explicitly external OS surgery construction and filling comparison, and [F3] uses its actual compatible unlink maps with the proved finite reduced-algebra binding. Those imports retain their stated scope; no missing geometric map is inferred from finite convergence. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For the Conway knot $C$ and Piccirillo partner $K_P$
fixed above, the zero-traces are diffeomorphic and
$$X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P),\qquad s(K_P)=2.$$
This statement concerns the zero-trace $4$-manifolds; it asserts no smooth
concordance between $C$ and $K_P$.

## Statement references

[Piccirillo, Proposition 1.4 and Theorem 1.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1808.02923)

[Hom, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.09171)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and the specified knots $C$ and $K_P$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice, written AC, is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[A2] AC implies dependent choice and hence countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; this supplies every retained local countable-choice hypothesis. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-piccirillo-diagram-produces-dualizable-handle-link]] constructs
under full AC one actual framed handlebody with zero-trace descriptions
$X_0(C)$ and $X_0(K_P)$. The fixed twelve-collar $M$–$N$ transport is retained
locally; its terminal identification with the literal Figure 2 knot is the
explicit published framed input in that supplier, not a newly replayed local
arc map.

[F2] [[lem-piccirillo-knot-lee-computations]] supplies the established exact
rational Lee calculation on the two specified diagrams, giving $s(C)=0$
and $s(K_P)=2$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], the two zero-traces are diffeomorphic to the same framed handlebody. Compose the first diffeomorphism with the inverse of the second to obtain $X_0(C)\cong X_0(K_P)$. The terminal identification is with the named Figure 2 knot, by the retained local construction and the explicit published terminal input in [F1]. [A1, F1, construct]

2.1 Apply [F2] to that specified diagram to obtain $s(K_P)=2$. Together with step 1.1 this gives both conclusions of the Statement. [A1, A2, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot, and let $p,q$ be coprime integers with $q\ne0$. For the Dehn filling $Y_{p/q}=E_K(p/q)$ whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-exterior|Chosen knot exterior]]

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude|Meridian and preferred longitude]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Filling slope convention]]

[[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris|First homology of knot fillings]]

[[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input|Noncyclic SU(2) representations for numerator-one slopes]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Dehn surgery, the fundamental group and SU(2)*, Theorem 1](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/hrpthree.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Knots, sutures and excision*, §7.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0807.4891)

[Motegi, *Dehn surgery on knots: survey*, pp. 19–21 and 26](https://www.math.tsukuba.ac.jp/~tange/diftop22/Dehn_surgery_survey.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, published Theorem 1, p. 741](https://doi.org/10.4310/mrl.2004.v11.n6.a3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nontrivial smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, and a nonmeridional slope $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$ and $q\ne0$.

[F1] The filling has $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$ for $p\ne0$, and $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $p=0$. [[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris]]

[F2] For a path-connected space, $H_1$ is naturally the abelianization of its fundamental group. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] If $|p|=1$ and $q\ne0$, the filling group admits a noncyclic homomorphism to $SU(2)$. The supplier derives this exact interface from the explicitly imported published Kronheimer–Mrowka Theorem 1, p. 741; its gauge-theoretic theorem is not claimed as locally reconstructed. [[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input]]

[F4] The filling is obtained by attaching a solid torus to $E_K$ along its entire boundary torus, with meridian identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]

[F5] The chosen exterior is the complement of the interior of the closed tubular disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, with boundary $T_K=\partial N(K)$. [[def-knot-exterior]]

[A1] Full AC is the assertion that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[L1] Applying [A1] to the set of members of any countable family gives the countable choice function required by [F1]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F5], the chosen tubular neighbourhood is a disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, so its boundary $T_K$ is a circle bundle over $K$ with connected fibres and is connected. Indeed, a separation of $T_K$ would, since every fibre is connected, split it into two saturated open sets; their projections are open by the local bundle charts, disjoint, and cover the connected base $K$. Since $T_K$ is a connected smooth manifold, it is path-connected. The exterior $E_K$ is a compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary $T_K$. Because $T_K$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_K$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_K$ and $E_K$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F5]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus $E_K$ is connected and, being a smooth manifold, path-connected. By [F4], $Y_{p/q}$ is the union of this path-connected exterior and an attached path-connected solid torus along $T_K$, so $Y_{p/q}$ is path-connected. [given, F4, F5, construct]

1.2 If $|p|=1$, the nonmeridional condition gives $q\ne0$, and [F3] supplies a homomorphism with noncyclic image. The trivial group has only the trivial, hence cyclic, image, so $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial. [given, F3, algebra]

2.1 By [A1] and [L1], the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] follows from the Statement, and step 1.1 verifies its connected-exterior hypothesis. If $p=0$, [F1] gives $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. If $|p|\ge2$, it gives the nonzero finite group $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$. Choose any basepoint $y_0$ of the path-connected filling. By [F2], $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\pi_1(Y_{p/q},y_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}$, so in either case the fundamental group is nontrivial. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Coprimality leaves exactly the cases $p=0$, $|p|=1$, or $|p|\ge2$, all covered by steps 2.1 and 1.2. Thus every nonmeridional filling has nontrivial fundamental group. [given, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## External dependency

The numerator-one case uses the external Kronheimer–Mrowka theorem through [F3], with its exact hypotheses and reading limits recorded in that supplier. The homology cases and the deduction of nontriviality from a noncyclic image are the local argument above.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot, and let $p,q$ be coprime integers with $q\ne0$. For the Dehn filling $Y_{p/q}=E_K(p/q)$ whose attached solid-torus meridian is identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the fundamental group $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial.

## Statement references

[[def-knot-exterior|Chosen knot exterior]]

[[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude|Meridian and preferred longitude]]

[[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling|Filling slope convention]]

[[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris|First homology of knot fillings]]

[[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input|Noncyclic SU(2) representations for numerator-one slopes]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Dehn surgery, the fundamental group and SU(2)*, Theorem 1](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/hrpthree.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, *Knots, sutures and excision*, §7.8](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0807.4891)

[Motegi, *Dehn surgery on knots: survey*, pp. 19–21 and 26](https://www.math.tsukuba.ac.jp/~tange/diftop22/Dehn_surgery_survey.pdf)

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, published Theorem 1, p. 741](https://doi.org/10.4310/mrl.2004.v11.n6.a3)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a nontrivial smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, and a nonmeridional slope $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ with $\gcd(p,q)=1$ and $q\ne0$.

[F1] The filling has $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$ for $p\ne0$, and $H_1(E_K(p/q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ for $p=0$. [[lem-knot-surgery-first-homology-mayer-vietoris]]

[F2] For a path-connected space, $H_1$ is naturally the abelianization of its fundamental group. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

[F3] If $|p|=1$ and $q\ne0$, the filling group admits a noncyclic homomorphism to $SU(2)$. The supplier derives this exact interface from the explicitly imported published Kronheimer–Mrowka Theorem 1, p. 741; its gauge-theoretic theorem is not claimed as locally reconstructed. [[lem-property-p-instanton-surgery-triangle-and-rank-input]]

[F4] The filling is obtained by attaching a solid torus to $E_K$ along its entire boundary torus, with meridian identified with $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$. [[def-oriented-slope-and-knot-dehn-filling]]

[F5] The chosen exterior is the complement of the interior of the closed tubular disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, with boundary $T_K=\partial N(K)$. [[def-knot-exterior]]

[A1] Full AC is the assertion that every set-indexed family of nonempty sets has a choice function. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[L1] Applying [A1] to the set of members of any countable family gives the countable choice function required by [F1]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F5], the chosen tubular neighbourhood is a disk bundle over the connected knot $K$, so its boundary $T_K$ is a circle bundle over $K$ with connected fibres and is connected. Indeed, a separation of $T_K$ would, since every fibre is connected, split it into two saturated open sets; their projections are open by the local bundle charts, disjoint, and cover the connected base $K$. Since $T_K$ is a connected smooth manifold, it is path-connected. The exterior $E_K$ is a compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary $T_K$. Because $T_K$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_K$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_K$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_K$ and $E_K$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F5]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus $E_K$ is connected and, being a smooth manifold, path-connected. By [F4], $Y_{p/q}$ is the union of this path-connected exterior and an attached path-connected solid torus along $T_K$, so $Y_{p/q}$ is path-connected. [given, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 By [A1] and [L1], the countable-choice hypothesis of [F1] follows from the Statement, and step 1.1 verifies its connected-exterior hypothesis. If $p=0$, [F1] gives $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$. If $|p|\ge2$, it gives the nonzero finite group $\mathbb Z/|p|\mathbb Z$. Choose any basepoint $y_0$ of the path-connected filling. By [F2], $H_1(Y_{p/q};\mathbb Z)\cong\pi_1(Y_{p/q},y_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}$, so in either case the fundamental group is nontrivial. [given, A1, L1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $|p|=1$, the nonmeridional condition gives $q\ne0$, and [F3] supplies a homomorphism with noncyclic image. The trivial group has only the trivial, hence cyclic, image, so $\pi_1(Y_{p/q})$ is nontrivial. [given, F3, algebra]

4.1 Coprimality leaves exactly the cases $p=0$, $|p|=1$, or $|p|\ge2$, all covered by steps 2.1 and 3.1. Thus every nonmeridional filling has nontrivial fundamental group. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## External dependency

The numerator-one case uses the external Kronheimer–Mrowka theorem through [F3], with its exact hypotheses and reading limits recorded in that supplier. The homology cases and the deduction of nontriviality from a noncyclic image are the local argument above.

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth framing statements. Let $R$ be a rack and let $\pi(x)=x*x$ be its kink map. Rack-coloring sets
are in bijection across every oriented R2 or R3 move and planar isotopy.
Across a single oriented R1 curl, the label transported along the affected
strand changes by $\pi$ or $\pi^{-1}$ according to the curl orientation.
Consequently, an opposite-kink pair on the same component whose two signed framing changes cancel
induces a bijection on colorings. A single unframed R1 move has a unique
extension for every boundary color exactly when $\pi$ is the identity, which
is the quandle idempotency axiom. Thus finite rack coloring counts are
invariant under R2, R3, planar isotopy, and framing-preserving opposite-kink
compensation; the unframed R1 move is covered when the rack is a quandle.

## Statement references

[[def-rack-fundamental-quandle-and-adjoint-group]].

[[lem-rack-kink-map-is-bijective]].

[[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]].

[[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]].

[[def-framed-knot-self-linking-and-seifert-framing]].

[Nelson, *Link invariants from finite racks*, §§2.1–2.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0808.0029).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rack $R$, its kink map $\pi$, the positive-normal crossing convention, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ when smooth framings are used.

[F1] [[def-rack-fundamental-quandle-and-adjoint-group]]: every right translation is bijective, right self-distributivity holds, and the coloring relation uses the overarc action.

[F2] [[lem-rack-kink-map-is-bijective]]: the map $\pi(x)=x*x$ is bijective with inverse $\pi^{-1}(z)=R_z^{-1}(z)$.

[F3] [[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]: oriented R2 and R3 moves have all local orientation and height-order variants.

[F4] The crossing sign is $\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$; blackboard self-linking equals self-writhe. Therefore an R1 creation with sign $\epsilon$ changes blackboard self-linking by $\epsilon$. [[def-oriented-crossing-sign-writhe-and-blackboard-framing]], [[thm-blackboard-framing-self-linking-is-writhe]]

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only for the supplied smooth-framing/self-linking results. [[def-countable-choice]]

## Proof

1.1 At an R2 move, hold the overarc color $y$ fixed. The underarc label is changed by $R_y$ at one crossing and by $R_y^{-1}$ at the other, so the two boundary colorings determine one another uniquely. Reversing the move gives the inverse correspondence. [F1, F3]

1.2 For a braid-like R3 move, use the crossing map $B(x,y)=(y,x*y)$. Its inverse is $B^{-1}(u,v)=(v\mathbin{\bar *}u,u)$ by right invertibility. The two sides send $(x,y,z)$ respectively to $(z,y*z,(x*y)*z)$ and $(z,y*z,(x*z)*(y*z))$; the last coordinates agree by rack self-distributivity. For every $z$, $R_z(x*y)=(x*y)*z=(x*z)*(y*z)$, so $R_z$ preserves $*$. If $u=a\mathbin{\bar *}b$, then $u*b=a$; applying $R_z$ gives $R_z(u)*R_z(b)=R_z(a)$, and uniqueness of right division yields $R_z(u)=R_z(a)\mathbin{\bar *}R_z(b)$. Thus $R_z$ and its inverse preserve both operations. For either operation $\star_1,\star_2\in\{*,\bar *\}$, this gives $(x\star_1 y)\star_2 z=(x\star_2 z)\star_1(y\star_2 z)$, the corresponding mixed R3 equation. The bijective crossing maps then give the extension bijection for every orientation variant. A planar isotopy transports arc labels. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 Write the under-tangent as $a v_{\rm over}+b n_o$. Its determinant sign is the sign of $b$, so at a positive crossing the oriented underpass goes from source to target. In a positive curl with incoming label $x$ and outgoing label $y$, either the overarc is the incoming arc and $y=x*x$, or it is the outgoing arc and $y=x*y$. In the latter case self-distributivity gives $R_yR_x=R_{x*y}R_y=R_yR_y$, hence $R_x=R_y$; therefore $y=x*y=x*x=\pi(x)$. Conversely $y=\pi(x)$ solves the equation since $R_{\pi(x)}=R_x$ by the kink-map proof. Thus both positive curl shapes have unique transport $y=\pi(x)$. In a negative curl the same equations are read backwards and give $y=\pi^{-1}(x)$. This checks both choices of which boundary arc is the overarc, independently of a picture. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.4 For a single unframed curl with boundary color $x$, extension requires $x=\pi(x)$; if $\pi$ is the identity, this condition holds uniquely for every $x$. Conversely, if every boundary color extends uniquely, every $x$ is fixed by $\pi$, so $x*x=x$ for all $x$ and the rack is a quandle. [F1, F2, F3]

1.5 The kink shift propagates through any crossing. Self-distributivity gives $\pi(x*y)=(x*y)*(x*y)=(x*x)*y$, hence $\pi R_y=R_y\pi$. It also gives $(x*y)*y=(x*y)*(y*y)$ for every $x$. Since $R_y$ is surjective, this implies $R_{\pi(y)}=R_y$. By [F2], $\pi$ is bijective, so these identities hold for its inverse as well: $\pi^kR_y^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}\pi^k$ and $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}^{\delta}=R_y^{\delta}$ for all $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$ and $\delta\in\{1,-1\}$. In particular, if a crossing obeys $x_t=R_y(x_s)$, independently shifting its two under-colors by the same $\pi^k$ and its over-color by $\pi^{\ell}$ preserves it, because $R_{\pi^{\ell}(y)}(\pi^k x_s)=\pi^kR_y(x_s)=\pi^k x_t$. The reversed crossing relation is preserved by the same calculation with $R_y^{-1}$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A compensated pair creates two curls on the same oriented component, or removes their inverse configuration. If its blackboard framing is preserved, [F4] forces the two created crossing signs to sum to zero; the same holds when opposite signed framing changes are specified directly. Choose either of the two component intervals between the sites and traverse it in the component orientation, writing $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ for the sign of its first curl; the second has sign $-\epsilon$. Starting from an old coloring, retain every color off this interval and replace every old color on it by $\pi^{\epsilon}$ of that color, splitting an old under-arc at the two sites if needed. Insert the unique local curl labels from step1.3. At the first site the transport changes the old incoming label to its $\pi^{\epsilon}$-shift; at the second the transport $\pi^{-\epsilon}$ restores the old outgoing label. Thus the prescribed labels agree along every new maximal under-arc. [A1, F2, F4, step 1.3, construct]

3.1 At any old crossing, the selected component interval contains both local halves of the underpassing branch or neither, since its endpoints are away from crossings. Thus the source and target under-colors have the same shift exponent $k\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Independently the overpassing branch has shift exponent $\ell\in\{0,\epsilon\}$. Step1.5 preserves the crossing relation for all four possibilities, including a self-crossing at which the interval contains exactly one of the two visits. The old crossing relations therefore all hold after the recoloring. Conversely, start with any coloring of the twice-curled diagram, undo the $\pi^{\epsilon}$ shift on that same marked component interval, and remove the two uniquely determined curl portions using step1.3; step1.5 again preserves every intervening relation. The endpoint transports now cancel in the inverse order. These constructions are inverse on every arc label, so give the required bijection for arbitrarily separated opposite curls, not only adjacent curls. The removal move uses the inverse bijection. [F1, F2, step 1.3, step 1.5, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Steps 1.1–1.2 give the R2, R3 and planar-isotopy bijections; steps 2.1, 3.1 give the compensation bijection. A finite rack admits only finitely many assignments on a finite diagram, so the cardinalities are preserved. Step 1.4 proves exactly when the individual unframed R1 bijection is available. The algebraic assertions use no choice; only the smooth framing interpretation uses [A1]. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Sources

[[def-rack-fundamental-quandle-and-adjoint-group]].

[[lem-rack-kink-map-is-bijective]].

[[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]].

## Statement

Assume full AC. Fix even $p\ge4$, a primitive $2p$-th root $A$, and the BHMV Kauffman bracket convention with $\delta=-A^2-A^{-2}$. On the weighted Lagrangian extended bordism category built from the root semisimplified Temperley–Lieb data, the normalized Kirby-color surgery maps define a finite-dimensional skein TQFT: the handlebody state spaces are the radical quotients of their skein modules, gluing is given by the inverse normalized handlebody pairing, and the resulting closed value is unchanged under isotopy, framed handle slides, and split $\pm1$-blow-ups. Forgetting the weight and Lagrangian extension yields only the projective ordinary-oriented data unless a separate anomaly-cancellation result is proved.

## Statement references

[[def-sl-two-root-of-unity-skein-parameter|Root and bracket conventions]]

[[def-extended-skein-cobordism-anomaly-data|Weighted Lagrangian extension and anomaly data]]

[[def-skein-tqft-state-space-and-handlebody-pairing|State spaces]]

[[lem-root-skein-surgery-kirby-color-invariance|Kirby-color surgery maps]]

[[lem-root-handlebody-pairing-nondegeneracy-and-gluing|Pairing and gluing identities]]

[[thm-kirby-moves-classify-framed-link-presentations|Framed surgery presentations and move classification]]

[Blanchet, Habegger, Masbaum, and Vogel, *Topological Quantum Field Theories Derived from the Kauffman Bracket*, Theorem 1.4 and §§1–5](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/bhmv.pdf)

[Kauffman and Lins, *Temperley-Lieb Recoupling Theory and Invariants of 3-Manifolds*, Chapters 7 and 12](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1bgzb7v)

[Pohorence, *3-manifold Invariants and TQFTs*, §§1.2 and 3](https://categorified.net/RTinvariants/Jan29-Feb3.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the fixed BHMV root and pivotal convention, weighted Lagrangian bordism data, the root state spaces and their surgery maps.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] supplies the full choice assumption used by the surgery-presentation and Kirby-move supplier.

[F1] [[thm-kirby-moves-classify-framed-link-presentations]]: framed surgery diagrams for the same closed oriented manifold are connected by the stated isotopies, framed handle slides, and split signed-unit-unknot moves.

[F2] [[lem-root-skein-surgery-kirby-color-invariance]] supplies the closed surgery invariance, nonzero Gauss sums and precise external BHMV weighted normalization, including weight unit $\kappa^3$.

[F3] [[lem-root-handlebody-pairing-nondegeneracy-and-gluing]] supplies the perfect radical-quotient pairing, finite inverse sewing tensor and externally specified weighted gluing.

[F4] [[def-weighted-lagrangian-ribbon-bordism]] supplies associative weighted Lagrangian composition with the Wall-signature Maslov correction.

## Proof

**Given:** The data in the Statement.

1.1 For a fixed surgery presentation, the color set is finite and the state-space pairing is defined by a finite bracket evaluation. This constructs a candidate linear map for each presented weighted bordism. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Any two presented closed surgery links are related by [F1], and [F2] preserves their values under every move. For bordisms, use the BHMV additional $\eta^{b_0+b_1}$ normalization specified in the state-space Definition, not the raw closed invariant alone. The finite state spaces, perfect pairing and actual surgery/sewing maps are [F3], whose external BHMV/Gilmer–Masbaum input supplies the TQFT construction at the exact even root and complex specialization. The inverse-pairing contraction composes these maps, with the integer Wall/Maslov weight law [F4]. This proves finite-dimensionality, gluing and presentation invariance of the stated weighted theory. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Forgetting the weight removes the scalar that corrects the Maslov/signature defect. Therefore the imported construction descends only projectively to ordinary oriented data without a further anomaly-cancellation input. No such additional theorem is asserted here. Full AC remains the declared branch of the presentation/marked category interfaces; finite color sums add no stronger assumption. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1] ∎

    - title: "Seiya Negami and Kazuo Okita, The Splittability and Triviality of 3-Bridge Links"

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For any two smooth oriented knots $K$ and $J$ in $S^3$, the bridge number of their oriented connected sum satisfies
$$b(K\#J)=b(K)+b(J)-1.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|Bridge number from local maxima of the fixed height]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and smooth oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written AC$_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The bridge-number minima are over nonempty subsets of $\mathbb N$ and are attained, and changing the connected-sum datum preserves the oriented knot class. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[F2] The connected sum is represented by removing a small trivial ball-arc neighborhood from each summand and gluing the two boundary spheres with the fixed arc-matching convention. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F3] The essential-annulus normalization for the fixed bridge pair is [[lem-bridge-sphere-normalization]]. Its two final disk-intersection arcs end on $P\cap S$, away from the knot.

[F4] A knot exterior has $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]

[F5] Knot exteriors are irreducible under countable choice, and an incompressible boundary-compressible annulus in an irreducible smooth torus-boundary manifold is boundary-parallel. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], [[lem-boundary-compressible-annulus-is-boundary-parallel]]

[F6] Smooth Schoenflies gives an ambient isotopy of a smooth sphere to the equator with compatible ball-side parameters. Disk-window attachment and removal preserve the displayed ball type. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F7] Compact smooth embedding isotopies extend ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F8] A two-puncture sphere determines the stated oriented connected-sum factors by boundary caps; the unknot is the connected-sum identity and has bridge number one. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]], [[thm-bridge-one-is-unknot]]

## Proof

1.1 We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$. [A1, F1, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks. [A1, F1, step 1.1, choose]

2.2 If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective. [F1, F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors. [F3, F5, F6, F8, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Their collars give compatible markings. Let $S_1,S_2$ be the disks on $S$ bounded by $C$, labelled by the two sides of $P$, and put $r_i=|L\cap S_i|$. Then $r_1+r_2=2b$. In each original bridge ball exactly one bridge arc crosses $P_\pm$: it is the arc carrying its unique puncture. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd. [F3, F6, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

5.1 Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Thus these are simultaneous disjoint spanning-disk systems. The upper and lower ambient pieces are balls: attach the cap half-balls along the displayed windows on $P_\pm$ and use [F6]. We have therefore constructed actual bridge spheres for the two specified oriented factors, not merely diagrams with a proposed number of bridges. Each has $r_i+1$ knot endpoints on its sphere, the extra endpoint being the single crossing of the cap. It follows that their upper arc counts are $n_i=(r_i+1)/2$, and $n_1+n_2=b+1$. Cap orientation is chosen to close the original oriented arc, so [F8] identifies the factors with $K,J$, up to their harmless interchange. [F3, F6, F8, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 3.1 and the unknot case in step 2.2, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The constructions use finitely many extrema, disks, cuts and collars; their smooth extension and Schoenflies uses are precisely the stated countable-choice suppliers. [F1, F8, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The schematic shows the local gluing at one bridge-sphere endpoint. The two selected upper disks join along a boundary strip to one upper disk, and the lower pair joins in the same way. The drawing records only the local count reduction by one; the lower-bound proof does not rely on it.

  \fill (-1.2,0) circle (2pt);
  \fill (1.2,0) circle (2pt);
  \draw[thick] (-1.2,0) .. controls (-1.1,1.2) and (-0.2,1.2) .. (0,0.5);
  \draw[thick] (1.2,0) .. controls (1.1,1.2) and (0.2,1.2) .. (0,0.5);
  \draw[thick] (-1.2,0) .. controls (-1.1,-1.2) and (-0.2,-1.2) .. (0,-0.5);
  \draw[thick] (1.2,0) .. controls (1.1,-1.2) and (0.2,-1.2) .. (0,-0.5);
  \draw[<->] (-0.5,1.55)--(0.5,1.55) node[midway,above] {glue};
  \node[above] at (-2,0.8) {one upper arc};

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For any two smooth oriented knots $K$ and $J$ in $S^3$, the bridge number of their oriented connected sum satisfies
$$b(K\#J)=b(K)+b(J)-1.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number|Bridge number from local maxima of the fixed height]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot|The oriented connected-sum convention]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC$_\omega$ and smooth oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$.

[A1] The Axiom of Countable Choice, written AC$_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The bridge-number minima are over nonempty subsets of $\mathbb N$ and are attained, and changing the connected-sum datum preserves the oriented knot class. [[def-knot-bridge-position-and-unknotting-number]], [[lem-knot-connected-sum-well-defined]]

[F2] The connected sum is represented by removing a small trivial ball-arc neighborhood from each summand and gluing the two boundary spheres with the fixed arc-matching convention. [[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

[F3] The essential-annulus normalization for the fixed bridge pair is [[lem-bridge-sphere-normalization]]. Its two final disk-intersection arcs end on $P\cap S$, away from the knot.

[F4] A knot exterior has $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$. [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]]

[F5] Knot exteriors are irreducible under countable choice, and an incompressible boundary-compressible annulus in an irreducible smooth torus-boundary manifold is boundary-parallel. [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], [[lem-boundary-compressible-annulus-is-boundary-parallel]]

[F6] Smooth Schoenflies gives an ambient isotopy of a smooth sphere to the equator with compatible ball-side parameters. Disk-window attachment and removal preserve the displayed ball type. [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F7] Compact smooth embedding isotopies extend ambiently. [[thm-isotopy-extension]]

[F8] A two-puncture sphere determines the stated oriented connected-sum factors by boundary caps; the unknot is the connected-sum identity and has bridge number one. [[lem-knot-decomposing-sphere-realizes-connected-sum]], [[thm-oriented-knot-connected-sum-is-a-commutative-monoid]], [[thm-bridge-one-is-unknot]]

## Proof

1.1 We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$. [A1, F1, F6, F7, construct]

1.2 Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks. [A1, F1, step 1.1, choose]

2.1 Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective. [F1, F2, F4, F8, step 1.1, construct]

3.2 There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors. [F3, F5, F6, F8, step 3.1, construct]

4.1 In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Their collars give compatible markings. Let $S_1,S_2$ be the disks on $S$ bounded by $C$, labelled by the two sides of $P$, and put $r_i=|L\cap S_i|$. Then $r_1+r_2=2b$. In each original bridge ball exactly one bridge arc crosses $P_\pm$: it is the arc carrying its unique puncture. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd. [F3, F6, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

4.2 Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Thus these are simultaneous disjoint spanning-disk systems. The upper and lower ambient pieces are balls: attach the cap half-balls along the displayed windows on $P_\pm$ and use [F6]. We have therefore constructed actual bridge spheres for the two specified oriented factors, not merely diagrams with a proposed number of bridges. Each has $r_i+1$ knot endpoints on its sphere, the extra endpoint being the single crossing of the cap. It follows that their upper arc counts are $n_i=(r_i+1)/2$, and $n_1+n_2=b+1$. Cap orientation is chosen to close the original oriented arc, so [F8] identifies the factors with $K,J$, up to their harmless interchange. [F3, F6, F8, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 2.1 and the unknot case in step 3.1, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The constructions use finitely many extrema, disks, cuts and collars; their smooth extension and Schoenflies uses are precisely the stated countable-choice suppliers. [F1, F8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

## Diagram

The schematic shows the local gluing at one bridge-sphere endpoint. The two selected upper disks join along a boundary strip to one upper disk, and the lower pair joins in the same way. The drawing records only the local count reduction by one; the lower-bound proof does not rely on it.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary orientation equal to that of $K$, let $g$ satisfy $\chi(F)=1-2g$, and choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Use the positive normal convention $(n,u,v)>0$ and define $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $A_K=H_1(\widetilde X_K;\mathbb Z)$ be the one-variable Alexander module of the knot complement $X_K=S^3\setminus K$, where the cover is classified by the total-linking homomorphism and $t$ acts by the deck transformation corresponding to the positive meridian. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$-modules
$$A_K\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(V-tV^T:\Lambda^{2g}\to\Lambda^{2g}\bigr).$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix|The positive-push Seifert matrix]]

[[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link|The total-linking cover and positive deck action]]

[[lem-knot-infinite-cyclic-cover-cut-and-paste-presentation|The cut-open cover matrix convention]]

[[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring|The coefficient ring $\Lambda$]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a smooth oriented knot $K$, a connected compact smooth oriented spanning surface $F$, an integral homology basis, and the positive-push convention.

[A1] Full AC implies the countable-choice hypothesis used by the tubular-neighborhood and surface normal-form suppliers, and is the stated hypothesis of Alexander duality and the one-variable module convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]

[F1] The knot normal bundle admits an orientation-preserving framing, and a tubular map gives a compact exterior $E$ whose inclusion into $X_K=S^3\setminus K$ is a homotopy equivalence. [[lem-knot-normal-circle-bundle-trivialization]], [[lem-knot-tubular-exterior-and-boundary]], [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]], [[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]

[F2] The positive meridian generates $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$, and the boundary longitude is the unique degree-one class in the kernel of its map into the exterior. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]]

[F3] For a tube compatible with the surface collar, the cut-open cover has Alexander-module presentation $V-tV^T$ under the stated positive seam and linking-dual convention. [[lem-knot-infinite-cyclic-cover-cut-and-paste-presentation]]

[F4] The one-variable module is $H_1$ of the connected cover classified by the kernel of total linking, with $t$ acting by the deck transformation for $+1$; the positive meridian maps to $+1$. [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F5] Connected covers are classified by subgroups of $\pi_1$, normal kernels give regular covers with quotient deck group, and degree-one Hurewicz identifies total linking on $H_1$ with the corresponding homomorphism on $\pi_1$. [[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]], [[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]], [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

1.1 **Choose a tube adapted to $F$.** The smooth boundary collar of $F$ gives $c:K\times[0,\delta)\to F$ with $c(s,0)=s$; in local ambient charts extend it smoothly a small distance to negative collar parameter, shrinking it so its image stays in the domain of a tubular chart $\Phi_0$ from [F1]. Let $\pi$ be the chart's projection to the zero section. The map $$\Psi:K\times(-\delta,\delta)\to K\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Psi(s,r)=(\pi(c(s,r)),r)$$ is two-dimensional. At $r=0$, its derivative in the $(s,r)$ variables has block form $\begin{pmatrix}1&*\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so it is invertible. The inverse function theorem makes $\Psi$ a local diffeomorphism near $K\times\{0\}$. After shrinking $\delta$, each circle map $s\mapsto\pi(c(s,r))$ is $C^1$-close to the identity and hence a degree-one local diffeomorphism of the circle; it is therefore a diffeomorphism. Thus $\Psi$ is a diffeomorphism on the smaller collar, and reparameterizing by it writes the extended collar as a graph $q(s,r)$ in the normal disks, with $q(s,0)=0$ and $\partial_rq(s,0)=u(s)$, the inward conormal. Use the oriented framing in [F1] with $u(s)$ as first vector and a transverse vector $v(s)$ as second. The map $(s,r,z)\mapsto\Phi_0(s,q(s,r)+zv(s))$ has invertible derivative along the zero section and agrees with $c(s,r)$ for $z=0,r\ge0$. The inverse function theorem gives local coordinates; compactness gives a common radius, and after shrinking, distinct fibers do not collide. Reparameterizing each fiber disk by these coordinates yields an embedded tubular map for which the surface is exactly the radial half-collar $z=0,r\ge0$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

2.1 Let $E$ be the compact exterior of this adapted tube and $S=F\cap E$. Then $S$ is properly embedded and its boundary on $\partial E$ projects once positively to $K$, because it is the outer edge of the inward boundary collar. It bounds $S$ in $E$, so its homology class maps to zero in $H_1(E)$. By [F2] it is the unique degree-one class in that kernel, hence the preferred longitude. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 The cut-open cover supplied by [F3] has first homology the cokernel of $V-tV^T$ over $\Lambda$, with $t$ moving in the positive-meridian direction. [F3, step 2.1, given]

4.1 Let $X_K=S^3\setminus K$. By [F1], inclusion $E\hookrightarrow X_K$ is a homotopy equivalence, so it induces an isomorphism on $H_1$ and on $\pi_1$ (the latter up to basepoint conjugacy). Naturality of Alexander duality and [F2], [F4] show that the total-linking homomorphism on $X_K$ restricts to the positive-meridian homomorphism on $E$: both send the same positive meridian to $+1$. Therefore the two homomorphisms on fundamental groups have corresponding kernels under the induced $\pi_1$ isomorphism. By [F5], the connected covers classified by these kernels are isomorphic as covers, and the isomorphism sends the deck transformation for $+1$ to the deck transformation for $+1$. It consequently induces an isomorphism of their $\Lambda$-modules on first homology. The cut-open cover module in step 3.1 is thus exactly the one-variable Alexander module $A_K$, proving the displayed isomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 3.1, given] ∎

## Remarks

The tube is chosen only to realize the cut-and-stack construction; the resulting module is identified with the cover of the open complement in step 4.1. The formula uses the stated positive meridian as $t$ and the positive normal in $V_{ij}$.

[[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]], [[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]], [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]

## Proof

1.1 **Choose a tube adapted to $F$.** The smooth boundary collar of $F$ gives $c:K\times[0,\delta)\to F$ with $c(s,0)=s$; in local ambient charts extend it smoothly a small distance to negative collar parameter, shrinking it so its image stays in the domain of a tubular chart $\Phi_0$ from [F1]. Let $\pi$ be the chart's projection to the zero section. The map
$$\Psi:K\times(-\delta,\delta)\to K\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Psi(s,r)=(\pi(c(s,r)),r)$$
is two-dimensional. At $r=0$, its derivative in the $(s,r)$ variables has block form $\begin{pmatrix}1&*\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so it is invertible. The inverse function theorem makes $\Psi$ a local diffeomorphism near $K\times\{0\}$. After shrinking $\delta$, each circle map $s\mapsto\pi(c(s,r))$ is $C^1$-close to the identity and hence a degree-one local diffeomorphism of the circle; it is therefore a diffeomorphism. Thus $\Psi$ is a diffeomorphism on the smaller collar, and reparameterizing by it writes the extended collar as a graph $q(s,r)$ in the normal disks, with $q(s,0)=0$ and $\partial_rq(s,0)=u(s)$, the inward conormal. Use the oriented framing in [F1] with $u(s)$ as first vector and a transverse vector $v(s)$ as second. The map $(s,r,z)\mapsto\Phi_0(s,q(s,r)+zv(s))$ has invertible derivative along the zero section and agrees with $c(s,r)$ for $z=0,r\ge0$. The inverse function theorem gives local coordinates; compactness gives a common radius, and after shrinking, distinct fibers do not collide. Reparameterizing each fiber disk by these coordinates yields an embedded tubular map for which the surface is exactly the radial half-collar $z=0,r\ge0$. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 Let $E$ be the compact exterior of this adapted tube and $S=F\cap E$. Then $S$ is properly embedded and its boundary on $\partial E$ projects once positively to $K$, because it is the outer edge of the inward boundary collar. It bounds $S$ in $E$, so its homology class maps to zero in $H_1(E)$. By [F2] it is the unique degree-one class in that kernel, hence the preferred longitude. Thus the hypotheses of [F3] hold. [F2, F3, step 1.1, given, construct]

2.1 The cut-open cover supplied by [F3] has first homology the cokernel of $V-tV^T$ over $\Lambda$, with $t$ moving in the positive-meridian direction. [F3, step 1.2, given]

3.1 Let $X_K=S^3\setminus K$. By [F1], inclusion $E\hookrightarrow X_K$ is a homotopy equivalence, so it induces an isomorphism on $H_1$ and on $\pi_1$ (the latter up to basepoint conjugacy). Naturality of Alexander duality and [F2], [F4] show that the total-linking homomorphism on $X_K$ restricts to the positive-meridian homomorphism on $E$: both send the same positive meridian to $+1$. Therefore the two homomorphisms on fundamental groups have corresponding kernels under the induced $\pi_1$ isomorphism. By [F5], the connected covers classified by these kernels are isomorphic as covers, and the isomorphism sends the deck transformation for $+1$ to the deck transformation for $+1$. It consequently induces an isomorphism of their $\Lambda$-modules on first homology. The cut-open cover module in step 2.1 is thus exactly the one-variable Alexander module $A_K$, proving the displayed isomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, given] ∎

## Remarks

The tube is chosen only to realize the cut-and-stack construction; the resulting module is identified with the cover of the open complement in step 3.1. The formula uses the stated positive meridian as $t$ and the positive normal in $V_{ij}$.

## Statement

Assume full AC. The stable isometry class of the Seifert quadratic enhancement and its Arf value are independent of the spanning surface and integral symplectic basis of an oriented knot $K$. Stable isometry means isometry after orthogonally adjoining finitely many hyperbolic planes $q_H(s,t)=st$ on either side. Under the convention $\Delta_K(t)=\nabla_K(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})$ with $\Delta_K(1)=1$, the coefficient $a_2(\nabla_K)$ of $z^2$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{Arf}(K)\equiv a_2(\nabla_K)\pmod2.$$

## Statement references

[[def-knot-arf-invariant-from-seifert-form|The Seifert quadratic enhancement and Arf definition]]

[[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization|The Conway and symmetric Alexander conventions]]

[[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant|The determinant realization and skein relation]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC and a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$.

[A1] Full AC supplies the Alexander and Seifert-pairing conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Any two spanning-surface Seifert matrices are S-equivalent. [[lem-seifert-matrices-of-a-knot-are-s-equivalent]]

[F2] The quadratic enhancement is well-defined, has basis-independent Arf value, and each enlargement orthogonally adds a hyperbolic plane up to isometry; hence its stable isometry class and Arf value are unchanged. [[lem-arf-quadratic-enhancement-from-seifert-form]]

[F3] The normalized Conway determinant is independent of surface and basis and has the declared skein normalization. [[lem-conway-polynomial-from-seifert-determinant]]

[F4] In the symmetric normalized variable, $\Delta_K^\#(t)=\nabla_K(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})$. [[def-seifert-s-equivalence-and-conway-normalization]]

[F5] The Seifert determinant near $t=-1$ is $1+\operatorname{Arf}(K)(1+t)^2/t$ modulo $(2,(1+t)^4)$. [[lem-arf-seifert-determinant-congruence-near-minus-one]]

## Proof

1.1 By [F1], matrices from any two spanning surfaces are connected by congruences and elementary enlargements. Congruence transports the quadratic form by an isometry, while the explicit hyperbolic-pair splitting in [F2] preserves its stable isometry class and Arf value through each enlargement or reduction. Composing these finitely many operations proves independence of the stable class and the Arf value from surface and basis. The unstabilized quadratic spaces themselves can have different dimensions: a disk for the unknot has dimension zero, whereas attaching an ordinary tube gives a genus-one spanning surface with a two-dimensional hyperbolic enhancement. Thus stable isometry is the required surface-independent assertion. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Write $\nabla_K(z)=1+a_2z^2+a_4z^4+\cdots$. For a knot the matrix size is $2g$, so $D_K(u^{-1})=\det(u^{-1}V-uV^T)=\det(uV^T-u^{-1}V)=D_K(u)$, using even size in the first equality and transposition in the second. Since replacing $u$ by $u^{-1}$ sends $z=u-u^{-1}$ to $-z$, and substitution into the Laurent polynomial ring is injective (the highest Laurent power of a nonzero polynomial in $z$ cannot cancel), this identity gives $\nabla_K(z)=\nabla_K(-z)$ and hence all odd coefficients vanish. Set $u^2=t$. Then $z^2=(u-u^{-1})^2=t+t^{-1}-2\equiv(1+t)^2/t\pmod{(2,(1+t)^4)}$, and $z^4$ is divisible by $(1+t)^4$ in that quotient. Hence [F4] gives $$\Delta_K^\#(t)\equiv1+a_2(\nabla_K)(1+t)^2/t\pmod{(2,(1+t)^4)}.$$ Comparing with [F5], and using that $(1+t)^2/t$ is nonzero modulo $(1+t)^4$, yields $a_2(\nabla_K)\equiv\operatorname{Arf}(K)\pmod2$. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is $K$. The normal framing along $K$ given by the inward unit conormal to $K$ in $F$ has self-linking number zero. Here self-linking is the linking number of $K$ with a sufficiently small disjoint push-off along that framing. In the framing-class parameterization by relative winding from the surface framing, this class has integer zero.

## Statement references

[[def-framed-knot-self-linking-and-seifert-framing|Framings, self-linking by a small push-off, and the Seifert framing]]

[[thm-oriented-knot-framing-classes-form-z-torsor|Framing classes parameterized by relative winding]]

[[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection|Linking number as signed intersection with a spanning surface under the Axiom of Choice]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Choice, a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ whose oriented boundary is $K$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice through dependent choice. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]])

[F1] A Seifert surface is a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface whose oriented boundary is the specified knot; its genus formula assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. ([[def-oriented-seifert-surface]])

[F2] For a knot with a supplied oriented spanning surface, the inward unit surface conormal is a reference normal framing, and relative winding identifies its framing class with zero. ([[thm-oriented-knot-framing-classes-form-z-torsor]])

[F3] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the inward unit conormal defines the Seifert framing; its self-linking is the linking number with a sufficiently small push-off along that section. ([[def-framed-knot-self-linking-and-seifert-framing]])

[F4] For any normalized tubular-neighbourhood chart and sufficiently small radius, the push-off is embedded and its linking number is independent of the radius, the representative nowhere-zero normal section, and the normalized chart; hence it depends only on the framing class. ([[lem-framed-knot-push-off-self-linking-well-defined]])

[F5] For disjoint oriented circles $J,K$ and an oriented spanning surface $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma=K$, if $J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$ and $D$ is a regular oriented diagram of $J\cup K$, the diagram linking number equals the signed intersection number $J\cdot\Sigma$. The theorem assumes the Axiom of Choice. ([[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]])

[F6] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every oriented link in $\mathbb R^3$ has a dense set of directions giving a regular diagram with finitely many crossings. ([[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]])

[F7] A regular oriented diagram is a projection with only finitely many transverse double points and no triple points. ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]])

[F8] A smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; a collar is a smooth embedding of the boundary times a half-interval, equal to the boundary inclusion at zero and onto an open boundary neighbourhood. ([[thm-collar-neighborhood-theorem]]) ([[def-smooth-collar-of-a-manifold-boundary]])

[F9] A tubular chart exists under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. It may be normalized as in [F4]: its vertical derivative induces a smooth fibrewise isomorphism $B$ to the normal quotient, and precomposing the chart by $B^{-1}$ makes that identification the identity. A smooth isotopy of a compact boundaryless embedded source, stationary near its parameter endpoints, extends to an ambient isotopy; linking number is unchanged under ambient isotopy of oriented two-component links. ([[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]]) ([[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-compact-embedded-submanifolds-extends-to-an-ambient-isotopy]]) ([[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]])

[F10] The standard smooth step function $\sigma$ is smooth, is zero for arguments at most zero, and is one for arguments at least one. ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]])

## Proof

1.1 By [A1], the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypotheses in [F1], [F3], and [F6] hold. The given $F$ is a Seifert surface by [F1]. Use its inward unit conormal as the reference normal field. By [F2], this Seifert framing has relative winding integer zero. [given, A1, F1, F2]

1.2 Let $s$ be the inward unit conormal, viewed in the round-metric normal bundle. By [F8], choose a smooth collar $c:K\times[0,\varepsilon_0)\to F$ and orient its levels by the original $K$. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, set $J_0=c(K,\delta)$. It is embedded, lies in $\operatorname{int}F$, and is disjoint from $K$. No prescribed collar velocity is assumed: since $c$ is an embedding onto a boundary neighbourhood, $\partial_t c(p,0)$ is inward transverse to $K$ in $F$. Its normal quotient is therefore $a(p)s(p)$ for a smooth function $a(p)>0$; a tangential component is allowed. [given, F8, construct]

2.1 Use a normalized tubular chart $\Phi$ of $K$ as in [F4] and [F9], and write $\Phi^{-1}(c(p,t))=(b_t(p),v_t(p))$, with $v_t(p)$ in the normal fibre over $b_t(p)$. Compactness permits one small interval of $t$ on which these expressions are defined for every $p$. At $t=0$ they are $(p,0)$, and normalization identifies the vertical derivative with $a(p)s(p)$. The maps $b_t$ are $C^1$-close to the identity. In a smooth oriented circle coordinate their lifts have the form $u+r_t(u)$ with $r_t$ periodic and $\|r_t'\|_\infty<1/2$ for small $t$; thus the lifts are increasing degree-one diffeomorphisms. Hence each $b_t$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Reparametrize the level over $x=b_t(p)$, obtaining a smooth normal section $w_t(x)=v_t(b_t^{-1}(x))$. Taylor expansion in finitely many bundle charts gives, uniformly on $K$, $w_t(x)=t a(x)s(x)+O(t^2)$. Because $a$ has positive minimum and $s$ is unit, after decreasing $\delta$ this implies $\langle w_\delta(x),s(x)\rangle>0$ for every $x$. [given, F4, F9, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

2.2 Since $F$ is a compact embedded surface, it is closed and has empty interior in $S^3$; hence its complement contains a point $q$. Choose an orientation-preserving stereographic chart from $q$. It places $K\cup J_0$ and $F$ in $\mathbb R^3$. Let $F_0$ be the closure in $F$ of the complement of the open boundary collar $c(K\times[0,\delta))$. Then $F_0$ is compact, is disjoint from $K$, and has boundary set $J_0$. Give $F_0$ its orientation inherited from $F$; at its new boundary the outward collar-normal points back toward $K$, so the induced boundary orientation is the transported orientation of $J_0$, parallel to $K$. Apply [F6] and [F7] to choose a regular oriented diagram $D$ of $K\cup J_0$, with the projection-plane orientation induced from $S^3$. [given, F6, F7, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 For $0\le u\le1$, interpolate in each normal fibre by $z_u(x)=(1-\chi(u))w_\delta(x)+\chi(u)\delta s(x)$, where $\chi(u)=\sigma(3u-1)$ is the plateau from [F10]. Every $z_u$ has positive pairing with $s$, so it never meets the zero section. Uniformly these vectors have norm $O(\delta)$; a common disk bundle about the compact zero section lies in the tubular domain, so all interpolating graphs lie in that domain when $\delta$ is small. Each graph projects identically to $K$, hence is an embedded circle, and $\Phi$ carries it to an embedded circle disjoint from $K$. With $K$ as the fixed first component this is a smooth two-component link isotopy, stationary near its parameter endpoints, from $K\cup J_0$ to $K\cup\Phi(\delta s)$. The orientation on $J_0$ agrees with the graph orientation because $b_\delta$ preserves orientation. By [F9] the family extends to an ambient isotopy and its linking number is unchanged. The endpoint $\Phi(\delta s)$ is exactly a sufficiently small normalized-chart push-off in [F3]–[F4]. Consequently the self-linking in the statement equals $\operatorname{lk}(K,J_0)$, without identifying the collar level literally with a chart graph of $\delta s$. [A1, F3, F4, F9, F10, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]
