$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S):=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{a_i:i\in S\},$$
with $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{\varnothing})=\{0\}$. The family $\Phi$ has the **complement property** if for every $S\subseteq[m]$,
$$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_S)=\mathbb R^d \quad\text{or}\quad \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Phi_{[m]\setminus S})=\mathbb R^d.$$
The definition applies to labeled families, including repeated or zero vectors.

Let $d\ge1$, $m\ge d$, and let $\Phi=(a_i)_{i\in[m]}$ be a finite family in $\mathbb R^d$. The family is **full spark** if for every list of distinct labels $i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[m]$, the vectors $a_{i_1},\ldots,a_{i_d}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb R$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

### Finite sums of vectors

By axiom (V1) the triple $(V, +, 0_V)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), hence
in particular a commutative monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]). So the finite
products of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] are available in it, and we write them
**additively**: for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite list $u : n \to V$, that is a
function on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]),

$$\sum_{i<n} u_i \;:=\; \prod_{i<n} u_i \quad \text{computed in } (V,+,0_V),$$

so that $\sum_{i<0} u_i = 0_V$ and $\sum_{i<\sigma(n)} u_i = \bigl(\sum_{i<n} u_i\bigr) + u_n$,
and the value depends only on $u_0, \dots, u_{n-1}$.

### Linear combinations

A **linear combination in $V$** is a vector of the form

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

where $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ is a finite list of scalars and
$v : n \to V$ is a finite list of vectors; the sum is the finite sum just
described, of the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. For $S \subseteq V$, a vector
$w \in V$ is a **linear combination of elements of $S$** when there are
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\lambda : n \to F$ and $v : n \to S$ with
$w = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$.

**The empty case is a real case.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), and at $n = 0$ the sum is the empty sum, which is
$0_V$. So $0_V$ is a linear combination of elements of every subset of $V$,
including $S = \varnothing$. The lists are indexed from $0$, so a linear
combination of length $n$ is $\lambda_0 v_0 + \dots + \lambda_{n-1}v_{n-1}$; no
statement here is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

### The span

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be commuting indeterminates over $\mathbb R$, and let $V_d$ be the $d\times d$ matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $t_j^{i-1}$. Then
$$\det V_d=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$
Consequently, for any distinct real numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the $d$ vectors
$$(1,s_j,s_j^2,\ldots,s_j^{d-1})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 1\le j\le d,$$
are linearly independent.
$\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is a field.

derivations.claim: Let $I\subseteq[m]$ have $q$ labels and enumerate them in increasing order as $i_0,\ldots,i_{q-1}$. Define $T_I:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^d$ by $T_I(c)=\sum_{j<q}c_j a_{i_j}$. This map is linear by distributivity of finite sums. Its image is a subspace: it contains zero, and if $u=T_I(c)$ and $v=T_I(c')$, then $\alpha u+\beta v=T_I(\alpha c+\beta c')$. For each $j<q$, the $j$th standard unit vector $e_j$ satisfies $T_I(e_j)=a_{i_j}$, so the smallest-subspace property gives $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)\subseteq\operatorname{im}T_I$. Conversely every $T_I(c)$ is a finite linear combination of the listed measurement vectors, so [F4] gives $\operatorname{im}T_I\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)$. Thus the image equals the span, also when $q=0$ because both are $\{0\}$.
If $q<d$, rank-nullity and [F5] give $\dim(\operatorname{im}T_I)\le q<d$, so by step 1.1 this span cannot equal $\mathbb R^d$.

Suppose $m\le2d-2$. Choose $S\subseteq[m]$ with $|S|=\min(m,d-1)$. Then $|S|\le d-1$; if $m>d-1$, the bound on $m$ gives $|[m]\setminus S|=m-d+1\le d-1$, and if $m\le d-1$ the complement is empty. Applying step 1.2 to both sides shows that neither side spans, so the complement property fails by [F2]. Hence phase retrieval fails by [F1].

The lower count is established in step 2.1. For the sufficient count, suppose $m\ge2d-1$ and $\Phi$ is full spark. For any $S\subseteq[m]$, the two sides cannot both have fewer than $d$ labels, since that would imply $m\le2d-2$. Thus one side contains $d$ distinct labels. By [F3], their vectors are independent. The coefficient map $T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ for these $d$ columns has trivial kernel by [F6]; by step 1.1 its image is their span, and rank-nullity [F4] and [F5] give that image dimension $d$. Hence the image, and therefore the span of the chosen vectors, is $\mathbb R^d$ by [F7]. The containing side also spans $\mathbb R^d$. Since $S$ was arbitrary, the complement property holds, and [F1] gives phase retrieval.

Set $m=2d-1$ and choose distinct real nodes $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. Every $d$-label subfamily is independent by [F8], so the family is full spark by [F3]. Since $m\ge2d-1$, step 3.1 proves it performs phase retrieval. For $d=1$, the same argument uses one node and the one-entry vector $(1)$; for all $d$, step 2.1 rules out any smaller count.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq V$. Write

$$L(S) \;:=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i \;:\; n \in \mathbb{N},\ \lambda : n \to F,\ v : n \to S \,\Bigr\}$$

for the set of linear combinations of elements of $S$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). Then

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;=\; L(S).$$

In particular $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$, and for every
$S \subseteq V$ the span of $S$ contains $0_V$ as the empty linear combination.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) that is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F V = n$ ([[def-dimension]]), and let $U$ be a
linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

**Nothing above uses a choice principle**, and claim 3 in particular is the
finite-dimensional substitute for the Zorn-based extension theorem stated earlier
on this page. In finite dimension the extension terminates on its own, because
[[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] bounds the size
of an independent set and [[thm-well-ordering-principle]] then supplies a largest
one; no selection is made anywhere.

**Finiteness is essential in claim 2.** Without it the equality case fails: the
companion page exhibits a
proper linear subspace of an infinite-dimensional space whose basis is
equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be commuting indeterminates over $\mathbb R$, and let $V_d$ be the $d\times d$ matrix with $(i,j)$ entry $t_j^{i-1}$. Then
$$\det V_d=\prod_{1\le p<q\le d}(t_q-t_p).$$
Consequently, for any distinct real numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_d$, the $d$ vectors
$$(1,s_j,s_j^2,\ldots,s_j^{d-1})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 1\le j\le d,$$
are linearly independent.
$\mathbb{R} = \mathcal{C}/\mathcal{N}$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is a field.

derivations.claim: Let $I\subseteq[m]$ have $q$ labels and enumerate them in increasing order as $i_0,\ldots,i_{q-1}$. Define $T_I:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^d$ by $T_I(c)=\sum_{j<q}c_j a_{i_j}$. This map is linear by distributivity of finite sums. Its image is a subspace: it contains zero, and if $u=T_I(c)$ and $v=T_I(c')$, then $\alpha u+\beta v=T_I(\alpha c+\beta c')$. For each $j<q$, the $j$th standard unit vector $e_j$ satisfies $T_I(e_j)=a_{i_j}$, so the smallest-subspace property gives $\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)\subseteq\operatorname{im}T_I$. Conversely every $T_I(c)$ is a finite linear combination of the listed measurement vectors, so [F4] gives $\operatorname{im}T_I\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\Phi_I)$. Thus the image equals the span, also when $q=0$ because both are $\{0\}$.
If $q<d$, rank-nullity and [F5] give $\dim(\operatorname{im}T_I)\le q<d$, so by step 1.1 this span cannot equal $\mathbb R^d$.

Suppose $m\le2d-2$. Choose $S\subseteq[m]$ with $|S|=\min(m,d-1)$. Then $|S|\le d-1$; if $m>d-1$, the bound on $m$ gives $|[m]\setminus S|=m-d+1\le d-1$, and if $m\le d-1$ the complement is empty. Applying step 2.1 to both sides shows that neither side spans, so the complement property fails by [F2]. Hence phase retrieval fails by [F1].

The lower count is established in step 3.1. For the sufficient count, suppose $m\ge2d-1$ and $\Phi$ is full spark. For any $S\subseteq[m]$, the two sides cannot both have fewer than $d$ labels, since that would imply $m\le2d-2$. Thus one side contains $d$ distinct labels. By [F3], their vectors are independent. The coefficient map $T:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ for these $d$ columns has trivial kernel by [F6]; by step 1.1 its image is their span, and rank-nullity [F4] and [F5] give that image dimension $d$. Hence the image, and therefore the span of the chosen vectors, is $\mathbb R^d$ by [F7]. The containing side also spans $\mathbb R^d$. Since $S$ was arbitrary, the complement property holds, and [F1] gives phase retrieval.

Set $m=2d-1$ and choose distinct real nodes $t_1,\ldots,t_m$. Every $d$-label subfamily is independent by [F8], so the family is full spark by [F3]. Since $m\ge2d-1$, step 4.1 proves it performs phase retrieval. For $d=1$, the same argument uses one node and the one-entry vector $(1)$; for all $d$, step 3.1 rules out any smaller count.

derivations.claim: Form the coefficientwise formal expression $C_D(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(D)z^j$ from [F1]. It is a diagram invariant, has value $1$ on an unknot, and satisfies $C_{D_+}-C_{D_-}=zC_{D_0}$ coefficientwise. A local positive and negative curl on any component of the $r$-component unlink are both that unlink; the oriented smoothing is the $(r+1)$-component unlink. Thus $c_j(U_r)-c_j(U_r)=c_{j-1}(U_{r+1})$ for every $j\ge1$. All coefficients of $U_{r+1}$ vanish. Therefore the unlink values of the formal expression are $1$ for one component and $0$ for more than one. This is also the forced unlink value for ANY polynomial-valued invariant satisfying the Definition.

Here is the finite argument that the expression is actually in $\mathbb Z[z]$. In a diagram choose finitely many component basepoints and an order. Call a crossing bad when its first encounter in this traversal is the underpass. If none is bad, the first component passes over every later component and has a descending self-diagram. Pull its successive arcs above everything they first encounter to isolate a round circle; repeat for the remaining components. Thus a descending diagram is an unlink. At a bad crossing the skein relation writes its value as the value of the switched diagram, plus or minus $z$ times its oriented smoothing. The switched diagram has one fewer bad crossing and the same number $N$ of crossings; the smoothing has $N-1$ crossings. Reset the finite component data on a smoothing if necessary. The nonnegative integer $N(N+1)/2+b$, with $b$ the number of bad crossings, decreases in each branch. Hence this is a FINITE resolution tree. Its leaves have values $0$ or $1$ by step1.1. Working back through the tree uses only integer addition/subtraction and multiplication by $z$, so $C_D\in\mathbb Z[z]$. In fact every branch has at most $N$ smoothing operations, giving degree at most $N$. This proves finiteness and integrality without assuming an integer-valued formal sequence theorem or making an infinite selection.

Apply the SAME finite tree to any two polynomial-valued invariants satisfying the stated normalization and skein relation. Their unlink leaves agree by step1.1, and each internal skein relation then forces agreement. Their values agree on every diagram. Existence follows from [F1], step1.2 and the ambient-link interpretation [F2], and this argument proves uniqueness. The separately fixed empty-link extension is unique as well, since its prescribed value is zero. Consequently the separate existence/uniqueness obligation mentioned in the Definition is now discharged: the resulting actual link invariant is exactly $\nabla$, and its coefficient $[z^k]\nabla_L$ is well-defined for every $k$. The finite local arguments use no choice axiom; the external constructive coefficient/diagram inputs are explicitly distinguished from them.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Supply finite balanced polygon Morse data of rank $m=h+k-1\ge1$, with common $w,z$ marks, and no triple intersection of the product tori. Fix a Spin-c structure on the polygon cobordism and use the STRICT all-$w$ normalized strong admissibility condition of the named geometric lattice theorem. Use the same condition for its relevant boundary-pair sectors. The boundary systems have their actual complete $k$-ball cuts, and nearly symmetric geometry has exact constant product-angle generator charts. No $S^3$ or torsion restriction on the intermediate three-manifolds is made.

In the smooth topology, the genuine constant-collar end paths having no nonconstant strip of index at most zero and regularity for every actual index-one strip in the relevant sectors form an open dense subset of the allowed protected end paths. With these paths, compatible coherent source-dependent polygon perturbations can be chosen generically, relative to their faces and any regular parameter endpoints. Their count-dimension-zero total sets are finite, and their count-dimension-one spaces compactify to actual compact one-manifolds. All nonnegative $w,z$ degrees are retained. These conclusions hold for the fixed total Spin-c label, across all its literal realized classes; they also hold for fixed degree vectors or fixed actual classes. The boundary consists exactly of the label-compatible rigid polygon–polygon faces and strip–polygon breakings, with additive marked vectors and actual exhaustive gluing collars. No sphere or one-torus disk bubble occurs in these polygon dimensions. This includes $k=1$.

For triangles the fixed count index is $\mu$, so rigid counts have $\mu=0$ and the chain-map boundary has $\mu=1$. In a generic one-parameter triangle family with fixed regular end data the universal count index is $\mu+1$: the index-minus-one universal counts are finite, and universal index-zero spaces have the parameter endpoints and strip–triangle boundaries. Thus the finite actual counts satisfy the weighted triangle chain-map equation and its auxiliary-data chain homotopy over $\mathbb F_2$. They may be specialized to the two-color ring by sending every $w$ variable to $U$ and every $z$ variable to $V$. No top-generator cycle, handle-map inverse, arbitrary diagram invariance or absolute grading is part of this assertion.

Assume countable choice. Let $(S,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma,w,z)$ be a strictly strongly admissible pointed Heegaard triple for a decorated knot cobordism, with the strong condition normalized at ALL $w$ marks. Fix one Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ and nonnegative $w,z$-multiplicities. In positive symmetric rank $m=h+k-1>0$, among the auxiliary Heegaard data first choose an arbitrarily small pointed Hamiltonian representative with no common intersection of three attaching families, following the pair generators and transporting the actual Spin-c label and strict admissibility. Such positive-rank representatives exist. Fix that representative; this is an explicit curve choice, not a claim that varying the almost-complex tensor alone regularizes constant triangles on the original arbitrary fixed triple.

At rank $m=0$, keep the original empty attaching systems: the target is one point and no triple-torus exclusion is imposed. Its unique constant triangle, when its assigned Spin-c label and zero marked-degree vectors match the specified ones, is regular of index zero and contributes one; all other specified-label or positive-degree sets are empty. The fixed index-one and universal index-minus-one spaces are empty, and a matching one-parameter family is the parameter interval.

In positive rank choose regular end data in the open dense set of allowed genuine constant-collar paths described in the proof. For generic fixed source-dependent almost-complex data compatible with those ends, the Maslov-index-zero triangle moduli spaces used in the triangle-count map are regular zero-manifolds and finite. For generic one-parameter families with those fixed regular ends, the universal triangle moduli spaces are regular with the parameter included in the expected dimension; slice counts are taken at regular parameter values. The compactified one-dimensional Maslov-index-one triangle spaces have precisely the broken triangle/strip strata, with actual gluing collars. In these dimensions no nonconstant one-torus boundary degeneration is allowed: its index contribution is at least two and the remaining triangle would have negative count dimension. In a one-parameter family the compactified universal index-zero spaces additionally have the two parameter-endpoint strata; the zero-dimensional universal index-minus-one spaces define the homotopy terms.

The mod-two boundary counts give the weighted bilinear triangle chain-map equation and its chain homotopy. Inserting an actual intermediate cycle gives the corresponding one-input chain-map equation. All nonnegative marked multiplicities and the fixed Spin-c extension are retained, including intermediate closed three-manifolds beyond $S^3$ and multiple mark pairs. No additional ends arise from sphere bubbling, escape through nonzero periodic domains or uncontrolled marked-point multiplicities. This analytic assertion does not itself establish that a named top generator is a cycle or prove invariance under changing the chosen attaching curves.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Supply finite balanced polygon Morse data of rank $m=h+k-1\ge1$, with common $w,z$ marks, and no triple intersection of the product tori. Fix a Spin-c structure on the polygon cobordism and use the STRICT all-$w$ normalized strong admissibility condition of the named geometric lattice theorem. Use the same condition for its relevant boundary-pair sectors. The boundary systems have their actual complete $k$-ball cuts, and nearly symmetric geometry has exact constant product-angle generator charts. No $S^3$ or torsion restriction on the intermediate three-manifolds is made.

In the smooth topology, the genuine constant-collar end paths having no nonconstant strip of index at most zero and regularity for every actual index-one strip in the relevant sectors form an open dense subset of the allowed protected end paths. With these paths, compatible coherent source-dependent polygon perturbations can be chosen generically, relative to their faces and any regular parameter endpoints. Their count-dimension-zero total sets are finite, and their count-dimension-one spaces compactify to actual compact one-manifolds. All nonnegative $w,z$ degrees are retained. These conclusions hold for the fixed total Spin-c label, across all its literal realized classes; they also hold for fixed degree vectors or fixed actual classes. The boundary consists exactly of the label-compatible rigid polygon–polygon faces and strip–polygon breakings, with additive marked vectors and actual exhaustive gluing collars. No sphere or one-torus disk bubble occurs in these polygon dimensions. This includes $k=1$.

For triangles the fixed count index is $\mu$, so rigid counts have $\mu=0$ and the chain-map boundary has $\mu=1$. In a generic one-parameter triangle family with fixed regular end data the universal count index is $\mu+1$: the index-minus-one universal counts are finite, and universal index-zero spaces have the parameter endpoints and strip–triangle boundaries. Thus the finite actual counts satisfy the weighted triangle chain-map equation and its auxiliary-data chain homotopy over $\mathbb F_2$. They may be specialized to the two-color ring by sending every $w$ variable to $U$ and every $z$ variable to $V$. No top-generator cycle, handle-map inverse, arbitrary diagram invariance or absolute grading is part of this assertion.

Assume countable choice. Let $(S,\boldsymbol\alpha,\boldsymbol\beta,\boldsymbol\gamma,w,z)$ be a strictly strongly admissible pointed Heegaard triple for a decorated knot cobordism, with the strong condition normalized at ALL $w$ marks. Fix one Spin-c structure $\mathfrak s$ and nonnegative $w,z$-multiplicities. In positive symmetric rank $m=h+k-1>0$, among the auxiliary Heegaard data first choose an arbitrarily small pointed Hamiltonian representative with no common intersection of three attaching families, following the pair generators and transporting the actual Spin-c label and strict admissibility. Such positive-rank representatives exist. Fix that representative; this is an explicit curve choice, not a claim that varying the almost-complex tensor alone regularizes constant triangles on the original arbitrary fixed triple.

At rank $m=0$, keep the original empty attaching systems: the target is one point and no triple-torus exclusion is imposed. Its unique constant triangle, when its assigned Spin-c label and zero marked-degree vectors match the specified ones, is regular of index zero and contributes one; all other specified-label or positive-degree sets are empty. The fixed index-one and universal index-minus-one spaces are empty, and a matching one-parameter family is the parameter interval.

In positive rank choose regular end data in the open dense set of allowed genuine constant-collar paths described in the proof. For generic fixed source-dependent almost-complex data compatible with those ends, the Maslov-index-zero triangle moduli spaces used in the triangle-count map are regular zero-manifolds and finite. For generic one-parameter families with those fixed regular ends, the universal triangle moduli spaces are regular with the parameter included in the expected dimension; slice counts are taken at regular parameter values. The compactified one-dimensional Maslov-index-one triangle spaces have precisely the broken triangle/strip strata, with actual gluing collars. In these dimensions no nonconstant one-torus boundary degeneration is allowed: its index contribution is at least two and the remaining triangle would have negative count dimension. In a one-parameter family the compactified universal index-zero spaces additionally have the two parameter-endpoint strata; the zero-dimensional universal index-minus-one spaces define the homotopy terms.

The mod-two boundary counts give the weighted bilinear triangle chain-map equation and its chain homotopy. Inserting an actual intermediate cycle gives the corresponding one-input chain-map equation. All nonnegative marked multiplicities and the fixed Spin-c extension are retained, including intermediate closed three-manifolds beyond $S^3$ and multiple mark pairs. No additional ends arise from sphere bubbling, escape through nonzero periodic domains or uncontrolled marked-point multiplicities. This analytic assertion does not itself establish that a named top generator is a cycle or prove invariance under changing the chosen attaching curves.

derivations.claim: **Choice scope.** Fix the actual compact smooth cobordism, decoration, Spin-c structure and, for a comparison, the two actual decompositions. A compact smooth input has finite atlas/handle data. A Morse decomposition has finitely many critical points; a generic Cerf comparison has finitely many exceptional times (Zemke Lemma 11.18, p.80, and Theorem 11.5, pp.74 and 84–85). Choosing a finite list of charts, gradient-like fields, band neighborhoods, puncturing balls and standard auxiliary classes uses finite choice only. No choice of one decomposition for every cobordism is required: existence and pairwise comparison are quantified separately for arbitrary given inputs.

The dividing surface and boundary data meet the source category in [F1]: basepoints alternate, the dividing set separates the two regions, every three-manifold component meets the link, and every four-manifold component meets the divided surface. Closed dividing curves are allowed by its properly embedded one-manifold definition. The two-color assignment in [F3] is compatible on every elementary piece, including multicomponent and multiply based intermediate links. Its curvature is zero, so the imported curved maps are genuine maps of complexes over $\mathbb F_2[U,V]$.

Use the elementary maps of [F1] for the chosen parametrized Kirby decomposition, with [F2]'s actual auxiliary cycles and the fixed restricted Spin-c labels. Their finite polynomial counts, chain-map property and compatibility with the natural Heegaard transition maps are supplied by that external construction. Thus their composition is the displayed representative. If a component has an empty incoming or outgoing end, apply [F1]'s standard puncturing prescription before composing, not an undefined intermediate empty-link Heegaard diagram. No graph-TQFT reduction or hat-only construction is substituted for this two-variable map.

For that finite list of diagrams, the homotopy and periodic-domain data are countably indexed: use the finite-cell models of the compact manifolds and finite products of circles, and integer words in their finite attaching data; Spin-c extensions form a subset of a finitely generated integral cohomology torsor. Integer degrees, multiplicities, polygon types and neck lengths in $\mathbb N$ are countable indices as well. The count theorem [F4] supplies coherent perturbations relative to faces and fixed ends, rather than making independent choices at every real parameter value. Model counts and the finite move identities of [F1] use such zero- and one-dimensional polygon families; the elementary top classes in [F2] are algebraic classes on specified standard diagrams. A cycle representative, if needed, may be selected as the first representative in the explicit enumeration of finite polynomial chains over the countable ring. Nonempty single choices and finite choices require no additional axiom; countably many choices are covered by the assumed Countable Choice.

The geometric generic functions and comparison families can be chosen in the separable smooth spaces on those finitely many compact charts, with their countable derivative seminorms. Their residual conditions are indexed by countable jet charts/exhaustions, the finite singularity types and the countable curve classes; the analytic regularity choices are already furnished by [F4]. For the geometric Baire choices one may recursively select the first basic ball whose closure lies in the preceding ball and in the next dense open set, with diameters tending to zero. Completeness supplies the limit, so this step requires no choice over an uncountable set of functions. Source model relations are imported as finite geometric/count identities, with these actual CC-regular counts; their use does not require a well-ordering of all diagrams or a full-Choice selection of a global transitive system. Consequently the external proof specializes to the declared CC setting. This is a bounded choice inventory of its use here; it is not a claim that the publication itself discusses foundational optimality.

The distinguished class notation in the formula never selects a canonical cycle on every diagram: choose a representative on the actual standard auxiliary pair and carry it by the transition maps. Its boundary ambiguity is exactly the homotopy in [F2]. The local analytic triangle theorem supplies its own weighted bilinear identity, but the existence and correctness of the required elementary inputs come from [F1]–[F2]. Independence of all chosen decomposition data and the Spin-c extension sum are established in the separate naturality lemma by the external Theorems A and B.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

derivations.claim: The rightmost factor is stacked lowest, so the factors from bottom to top are $\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1},\sigma_2,\sigma_1^{-1}$. Starting from the bottom positions, the component-position sequence after successive crossings is $(1,2,3)$, $(1,3,2)$, $(3,1,2)$, $(3,2,1)$, $(2,3,1)$, $(2,1,3)$, $(1,2,3)$. The six crossing-label pairs and signs in that order are respectively $(2,3,+1)$, $(1,3,-1)$, $(1,2,+1)$, $(2,3,-1)$, $(1,3,+1)$, and $(1,2,-1)$, as determined by the signed generators in the braid word and [F1]. Thus the closure returns each label to its own endpoint, and each component pair crosses twice with opposite signs. By [F4] each pairwise linking number is half the signed mixed-crossing sum, hence is zero.

At crossing 1, component 2 passes under component 3, so its meridian becomes $B=x_3^{-1}x_2x_3$. At crossing 2, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the longitude factor $x_1^{-1}$. At crossing 3, component 1 passes under component 2, so its meridian becomes $C=B^{-1}x_1B$. At crossing 5, component 3 passes under component 1 and contributes the factor $C$. The other crossings do not put component 3 under. Hence $\lambda_3=x_1^{-1}C=x_1^{-1}B^{-1}x_1B$.

In $R_2$, $E(B)\equiv1+X_2\pmod{\mathfrak m^2}$, so
$$E(C)=E(B)^{-1}(1+X_1)E(B)=1+X_1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Since $E(x_1^{-1})=1-X_1+X_1^2$, multiplication gives
$$E(\lambda_3)=E(x_1^{-1})E(C)=1+X_1X_2-X_2X_1\pmod{\mathfrak m^3}.$$
Under [A1], the $X_1X_2$ coefficient is $+1$, so [F3] gives $\mu_{\tau_B}(1,2,3)=1$.

The computed longitude has zero degree-one term, as required by the chosen untwisted based peripheral system. Closing the endpoints along crossing-free arcs adds no undercrossing factor, and component 3 has self-writhe zero, so the same word is its based closed-link preferred longitude by [F2]. Every proper length-two subsequence in $\Delta_{123}^b$ is a pairwise linking number, so step 1.1 makes $\Delta_{123}^b=0$. Thus the same coefficient gives the closed-link residue candidate $1$.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. (from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set

zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group

based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred

$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return

iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
