citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Every orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $g:S^2\to S^2$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth isotopy of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, stationary near its time endpoints. Consequently every smooth diffeomorphism $b:\partial B_0\to\partial B_1$ between the boundaries of two parametrized smooth $3$-balls extends to a smooth diffeomorphism $B_0\to B_1$. In the radial boundary collars supplied by their parametrizations, the extension can be required to have the product form $(x,r)\mapsto(b(x),r)$ on one smaller collar. Its orientation agrees with the orientation of $b$ on the boundaries, using the outward-normal convention.

This asserts existence of an isotopy for each given map; it does not assert a deformation retraction parametrized by the entire diffeomorphism group.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

All isotopies below are jointly smooth diffeotopies, stationary near the time endpoints.

1. On $A=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times[0,1]$, every smooth diffeomorphism fixing both boundary circles pointwise is isotopic relative to the boundary to exactly one twist
$$D_k(\theta,u)=(\theta+k\rho(u),u),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $\rho$ is a fixed smooth function equal to zero near $0$ and one near $1$. If the map initially fixes a boundary collar, a common smaller collar can be fixed throughout this isotopy. Without fixing the boundary, every annulus diffeomorphism is isotopic to one of the four maps $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,u)$ or $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,1-u)$, with $\varepsilon=\pm1$.
2. Every smooth diffeomorphism of $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ inducing the identity on $H_1(T^2;\mathbb Z)$ is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Consequently every torus diffeomorphism is smoothly isotopic to the linear torus map inducing its integral unimodular matrix on $H_1$.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact orientable smooth three-manifold and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite disjoint family of properly embedded two-sided annuli. Suppose each map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(M)$ is injective and every component of the cut-open manifold $M\mathbin{\|}\mathcal A$, with its boundary corners rounded, is irreducible. Then $M$ is irreducible. The family may be empty, and its annuli need not be separating or boundary-incompressible.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Fix an HNN extension in associated-subgroup notation and choose transversal data
$(S_-,S_+)$ as in [[def-choice-of-transversals-for-hnn-normal-forms]]. Then
every element of the HNN extension is represented by a unique transversal normal
form

$$a_0t^{\varepsilon_1}a_1\cdots t^{\varepsilon_n}a_n.$$

In particular, the identity has the unique normal form with $n=0$ and
$a_0=e_A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

For pointed topological spaces $(X,x_0)$ and $(Y,y_0)$, the coordinate projections induce a natural group isomorphism

$$\Theta:\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0),\qquad [\gamma]\longmapsto([\pi_X\gamma],[\pi_Y\gamma]).$$

Its inverse sends $([\alpha],[\beta])$ to the class of the paired loop $s\mapsto(\alpha(s),\beta(s))$.

derivations.claim: The solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as a standard unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior has two ball sides by [F2]. Its exterior solid torus is connected and misses the sphere, so lies entirely on one side; the other ball is contained in $V$. We will use the following disk-push consequence with its smooth interpretation. If two smooth disks meet just along their common boundary and bound such a ball, their faces admit a common-boundary disk sweep through the ball. To retain the actual faces, take a thin rim collar first. At a transverse rim its normal section is a quadrant; at a previously shared collar first separate the two faces by a small normal graph. Parametrize the two faces by smooth disks with their prescribed rim collars, using [F3]. Round and truncate the rim; the remaining boundary is a smooth sphere with these marked disk and collar portions. The two disk maps and the intervening product annulus give a smooth boundary diffeomorphism to the corresponding standard rounded lens; [F3] extends it over the ball. Restore the quadrant rim using those same product collars. This gives a lens parameter retaining both faces and their rim coordinates. In this parameter use [F4]'s spherical-cap sweep; in the rim section its inward tangent runs between the two face tangents and stays nonzero. The sweep is jointly smooth, including at the disk center, by [F4]'s displayed formulas. It can be continued just past either face in its normal collar and extended ambiently by [F5]. If another surface misses the ball except in one face, the push removes that face's intersections and creates none. The support can be restricted to the ball and arbitrarily thin face and rim collars.

For the classification first replace $F$ by its neat representative using [F9]; both disk-obstruction hypotheses pass to it. Its boundary and abstract surface are unchanged. The topological ambient extension pulls a boundary-parallel product back to the original surface, and no smooth product at an original tangency is asserted. In the rest of the classification denote this neat representative again by $F$. The surface $F$ is compact, since its inclusion is proper and $V$ is compact, and it is orientable, since it is two-sided in oriented $V$. If some component $c$ of $\partial F$ is nullhomotopic on $\partial V$, choose one with an innermost boundary disk $Q$ whose interior misses all of $\partial F$. A short inward push gives a disk with boundary $c$ on $F$ and interior disjoint from $F$. If $F$ is not a disk, $c$ is essential on $F$: a boundary circle of a connected surface can bound a disk in that surface only when that disk is the entire surface, by the local half-disk charts and connectedness. The pushed disk would therefore compress $F$. Thus in this case $F$ is a disk. For the rest of the classification suppose $F$ is not a disk; then every boundary circle is essential on $\partial V$. Disjoint essential circles on a torus have the same primitive unoriented slope, as the strip reductions of [F4] show. Use those reductions for the finite family and extend into a boundary collar by [F5] to make them parallel affine circles in coordinates $(\mu,\phi)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, where $\phi$ is the longitude coordinate of $V$. If the slope is meridional, choose a standard meridian disk $D_0$ with boundary disjoint from them. Otherwise the affine circles have nonzero $\phi$ derivative and meet $\partial D_0=\{\phi=0\}$ transversely.

Put the interiors of $F$ and $D_0$ in finite transverse position. An innermost intersection circle on $D_0$ bounds a disk $D$ with interior missing $F$. Incompressibility makes its boundary bound a disk $D'$ on $F$. The sphere $D\cup D'$ bounds a ball in $V$ by step 1.1, with the corner interpreted there. The connected surface $F\setminus\operatorname{Int}D'$ reaches $\partial V$, misses the sphere off its rim, and hence lies on the exterior side of that ball. The disk push of step 1.1 replaces $D'$ by a disk just past $D$. It removes this circle and any additional circles in $D'$, and creates none. After finitely many pushes no circle remains. The isotopies have interior support and retain the normalized boundary curves.

Suppose an intersection arc remains. An outermost arc $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D$ in $D_0$, with other boundary arc $\beta\subset\partial D_0$ and interior missing $F$. Boundary-incompressibility implies that $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D'$ on $F$, with other boundary arc $\gamma$ contained in one component of $\partial F$. If the slope were meridional there would be no arc endpoints, by the chosen disjoint boundaries. Otherwise $\gamma$ is a nonconstant subarc of an affine boundary circle whose longitude coordinate is strictly monotone on its lift. Both its endpoints have $\phi=0$, so its lifted longitude displacement is a nonzero integer. But $\beta$ has constant longitude. The union $D\cup D'$, pushed a little along its common edge if necessary, gives a continuous disk cap for the loop $\beta\cup\gamma$ in $V$. Its longitude degree would therefore be zero, contradicting that nonzero integer. Thus there are no arcs. If the slope were nonmeridional, the affine boundary curves would necessarily meet $\partial D_0$, so this case is impossible. We have made $F$ disjoint from $D_0$. Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ leaves a ball. An innermost boundary circle of $F$ on its boundary sphere has a disk there with interior missing all boundary circles of $F$. Push it inward. Unless $F$ is a disk it is a compressing disk, by the boundary-circle argument of step 2.1. This contradicts our supposition that $F$ was not a disk.

Let $D_1,D_2$ be meridian disks with the same boundary $C$. If either disk is not neat, first neatify each separately by [F9], fixing $C$. Apply the following neat-disk argument and then reverse the second embedding path. This gives a smooth embedding isotopy for the broad inputs; their two explicit topological ambient extensions and the middle smooth ambient path give a topological ambient extension. For neat inputs no preliminary change is necessary, and the entire argument below is smooth ambient. Now suppose both disks neat. In coordinates along $C$, use a small normal graph to separate their interior collars while fixing $C$ pointwise: with inward boundary coordinate $q\ge0$ and a transverse coordinate $y$ on $\partial V$, the two collars can be arranged as $y=\pm\varepsilon q$ on a common smaller strip. First each neat disk is straightened to such a graph by its full-rank collar coordinates; interpolation of the positive inward derivative gives an embedding path on a common compact strip, extended by [F5]. This keeps every boundary point fixed. General position relative to those collars then leaves only finitely many interior intersection circles. An innermost one on $D_1$ and its subdisk on $D_2$ bound a ball by irreducibility. The complement of that subdisk in $D_2$ reaches $C$ outside the ball, so the disk push from step 1.1 removes the circle and any circles inside that subdisk. Repeat until the interiors are disjoint. The resulting disks bound a ball with rim $C$, again by step 1.1 after the rim is rounded. Its common-boundary cap sweep carries one disk to the other, fixing $C$ throughout; at the rim every intermediate tangent is an inward direction between the two collar tangents, so the family remains neat in $V$. Undo the preliminary isotopies of $D_2$ and concatenate with stationary time changes. This gives a jointly smooth isotopy relative to $C$; The velocity vanishes on $C$ throughout this neat path. In a neat boundary chart it is $q$ times a smooth coefficient, as in [F9] and its neatification supplier Proof 5.2. Extend that coefficient and retain the factor $q$; the finite compact flow gives a smooth ambient isotopy fixing all of $\partial V$, not only $C$.

We have proved that $F$ is a disk. If $\partial F$ is essential on $\partial V$, it is a primitive class in the kernel of $\pi_1(\partial V)=\mathbb Z\mu\oplus\mathbb Z\phi\to\pi_1(V)=\mathbb Z\phi$, since $F$ caps it. It is therefore $\pm\mu$, so $F$ is a meridian disk. If $\partial F$ is inessential, let $Q$ be its disk on $\partial V$. The sphere $F\cup Q$, pushed slightly into the interior and rounded, bounds a ball there. Restore the boundary collar as in step 1.1 to get a ball with these two disk faces. Its marked lens parameter gives the boundary-parallel product: extend $Q$ a short distance beyond its rim in $\partial V$ and retain a smaller collar on $F$; in the normal section the two disk faces are separated by a rectangle, with its outer edge on $\partial V$. The lens parameter away from that rim and this rectangle near it identify the region with $D^2\times[0,1]$, with $D^2\times\{0\}=F$ and the other disk and lateral annulus in $\partial V$. Thus $F$ is boundary-parallel in exactly [F1]'s product sense. Conversely a boundary-parallel disk has no essential circle or essential proper arc, so it does satisfy both disk-obstruction hypotheses; this is why it must be retained in the conclusion.

Finally, if a two-sided torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ had no compressing disk, [F6] would inject $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ into $\pi_1(V)\cong\mathbb Z$. No such injection exists: for images $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ of the two generators, $(b,-a)$ is in the kernel when $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and otherwise the entire group is the kernel. This contradiction yields a smooth compressing disk. This use of [F6] is within its compact smooth scope and does not turn a PL disk into a smooth disk without the supplied bridge. All earlier isotopies are smooth by the explicit cap, graph and finite extension constructions; the full AC assumption covers [F6] and implies the countable choice used elsewhere.

Finally allow the torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ to be TOP two-sided with its given product neighborhood, without assuming it smooth. Cut along that TOP collar. The cut pieces are compact orientable TOP3-manifolds; there are either two connected pieces with one torus face each, or one connected piece with two torus faces. Indeed every piece meets a face, and each face is connected. If any face map has nontrivial fundamental-group kernel, [F10] gives a proper disk in that cut piece whose boundary has nontrivial class on the face. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

derivations.claim: If $g=0$, $V$ is the empty matrix and a disk with its empty homology basis realizes it. Assume $g>0$. Put $J=V-V^T$ and $H=\mathbb Z^{2g}$. Choose a primitive vector $e\in H$. Since $J:H\to\operatorname{Hom}(H,\mathbb Z)$ is an isomorphism, the functional $J(e,-)$ is primitive, so Bezout's identity gives $f\in H$ with $J(e,f)=1$. For every $x\in H$, the vector $x'=x-J(x,f)e+J(x,e)f$ satisfies $J(x',e)=J(x',f)=0$. Thus $H=\langle e,f\rangle\oplus\langle e,f\rangle^\perp$, and the restricted alternating form on the second summand is unimodular. Induction gives a basis with matrix $J_0=\bigoplus_{k=1}^g\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Let $P\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ be the corresponding change of basis and put $W=P^TVP$; then $W-W^T=J_0$.

Start with a disk and attach $2g$ oriented bands in the standard one-boundary handle pattern. Their core curves form an integral basis with intersection matrix $J_0$. The result is a connected compact smooth oriented surface with one boundary component. Write $W_0$ for its positive-push matrix; by [F1], $W_0-W_0^T=J_0$.

For each band core, inserting an integer number of full twists in a small subarc changes only its self-linking entry by the chosen integer. The twist box is disjoint from the other core arcs, and the surface intersection matrix is unchanged. Perform these finitely many modifications to make every diagonal entry of $W_0$ equal the corresponding diagonal entry of $W$.

For each pair $i<j$, choose subarcs of bands $i$ and $j$ in a ball disjoint from every other core and every earlier modification. Insert the oriented local clasp whose two new mixed crossings between $a_i^+$ and $a_j$ have the same sign $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$. By [F2], their signed sum changes by $2\varepsilon$, so $W_{ij}$ changes by $\varepsilon$. The clasp preserves the abstract surface intersection form; by [F1], $W_{ij}-W_{ji}$ is unchanged, and therefore $W_{ji}$ also changes by $\varepsilon$. The move is supported away from every other core, so all other pair entries and all diagonal entries stay fixed. The target equation $W-W_0=(W-W_0)^T$ off the diagonal holds because both skew parts are $J_0$. A finite number of positive or negative clasps thus sets both entries to their target values for each pair, without changing previously treated pairs. The resulting surface has positive-push matrix exactly $W$.

The basis change $P^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$ on this surface changes its matrix from $W$ to $(P^{-1})^TW P^{-1}=V$. The constructed surface has one boundary component, so its boundary is an oriented knot and the matrix is a Seifert matrix for that knot.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$.

Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives
$$
T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B,
$$
because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry.
Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. Let $J_F$ be the matrix of the algebraic intersection form on $F$, with a transverse intersection of oriented curves $u,v$ counted positively exactly when their ordered tangent vectors form a positive basis of $TF$. Then $V-V^T=J_F$. The matrix $J_F$ is skew-symmetric and unimodular; when $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ is a standard handle basis, it is a direct sum of blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice when an integral Seifert lattice comes from a knot's positive-push pairing. For an integral Seifert lattice $(H,V)$, its integral Witt class is its class in $G_{\mathbb Z}$ from the definition of metabolic Seifert form and algebraic knot concordance. An isomorphism $(W,B,T)\to(W',B',T')$ of rational isometric structures is a rational-linear bijection $P:W\to W'$ such that $B'(Px,Py)=B(x,y)$ and $PT=T'P$. A rational isometric structure is a triple $(W,B,T)$ in which $W$ is a finite-dimensional even-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-vector space, $B:W\times W\to\mathbb Q$ is a nonsingular symmetric bilinear form, $T:W\to W$ is an invertible linear map satisfying $B(Tx,Ty)=B(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in W$, and $I-T$ is invertible. Such a structure is metabolic if it has a $T$-invariant subspace $L\subset W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb Q}L=\frac12\dim_{\mathbb Q}W$ and $B|_{L\times L}=0$. Define the rational Witt group $G_{\mathbb Q}$ by direct sum of isomorphism classes, with metabolic structures set equal to zero. For a nonsingular integral Seifert matrix $V$, the associated matrix pair is $(B,T)=(V+V^T,V^{-1}V^T)$; whether this pair is a rational isometric structure is established separately.

The definition concerns finite-rank bilinear forms and isometry data. It does not identify the unrelated Witt Lie algebra with either $G_{\mathbb Z}$ or $G_{\mathbb Q}$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $B=V+V^T$ is symmetric. Modulo $2$, $V+V^T\equiv V-V^T$; by [F1] the determinant of $V-V^T$ is odd, so $\det B$ is odd and in particular nonzero. Thus $B$ is nonsingular over $\mathbb Q$.

Since $V$ and $V^T$ are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, $T=V^{-1}V^T$ is invertible. Direct multiplication gives $$ T^TBT=V(V^T)^{-1}(V+V^T)V^{-1}V^T=V+V^T=B, $$ because the two summands in the middle expression simplify respectively to $V$ and $V^T$. Therefore $T$ is a $B$-isometry.
Finally $I-T=V^{-1}(V-V^T)$, which is invertible by invertibility of $V$ and [F1]. The three defining conditions in [F2] hold, proving the claim.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

abla_gw\|_{L^2(M)}$ for every $w\in H_0^1(M)$. For every $h\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique $v\in H^1(M)$ with trace $f$ satisfying $\int_M\gamma\,g(
abla_gv,
abla_g\overline z)\,dV_g=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g$ for every $z\in H_0^1(M)$. If $h$ and $f$ are smooth, this weak solution is smooth up to the boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary and no orientability assumption, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and suppose the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$. For every $F\in L^2(M)$ and $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ there is a unique weak solution $u\in H^1(M)$ of $(-\Delta_g+q)u=F$ with trace $f$. If $f=0$, $F\in H^m(M)$ and $m\geq0$ is an integer, then $u\in H^{m+2}(M)$ and $\|u\|_{H^{m+2}}\leq C_m\|F\|_{H^m}$. If $F$ and $f$ are smooth, this solution belongs to $H^m(M)$ for every integer $m\geq0$.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

derivations.claim: Write $a_{\gamma_j}(v,w)=\int_M\gamma_jg(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_1}(u_1,u_2)$, since $u_2$ is an extension of $f_2$. Let $\widetilde u_1$ solve the $\gamma_2$ equation with boundary value $f_1$, which exists by [F2]. Then $\langle\Lambda_{\gamma_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{\gamma_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $\gamma_2$ weak equation, Hermitian symmetry gives $a_{\gamma_2}(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_{\gamma_2}(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$. Hence $a_{\gamma_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)=a_{\gamma_2}(u_1,u_2)$. Subtracting the two equalities gives the conductivity identity.

Write $a_{q_j}(v,w)=\int_M(g(\nabla v,\nabla\bar w)+q_jv\bar w)\,dV_g$. By [F1], $\langle\Lambda_{q_1}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_1}(u_1,u_2)$ because $u_2$ extends $f_2$. Let $\widetilde u_1$ be the $q_2$ solution with boundary value $f_1$, which exists by [F3]. Then $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_2}(\widetilde u_1,u_2)$. Since $u_1-\widetilde u_1\in H_0^1(M)$ and $u_2$ solves the $q_2$ weak equation, real-valuedness of $q_2$ gives $a_{q_2}(u_1-\widetilde u_1,u_2)=\overline{a_{q_2}(u_2,u_1-\widetilde u_1)}=0$. Thus $\langle\Lambda_{q_2}f_1,f_2\rangle=a_{q_2}(u_1,u_2)$.
Subtract the identities in step 2.1. The gradient terms cancel and the remaining volume term is $\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g$, which proves the Schrödinger identity.

Define the boundary trace-data space $\mathcal B_\Omega:=H^1(\Omega)/H_0^1(\Omega)$ with quotient norm; the trace-quotient lemma identifies this quotient with the fixed-atlas $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ boundary data convention of the scalar conductivity map. For $f=[U]\in\mathcal B_\Omega$, a weak solution with boundary datum $f$ is a class $u_{\gamma,f}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $[u_{\gamma,f}]=f$ and

$$\int_\Omega \gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla\varphi\,dx=0\qquad(\varphi\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle:=\int_\Omega\gamma\nabla u_{\gamma,f}\cdot\nabla V_h\,dx,$$

$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying

invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,

[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$

context.

almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev

for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;

Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The space $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a closed linear subspace of the complete space $H^1(\Omega)$ by [F1] and [F3]. Since $\Omega$ is bounded, it lies in a slab $a<x\cdot e<b$ for some unit vector $e$ and finite $a<b$; applying [F2] with $p=2$ gives $\|v\|_{L^2}\le C(2)(b-a)\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Thus $\|v\|_H:=\|
abla v\|_{L^2}$ is a norm equivalent to the inherited $H^1$ norm, and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ is a real Hilbert space for $(v,w)_H=\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot
abla w\,dx$.

Fix any representative $U\in H^1(\Omega)$ of $f$; the existence argument below is independent of which representative is fixed. On $H_0^1(\Omega)$ define $a_\gamma(z,v)=\int_\Omega\gamma
abla z\cdot
abla v\,dx$ and $F_U(v)=-\int_\Omega\gamma
abla U\cdot
abla v\,dx$. By [F6], $a_\gamma$ is bounded by $C\|z\|_H\|v\|_H$, coercive by $c\|z\|_H^2$, and $F_U$ is bounded by $C\|
abla U\|_{L^2}\|v\|_H$. Countable Choice follows from [F5], so [F4] gives a unique $z\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $a_\gamma(z,v)=F_U(v)$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Then $u_{\gamma,f}:=U+z$ has quotient class $f$ and satisfies the stated weak equation.

abla w\cdot
abla v\,dx=0$ for every $v\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Taking $v=w$ and using [F6] gives $c\|
abla w\|_{L^2}^2\le0$, so $\|w\|_H=0$ and hence $w=0$ by the norm property in step 1.1.

abla W|^2\,dx=\int_\Omega\gamma|

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Assume AC. Let $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$ with positive-definite covariance
$\Sigma$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable and symmetric,
$L(-x)=L(x)$, and quasi-convex, meaning each sublevel set
$\{x:L(x)\le t\}$ is convex. Then for every $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$E L(X-a)\ge E L(X-m).$$
Thus the Gaussian center $m$ minimizes expected loss. The result includes
quasi-convex losses whose sublevel sets are not closed.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Write $Y_n=(\ell_1(W),\ldots,\ell_n(W))$, let $\Sigma_n$ be its covariance matrix, and put $a_n=(\ell_1(ih),\ldots,\ell_n(ih))$. The vector $Y_n$ is centered Gaussian by [F1]. If $c\in\ker\Sigma_n$, then $\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j(W)$ has variance zero and hence is zero almost surely. For $\ell_c=\sum_{j\le n}c_j\ell_j$, this gives $C\ell_c=0$ and $[\ell_c]=0$ in $E$; therefore [F2] gives $c\cdot a_n=\ell_c(ih)=\langle h,[\ell_c]\rangle_E=0$. Thus $a_n\perp\ker\Sigma_n$, so $a_n\in S_n:=\operatorname{ran}(\Sigma_n)$, the support subspace of $Y_n$.

In the finite-dimensional space $S_n$, the restriction of $Y_n$ is a nondegenerate Gaussian vector. Let $Q_n=[-r,r]^n$ and $D_n=Q_n\cap S_n$, a closed symmetric convex set. Since $a_n\in S_n$, the event $Y_n-a_n\in Q_n$ is the translate by $a_n$ of $D_n$ inside $S_n$. An invertible linear change of coordinates turns the centered law on $S_n$ into a nondegenerate Gaussian law and preserves symmetry and convexity of $D_n$. Apply [F4] to the bounded loss $1_{D_n^c}$ in those coordinates: its sublevel sets are $D_n$ and the whole space, so it is symmetric and quasi-convex. This yields
$$ \mathbb P(Y_n-a_n\in Q_n)\le\mathbb P(Y_n\in Q_n). $$
If $S_n=\{0\}$, then $Y_n=a_n=0$ almost surely and the same inequality is equality.

Define $A_n(h)=\{\max_{j\le n}|\ell_j(W-ih)|\le r\}$. Step 2.1 says $\mathbb P(A_n(h))\le\mathbb P(A_n(0))$. The sets $A_n(h)$ decrease with $n$, and [F3] gives $\bigcap_n A_n(h)=\{\|W-ih\|_B\le r\}$; likewise $\bigcap_n A_n(0)=\{\|W\|_B\le r\}$. Apply [F5] to both decreasing sequences and pass to their limits in the finite-dimensional inequalities. This proves the stated ball-mass bound.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. Let $\Omega\subset(0,1)^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open domain with $C^\infty$ boundary, and let $\Omega'\subset\Omega$ be an open domain whose closure is compact and contained in $\Omega$. Fix real parameters $m>0$, $M\ge\max\{1,m\}$, $R>0$, and $0<\alpha<1$. Define
$$\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):=\{\gamma\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R):m\le\gamma(x)\le M\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\}$$
and
$$\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega'):=\{\gamma\in\Gamma_{m,M}(\Omega):\gamma=1\text{ almost everywhere on }\Omega\setminus\Omega'\}.$$
For $\gamma\in BV(\Omega)$ set $\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}:=\max\{\|\gamma\|_{L^1(\Omega)},TV(\gamma;\Omega)\}$. For a continuously differentiable function on $\overline\Omega$ whose first derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder continuous, set
$$\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\max\left\{\max_{|\beta|\le1}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)|,\ \max_{|\beta|=1}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|\partial^\beta\gamma(x)-\partial^\beta\gamma(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}\right\}.$$
Define
$$X_d(R):=\begin{cases}\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap BV(\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{BV(\Omega)}\le R\},&d=2,\\[2mm]\{\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')\cap C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega):\|\gamma\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le R\},&d\ge3.\end{cases}$$
For $\gamma\in\Gamma'_{m,M}(\Omega,\Omega')$, define its measurable background extension $\gamma_e:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ by $\gamma_e=\gamma$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$ and $\gamma_e=1$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\Omega$. Then $\gamma_e-1$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\Omega'$. No pointwise continuity of $\gamma_e$ is asserted. The classes $X_d(R)$ are not assumed nonempty.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, where elements of $L^1$ are almost-everywhere equivalence classes. For each $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, its distributional derivative $D_i u$ acts on $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by
$$\langle D_i u,\varphi\rangle:=-\int_\Omega u\,\partial_i\varphi\,dx.$$
The function $u$ is in $BV(\Omega)$ when each $D_i u$ is represented by a finite signed Radon measure and the resulting vector-valued measure $Du=(D_1u,\ldots,D_nu)$ has finite total variation. Here a finite vector-valued Radon measure means that its partition variation is a finite Radon measure. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, define
$$|Du|(A):=\sup\left\{\sum_{j=1}^\infty |Du(A_j)|:\ (A_j)_{j\ge1}\text{ is a Borel partition of }A\right\},$$
using the Euclidean norm on each vector value. Define the spatial total variation by $TV(u;\Omega):=|Du|(\Omega)$. A Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\Omega$ of finite measure has finite perimeter relative to $\Omega$ when $\chi_E\in BV(\Omega)$; its relative perimeter is $P(E;\Omega):=TV(\chi_E;\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain, meaning a bounded open set whose boundary has a finite cover by Lipschitz graph neighborhoods with $\Omega$ on one side of each graph. The zero-extension map is bounded from $BV(\Omega)$ to $BV(\mathbb R^n)$, with support in $\overline\Omega$, and there is a finite $C_\Omega$ such that $$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}+TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^n)\le C_\Omega\bigl(\|u\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+TV(u;\Omega)\bigr)$$ for every $u\in BV(\Omega)$. For every $v\in BV(\mathbb R^n)$ and $h\in\mathbb R^n$, $$\|v(\cdot+h)-v\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^n)}\le |h|TV(v;\mathbb R^n).$$

Let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be a function.
The **translate** of $f$ by $h$ is the function $\tau_h f$ defined by

$$ (\tau_h f)(x) := f(x-h)\qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

This fixes the sign convention used throughout the page: translating by $h$
shifts the graph of $f$ in the positive $h$-direction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

By the zero-extension part of [F2], $\widetilde u\in BV(\mathbb R^2)$ and
$$TV(\widetilde u;\mathbb R^2)\le C_\Omega\bigl(|\Omega|(M+1)+R\bigr)=:V_0.$$
Since $\gamma_e=1+\widetilde u$, [F3] gives $\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_1=\|\widetilde u(\cdot+h)-\widetilde u\|_1\le V_0|h|$. Thus the first inequality holds with $C_1=V_0$.

The bound $m\le\gamma\le M$ inside $\Omega$ and the background value $1$ outside show $|\gamma_e|\le B$ almost everywhere; hence $|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e|\le2B$ almost everywhere. Applying [F3] and step 1.2 yields
$$\|\gamma_e(\cdot+h)-\gamma_e\|_p^p\le(2B)^{p-1}V_0|h|.$$
Taking $p$-th roots and then the supremum over $|h|\le t$ gives the second inequality with $C_p=((2B)^{p-1}V_0)^{1/p}$. At $t=0$ both sides vanish.

$$U_\zeta(x)=e^{x\cdot\zeta}(1+r_\zeta(x)),\qquad (-\Delta+q)U_\zeta=0,\qquad \|r_\zeta\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{1/2}}\le2\|q\|_{\dot X_\zeta^{-1/2}}.$$

$$\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\left(\|q\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{-1/2}}^2+\|r_{\zeta_\pm}\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm}^{1/2}}^2\right)ds\,d\eta\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\lambda^{-\alpha/(1+\alpha)}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge3$, $k\in\mathbb R^d$, and fix an oriented two-plane $P\perp k$. For a unit vector $\eta\in P$, let $\eta^\perp$ be its positive quarter turn. For $s\ge|k|/2$, put $r(s)=\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}$ and
$$\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)=\pm s\eta+i(k/2\pm r(s)\eta^\perp).$$
These phases are null, have length $\sqrt2s$, and sum to $ik$. Use the unitary angular Fourier convention and the norms $\dot X_\zeta^b,X_\zeta^b$ with inhomogeneous weight $s+|p_\zeta|$, where $p_\zeta(\xi)=-|\xi|^2+2i\zeta\cdot\xi$. For a fixed $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, define
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f):=\frac1\lambda\int_{S^1(P)}\int_\lambda^{2\lambda}\|\phi\operatorname{div}f\|_{\dot X_{\zeta_\pm(s,\eta)}^{-1/2}}^2\,ds\,d\eta.$$
Here $d\eta$ is arclength, either sign can be used, and the derivative is distributional. For $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+|k|^2}$ and $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C^d)$,
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\|f\|_2^2,$$
where $C$ depends only on $d,\phi$. If $f\in H^1$, also
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le\frac C\lambda\|\nabla f\|_2^2.$$
Let $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$ be nonnegative with integral $1$, put $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$, and define $\omega_2(f,h)=\sup_{|y|\le h}\|f(\cdot-y)-f\|_2$. For $h>0$ one consequently has
$$\mathcal A_{\lambda,k}(f)\le C_\rho\left[\frac{\|f\|_2^2}{\lambda h^2}+\left(1+\frac{1+|k|^2}{\lambda}\right)\omega_2(f,h)^2\right].$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Extend both coefficients by $1$ using [F1], and fix a ball $B$ containing $[0,1]^d$ and a neighborhood of it. Put $g_j=\sqrt{\gamma_j}$ and $a_j=
abla\log\gamma_j$. These are globally $C^1$ and $C^{0,\alpha}$, respectively, and $a_j$ has support in $\overline{\Omega'}$. Their supremum and Hölder bounds are uniform: the positive lower bound $m_*:=\min\{m,1\}$ gives $|a_j|\le C_dR/m_*$; on $|x-y|\le1$, expand $
abla\gamma_j(x)/\gamma_j(x)-
abla\gamma_j(y)/\gamma_j(y)$, using the derivative Hölder bound and $|\gamma_j(x)-\gamma_j(y)|\le\sqrt dR|x-y|$; on larger distances use twice the supremum. Thus [F4] applies uniformly. Let $q_j=	frac12\operatorname{div}a_j+	frac14|a_j|^2$ and $Q=q_1-q_2$, with bilinear distribution pairings as in [F4].

The Liouville form identity is $\int
abla v\cdot
abla w+\langle q_j,vwangle=\int\gamma_j
abla(v/g_j)\cdot
abla(w/g_j)$ for $v,w\in H^1$ on a bounded set. Indeed $q_j=g_j^{-1}\Delta g_j$ means $\langle q_j,vwangle=-\int
abla g_j\cdot
abla(g_j^{-1}vw)$; expanding this derivative gives the displayed identity term by term. All products are integrable since $g_j,g_j^{-1},
abla g_j$ are bounded and the factors are in $H^1$. The identity extends from smooth factors by local $H^1$ approximation; multiplication by a bounded $C^1$ function with bounded derivative is continuous on $H^1$, as follows from the product rule and the same approximation. Since $g_j=1$ near $\partial\Omega$, the trace of $U_j$ equals that of $u_j:=U_j/g_j$. A solution $U_j$ of the Schrödinger form equation therefore gives a weak conductivity solution $u_j$: test the form identity with $w=g_jz$, first for compactly supported tests and then in $H_0^1$ by density. Subtracting the two Schrödinger forms for solutions $U_1,U_2$, or repeating the weak-solution subtraction in [F2], gives $\langle Q,U_1U_2angle=((\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1)(\overline{f_2})$. Here $f_j$ is the trace class of $u_j$, and the conjugation converts the sesquilinear DN convention to the bilinear interior form. The compact support of $Q$ makes its whole-space pairing identical to its pairing on $\Omega$. Consequently $|\langle Q,U_1U_2angle|\le\delta\|u_1\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\|u_2\|_{H^1(\Omega)}$.

Use the paired phases $\zeta_\pm=s(\pm\eta)+i(k/2\pm\sqrt{s^2-|k|^2/4}\,\eta^\perp)$ of [F4]. For fixed $s$ their remainders satisfy $\|r_j\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. To verify this last uniform bound, the symbol inequality $|\xi|^2/(s+|p_{\zeta_j}(\xi)|)\le Cs$ follows by splitting $|\xi|\le8s$ and its complement. Apply the negative cutoff bound in [F3] to $\operatorname{div}a_j$ and $|a_j|^2$ as in [F4] to obtain $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_j}}\le C\sqrt s$. The two positive cutoff bounds then give $\|r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le C$ and $\|\nabla r_j\|_{L^2(B)}\le Cs$. Multiplication by $g_j^{-1}e^{x\cdot\zeta_j}$ yields $\|u_j\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le Ce^{Cs}s$. Thus step 2.1 bounds the exact interior product by $C\delta e^{Cs}s^2$.

Fix a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\phi=1$ near $\overline{\Omega'}$. We first prove the modulated cutoff bound used for each linear remainder term. Let $u$ be Schwartz and write the Fourier convolution for $\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u$ with $h=\xi-\eta-k$. The symbol comparison and characteristic-sphere estimate proved in [F3] give, uniformly in the center $y$, $\int\langle\xi-y\rangle^{-L}(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})\,d\xi\le C_L$ for sufficiently large $L$, and $s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|\le C(s+|p_\zeta(\xi)|)\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^2$, where $D_\zeta$ is distance to the characteristic sphere of $p_\zeta$. Since $s/|p_\zeta(\xi)|\le C(1+D_\zeta(\xi)^{-1})$, these estimates imply
 $\sup_\eta\int |\widehat\phi(\xi-\eta-k)|\frac{s+|p_\zeta(\eta)|}{|p_\zeta(\xi)|}\,d\xi\le C\langle k\rangle^2$.
Indeed, after substituting $h=\xi-\eta-k$, the integrand is bounded by $C|\widehat\phi(h)|\langle k+h\rangle^2(1+D_\zeta(\eta+k+h)^{-1})$; use $\langle k+h\rangle^2\le C\langle k\rangle^2\langle h\rangle^2$, the rapid decay of $\widehat\phi$, and the uniform-center estimate. The same weighted Schur argument as in [F3] gives $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}u\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|u\|_{X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Applying the dual argument of [F3] to $\overline\phi e^{-ik\cdot x}$ yields $\|\phi e^{ik\cdot x}v\|_{X^{1/2}_\zeta}\le C\langle k\rangle^2\|v\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_\zeta}$, and hence also the same bound with the homogeneous positive-half norm on the left. Density in the weighted Fourier completions follows by truncating away from the characteristic sphere, as in [F3]. Since $2\le N=d+10$, this proves the modulation estimate used below with the stated exponent. Because $q_j$ is real, $\widehat q_j(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat q_j(\xi)}$, and $p_{-\zeta}(\xi)=p_\zeta(-\xi)$, so $\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{-\zeta}}=\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_\zeta}$. Weighted Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz in the bilinear pairing therefore gives $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_l\rangle|\le C\langle k\rangle^N\|q_j\|_{\dot X^{-1/2}_{\zeta_l}}\|r_l\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_l}}$. For the quadratic term, expand the definition of $q_j$ on $e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2$ and use [F3] on each factor with its own phase. The product and differentiated product have $L^1$ norms at most $Cs^{-1}$ and $C$, respectively, times the two remainder norms. The derivative of the exponential adds $C|k|s^{-1}$, giving $|\langle q_j,e^{ik\cdot x}r_1r_2\rangle|\le C(1+|k|)\|r_1\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_1}}\|r_2\|_{\dot X^{1/2}_{\zeta_2}}$.

Since $\zeta_1+\zeta_2=ik$, expand $U_1U_2=e^{ik\cdot x}(1+r_1+r_2+r_1r_2)$ in step 3.1. Move the three remainder terms to the other side and apply step 4.1. Average over $\lambda\le s\le2\lambda$ and the unit circle in the fixed plane $P\perp k$, dividing by its total measure $2\pi\lambda$. The left side $|\langle Q,e^{ik\cdot x}\rangle|$ is independent of these parameters. For each linear or quadratic product, integral Cauchy–Schwarz and [F4] bound its average by $C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$, where $\beta=\alpha/(1+\alpha)$. The same bound applies when the potential $q_j$ and remainder $r_l$ have different indices, because [F4] holds for either coefficient and either phase. Absorbing the fixed Fourier normalization gives $|\widehat Q(k)|\le C\delta e^{C\lambda}\lambda^2+C\langle k\rangle^N(1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda)\lambda^{-\beta}$ whenever $\lambda\ge\max\{s_0,100\langle k\rangle\}$. Replacing $k$ by $-k$ if needed accounts for the negative-sign Fourier convention.

Define $\mathcal Q:=\|(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1/2}\widehat Q(\xi)\|_2$. This is finite since $Q=\tfrac12\operatorname{div}(a_1-a_2)+\tfrac14(|a_1|^2-|a_2|^2)$ with both coefficient fields in $L^2$. For $t\ge1$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $Ct^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|$. The high-frequency contribution of the zero-order field is at most $Ct^{-1}$. Plancherel bounds its high-frequency contribution by $Ct^{-1}\|\operatorname{div}(\rho_h*f)\|_2+\|f-\rho_h*f\|_2\le C(t^{-1}h^{-1}+h^\alpha)$. The last two bounds follow by differentiating the convolution kernel and by the uniform Hölder estimate with fixed compact support, exactly as in [F4]. Taking $h=t^{-1/(1+\alpha)}$ gives $\mathcal Q\le C[t^{d/2}\sup_{|k|\le t}|\widehat Q(k)|+t^{-\beta}]$.

Choose $A=2+(N+d+1)/\beta$ and a fixed $L\ge\max\{s_0,200\}$. Set $\lambda=Lt^A$. Then $\lambda\ge100\sqrt{1+t^2}$, $1+\langle k\rangle^2/\lambda\le C$ for $|k|\le t$, and $t^{N+d/2}\lambda^{-\beta}\le Ct^{-\beta}$. If $\delta=0$, let $t\to\infty$ in the estimate before this choice to obtain $\mathcal Q=0$.

Put $w=\log g_1-\log g_2$ and $H=g_1g_2$. Both $w$ and $
abla w$ have compact support in $\overline{\Omega'}$, and $w\in H_0^1(B)$. Expanding the formula for $Q$ gives the distribution identity $HQ=\operatorname{div}(H
abla w)$: the divergence part is $\Delta w$, while the zero-order part is $
