citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume full AC, matching the chosen finite twisted-chain and maximal-abelian-cover conventions. Let K be a smooth oriented knot, M(K) its preferred-longitude zero-framed surgery, W a compact connected oriented smooth 4-manifold with boundary M(K), and π=π₁(W). Put π^(0)=π and π^(j+1)=[π^(j),π^(j)]. A right Zπ-chain complex with coefficients in a left Z[π/π^(j)]-module is formed by tensoring over Zπ with that module.

For n≥0, W is an integral n-solution for K when H₁(M(K);Z)→H₁(W;Z) is an isomorphism, H₂(W;Z) is free of rank 2r for some finite r, and there are classes x₁,…,x_r,y₁,…,y_r in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n)]) whose equivariant intersection pairings satisfy λ_n(x_i,x_j)=0 and λ_n(x_i,y_j)=δ_ij. It is an integral (n+1/2)-solution when, in addition, each x_i is the image of a class x̃_i in H₂(W;Z[π/π^(n+1)]) and λ_{n+1}(x̃_i,x̃_j)=0 for all i,j. Here λ_j is the equivariant intersection pairing induced by the orientation of W.

For a commutative ring R with 1≠0, a group G belongs to Strebel's class D(R) if every homomorphism between projective RG-modules is injective whenever its tensor with the trivial G-module R is injective. In this page R is Q or F_p for a prime p. For a countable discrete group G, its group von Neumann algebra N G is the weak-operator closure of CG in the left regular representation on ℓ²(G), with trace τ_G(T)=⟨Tδ_e,δ_e⟩. The von Neumann dimension of a finitely generated projective N G-module represented by a projection E is τ_G(E); for an arbitrary module it is the supremum of the dimensions of its finitely generated projective submodules.

For a compact oriented 4-manifold W with boundary, sign(W) is the inertia difference of the symmetric intersection form on H₂(W;R) modulo its radical (the subspace pairing to zero with every class), equivalently on the image of H₂(W;R)→H₂(W,∂W;R). Given a closed oriented 3-manifold M, a homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→G, a compact oriented 4-manifold W with ∂W=M, and an extension ψ:π₁(W)→G of φ, the L²-signature sign_G^(2)(W,ψ) is the von Neumann signature of the nonsingular part of the N G-coefficient intersection form. When such a W and extension exist, the signature defect is sign_G^(2)(W,ψ)−sign(W). It is called the rho invariant of (M,φ) only after its independence of the bounding data is established by a separate bordism argument.

Supply a finite polygonal oriented disk-band Seifert-surface model and local ambient smooth roundings for a smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, with compatible closed product tube, positive meridian $\mu$, preferred longitude $\lambda$, collars and peripheral paths. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T=\partial X$, and let $M=X\cup_T V$ be its actual preferred zero-longitude surgery, oriented to extend $X$. Let $k=\mathbb Z$ or a commutative field, $R=k[t,t^{-1}]$, and let $F$ be its fraction field, so $F=\mathbb Q(t)$ when $k=\mathbb Z$. Use the associated based right coefficient systems sending $\mu$ to $t$ with transport by the inverse unit, and their standard parallel Hermitian form.

The actual maps induce isomorphisms
$$i_*:H_1(X;R)\cong H_1(M;R),\qquad j_*:H_1(X;R)\cong H_1(X,T;R).$$
The closed Bockstein–duality pairing $B_M$ is defined on the whole first homology and is nonsingular. On $X$ use the following explicit classical cocycle rule: take an integral $R^\vee$-valued two-cocycle $a$ whose cap class is $\overline{j_*x}$, take one whole $F^\vee$-valued one-cochain $b$ with $\partial^*b=a$, and set $B_X(x,y)=[b(y)]\in F/R$. Such primitives exist, this rule is independent of all representatives and choices, and
$$B_X(x,y)=B_M(i_*x,i_*y).$$
Thus it is the nonsingular exterior classical Blanchfield form with the same positive-meridian, positive-push and first-variable conjugate-linear conventions. Based axis classes in the exterior are carried to their actual surgery classes. The constructions commute with the rational and prime coefficient maps wherever the displayed forms are compared; no choice principle, arbitrary knot projection theorem or four-dimensional normal-neighborhood claim is assumed.

Assume AC. For an integer $h\ge0$ or a half-integer $h=n+1/2$, let $\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ be the set of smooth concordance classes whose preferred-longitude zero surgery bounds an integral $h$-solution. Use the integral lifted-pair definition: $H_1$ is identified with the boundary meridian $\mathbb Z$, $H_2$ is free of rank $2r$, there are exactly $r$ zero/unit pairs over the indicated derived quotient, and at a half level the isotropic classes lift one further derived stage. Every smooth pattern preserves smooth knot concordance. Then $\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ is a subgroup of smooth knot concordance, $\mathcal F_{h'}^{\mathrm{sm}}\subseteq\mathcal F_h^{\mathrm{sm}}$ for $h'\ge h$, and every smooth knot lies in $\mathcal F_0^{\mathrm{sm}}$.

More specifically, let $R$ be a smooth slice knot and let $\eta$ be a supplied unknotted infection axis in its exterior with $[\eta]\in\pi_1(S^3\setminus R)^{(k)}$, where $k\ge1$. For every smooth knot $J$, the infection $R(\eta,J)$ has an actual smooth integral $k$-solution. All constructions use finite smooth disk-band, peripheral product-tube, collar and path data; these data may be chosen under the stated AC.

Consequently, if $P$ is a winding-zero smooth pattern, then for every $k\ge1$ and every smooth knot $J$,
$$[P^k(J)]-[P^k(U)]\in\mathcal F_k^{\mathrm{sm}},\qquad \langle P^k(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle\subseteq\mathcal F_k^{\mathrm{sm}}+\langle[P^k(U)]\rangle.$$
No locally flat tubular neighborhood or TOP realization theorem is assumed or concluded.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge1$ and a smooth winding-zero pattern $P$ whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-value, equivalently using the actual exterior-to-zero-surgery identification. Supply finite smooth disk-band models, peripheral product tubes, paths and compatible collars for the finitely many knots and infection pieces used below.

For every $m\ge1$ there are smooth knots $J_1,\ldots,J_m$ with explicit finite disk-band surfaces such that no nonzero signed connected sum
$$K=\mathop{\#}_{i=1}^m a_i P^n(J_i),\qquad (a_1,\ldots,a_m)\in\mathbb Z^m\setminus\{0\},$$
bounds a compact connected oriented smooth four-manifold $V$ with collared boundary $M(K)$ and the following lifted half-pair data: boundary inclusion identifies $H_1(M(K);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ with $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$, $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, there are exactly $r$ height-$n$ equivariant pairs $x_i,y_i$ with zero $x$-pairings and unit $x,y$-pairings, and the $x_i$ lift to height $n+1$ with zero pairings. Height $h$ means coefficients $\mathbb Z[\pi_1(V)/\pi_1(V)^{(h)}]$. Signed knots use the marked mirror-and-reverse inverse convention.

There is also one smooth knot $J$, with explicit finite disk-band surface, for which
$$P^n(J)\#P^n(J)\#\bigl(-P^n(J\#J)\bigr)$$
is not smoothly slice. More generally its zero surgery bounds no compact connected smooth integral homology-circle four-manifold with boundary-meridian $H_1$ isomorphism.

The coefficient maps and all signature sums used to obtain these obstructions are maps on the actual smooth bounding manifolds and infection pieces. No TOP-to-smooth rho comparison, choice-free analytic conclusion, integral-filtration subgroup construction, or quotient-rank conclusion is implicit in this supplied-data obstruction theorem.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented collared topological four-manifold with connected boundary $M$, with $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$ the isomorphism $\mathbb Z[\mu]\to\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$. Supply $r$ ordinary zero/unit pairs $x_i,y_i$, and supply isotropic lifts of the $x_i$ to the abelian cover of $V$. Let $p$ be any prime, let $C_p$ be the cyclic group of order $p$, and let $\phi:\pi_1(V)\to\mathbb Z\to C_p$ send the meridian to its positive generator. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}_{C_p}^{(2)}(V,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}(V)=0.$$
The completed coefficient homology has $b_0^{(2)}(V)=b_1^{(2)}(V)=1/p$, $b_2^{(2)}(V)=2r$ and $b_3^{(2)}(V)=b_4^{(2)}(V)=0$, and the middle intersection form has zero radical. In particular, when $V$ is smooth, its boundary restriction has $\rho_{\mathrm{sm}}(M,\phi|_M)=0$. Every smooth integral $1$-solution satisfies the supplied pair hypotheses. No comparison between a nonsmooth TOP defect and a smooth bounding-defect invariant is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a smooth winding-zero pattern whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-pairing in the Alexander module of $P(U)$. Let $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$ denote smooth oriented knot concordance with its reverse-mirror inverse, and let $P^0$ be the identity. Then for every $n\ge0$ the abelian-group quotient
$$\langle P^n(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle/\langle P^{n+1}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}})\rangle$$
has infinite rational rank. For every $n\ge1$ the smooth satellite map $P^n$ is not a group homomorphism. The proof uses finite companion families depending on a prescribed rank bound; no infinite choice of an explicit independent sequence is required. No coprime Alexander-polynomial condition is imposed. This theorem retains full AC and makes no assertion identifying nonsmooth TOP defects with smooth bounding invariants.

Let $n\ge1$. Supply a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold $V$ with boundary a marked knot zero surgery, $H_1(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$, and exactly $r$ integral pairs $x_i,y_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n)}])$, $\pi=\pi_1(V)$, satisfying $\lambda(x_i,x_j)=0$ and $\lambda(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Form $W$ by any finite sequence of the actual marked standard connected-sum and winding-zero infection cobordism adjunctions along outgoing knot-surgery components, including orientation reversals, using supplied smooth peripheral products and collars. Let $\phi:\pi_1(W)\to\Gamma$ have PTFA target and restrict on $V$ through $\pi/\pi^{(n)}$. Take $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ and put $A=k[\Gamma]$, with involutive Ore fraction division ring $K$ and the based standard parallel Hermitian structure.

The image pairs $\ell_i,d_i\in H_2(W;A)$ satisfy $\lambda(\ell_i,\ell_j)=0$ and $\lambda(\ell_i,d_j)=\lambda(d_j,\ell_i)=\delta_{ij}$. Their localized boundary-intersection cokernel has dimension at most $2r$. For each boundary component $M_0$ on which $\phi$ is nontrivial, $H_1(M_0;K)=0$, its coefficient Bockstein–duality linking form is defined, and its actual inclusion kernel is isotropic:
$$B_{M_0}(z,w)=0\quad\text{for all }z,w\in\ker\{H_1(M_0;A)\to H_1(W;A)\}.$$
Thus every boundary class with nonzero self-pairing survives in $H_1(W;A)$ and lies outside every isotropic submodule. If a component's coefficient image is cyclic, its form additionally has the nonsingularity furnished by the cyclic-image coefficient theorem; no unrestricted PTFA nonsingularity is asserted.

For a finite forest of iterated winding-zero infections with these initial data, suppose each top meridian generates $H_1(W_n;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ up to sign, and each pattern-axis integral classical self-pairing is nonzero. Use the actual intermediate $W_j$, rational mixed coefficients through index $n$, and one bottom field $\mathbb F_p$. For every odd prime outside the explicit finite exceptional set of the axis values, every branch meridian has a nonzero class in $P^{n-j}\pi_1(W_j)/P^{n-j+1}\pi_1(W_j)$, of infinite order when $j>0$ and order $p$ when $j=0$. All these conclusions hold for the supplied locally flat topological bordisms and smooth bordisms without a choice principle. Existence of the initial $V$ and its lifted pairs from a concordance relation is a separate hypothesis, as are analytic rho invariance and signature vanishing.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact oriented Hausdorff topological manifold with supplied boundary collar, and supply a based homomorphism on each component to a discrete group $G$, with compatible paths when maps or gluings are considered. Use $R=\mathbb CG$, with involution conjugating complex scalars and sending $g$ to $g^{-1}$, and its based right regular local system with standard parallel Hermitian form. Let $A=\mathcal NG$ have the canonical group trace. Then its singular coefficient complex has an actual bounded finite-projective $R$ chain-homotopy model. Absolute, relative and finite whole-component gluing diagrams admit such models and finite matrix comparison maps.

After extending these finite projective matrices to $\ell^2(G)$, write $\mathscr H_i(M)$ for completed reduced homology, with boundaries replaced by their Hilbert closures. If $p_Z,p_B$ are the cycle and boundary-closure projections in a finite ambient projection module, the corresponding algebraic reduced module is $P_i=(p_Z-p_B)A^r$, and
$$H_i(M;A)\twoheadrightarrow P_i\hookrightarrow\mathscr H_i(M)=(p_Z-p_B)\ell^2(G)^r.$$
The first map has dimension-zero kernel, and the second is injective with dense image and need not be onto. Pair and whole-component Mayer–Vietoris sequences are weakly exact on the completed modules. Oriented cap duality gives bounded mutually inverse maps on their completed reduced homology and cohomology, with the cap-boundary and restriction identities. These structures and the resulting spectral signature do not depend on the finite-projective model.

For a four-manifold the middle intersection form is the bounded Hermitian form defined by inverse relative cap duality, restriction and evaluation. Its Hilbert radical is the kernel of its self-adjoint operator. Its signature is the trace of the positive spectral projection minus the trace of the negative projection; no closed range or bounded inverse is required for a manifold with boundary. For a closed four-manifold its middle intersection operator is boundedly invertible.

Let $W_0,W_1$ be compact oriented topological four-manifolds, let $N$ be a union of entire closed boundary components, and glue the two marked copies of $N$ by an orientation-reversing identification and the supplied collars. Put $W=W_0\cup_N W_1$ and supply one compatible regular coefficient system on $W$. Other boundary components may remain. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W)=\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(W_1),\qquad\operatorname{sign}(W)=\operatorname{sign}(W_0)+\operatorname{sign}(W_1).$$
Orientation reversal changes the corresponding sign. No finite CW type, triangulation, smoothing of a topological four-manifold, equality of ordinary and $L^2$ signatures on arbitrary closed manifolds, or analytic eta-to-defect comparison is asserted or assumed. For an arbitrary possibly uncountable $G$, the finite-matrix construction has the same dimensions and signatures as its countable coefficient image, so it agrees with the countable-group convention.

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented topological four-manifold with a supplied collar and connected boundary $M$, and choose a based loop $\mu\subset M$ such that
$$H_1(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu],\qquad H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(V;\mathbb Z),\qquad H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}.$$
Put $\pi=\pi_1(V)$, take $n\ge0$, and supply classes $x_i,y_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n)}])$, $1\le i\le r$, satisfying $\lambda_n(x_i,x_j)=0$ and $\lambda_n(x_i,y_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Supply classes $\widetilde x_i\in H_2(V;\mathbb Z[\pi/\pi^{(n+1)}])$ mapping to $x_i$ with $\lambda_{n+1}(\widetilde x_i,\widetilde x_j)=0$. These are actual lifted half-pair data on the supplied manifold; existence of such a manifold or lifts is not asserted.

Let $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb F_p$ for any prime $p$. Let $G$ be a discrete amenable group in $D(k)$ with $G^{(n+1)}=1$, and supply $\phi:\pi\to G$ such that $\phi(\mu)$ has infinite order. Use its based regular unitary local system and the finite-projective topological intersection convention. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}^{(2)}_G(V,\phi)=0=\operatorname{sign}(V),$$
so its actual bounding signature defect is zero. This applies to the full supplied locally flat topological category as well as smooth manifolds; no finite CW type, smoothing, closed-manifold ordinary-versus-$L^2$ index equality or rho bordism-independence theorem is assumed. If a separately applicable bordism-independence result identifies a rho invariant with this bounding defect, that invariant is consequently zero.

Assume full AC and a smooth winding-zero pattern $P$ whose axis has nonzero integral classical Blanchfield self-value. Use oriented zero surgery $M(K)$ and the first-positive-push Levine–Tristram signature function $\sigma_J$. Let $L>0$ exceed the uniform Cheeger–Gromov bound for every rho value of $M(P(U))$ under every group representation. For every $n,m\ge1$, there are distinct odd primes $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ outside the finite exceptional set for reduction of this self-value and finite disk-band companion knots $J_i$ such that, writing $\zeta_p=\exp(2\pi i/p)$,
$$D_i=\frac1{p_i}\sum_{r=0}^{p_i-1}\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{r})>mnL,$$
with $\sigma_{J_i}(1)=0$, $\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i})=\sigma_{J_i}(\zeta_{p_i}^{-1})>p_i mnL/2$, all other nonidentity $p_i$-th-root signatures zero, and every $p_j$-th-root signature zero for $j\ne i$. Thus $D_i$ is the canonical $\mathbb Z/p_i$ cyclic defect of $M(J_i)$. In any candidate smooth bounding bordism for a nonzero integer vector $(a_i)$ used in the actual finite-prime infection obstruction assembly, choose $i_*$ with $|a_{i_*}|=\max_i|a_i|$. Its supplied quotient using $p_{i_*}$ gives signed bottom boundary contribution $a_{i_*}D_{i_*}$; the remaining $n\sum_i|a_i|$ pattern terms have total absolute value less than $nL\sum_i|a_i|\le nmL|a_{i_*}|<|a_{i_*}|D_{i_*}$. Thus the total signed boundary rho value has the sign of $a_{i_*}$ and is nonzero.

For every $n\ge1$, the three-branch obstruction assembly also admits a finite disk-band companion knot with a canonical cyclic defect $D>3nL$. For any supplied candidate smooth homology-circle bound in that assembly, its quotient kills the distinguished negative bottom branch and gives either $0$ or $D$ on each positive bottom branch, with at least one value $D$. Its $3n$ remaining pattern terms have total absolute value less than $3nL$, so the total boundary rho value is positive. For a locally flat TOP pair-family application, the initial bordism must supply the actual height-$n$ pairs and height-$(n+1)$ isotropic lifts; for a TOP three-branch application it must supply the actual homology-circle bound. In either case the finite-projective coefficient quotient must satisfy the stated survival and vanishing hypotheses, and the boundary rho values must agree with the smooth bounding defects by the closed TOP bordism equality. Pairwise relatively prime Alexander polynomials belong only to the separate Theorem C comparison of distinct patterns; they are not hypotheses of Theorems A or B.

Assume full AC. Let M be a closed oriented 3-manifold, Γ a discrete group, and φ:π₁(M)→Γ. If (W₀,ψ₀) and (W₁,ψ₁) are compact oriented 4-manifolds with boundary M over which φ extends, then sign_Γ^(2)(W₀,ψ₀)−sign(W₀)=sign_Γ^(2)(W₁,ψ₁)−sign(W₁). Hence the signature defect depends only on (M,φ).

Assume full AC. For every closed oriented 3-manifold M there exists a finite constant C_M such that for every discrete group Γ and every homomorphism φ:π₁(M)→Γ for which the rho invariant is defined, |ρ(M,φ)|≤C_M. The constant may depend on M but not on Γ or φ.

Assume AC. Let $V$ be a compact connected oriented collared topological four-manifold with connected boundary $M$, with $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(V;\mathbb Z)$ the isomorphism $\mathbb Z[\mu]\to\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_2(V;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2r}$. Supply $r$ ordinary zero/unit pairs $x_i,y_i$, and supply isotropic lifts of the $x_i$ to the abelian cover of $V$. Let $p$ be any prime, let $C_p$ be the cyclic group of order $p$, and let $\phi:\pi_1(V)\to\mathbb Z\to C_p$ send the meridian to its positive generator. Then
$$\operatorname{sign}_{C_p}^{(2)}(V,\phi)=\operatorname{sign}(V)=0.$$
The completed coefficient homology has $b_0^{(2)}(V)=b_1^{(2)}(V)=1/p$, $b_2^{(2)}(V)=2r$ and $b_3^{(2)}(V)=b_4^{(2)}(V)=0$, and the middle intersection form has zero radical. citations.quote:
Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Let P be a pattern of nonzero winding n. If P(U) is smoothly slice in an R_n-homology 4-ball, then P is weakly injective on C^{1/n}, meaning P(K)=P(U) implies K=U in that category. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then P is weakly injective on C_ex (respectively C_top). In ordinary smooth concordance, if P(U) is smoothly slice in standard B⁴ and P has strong winding number ±1, then P is weakly injective on C_sm provided the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture holds.

For any pattern P and knots K,J with P(K)=P(J) in one of these concordance groups, the connected-sum reduction constructs a pattern R for which R(−K#J) is concordant to U, whose closure R(U)=−P(K)#P(K) is ribbon, and whose winding w(R)=w(P). If P is strong winding ±1, then R is strong winding ±1. This reduction turns injectivity of P into weak injectivity of R; it does not assert that P itself is weakly injective without the closure hypotheses above.

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

Let B be a smooth 4-ball embedded in the standard smooth 4-sphere S⁴. The closure of S⁴\B is diffeomorphic to the standard 4-ball. This is the special smooth Schoenflies complement assertion used after a capped contractible 4-manifold has been identified with standard S⁴; it does not assert the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary, let $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ be a connected boundary region, and let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M$ by embeddings $f_1,f_2$ with disjoint images, where $1\le k\le n-2$. A **slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$** is determined by a band datum: points $x_i$ in the attaching spheres $f_i(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})$, trivializations of the normal bundles of the attaching spheres near $x_i$ compatible with the framings of $f_i$, and an embedded band $\beta$ whose rank-$(n-k-1)$ normal framing matches the sphere framings after quotienting out the transverse band direction, as supplied by the band lemma. The datum also includes the full framing gluing convention described below; quotient compatibility alone is insufficient. The slid handle $h_1'$ is the $k$-handle attached to $M$ by the embedding $f_1'$ whose core sphere is obtained from $f_1(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_0$ and from $f_2(S^{k-1}\times\{0\})\setminus\operatorname{int}\beta_1$ pushed off along the band framing, where $\beta_0,\beta_1$ are the two end discs, together with the side $\partial D^{k-1}\times I$ of the band, smoothed along the gluing circles; the framing of $f_1'$ is built from the framing of $f_1$, the signed framing of the parallel copy of $f_2$, and the band framing, and extends to an embedding of the attaching region. Equivalently, in the band-sum picture, the attaching sphere of $h_1'$ is the connected sum of the attaching sphere of $h_1$ with a signed framed parallel copy of the attaching sphere of $h_2$ along the band, so that the slid attachment is disjoint from the attachment of $h_2$. Different band data may give different slides; all of them are called slides of $h_1$ over $h_2$. For $k=1$ the general formula is read in the $0$-dimensional sense: the band is an arc joining a point of the first attaching $0$-sphere to a framed parallel point of the second, and the slid attaching $0$-sphere is obtained from the first by replacing that point with a parallel copy of the other point of the second attaching $0$-sphere.

For $k\ge2$, write the old ordered normal framings as $(v_{i1},\ldots,v_{iq})$, $q=n-k$, choosing the first normal line to be the transverse band line at each end. The band framing matches the classes of $(v_{i2},\ldots,v_{iq})$. Round the seams in the two-dimensional plane formed by the end disk's radial direction and the transverse band direction. The first normal to the rounded sphere is the complementary normal in this plane; choose its sign to match $v_{11}$ on the first sphere. At the other end it agrees with $\sigma v_{21}$ for a uniquely determined $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$. Use $(\sigma v_{21},v_{22},\ldots,v_{2q})$ on the entire parallel copy of the second sphere. Equivalently, when $\sigma=-1$, precompose its normal disk coordinate with $(z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)\mapsto(-z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_q)$. This reflection concerns the copy used in the band sum; the retained handle $h_2$ keeps its original attaching embedding. Require these full ordered frames to glue across the rounded seams, rather than requiring agreement with both unreflected old frames. In an oriented boundary, this is the usual condition that the orientations induced on the two removed end disks by the framed spheres and the band have opposite boundary-gluing signs. Both addition and subtraction are allowed by the choice of band-end coordinates and this sign convention.

The seam rotation in the indicated plane, together with the remaining band normal vectors, gives a full framing agreeing with the first old framing and the signed second-copy framing. A sufficiently thin normal thickening is then an attaching embedding; take the parallel copy outside the retained attaching region and the thickening small enough to be disjoint from it. For $k=1$, use the full normal framing transported when the chosen foot is pushed along the band and across the parallel interval core of $h_2$ to its other foot; this fixes the analogous sign convention without using a positive-dimensional seam. The band lemma supplies the embedded band and its quotient framing, while the full-frame convention supplies the additional gluing data. No uniqueness of the slide is asserted. Countable Choice is inherited through the band-existence and smooth-attachment conventions.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $h_1,h_2$ be $k$-handles attached to $M\subseteq\partial_+W$ as in the slide definition, with $1\le k\le n-2$, and let $h_1'$ be a slide of $h_1$ over $h_2$ (the slid handle attached to $M$ by the band move). Then $W\cup_{f_1}h_1\cup_{f_2}h_2$ and $W\cup_{f_1'}h_1'\cup_{f_2}h_2$ are diffeomorphic relative to $\partial_0W$; more precisely there is a diffeomorphism supported in a neighbourhood of the two handles and the band region carrying the first presentation to the second. Consequently a handle slide does not change the diffeomorphism type of the presented manifold and may be performed on any of two equal-index handles.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary $\partial W=\partial_0W\sqcup\partial_1W$, let $\varphi:S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}\to\partial_1W$ be an attaching embedding of a $k$-handle and let $\psi:S^k\times D^{n-k-1}\to\partial_1(W\cup_\varphi h^k)$ be an attaching embedding of a $(k+1)$-handle attached after it, where $0\le k\le n-1$. If the attaching sphere of $h^{k+1}$ meets the belt sphere of $h^k$ transversely in exactly one point, then $W\cup_\varphi h^k\cup_\psi h^{k+1}$ is diffeomorphic to $W$ relative to $\partial_0W$. Consequently a geometrically cancelling consecutive pair may be deleted from, or added to, any handle presentation of the same manifold; the diffeomorphism may be taken to act only in a collar of the affected boundary disc and in the two handles, so the attaching data of all later handles are carried along.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link, and
isotope $R$ to an unknot bounding a disk $D_R$ that meets $B$ transversely in
one point. Then there is a finite sequence of slides of the $2$-handle $G$ over
the $2$-handle $B$, together with link isotopies, after which the attaching
circle for $G$ is disjoint from $D_R$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

derivations.claim: Fix disjoint oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$ with a regular oriented diagram $D$, and write $[J]=m[\mu_K]$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ using [F7]. The inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ is a homotopy equivalence: in the punctured tube $N(K)\setminus K$, radial motion in each normal disk retracts onto its boundary torus. Thus the same coefficient $m$ is obtained in the open complement. Let $\ell(D)$ be the half-sum of mixed crossing signs. At a mixed crossing where $K$ passes over $J$ with sign $\epsilon$, switching the crossing changes $\ell$ by $-\epsilon$. In an oriented crossing ball straighten $K$ to the positive $x$-axis. When $\epsilon=+1$, the old underpassing arc of $J$ runs in the positive $y$ direction, and the new arc above $K$ minus the old arc represents the negative positive-meridian class; when $\epsilon=-1$, reversing that tangent reverses the class. Hence the same switch changes $[J]$ by $-\epsilon[\mu_K]$, so it changes $m$ by $-\epsilon$. After switching all mixed crossings, $J$ passes over $K$ at every projected intersection. Raise $J$ in the viewing-normal direction and move its projection into a disk disjoint from the projection of $K$; this is an isotopy in $S^3\setminus K$. The final $J$ lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from $K$, so its homology class is zero, and a regular diagram with separated projections has half-sum zero. By [F6] the half-sum is unchanged by this isotopy. Since every crossing switch changed the half-sum and meridian coefficient by the same integer, their initial values agree: $\ell(D)=m$. In particular, for any framed parallel $L_f$ of a knot $L$, its framing integer measured by this half-sum is its meridian coefficient in $H_1(E_L)$; it is zero exactly when $[L_f]=0$. A degree-one parallel with zero class is a preferred longitude by [F8].

Choose a spanning disk $D_R$ for the unknotted dotted circle $R$ so that $B$ meets it once, as allowed by [F1]. Apply [F5] to obtain a finite sequence of slides of $G$ over $B$ and isotopies after which the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from $D_R$. The supplier clears actual intersections one at a time; it does not infer geometric disjointness from a zero signed count.

At each slide of $G$ over $B$, the oriented band sum represents $[G]\pm[B_f]$ in $H_1(E_B)$, where $B_f$ is the signed framed parallel of $B$. By step 1.1, the meridian coordinate of $[B_f]$ is its framing integer $f(B)$. Thus the new linking number is $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)\pm f(B)$. The initial framing pushoff of $B$ is its preferred longitude by [F1], so [F8] makes its class zero and step 1.1 gives $f(B)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ remains zero after every slide.

For the same band sum, expanding the linking of the new attaching circle with its transported pushoff gives $$ f(G\#(\pm B))=f(G)+f(B)\pm2\operatorname{lk}(B,G). $$ The two self-pairings are the old framings and the two cross-pairings are equal by the symmetry in [F4]. The expansion is valid because the band and its pushoff are carried in disjoint product strips, so the four old pairings are unchanged outside the strips. Each framing integer is the meridian coordinate of its pushoff by step 1.1. All framing terms are zero initially by [F1], [F8] and step 1.1, and the mutual linking remains zero by step 3.1. Induction over the finite sequence in [F5] shows the final attaching framing is zero; isotopies preserve it.

The circle $B$ still goes geometrically once over the $1$-handle $R$, while the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from the cancellation disk. Therefore the attaching sphere of the $2$-handle $B$ meets the belt sphere of the $1$-handle once, and [F3] cancels this pair. Since the remaining attaching circle and its framing lie outside the cancellation neighborhood, the transported remaining handle is a single $0$-framed $2$-handle on a $4$-ball. By [F1] this is $X_0(K_G)$. Slides preserve the handlebody by [F2], so $X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

derivations.claim: Fix disjoint oriented knots $K,J\subset S^3$ with a regular oriented diagram $D$, and write $[J]=m[\mu_K]$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ using [F7]. The inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow S^3\setminus K$ is a homotopy equivalence: in the punctured tube $N(K)\setminus K$, radial motion in each normal disk retracts onto its boundary torus. Thus the same coefficient $m$ is obtained in the open complement. Let $\ell(D)$ be the half-sum of mixed crossing signs. At a mixed crossing where $K$ passes over $J$ with sign $\epsilon$, switching the crossing changes $\ell$ by $-\epsilon$. In an oriented crossing ball straighten $K$ to the positive $x$-axis. When $\epsilon=+1$, the old underpassing arc of $J$ runs in the positive $y$ direction, and the new arc above $K$ minus the old arc represents the negative positive-meridian class; when $\epsilon=-1$, reversing that tangent reverses the class. Hence the same switch changes $[J]$ by $-\epsilon[\mu_K]$, so it changes $m$ by $-\epsilon$. After switching all mixed crossings, $J$ passes over $K$ at every projected intersection. Raise $J$ in the viewing-normal direction and move its projection into a disk disjoint from the projection of $K$; this is an isotopy in $S^3\setminus K$. The final $J$ lies in a $3$-ball disjoint from $K$, so its homology class is zero, and a regular diagram with separated projections has half-sum zero. By [F6] the half-sum is unchanged by this isotopy. Since every crossing switch changed the half-sum and meridian coefficient by the same integer, their initial values agree: $\ell(D)=m$. In particular, for any framed parallel $L_f$ of a knot $L$, its framing integer measured by this half-sum is its meridian coefficient in $H_1(E_L)$; it is zero exactly when $[L_f]=0$. A degree-one parallel with zero class is a preferred longitude by [F8].

Choose a spanning disk $D_R$ for the unknotted dotted circle $R$ so that $B$ meets it once, as allowed by [F1]. Apply [F5] to obtain a finite sequence of slides of $G$ over $B$ and isotopies after which the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from $D_R$. The supplier clears actual intersections one at a time; it does not infer geometric disjointness from a zero signed count.

At each slide of $G$ over $B$, the oriented band sum represents $[G]\pm[B_f]$ in $H_1(E_B)$, where $B_f$ is the signed framed parallel of $B$. By step 1.1, the meridian coordinate of $[B_f]$ is its framing integer $f(B)$. Thus the new linking number is $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)\pm f(B)$. The initial framing pushoff of $B$ is its preferred longitude by [F1], so [F8] makes its class zero and step 1.1 gives $f(B)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ remains zero after every slide.

For the same band sum, expanding the linking of the new attaching circle with its transported pushoff gives $$ f(G\#(\pm B))=f(G)+f(B)\pm2\operatorname{lk}(B,G). $$ The two self-pairings are the old framings and the two cross-pairings are equal by the symmetry in [F4]. The expansion is valid because the band and its pushoff are carried in disjoint product strips, so the four old pairings are unchanged outside the strips. Each framing integer is the meridian coordinate of its pushoff by step 1.1. All framing terms are zero initially by [F1], [F8] and step 1.1, and the mutual linking remains zero by step 2.1. Induction over the finite sequence in [F5] shows the final attaching framing is zero; isotopies preserve it.

The circle $B$ still goes geometrically once over the $1$-handle $R$, while the remaining attaching circle is disjoint from the cancellation disk. Therefore the attaching sphere of the $2$-handle $B$ meets the belt sphere of the $1$-handle once, and [F3] cancels this pair. Since the remaining attaching circle and its framing lie outside the cancellation neighborhood, the transported remaining handle is a single $0$-framed $2$-handle on a $4$-ball. By [F1] this is $X_0(K_G)$. Slides preserve the handlebody by [F2], so $X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)$.

Interchange $B$ and $G$. The other meridional condition supplies the starting intersection for [F5], and the linking number remains zero by [F4]. The reversed slide sequence preserves both the zero mutual linking and zero framing by the calculations in steps 2.1 and 3.1. Cancel $(R,G)$ by the same one-intersection argument as in step 4.1. This gives $X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_B)$; combining with step 4.1 yields both trace descriptions.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, let $L$ be a free abelian group of rank $n$ with an integer-valued symmetric bilinear form whose Gram determinant is $1$ or $-1$, and let $f:L\to\mathbb Z^n$ be an isometric homomorphism, where $\mathbb Z^n$ has its standard dot product. Then $f(L)=\mathbb Z^n$.

derivations.claim: Let $A_7$ be the $7\times7$ leading principal block on vertices $1,\ldots,7$. Its leading principal determinants $d_k$ satisfy $d_0=1$, $d_1=2$, and $d_k=2d_{k-1}-d_{k-2}$ for $2\le k\le7$, by expansion along the last row of the tridiagonal chain matrix. Induction gives $d_k=k+1$, so these seven determinants are positive.

The vector $x=A_7^{-1}e_3$ has coordinates $x_i=\min(i,3)(8-\max(i,3))/8$ for $1\le i\le7$: substitution into $2x_i-x_{i-1}-x_{i+1}=\delta_{i3}$ with $x_0=x_8=0$ verifies $A_7x=e_3$. Hence $e_3^{\mathsf T}A_7^{-1}e_3=15/8$. The Schur-complement determinant of $C=\begin{pmatrix}A_7&-e_3\\-e_3^{\mathsf T}&2\end{pmatrix}$ is $\det(A_7)(2-15/8)=8/8=1$.

By Sylvester's criterion, the positive leading principal determinants $d_1,\ldots,d_7$ from step 1.1 and $\det C=1$ from step 1.2 make $C$ positive definite. For any $z\in\mathbb Z^8$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=2\sum_i z_i^2-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\text{ an edge}}z_i z_j$ is even. Every nonzero vector therefore has positive even integral norm, hence norm at least $2$; in particular there is no norm-one vector.

The standard lattice $\mathbb Z^8$ contains norm-one basis vectors, so no isometry from $L_{E_8}$ onto $\mathbb Z^8$ exists by step 2.1. If there were an isometric full-rank embedding, its Gram determinant would be $1$ by step 1.2, and [F2] would force its image to be all of $\mathbb Z^8$, which would be an isometry, again contradicting step 2.1.
