The composites $\psi\phi$ fix each $g_a$. The other composite fixes each generator $e_q$: every $q\in Q(D)$ is represented by a term in the arc generators using $*$ and $\bar *$, and the adjoint relations give $e_{u*v}=e_v^{-1}e_ue_v$ and $e_{u\bar *v}=e_ve_ue_v^{-1}$, so induction on the term gives $\phi\psi(e_q)=e_q$. citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot and let $p,q$ be coprime integers, not both zero. The Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$ if and only if $q=0$, in which case $p=\pm1$ and the slope is the meridional slope $1/0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $S\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded submanifold, let $
u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(
u(S))$ whose restrictions to the zero section are the inclusion of $S$ ([[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Assume that $d\Phi_1$ and $d\Phi_2$ induce the same isomorphism from each vertical fibre $
u(S)_p$ to the ambient normal quotient $T_pN/T_pS$. (The usual normalization makes both induced maps the identity; merely fixing the zero section is insufficient.) Then, after shrinking $\Omega$ around the zero section, the two embeddings are isotopic through tubular neighbourhood embeddings fixing $S$ pointwise. Consequently, for every compact $A\subseteq S$ there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, compact support, $H_t\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$ (in particular $H_1\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_2$ there), and $H_t$ fixing a neighbourhood of $A$ in $S$ pointwise; when $S$ is compact one may take $A=S$ and obtain the agreement on a neighbourhood of all of $S$, with support in any prescribed neighbourhood of $\Phi_1(\Omega)\cup\Phi_2(\Omega)$.

Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: For each $J\in\{K,K'\}$, the boundary $T_J$ is a circle bundle over the connected knot $J$ with connected fibres, hence is connected: a separation would split the boundary into saturated open sets whose projections, by local bundle charts, separate $J$. By [F10], $E_J$ is a compact smooth orientable $3$-manifold with boundary $T_J$. Since $T_J$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_J$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_J$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_J$ and $E_J$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F10]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus both exteriors are connected and, being manifolds, path-connected.

Suppose one knot is unknotted. By [F4] its standard radius-tube exterior is a solid torus with the displayed proper meridian disk. Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. If the other knot were nontrivial, apply [F9] to its compact connected orientable smooth exterior (connectedness was proved in step 1.1), the whole smooth boundary torus as the boundary subsurface, and the trivial normal subgroup. Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.

constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept

$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

derivations.claim: For each $J\in\{K,K'\}$, the boundary $T_J$ is a circle bundle over the connected knot $J$ with connected fibres, hence is connected: a separation would split the boundary into saturated open sets whose projections, by local bundle charts, separate $J$. By [F10], $E_J$ is a compact smooth orientable $3$-manifold with boundary $T_J$. Since $T_J$ is connected, it lies in one component of $E_J$. Any other component is boundaryless, hence lies in $\operatorname{int}E_J$ and is open in $S^3$; it is also closed in $S^3$, since it is closed in $E_J$ and $E_J$ is closed in $S^3$ by [F10]. This contradicts connectedness of $S^3$. Thus both exteriors are connected and, being manifolds, path-connected.

Suppose one knot is unknotted. By [F4] its standard radius-tube exterior is a solid torus with the displayed proper meridian disk. Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. If the other knot were nontrivial, apply [F9] to its compact connected orientable smooth exterior (connectedness was proved in step 1.1), the whole smooth boundary torus as the boundary subsurface, and the trivial normal subgroup. The disk boundary lies in the relative interior of that torus, so [F9] gives a new smoothly properly embedded disk with essential boundary. This contradicts [F2]. No smoothing of the homeomorphic image disk and no replacement of $h$ by a diffeomorphism is required. Thus either both are unknotted or both are nontrivial.

Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Together with steps 2.1, 1.2, and 3.1 this proves every case.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

$$ \pi_1(BG)\cong G,\qquad \pi_n(BG)=0\quad(n>1). $$

Consequently any connected CW model of $BG$ is an Eilenberg--Mac Lane space $K(G,1)$.

$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. let $R$ be a commutative unital ring. The skeletal filtration gives a
choice-free natural first-quadrant homological spectral sequence
$$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a\bigl(B;\mathcal H_b(p;R)\bigr), \qquad d_r:E^r_{a,b}\longrightarrow E^r_{a-r,b+r-1},$$

$$F_aH_n(E;R)=\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_n(E_a;R)\to H_n(E;R)\bigr), \qquad 0=F_{-1}H_n\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_nH_n=H_n(E;R).$$
Its stable terms have the specified natural identifications
$$E^\infty_{a,n-a}\cong F_aH_n(E;R)/F_{a-1}H_n(E;R).$$
If $B$ is simply connected, transport between two fiber stalks is independent
of the path class, so after choosing one fiber identification the local
system is constant. The displayed spectral sequence then has
$E^2_{a,b}\cong H_a(B;H_b(F;R))$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a nonempty compact connected smooth Riemannian domain with nonempty smooth boundary. For a real-valued $\gamma\in C^\infty(M)$ with $\gamma(x)>0$ at every $x\in M$, let $v_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gv_f)=0$ with trace $f\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, whose existence is supplied by the positive-conductivity solvability lemma. Define the full-data physical conductivity Dirichlet-to-Neumann map $\Lambda_\gamma:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_\gamma f,h\rangle=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla_gv_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})\,dV_g,$$
where $V_h\in H^1(M)$ is any extension of $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. The weak equation makes this value independent of the extension. For smooth data, $\Lambda_\gamma f=\gamma\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}v_f|_{\partial M}$; this is the full physical flux convention. When $M=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean metric, this is the scalar Euclidean conductivity DN map.

For a real $q\in C^\infty(M)$ such that the only $w\in H_0^1(M)$ satisfying $(-\Delta_g+q)w=0$ weakly is $w=0$, let $u_f\in H^1(M)$ be the unique weak solution of $(-\Delta_g+q)u_f=0$ with trace $f$, whose existence follows from the nonresonant regularity lemma. Define the Schrödinger DN map $\Lambda_q:H^{1/2}(\partial M)\to H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ by
$$\langle\Lambda_qf,h\rangle=\int_M\big(g(\nabla_gu_f,\nabla_g\overline{V_h})+qu_f\overline{V_h}\big)\,dV_g.$$
For smooth data this is $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_f|_{\partial M}$. Equality of these operators means equality on all of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$, not equality for a restricted set of boundary inputs.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ are strictly positive and $u_j$ solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma_j\nabla_gu_j)=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{\gamma_1}-\Lambda_{\gamma_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)g(\nabla_gu_1,\nabla_g\overline{u_2})\,dV_g.$$
If instead $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$ have trivial Dirichlet kernels for $-\Delta_g+q_j$ and $u_j$ solves $(-\Delta_g+q_j)u_j=0$ with smooth boundary value $f_j$, then
$$\langle(\Lambda_{q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2})f_1,f_2\rangle_{\partial M} =\int_M(q_1-q_2)u_1\overline{u_2}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\geq2$, be a bounded smooth domain, let $\gamma,\widetilde\gamma\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathbb R)$ be strictly positive, let $x_0\in\partial\Omega$, and let $\xi_0\in T_{x_0}^*\partial\Omega$ have unit norm in the induced boundary metric. Choose a sufficiently small boundary patch and $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported there with $\chi=1$ near $x_0$. For every integer $N\geq1$ there are a smooth complex phase $\Phi$ in a collar of the patch and amplitudes $b_{\lambda,\gamma}$, $b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$, defined for $\lambda\geq1$, such that
$$v_{\lambda,\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\gamma},\qquad v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}=\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\Phi}b_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma},$$
have boundary values $\lambda^{-1/2}e^{i\lambda\phi}\chi$, where $\phi$ is real with $|d\phi|=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\chi$, have $H^1(\Omega)$ norms bounded above and below by positive constants, and satisfy
$$\|\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} +\|\operatorname{div}(\widetilde\gamma\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma})\|_{L^2(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
Here $\phi=\Phi|_{\partial\Omega}$ is real, $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$, and $\operatorname{Im}\Phi$ is comparable to the inward distance to the boundary on the collar. Let $u_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ be the exact conductivity solutions with the same respective boundary values. Their corrections satisfy
$$\|u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} +\|u_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}\|_{H^1(\Omega)} =O(\lambda^{-N}).$$
For every fixed integer $k\geq0$ and continuous $F$ on $\overline\Omega$, choosing $N>k$ gives
$$\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\lambda^k \int_\Omega \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k F(x) \nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}}\,dx =c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,\qquad c_k=2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt=\frac{k!}{2^k}>0.$$
The same limit holds with $v_{\lambda,\gamma},v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ replaced by their exact corrections.

Fix $x_0\in\partial\Omega$ and a sufficiently small patch. Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ supported in the patch and equal to one near $x_0$, and use [F3] to construct approximate beams for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ with the same boundary trace. Let $u_{\lambda,j}$ be their exact conductivity solutions. Equality of the DN maps and [F2] give
$$\int_\Omega(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)\nabla u_{\lambda,1}\cdot\overline{\nabla u_{\lambda,2}}\,dx=0.$$
Replacing each exact solution by its approximate beam changes this integral by $O(\lambda^{-N})$: the coefficient is bounded, the beam $H^1$ norms are uniformly bounded, and each exact correction is $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$ by [F3].

Set $k=0$ in [F3] and let $\lambda\to\infty$ in step 1.1. Since $c_0>0$,
$$\int_{\partial\Omega}(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)|\chi|^2\,dS=0.$$
If $\gamma_1-\gamma_2$ were positive or negative at any boundary point, continuity would give a patch on which it has that strict sign; choosing $\chi$ supported in that patch and equal to one near the point would make this integral nonzero. Thus $\gamma_1=\gamma_2$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Fix an integer $k\geq1$ and suppose inductively that $\partial_{x_n}^j(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)=0$ on a boundary patch for every $j<k$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the inward normal coordinate gives
$$\gamma_1(y,x_n)-\gamma_2(y,x_n)=x_n^kF_k(y,x_n),\qquad F_k(y,0)=\frac{\partial_{x_n}^k(\gamma_1-\gamma_2)(y,0)}{k!},$$
for a smooth $F_k$. Apply [F2] to the exact beams from [F3], replace them by their approximate beams, and multiply the resulting integral identity by $\lambda^k$. The replacement error is $O(\lambda^{k-N})$, since the weight $x_n^k$ is bounded and the corrections are $O(\lambda^{-N})$ in $H^1$. Choose $N>k$ and apply the weighted limit in [F3]; then
$$c_k\int_{\partial\Omega}F_k(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2\,dS(y)=0.$$
Since $c_k>0$, the same localized sign argument as in step 1.2 gives $F_k(y,0)=0$ throughout the patch. Therefore the $k$th inward normal derivatives agree there.

Step 1.2 is the base case for the induction. Step 2.1 proves each subsequent order on a patch that may be chosen around any prescribed boundary point. Thus every boundary point has a neighborhood on which the order-$k$ normal derivative difference is zero for every integer $k\geq0$, proving the full boundary-jet assertion.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define
$$P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}.$$
There is a constant $C$ such that every $w\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|P_{\varphi,h,q}w\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
Moreover, for every $F\in L^2(M)$ there is an $R\in L^2(M)$ solving $P_{\varphi,h,q}R=F$ in distributions on $M^\circ$ and satisfying
$$\|R\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
No boundary trace is prescribed for $R$.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

derivations.claim:
Put $\Phi=x_1+i\psi$. By [F1] and $|d\psi|_{g_0}=1$,
$$g(d\Phi,d\Phi)=1+i^2|d\psi|_{g_0}^2=0.$$
Direct conjugation gives
$$(-\Delta_g+q)(e^{-\tau\Phi}a) =e^{-\tau\Phi}\left[\tau^2g(d\Phi,d\Phi)a+ \tau\left(2g(\nabla_g\Phi,\nabla_ga)+(\Delta_g\Phi)a\right) +(-\Delta_g+q)a\right].$$
The $\tau^2$ term vanishes by the eikonal equality, and the coefficient of $\tau$ is exactly the transport equation in the statement. Hence the residual is $e^{-\tau\Phi}(-\Delta_g+q)a$.

Set $h=\tau^{-1}$ and conjugate by the real weight $e^{-\tau x_1}$. The equation for the correction is
$$P_{x_1,h,q}r_\tau=-h^2e^{-i\tau\psi}(-\Delta_g+q)a.$$
The right side is in $L^2$ and has norm $h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2$. By [F4]--[F5], with the equation divided by $h^2$, there is an $H^1$ correction (and hence a distributional) $r_\tau\in L^2(M)$ with
$$\|r_\tau\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}h^2\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2 =C\tau^{-1}\|(-\Delta_g+q)a\|_2.$$
Thus the asserted remainder estimate and the equation hold distributionally.

Choose the $H^1$ correction from step 1.2. Multiplication by the smooth exponentials preserves $H^1(M)$ for each fixed $\tau$, and the correction equation cancels the residual computed in step 1.1. Thus $u_\tau$ is exact, has the stated remainder bound, and has no imposed correction boundary value. The additional boundary regularity is the external input [F4], rather than a consequence asserted for the $L^2$ solver [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $K:X\to Y$ be a compact linear operator of infinite rank, viewed as an inverse model with exact datum $Kx$. Here compact means that the image of every bounded subset has compact closure. Write $N(K)=\{x\in X:Kx=0\}$ and $H_0=\overline{\operatorname{ran}K}$. Fix a positive singular system $(s_j,v_j,u_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ for $K$, where $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, $s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots>0$, $s_j\to0$, $Kv_j=s_ju_j$, $(v_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $N(K)^\perp$, and $(u_j)$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $H_0$. A complete orthonormal basis is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is the whole indicated subspace. These are the compact SVD conventions; in particular, this model concerns minimum-norm representatives in $N(K)^\perp$ and does not estimate a kernel component.

For a truth $x\in N(K)^\perp$, let $\theta_j=\langle x,v_j\rangle_X$. The complete-basis coefficient map identifies $N(K)^\perp$ bijectively and isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, so every $\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ is a model parameter. For $\epsilon>0$, take the functional white-noise experiment on the separable Hilbert space $H_0$ with observations $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_Y+\epsilon W(g)$, where $W$ is centered, has covariance $\mathbb E[W(g)W(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_Y$, and has independent standard-normal values on every finite orthonormal tuple. The countable complete basis makes $H_0$ separable. Define $\xi_j=W(u_j)$ and $Z_j=Y_x(u_j)/s_j$. The sequence sample space is $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ with the product Borel sigma-algebra, meaning the sigma-algebra generated by its coordinate projections. The coordinate law is the pushforward of the functional experiment under $y\mapsto(y(u_j)/s_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$; this map is measurable because each coordinate is a cylinder evaluation followed by scalar multiplication. The compact SVD expansion gives $\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_Y=s_j\theta_j$, and the positive-noise white-noise coordinate theorem gives the independent standard-normal coordinates $\xi_j$. Hence the normalized coordinates satisfy $Z_j=\theta_j+\epsilon s_j^{-1}\xi_j,\qquad j\in\mathbb N.$

For the zero-noise boundary $\epsilon=0$, define the sequence experiment separately by the point mass at $\theta$, so $Z_j=\theta_j$. This boundary is not an instance of the positive-noise functional experiment.

Assume AC. Let $n,m\ge1$, $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let
$C_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric with $v^TC_0v\ge0$ for every
$v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let
$A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ and let
$\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, meaning
$u^T\Gamma u>0$ for every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^m$. Suppose
$X$ and $\eta$ are independent random vectors with laws
$X\sim N_n(m_0,C_0)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$, and set
$Y=AX+\eta$. Define $\mu_0(E)=\mathbb P(X\in E)$ for Borel
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and set
$S=AC_0A^T+\Gamma$. Then $S$ is positive definite. For each
$y\in\mathbb R^m$, define
$$ \Phi_y(x)=\tfrac12(y-Ax)^T\Gamma^{-1}(y-Ax),\qquad Z(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx). $$
For every $y$, $0<Z(y)<\infty$, so the normalized potential update
$$ \Pi^y(E)=\frac{\int_E e^{-\Phi_y(x)}\,\mu_0(dx)}{Z(y)} \quad(E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)) $$
is a probability measure and equals the conditional-law version obtained by
conditioning the observation model at $y$. Its Gaussian formula, defined for
every $y$, is
$$ N_n\!\left( m_0+C_0A^TS^{-1}(y-Am_0),\ C_0-C_0A^TS^{-1}AC_0 \right). $$
Let $P_Y(B)=\mathbb P(Y\in B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^m$.
Conditional-law versions are unique only $P_Y$-almost surely. The displayed
mean and covariance formulas invert only $S$, not $C_0$; $C_0$ and the
posterior covariance may be singular. The prior support is
$m_0+\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. For each positive noise level $\epsilon$, let $\Pi_{0,\epsilon}$ be a proper Borel prior on $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ in the Gaussian sequence inverse experiment, and let $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}$ be the resulting prior-predictive joint law of parameter and data. A posterior kernel is a data-measurable assignment $y\mapsto\Pi_\epsilon(\cdot\mid y)$ of Borel probability measures on $\ell^2$ satisfying
$$\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}(\theta\in A,\,Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid y)\,\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y(dy)$$
for every Borel $A\subseteq\ell^2$ and every product-Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$, where $\mathbb P_{\Pi_{0,\epsilon}}^Y$ is the prior-predictive data marginal. Fix a truth $\theta^\dagger\in\ell^2$ and write $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ for its data law. Since a conditional-law version is specified only up to a prior-predictive null set, any contraction claim under $\mathbb P_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon$ refers to the stated version. A positive function $r_\epsilon\to0$ is a posterior contraction rate in the $\ell^2$ norm at $\theta^\dagger$ if, for every positive function $M_\epsilon\to\infty$,
$$\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}^\epsilon\!\left[\Pi_\epsilon\!\left(\{\theta\in\ell^2:\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2>M_\epsilon r_\epsilon\}\mid Y\right)\right]\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }\epsilon\downarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

derivations.claim: For each fixed coordinate $j$, apply [F2] with one-dimensional prior variance $C_0=\tau_j^2$, observation map $A=s_j$, and noise variance $\Gamma=\epsilon^2$. Then $AC_0A^T+\Gamma=s_j^2\tau_j^2+\epsilon^2>0$, and [F2] gives posterior mean $\tau_j^2s_jY_j/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=\lambda_jY_j/s_j$ and variance $\tau_j^2-\tau_j^4s_j^2/(\epsilon^2+\tau_j^2s_j^2)=v_j$.

For every finite coordinate set $J$, the prior/noise pairs indexed by $J$ are independent of the pairs outside $J$: independence of the prior element from the noise element and independence within each coordinate family factor the probabilities of finite coordinate rectangles into the product of the pair marginals, and [F5] extends this factorization from the generating rectangles to the corresponding product-Borel events. Each $Y_j$ is a measurable function of its pair $(\theta_j,\xi_j)$, so $(\theta_J,Y_J)$ is independent of $Y_{J^c}$. For the finite block, put $D_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_j^2)_{j\in J}$ and $D_s=\operatorname{diag}(s_j)_{j\in J}$. [F2] gives posterior covariance
$$D_\tau-D_\tau D_s^T(D_sD_\tau D_s^T+\epsilon^2I)^{-1}D_sD_\tau=\operatorname{diag}(v_j)_{j\in J},$$
and posterior mean with coordinates $\lambda_jY_j/s_j$. Since each $v_j>0$, the Gaussian coordinates have zero cross-covariance, and repeated application of [F10] shows they are independent. Thus the finite-block conditional law is the product of the scalar laws from step 1.1. Independence of the complement makes this also the conditional law given the full data: the conditional identity first holds on data rectangles by finite-block conditioning and independence, and [F5] extends it to all product-Borel data events. The product Gaussian law $Q_y=\bigotimes_{j\ge1}N(\lambda_jy_j/s_j,v_j)$ exists on $\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ by [F3]. On finite-coordinate cylinders its evaluations are Borel functions of $y$; the class of Borel sets $B$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(B)$ is measurable is a Dynkin system containing the generating cylinder $\pi$-system, so [F6] makes $Q$ a probability kernel. The same finite-block conditional identity holds on data cylinders, and [F5] applied successively in the data and parameter coordinates extends it to all product-Borel events. Thus $Q_y$ is the prior-predictive conditional law on the product coordinate space.

Put $m_j(y)=\lambda_jy_j/s_j$ and $Y_0=\{y:\sum_jm_j(y)^2<\infty\}$. This is Borel because each $m_j$ is coordinate-measurable and $\ell^2=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\bigcap_{N\ge1}\{x:\sum_{j=1}^Nx_j^2\le k\}$. Since $v_j\le\tau_j^2$, [F7] gives $\int\sum_jx_j^2\,Q_y(dx)=\sum_j(m_j(y)^2+v_j)<\infty$ on $Y_0$, so $Q_y(\ell^2)=1$ there. Under the prior-predictive law, $\mathbb E m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2\tau_j^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=\lambda_j\tau_j^2\le\tau_j^2$; under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)=\lambda_j\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$ and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}m_j(Y)^2=\lambda_j^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2\le(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\tau_j^2$. Applying [F7] to the partial sums shows $Y_0$ has full measure under both laws. Restrict $Q_y$ to $\ell^2$ on $Y_0$ and set it equal to $\delta_0$ outside $Y_0$; this is a posterior version on $\ell^2$ and is defined for fixed-truth-almost every observation.

For $y\in Y_0$, the product posterior has coordinate mean $m_j(y)$ and variance $v_j$, so its expected squared coordinate error is $(m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j$. The partial sums of these nonnegative errors increase to $\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$; [F7] therefore gives $\int\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2\,\Pi_\epsilon(d\theta\mid y)=\sum_j((m_j(y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2+v_j)$, with the value $+\infty$ allowed.

Under the fixed truth, $m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger=-(1-\lambda_j)\theta_j^\dagger+\lambda_j\epsilon\xi_j/s_j$. The noise has mean zero and variance one, so its cross term has expectation zero and $\mathbb E_{\theta^\dagger}(m_j(Y)-\theta_j^\dagger)^2=(1-\lambda_j)^2(\theta_j^\dagger)^2+\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2$. The identity $v_js_j^2/\epsilon^2=\lambda_j$ gives $\lambda_j^2\epsilon^2/s_j^2=v_j^2s_j^2/\epsilon^2$. Taking expectations in step 4.1 and applying [F7] to the nonnegative partial sums proves the displayed exact series identity.

For each fixed data sequence, apply [F8] to the posterior probability measure with $f(\theta)=\|\theta-\theta^\dagger\|_2^2$ and threshold $R^2>0$. This gives posterior tail mass at most $R^{-2}$ times the posterior second moment. Taking fixed-truth expectation and using step 5.1 yields the stated bound. If $S_\epsilon(\theta^\dagger)\le C r_\epsilon^2$, substitute $R=M_\epsilon r_\epsilon$ to obtain expected tail mass at most $C/M_\epsilon^2\to0$ for every $M_\epsilon\to\infty$; [F9] identifies $r_\epsilon$ as a posterior contraction rate.
